Sir John Pringle supposes, with great <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, that the frequent use of sugar and fresh vegetables, which at this time make up a considerable part of the diet of the European nations, prevents those putrid diseases and plagues which formerly were rather frequent.—Dr Macbride, flowing experimentally that fixed air is discharged by such substances as form our common food, attributes the preservation of the body from putrefaction in great measure to the fixed air, which in the ordinary process of digestion is disengaged from the aliment, and incorporates with the fluids of the body. From the same property it may be also usefully applied to several economical purposes. Mr Henry found, that fixed air can preserve fruit incorrupt for a considerable time. He tried a bunch of Italian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, which being suspended in the middle part of Dr Nooth's apparatus, and being supplied with plentiful streams of fixed air every day, was preserved without any signs of decay for about one month longer than a similar bunch suspended in a decanter containing common air. Strawberries and cherries he also found to be preserved without decay some days longer in fixed than in common air. Indeed, fixed air preserves not only fruit, but resists putrefaction in general. Dr Macbride, in his elegant Essays on Medical and Philosophical Subjects, has published various experiments which demonstrate this property of fixed air. He found, that not only good meat was preserved incorrupt for a considerable time, when exposed to fixed air; but that the putrefaction of substances actually putrid was impeded by this means, and even that those substances were restored from the putrefact to a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> state. That putrefaction was checked by fermentation, was discovered by Sir John Pringle; and Dr Macbride observed, that this effect was owing to the fixed air produced in the act of fermentation. But it must be observed, that when the sound, or even putrid substances, expose a very great surface to the fixed air, as is the case with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, bile, and other fluids impregnated with fixed air, and also with small bits of meat, then they are preserved for a considerable time; but large pieces of solid animal substances, as for instance roundish pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of about half a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POUND">pound</a> weight, do not seem to remain incorrupt much longer in fixed than in common air; at least the difference is inconsiderable. Sir William <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEE">Lee</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARONET">baronet</a>, in two of his letters to Dr Priestley, informs him of his having found, that flesh-meat, even in the hot season, could be preserved wholesome for several days, by only washing it two or three times a-day in water impregnated with fixed air. "We have been enabled," says he, "to preserve meat as perfectly sweet and good to the extent of ten days, as at the first killing; and there seems no doubt it might be preserved much longer." He has even recovered some meat that had begun to change. This useful discovery, Sir William justly observes, may be very beneficial to the public, especially to butchers. "Particularly a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUTCHER">butcher</a>," says he, "who deals pretty largely, assures me, he found the greatest success from it, and only objects that the veal was a little discoloured, though kept perfectly sweet." II. Inflammable Air is produced, like fixed air, both naturally and artificially. It is yielded abundantly by putrid animal and vegetable substances, and in general by those inflammable bodies which part easily with their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHLOGISTON">phlogiston</a>. Hence, in caverns and mines, especially in coal-mines, this fluid is often found. Sometimes, when the miners <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> a piece of the mineral, thereby probably disclosing some hidden cavity, the inflammable air rushes out in great quantity. Being specifically lighter than common air, it always ascends, and escapes through fissures, except in those places... which are closely vaulted. Being generally mixed with a considerable quantity of common air, it is less noxious than fixed air; so that the miners breathe it with impunity; though, by reason of its inflammable property, it often produces terrible explosions; from whence the miners have called it the fire-damp. Inflammable air is often produced in ditches, exhaling from the surface of putrid water; in burying-places and houses of office, where putrefying animal or vegetable matters are collected. It may also be extracted from the waters of most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> and rivers wherein great quantities of fermentable and putrefying matters are thrown, as in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a>, &c. In warm climates this kind of air is produced in much greater quantities, as the processes of fermentation and putrefaction there go on much more rapidly than in colder countries. So rapid is the production of this kind of air indeed in hot climates, that if the mud at the bottom of a pond is well stirred, and a lighted candle immediately afterwards brought near to the surface of the water, the inflammable air will take fire, and a flame instantly spread over the surface of the pond, affording a very curious spectacle in the nighttime. Inflammable and fixed air, as also phlogisticated air, are discharged by our aliments in the natural course of digestion, and afterwards discharged from the intestines. There is scarce any substance from which, by one process or other, inflammable air may not be obtained. But to the inflammable elastic fluids thus obtained, perhaps no other properties in common can be ascribed than those of being inflammable, and being specifically lighter than common air. In other respects they show a material difference between each other, both in weight, smell, power of burning, of preferring their properties, and the phenomena attending their combustion. Hence various <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of this fluid might be enumerated. As yet, however, there have not been a sufficient number of observations to enable us to make these distinctions properly. We shall therefore only remark the difference between a real inflammable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GAS">gas</a>, and that which is evidently formed by mixing a volatile inflammable fluid with the common atmosphere. A drop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETHER">ether</a> put into a quantity of common air, diffuses itself by evaporation through the whole, taking fire at the approach of a candle like true inflammable air. In like manner Mr Cigna observes, that air saturated with volatile alkali is inflammable; and Dr Priestley has found, that alkaline air is itself weakly inflammable. To produce Inflammable Air. The process for making this sort of gas is the same as that for making fixed air: one of the materials only must be different, viz. iron filings, or grossly powdered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZINC">zinc</a>, must be used instead of chalk; to which filings some oil of vitriol and water must be added, in the same proportion as in the fixed air, or rather a little more of oil of vitriol. N.B. Instead of the filings of iron, small nails, or small bits of iron-wire, answer equally well. The inflammable elastic fluid produced by this mixture, has a displeasing smell, even when mixed with a very large quantity of common air; so that if any considerable quantity of it comes out of the bottle, before the cork with the bent tube be applied to it, &c., its smell may be perceived all over the room in which the experiment is made; but this smell is not particularly offensive. When a bottle has been filled with this elastic fluid, stop the mouth of it with your thumb, or any stopper, and taking it out of the basin, bring it near the flame of a candle; and when the mouth of the bottle is very near it, remove the stopper, and the elastic fluid contained in the bottle will be immediately inflamed; and if the capacity of the bottle is nearly equal to four ounces measure, it will continue burning quietly for about half a minute, the flame gradually descending lower and lower, as far as about the middle of the bottle, in proportion as the inflammable gas is consumed. In this experiment we see, that inflammable air follows the general rule of all other combustible substances, namely, that of burning only when in contact with common air: thus the flame of this gas, whilst burning, is observable only on that surface of it which is contiguous to the common air; so that if the bottle be closed, the flame is put out immediately, because the air is intercepted from it. But if the inflammable air were put in such a situation as to expose a very great surface to the common air, it is plain, that by this means its combustion would be accelerated, so as to let it burn instantly, and go off with an <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPLOSION">explosion</a>, caused by the sudden rarefaction of the air. In fact, this effect may be easily observed in the following manner: When the bottle is to be inverted into the basin, in order to let it be filled with the inflammable gas, instead of filling it entirely with water, let half of it remain filled with common air; then invert it, and let the other half, which now is filled with water, be filled with inflammable air after the usual manner; and when the bottle is full, remove it in the manner shown above, and approach it to the flame of the candle, by which means the inflammable air takes fire; but now it explodes all at once with a large flame and a considerable report, sometimes breaking the bottle in which it is contained. In this case, the bottle being filled with equal parts of inflammable and common air, these two elastic fluids were mixed together, so that almost every particle of the one touched every particle of the other, and hence the sudden combustion was occasioned. The force of this explosion is so very considerable, that some pistols have been contrived, which are <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with a mixture of air and inflammable gas, and being fired by means of an electric spark, are capable to drive a leaden bullet with great violence. Sometimes those pistols are made of glass (but in this case they are not charged with a bullet), and it is very diverting to show, that pistols are charged and explode by the combustion of an invisible substance. When a slender pipe is tied to the neck of a bladder, and the bladder is filled with inflammable air, after the manner described in the preceding experiment (viz. when the bladder was required to be filled with fixed air), two very pleasing experiments may be performed with it. First, the inflammable gas may be inflamed by applying the flame of the candle to the extremity of the pipe; and squeezing at the same time the bladder, a stream of fire will be formed in the air, which will last as long as the bladder contains any inflammable air; for this gas coming out of the pipe with violence, will continue inflamed for a considerable way. way in the air. Secondly, the extremity of the pipe may be dipped into a solution of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>, then removing it from the solution, and squeezing the bladder very gently, a ball of soap-water may be formed, including inflammable air; which ball, on account of the inflammable gas being much lighter than common air, as soon as it is detached from the pipe will ascend upwards, and will break by dashing against the ceiling, contrary to those commonly made by children, which in still air go downwards.—Whilst the ball is ascending, if the flame of the candle be approached to it, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FILM">film</a> of soap-water will be instantly broke, and the inflammable air will take fire; thus a flame may be shown to be seemingly produced from a soap-ball. In stagnant waters where inflammable air is naturally produced, it may, especially in the hot months, be caught in great plenty in the following manner. Fill a wide-mouthed bottle with the water of the pond, and keep it inverted therein; then with a stick stir the mud at the bottom of the pond, just under the inverted bottle, so as to let the bubbles of air which come out of it enter into the bottle: which air is inflammable. When by thus stirring the mud in various places, and catching the air in the bottle until this is filled, a cork or glass-stopper must be put over it whilst standing in water, and then the bottle may be taken home, in order to examine the contained inflammable fluid at leisure. Heat alone is capable to extract a good deal of inflammable air out of most inflammable substances, even from some of the metals. Dr Hales obtained inflammable air by simply distilling wax, pitch, pease, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBER">amber</a>, coals, and oyster-shells. Mr Fontana says he extracted a considerable quantity of inflammable air from spathoic iron, by the action of fire only, applied to a matrix. But Dr Priestley has obtained it from a vast many more substances. His method is, to introduce the required substance into a gun-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a>, to the extremity of which a tube of glass, or of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>-pipe, was fitted, and a bladder bladder was tied to the end of this tube, which received the elastic fluid produced, when the gun-barrel was put into the fire. The Doctor observes, that in order to get a considerable quantity of inflammable air from various substances, the heat must be applied suddenly. "For," says he, "notwithstanding the same care be taken in luting, and in every other respect, fix or even ten times more air may be got by a sudden heat than by a slow one, though the heat that is last applied be as intense as that which was applied suddenly. A bit of dry oak, weighing about twelve grains, will generally yield about a sheep's bladder full of inflammable air with a brisk heat, when it will only give about two or three ounce <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>, if the same heat be applied to it very gradually. To what this difference is owing, I cannot tell. Perhaps the phlogiston, being extricated more slowly, may not be entirely expelled, but form another kind of union with its base."

ALBINUS

Pages 1090-1091

a celebrated physician and anatomist, was born, of an illustrious family, at Francfort on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ODER">Oder</a> in 1697. His father was then professor of the practice of medicine in the university of Francfort; but in the year 1702 he repaired to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, den, being nominated professor of anatomy and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a> in that university. Here his son had an opportunity of studying under the most eminent masters in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, who, from the singular abilities which he then displayed, had no difficulty in prognosticating his future eminence. But while he was distinguished in every branch of literature, his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> was particularly turned to anatomy and surgery. His peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to these branches of knowledge gained him the intimate friendship of Ruyssch and Rau, who at that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> flourished in Leyden; and the latter, so justly celebrated as a lithotomist, is said to have seldom performed a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> operation without inviting him to be present. Having finished his studies at Leyden, he went to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, where he attended the lectures of Du Verney, Vaillant, and other celebrated professors. But he had scarce spent a year there, when he was invited by the curators of the university of Leyden, to be a lecturer in anatomy and surgery at that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. Though contrary to his own inclination, he complied with their request, and upon that occasion was created Dr of physic without any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>. Soon after, upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his father, he was appointed to succeed him as professor of anatomy; and upon being admitted into that office on the 9th of November 1721, he delivered an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORATION">oration</a>, De vera via <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> fabricae humani corporis cognitionem ducente; which was heard with universal approbation. In the capacity of a professor, he not only bestowed the greatest attention upon the instruction of the youth entrusted to his care, but in the improvement of the medical art. With this view, he published many important discoveries of his own; and by elegant editions, turned the attention of physicians to works of merit, which might otherwise have been neglected. By these means his fame was soon extended over Europe; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETERBURGH">Peterburgh</a>, and Harlem, cheerfully received him as an associate. In 1745, he was appointed professor of the practice of medicine at Leyden, and was succeeded in the anatomical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Frid. Bern. Albinus. He was twice rector of the university, and as often he refused that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> when it was voluntarily offered him. At length, worn out by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> and intense <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, he died on the 9th of September 1770, in the 74th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. ALBUGO. Delo the marginal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>. Some distinguish this disorder by nubeculae, when its seat is superficial; and albugo, when it is deep. Others make the following distinctions, viz. when the speck appears of a thinning <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, and without pain, it is called a cicatrice; when of an opaque whiteness, an albugo. Seated superficially, it hath been termed a speck; and more deeply, a dragon. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> an abscess was the cause, its contents hardening between the laminae of the cornea, causes it to project a little; and then it is called a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PEARL">pearl</a>. The causes are various; as inflammation in the eye, abscess in the cornea, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EROSION">erosion</a>, measles, small-pox, wounds, burns, &c. When deep, the cure is difficult; when the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of a wound <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> ulcer, they are rarely cured; when caused by an imprudent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of vitriolic collyriums, and when they alter the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> shape of the eye, the prognostic is as unfavourable. Those which follow an inflammation, generally disappear spontaneously. Happening after the small-pox, measles, or other inflammatory causes, the utmost haste should be made to relieve, by bleeding, purging, blistering, diuretics, and an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSTINENCE">abstinence</a> diet. Avoid <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and astringent collyriums; but the fumes of coffee, or of the decoction of the woods, may be useful. When these specks Motherby, are very small, they often ulcerate; but these ulcerations are soon healed by the application of the pulv. rad. irid. paulul. fac. chrysal. or, as is justly preferred by many, the agg. sapph. If the disorder hath been of long standing, the cure is very difficult; however, the following methods may be attempted: expose the diseased <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the eye to the fumes of camphorated spirit of wine directed through a quill; this, by a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> use, may abrade the speck. This method seldom fails to excite some <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of inflammation, by which the cure is effected; though when the inflammation is thus produced, it must be removed by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> methods with all possible speed. To this end, the following have been also applied with some degree of success, viz. the juice of celandine, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GALL">gall</a> of eels, or of the pike, or of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARTRIDGE">partridge</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of box: if these prove too sharp, let them be diluted with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, or with a thin solution of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUM">gum</a> dragon: apply any of these once in 24 hours; and half an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> after the application, wash it off with a little brandy and water. The agg. sapph. alone sometimes succeeds. When the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FILM">film</a> is very tough, and the eye not inflamed, common glas finely levigated may be blown upon it through a quill, and repeated once in a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> or two.

ALBURNUM

Pages 1091-1091

the soft <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> substance which in trees is found between the liber <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> inner bark and the wood, and in progress of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> acquiring solidity, becomes itself the wood. From its <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> and comparative softness, it has been styled by some writers the fat of trees, adeps arborum. The albumen is found in largest quantities in trees that are vigorous; though in such as languish, or are sickly, there is a greater <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of seeds. In an oak six inches in diameter, this substance is nearly equal in bulk to the wood. In a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> of one foot diameter, it is as one to three and a half; of two and a half feet diameter, as one to four and a half, &c. but these proportions vary according to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of the trees.—The albumen is frequently gnawed in pieces by insects which lodge in the substance, and are nourished from it.

ALDER

Pages 1091-1092

(Encycl.) The bark of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> berry-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> alder is said to be the most certain purge for the horned cattle in obstinate constipations of the bowels. Gunner says, that horses do not eat the leaves, but that cows sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a>, and that it greatly increases the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILK">milk</a>. ALGÆ, flags; one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> families <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> tribes into which the whole vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> is divided by Linnæus, in his Philosophia Botanica. They are defined to be <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, whose root, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>, and stem are all one. Under this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> are comprehended all the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-weeds, and some other aquatic plants. In the sexual system, they constitute the third order of the 24th class cryptogamia; in Tournefort, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> genus of the second <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECTION">section</a>, marine, aut fluviatiles, of the 17th class, asperme vulgo habita; and the 57th order in Linnæus's Fragments of a Natural Method. The discoveries made in this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the vegetable kingdom are Aliment, uncertain, and imperfect; and the attempts, in particular, to arrange flags by the parts of the fructification, have not been attended with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> success. Dillenius has arranged this order of plants from their general <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> and structure; Michelius from the parts of fructification.—Each has considerable merit. ALIMENT. Marginal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, for no. 438, &c. read 440—442. A considerable change has now taken <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the vegetables made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of as food by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, by substituting, instead of what were then used, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of more bland, agreeable, and nutritive juices. The acorns and nuts of the primitive times have given way to a variety of sweeter farinaceous seeds and roots. To the malvaceous tribe of plants so much used by the Greeks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, hath succeeded the more grateful spinach; and to the blite, the garden orach. The rough borage is supplanted by the acercent <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SORREL">sorrel</a>; and asparagus has banished a number of roots recorded by the Roman writers under the name of bulbus; but Linnaeus is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that the parsnip has undervaluedly usurped the place of the skirret. The bean of the ancients, improperly so called, being the root, as well as other parts of the nymphoea melampoda, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>-lily, is superseded by the kidney-bean. The garden rocket, eaten with, and as an antidote against the chilling qualities of the lettuce, is banished by the more agreeable cress and tarragon; the apium by the meliorated celery; the pompion, and others of the cucurbitaceous tribe, by the melon; and the fumach berries, by the fragrant <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NUTMEG">nutmeg</a>. The filipendula, or locosus Cyrenaicus, which the Romans purchased from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a> at a great price, and is thought by some to have been the asafoetida of the present <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, is no longer used in preference to the alliaceous tribe. To turn from the vegetable to some of the animal substitutes, we may mention the carp among fishes, as having excluded a great number held in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> estimation among the Romans. The change of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>; of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>; of mulia, or liquors made of wine, water, and honey, for the wines of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times; and that of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> zythus for the present improved malt liquors; not to mention also the calida of the Roman taverns, analogous to our <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TEA">tea</a> and coffee.

ALKADARII

Pages 1092-1092

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> among the Mahometans, who deny any eternal, fixed, divine decrees, and are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-BELIEVERS">believers</a> of free <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a>. The word is formed from the Arabic alkadar, which signifies "<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECREE">decree</a>." The Alkadarii are a branch of Morazalites, and stand opposed to the Algiabarii. See Algiabarii (Encycl.)

ALKALI

Pages 1092-1093

(Encycl.) Alkalis comprehend one class of the chemical elements, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> component parts or neutral salts, as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a> do another. Concerning the origin of alkalis there have been a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of various conjectures, as well as concerning that of acids; but nothing certain has been, or in all <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> be, discovered. They are distinguished from other bodies of the saline kind by the following properties. 1. They combine with acids more readily than any other known substance, excepting the pure ponderous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, occasioning an effervescence and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>. 2. When they are in a concrete form, into which they may be easily reduced by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> exposed to the open <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, they attract the moisture from it, though not so strongly as concentrated acids; and generally delicate, that is, become a fluid. But if they are mixed with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> all at once, a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of heat is produced. 3. They generally change the blue and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of vegetables to a green; whereas the acids change it to red, or to a stronger red. 4. They have an acid <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, which has something of urinous. 5. They partly exhale with water, especially when boiled in open vessels. 6. They may be fused by a moderate heat; and in that state they dissolve all sorts of earths, especially those called vitrifiable; and if the heat is sufficient, they and the earth form a brittle substance called glas; and upon this principle <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> glass is made. Alkalis are principally distinguished into fixed and volatile; the former being not so easily dissipated even by a strong fire; for which reason they are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> employed in making glass, and other compositions. But the volatile alkalis are so easily dissipated, that they may be almost entirely evaporated by a much less degree of heat than that of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> water. Notwithstanding that various sorts of alkali are enumerated, it is supposed that there is but one alkaline principle in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, which, by being variously combined with sundry substances, attunes various particular properties. However, an alkali is never found pure in nature, but it is always combined with other substances, from which it must be separated by art, in order to obtain it sufficiently pure. The fixed alkali is obtained either from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, or from vegetables; hence it is called fixed mineral alkali in the first <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>, and fixed vegetable alkali in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a>. The volatile alkali is obtained, by means of decomposition and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a>, from all animal substances, and may be also obtained by decomposition and other means from some vegetable and a few other matters. Fixed alkali, whether vegetable or mineral, has always the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> properties; yet they differ from one another in degree, viz. the mineral alkali possesses the alkaline properties in a less degree than the vegetable alkali; for when it is exposed to the open air, it will not attract the moisture from it in such a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> as to deliquesce; when mixed with water, it will not occasion so much heat as the fixed vegetable alkali, &c.—Its <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> with other substances is exhibited below: 1. Vitriolic acid, 8. Oils, 2. Nitrous acid, 9. Tin, 3. Marine acid, 10. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">Lead</a>, 4. Phosphoric acid, 11. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">Copper</a>, 5. Acid of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, 12. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a>, and 6. Other vegetable acids, 13. Water. 7. Sulphur, The fixed vegetable alkali has an affinity with the following substances: 1. Vitriolic acid, 8. Oils, 2. Nitrous acid, 9. Tin, 3. Marine acid, 10. Lead, 4. Phosphoric acid, 11. Copper, 5. Acid of sugar, 12. Gold, and 6. Other vegetable acids, 13. Water. 7. Sulphur, Alkaline salts are of great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, not only because they counteract the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of acids, but also because they are powerful solvents; and, when combined with other substances, communicate to them <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of their saline properties. Thus, when they are combined with sulphur, they make a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> called hepatic sulphuris, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a> of sulphur, which is dissoluble in water, whereas sulphur by itself is not; and when they are combined with oils, form compounds called soaps, which are dissoluble in water, whereas <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> by itself is not. The fixed alkali, more commonly used, by reason of its greatest purity, is that extracted from tartar, which is a substance found adhering to the sides of casks that have contained wine, and is considered as the essential salt of that liquor. This alkali, when it is in a liquid form by its <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> with a sufficient quantity of water, is commonly, but improperly, called oil of tartar. Volatile alkali, when first extracted from animal or vegetable substances, is very impure; but by proper methods it may be purified to a great degree; and in that purified state it differs from fixed alkali, principally because it is very volatile; it has a strong penetrating smell, which occasions coughs, suffocation, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HART">hart</a>'s-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a> drops commonly used, the smell of which almost every body knows, are a volatile alkali.

ALOPECIA

Pages 1094-1094

(Encycl.) Dele the marginal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> is used among physicians to denote a total falling off of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> from certain parts, occasioned either by the defect of nutritious juice, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> by its vicious <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> corroding the roots of it, and leaving the skin rough and colourless. The word is formed from αλοπεξ, vulpes, "a fox;" whose urine, it is said, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> occasion baldness; or because it is a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> which is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to that creature. The alopecia properly differs from defluvium capillorum; as in the former certain parts or patches are left entirely bald, whereas in the latter, the hair only grows immoderately thin. It also differs from the ophiasis, as this latter creeps in spires about the head, like the windings of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a>; whereas the former is not confined to any <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. The remedies which remove the proximate cause of this malady, are called παρασκευής, metafascritica. Here, first, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any corrupt hairs still remain, they are to be drawn out either with tweezers, or by dropacism; or the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> must be shaved by a razor. Then the head is to be washed every night at going to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a> with a ley, prepared by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> the ashes of vine branches in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> wine. A powder made by reducing hermodactyls to fine flour, is also recommended for the same purpose. In <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> where the baldness is total, a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the finest burdock roots are to be bruised in a marble <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>, and then boiled in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> wine until there remains only as much as will cover them. This liquor, carefully strained off, is said to cure baldness, by washing the head every night with some of it warm. A ley made by boiling ashes of vine branches in common <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, is also recommended with this intention. A fresh cut onion, rubbed on the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> until it be red and itch, is likewise said to cure baldness. A multitude of such remedies are everywhere to be found in the works of Valerius de Taranta, Rondeletius, Hollerius, Trincavellius, Celsus, Senecracy, and other practical physicians. See Buxus, (Encycl.) <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERANTS">ALTERANTS</a>. In the marginal note, for Medicine, &c. read <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a>, p. 4475. col. i. par. 2. ALTHAEA. Marginal note, for n° 90, read The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">Table</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">ALUM</a>. Marginal note, for n° 91, read The Table.

AMALGAMATION

Pages 1094-1094

(Encycl.) The proper method of making amalgams is, by first melting the metal with as little <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> as possible, and then pouring the quicksilver into it. During this operation <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the metal undergoes a kind of calcination, whence the surface of some amalgams become <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> and dusty in a very short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>. This is effectually prevented by adding a small <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of tallow <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOG">hog</a>'s-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-LARD">lard</a> to the mixture whilst hot; which restores the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHLOGISTON">phlogiston</a> lost by the metal, and preserves the mixture always of a metallic splendor. This is especially necessary in making an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMALGAM">amalgam</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZINC">zinc</a>, which is found to excite the electrical power of glass more than any other. It requires at least four parts of zinc to one of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>. AMAUROSIS. Marginal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, for 790, read 455.

AMBERGRIS

Pages 1094-1094

(Encycl.) In the Philosophical Transactions we meet with an account of the origin of substance, very different from the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> received one of its being a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> bitumen. This account was communicated to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> by Paul <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUDLEY">Dudley</a>, Esq.; who had it from an American shipmaster. It is in substance the same with the account given by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a> Douglas in his Historical and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">Political</a> Summary of the English Colonies, vol. i. p. 57. "Ambergris," says he, "is now fully discovered to be some production of the spermaceti whale; for some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> it was imagined some peculiar concreted juice lodged in a peculiar cystis, in the same manner as is the castoreum of the beaver <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> fiber canadensis, and the zibethum of the civet-cat or hyæna, in cystis on both sides in the animal. Thus, not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> since, some of our Nantucket whalers imagined, that in some (very few and rare) of these <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> or bull-whales, they had found the gland or cystis in the loins near the spermatic organs: late and more accurate observations seem to declare it to be some <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the ordure, dung, or alvine <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXCREMENT">excrement</a> of the whale. Squid fish, one of the Newfoundland baits for cod, are sometimes in Newfoundland <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> ashore in quantities; and as they corrupt and fry in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, they become a jelly or substance of an ambergris smell; therefore, as squid bills are sometimes found in the lumps of ambergris, it may be inferred, that ambergris is some of the excrement from liquid food, with some singular circumstances or dispositions that procure this <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> seldom occurring. Thus the Nantucket whalers, for some years last past, have found no ambergris in their whales." In the fifth volume of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDSMITH">Goldsmith</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY">Natural <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, we find an account somewhat different from the foregoing. He tells us, that it is found in the cachalot or spermaceti whale, in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the seminal vesicles are usually situated in other animals. It is found in a bag of three or four feet long, in round lumps, from one to 20 pounds <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, floating in a fluid rather thinner than <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and of a yellowish <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. There are never more seen than four at a time in one of these bags; and that which weighed 20 pounds, and which was the largest ever seen, was found single. These balls of ambergris are not found in all fishes of this kind, but chiefly in the oldest and strongest. In the 73rd volume of Philosophical Transactions, Dr Schwedauer gives an account very similar to the former one. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">AMERICA</a>. Marginal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, n° 11. for cool, read moderate.

AMNIOS

Pages 1094-1094

(Encycl.). See <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENERATION">Generation</a>, footnote (c), (Encycl.) AMOMUM. At the end, for n° 97, read The Catalogue of Simples. AMPUTATION. Marginal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, for n° 28, 29, read feet. xviii. p. 8453.

AMSTERDAM ISLAND

Pages 1094-1095

(Encycl.) said there, by mistake, not to be taken notice of in our later discoveries. It was visited by Capt. Cook in his late voyages. Its greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> from east to west is about 21 miles, and from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to south about 13. It is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> at the east end, and runs <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAPER">taper</a> towards the west, where it turns, and runs to a point due north. It is about six leagues to the west of Middleburgh. The shore is surrounded by a coral rock, and its most elevated parts are not above six <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> eight yards above the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. S. Lat. 21. 11. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 175. It is wholly laid out in plantations, in which are cultivated some of the richest productions of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. Here are <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>-fruit, cocoa-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a> trees, plantains, bananas, shaddock, yams, and some other roots; <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-canes, and a fruit like a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NECTARINE">nectarine</a>, called by the natives fighega. There did not appear an inch of waste ground: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> occupied no more space than was absolutely necessary: the fences did not take up above four inches each; and even these were not wholly lost, for in many grew some useful trees or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>: it was everywhere the same, change of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> altered not the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>: nature, assisted by a little art, nowhere appeared in more splendor than on this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">Water</a> is not so plentiful here as at the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>; but the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> pointed out a pool of fresh water unasked, to supply the ships with that necessary article. Casuarinas, pandangs, and wild sago-palms, appear here with their various tints of green, and barringtonize as big as the loftiest oaks. The bread-fruit does not, however, thrive here with the same luxuriance as at the Society-islands, the coral rock, which composes the basis of this spot, being much more thinly covered with mould. Both men and women are of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> size of Europeans, and their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> is that of a lightish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>; they are well-shaped, have regular features, are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>, brisk, and lively. They have fine eyes, and in general good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, even to an advanced <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. The women are the merriest creatures imaginable, and incessant talkers. In general, they appear to be modest; although there was no want of those of a different stamp. Among the natives, who swam about the ship very vociferously, were a considerable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of women, who wanted in the water like amphibious creatures, and were easily persuaded to come on board perfectly naked; but none of them ventured to stay there after sunset, but returned to the shore to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the night, like the greater <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the inhabitants, under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> of the wild wood which lined the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a>. There they lighted <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> fires, and were heard conversing almost the whole night. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> of both sexes in general is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, but especially that of the women; both sexes wear it short, except a single lock on the top of the head, and a small <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> on each side. The men cut or shave their beards quite <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>, which operation they perform with two shells. The hair of many was observed to burnt at the ends, and strewed with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> powder, which was found, on examining it, to be lime made of shell or coral, which had corroded or burnt the hair; some made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of a blue powder, and others, both men and women, of an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a>-coloured powder made of turmeric. The dress of both sexes consists of a piece of cloth or matting wrapped round the waist, and hanging <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> below the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a>. From the waist upwards they are generally naked, and it seems to be a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> to anoint these parts every morning. The practice of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TATTOOING">tattooing</a>, or puncturing the skin, likewise prevails. The men are tattooed from the middle of the thigh to above the hips; the women have it only on their arms and fingers, and on those parts but very slightly. Their ornaments are amulets, necklaces, and bracelets, the bone, shells, and beads of mother-of-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PEARL">pearl</a>, tortoiseshell, &c., which are worn by men as well as women. The women also wear on their fingers neat rings made of tortoiseshell, and pieces in their ears about the size of a small quill: but here ornaments are not <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> worn, though all have their ears pierced. They have also a curious apron, made of the outside feathers of the cocoa-nut shell, and composed of a number of small pieces sewed together in such a manner as to form stars, half-moons, little squares, &c.; it is studded with beads and shells, and covered with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> feathers, so as to have a pleasing effect. They make the same kind of cloth, and of the same materials, as at O-Taheite, though they have not such a variety, nor do they make any so fine; but as they have a method of glazing it, it is more durable, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> resist <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> for some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, which the other cloth would not. Their colours are black, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, purple, and red; all made from vegetables. They make various sorts of matting, some of a very fine texture, which is generally used for clothing; and the thick and stronger sort serves to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> upon, and to make sails for their canoes, &c. Among other useful utensils, they have various sorts of baskets, some made of the same materials as their mats, and others of the twisted fibres of cocoa-nuts. These are not only durable, but beautiful, being generally composed of different colours, and studded with beads made of shells or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BONES">bones</a>. They have many little nicknacks among them, which show that they neither want <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, nor skill to execute, whatever they take in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. Their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> implements are much the same as in other islands: here was purchased a fish-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NET">net</a> made like our casting-nets, knit of very firm though slender threads. Notwithstanding their very friendly disposition, these people have very formidable weapons; some of their spears have many barbs, and must be very dangerous weapons when they take effect. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> flat shell or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREASTPLATE">breastplate</a> was purchased, made of a roundish bone, white and polished like <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>, about 18 inches in diameter, which appeared to have belonged to an animal of the whale tribe. AMYGDALUS. At the end of the article, for no. 99, read The Catalogue of Simples.

AMYLACEOUS

Pages 1095-1095

from amyllum, "flour;" a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to the fine flour of farinaceous seeds, in which consists their nutritive <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREAD">BREAD</a>, (Encycl.)

ANALYSIS

Pages 1095-1097

(Encycl.) Rhetorical analysis, is that which examines the connections, tropes, figures, and the like, inquiring into the proposition, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>, passions, arguments, and other <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>. Several authors, as Freigius and others, have given analyses of Cicero's Orations, wherein they reduce them to their grammatical and logical principles; strip them of all the ornaments and additions of rhetoric which which otherwise <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a> their true form, and conceal the connection between one <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> and another. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of these authors is to have those admired harangues <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> such as the judgment disposed them, without the help of imagination; so that here we may coolly view the force of each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>, and admire the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> Cicero made of rhetorical figures to conceal the weak part of a cause. A collection has been made of the analyses formed by the most celebrated authors of the 16th century, in 3 vols folio. Analysis is also used, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, for the decomposing of a mixed body, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the separation of the principles and constituent parts of a compounded substance. To analyze bodies, or resolve them into their component parts, is indeed the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> object of the art of chemistry. Chemistry furnishes several means for the decomposition of bodies, which are all founded on the differences of the properties belonging to the different principles of which the body to be analyzed is composed. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a>, for example, a body be composed of several principles, some of which have a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, and others a moderate <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of volatility, and, lastly, others are fixed, its most volatile parts may be first separated by a gradual <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> in distilling vessels; and then the parts which are next in volatility <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> over in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a>; and lastly, those parts which are fixed, and capable of resisting the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of fire, will remain at the bottom of the vessel. Analysis is also used for a kind of syllabus, or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> heads or <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> discourse, disposed in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> order and dependency. Analyses are more scientific than alphabetical indexes; but they are less used, as being more intricate. Analysis is likewise used for a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a>, but methodical, illustration of the principles of a science; in which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it is nearly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a> with what we otherwise call a synopser. ANASARCA. (Encycl.) Dele the references.—In this distemper the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> is contained in the cellular membrane between the skin and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>. Its cure is the same with that of the scrofula. See Medicine, no 441—444, and p. 4870, col. 2. (Encycl.) <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANEMONE">ANEMONE</a>. (Encycl.) Horned cattle, when removed from the higher grounds into woods and woody pastures, frequently eat the wood-anemone; and, according to Linnaeus and Gunner, many observations have proved that it causes the bloody <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLUX">flux</a> among them. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>-Anemone. See Animal-Flower and Sea-Anemone. (Encycl.) ANETHUM. For no 103. read Catalogue of Simples. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANEURISM">ANEURISM</a>. For no 38. read p. 8416. ANGELICA. For no 104. read The Catalogue of Simples. ANGINA PECTORIS. See Medicine, no 70, 480. (Encycl.) ANTIMONIALS. For "References at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a>, no 110," read "See Materia Medica, The Catalogue of Simples." <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANTIMONY">ANTIMONY</a>. For References, &c. read "See Materia Medica, The Catalogue of Simples." ANTIQUITIES. Marginal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>: For VII. read Antiquities III. ANVIL. (Encycl.) A smith's utensil, serving to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> their <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> on to be hammered or forged. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a> or uppermost surface of the anvil must be very flat and smooth, without flaws; and so hard that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FILE">file</a> will not touch it.—At one end is sometimes a pike, bickern or beak-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, for the rounding of hollow work. The whole is usually mounted on a firm wooden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a>. APHIS*. (Encycl.) These insects are found in great numbers on the stems, leaves, and even roots of many trees and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. Those trees that are most loaded with the insects, suffer greatly from them. The plant-<a class="xref" href="../1823/vol0.html#article-LICE">lice</a> thrust their sharp-pointed rostrum into the substance of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> to draw out their sustenance, which warps the stems and leaves, and occasions in the latter cavities underneath, and swellings above; nay, even in some, a kind of hollow <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GALL">gall</a> filled with insects, as is often seen on elm-leaves. It appears astonishing, that the slight puncture of so small an animal should so greatly disfigure a plant; but it must be remembered, that plant-lice always live in numerous associations, which increase visibly by the prodigious fruitfulness of those insects; so that although each puncture be slight, yet the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of them is so great, so reiterated, that it is no longer a wonder the leaves should be disfigured. And indeed lovers of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GARDENING">gardening</a> and plants seek to free and cleanse their trees from this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERMIN">vermin</a>; but their care often proves unavailing, the insect is so fruitful that it soon produces a fresh colony. The best and surest method of extirpating it, is to put on the trees infected with them some larva of the plant-louse-lion, or aphidivorous flies; for those voracious larva destroy every <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> a great number of the insects, and that with so much facility, as the latter remain quiet and motionless in the neighbourhood of these dangerous enemies, who range over heaps of plant-lice, which they gradually waste and diminish. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-APIS">APIS</a>. (Encycl.) See also <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEE">Bee</a>.—P. 515, col. 1. par. 2. for no 2. read no 21. And p. 554, col. 1. line 31. for fig. 12. read fig. 17. APPLE. (Encycl.) For Malus read Pyrus. The best method of preserving apples for winter use, is to let them hang upon the trees until there is danger of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FROST">frost</a>, to gather them in dry <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, and then to lay them in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> heaps to sweat for a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> or six weeks. They ought then to be carefully looked over, all which have the least appearance of decay taken out, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> fruit wiped dry, and packed up in large <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> jars, which have been thoroughly scalded and dry, and then stopped <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to exclude the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>. If this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> is duly observed, the fruit will keep a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> sound, and their flesh remain plump; whereas, when exposed to the air, their skins will shrivel, and their pulp soften. Among the various kinds of apples, some are used for the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESSERT">dessert</a>, some for the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a>, and some for cider-making. Those used for the dessert are the following, placed as they successively <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIPEN">ripen</a> after one another: The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> juncating, the margaret apple, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> pearmain, the summer queening, the embroidered apple, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> rennet, the summer white calville, the summer <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> calville, the silver pippen, the aromatic... aromatic pippen, la reine de grise, la haute <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONNE">bonne</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> russetting. Wheeler's russet, Sharp's russet, the spine apple, the golden pippen, the nonpareil, the papi or pomme d'api. Those for the kitchen use, in the order of their ripening are these: The codling, the summer marygold, the summer red pearmain, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> pippen, the Kentish pippen, the courpendu, Loan's pearmain, the French rennet, the French pippen, the royal russet, the monstrous rennet, the winter pearmain, the prune violette, Spencer's pippen, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> pippen, and the oaken pippen. Those most esteemed for cider are, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a> royal wilding, the redtreak apple, the whitfour, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEREFORDSHIRE">Herefordshire</a> under-leaf, and the John apple, or deux anner, everlasting hanger, and gennet moyle. The apple is composed of four distinct parts, viz., the pill, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARENCHYMA">parenchyma</a>, the branchery, and the core. The pill or skin is only a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DILATATION">dilatation</a> of the outermost skin or rind of the bark of the branch on which it grew. The parenchyma or pulp, as tender and delicious as it is found, is only a dilatation, or, as Dr Grew calls it, a swelth or superbiency of the inner part of the bark of the branch. This appears not only from the visible continuation of the bark from the one through the pedicle or stalk to the other, but also from the structure <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to both. The branchery or vessels, are only ramifications of the woody part of the branch, sent throughout all the parts of the parenchyma, the greater branches being made to communicate with each other by inoculations of the leafs. The apple core is originally from the pith of the branch; the sap of which finding room enough in the parenchyma through which to diffuse itself, quits the pith, which by this means hardens into core. The juice of apples is a menstruum for iron. A solution of iron in the juice of the apples called golden rennet, evaporated to a thick consistence, proves an elegant chalybeate, which keeps well. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AQUA">AQUA</a>. For no 501. read 541.
