ARCHBISHOP

Pages 1097-1097

(Encycl.) Archbishops were not known in the east till about the year 320; and though there were some soon after this who had the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, yet that was only a personal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, by which the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> of considerable cities were distinguished. It was not till of late that archbishops became metropolitans, and had suffragans under them. Athanasius appears to be the first who used the title archbishop, which he gave occasionally to his predecessor; Gregory Nazianzen, in like manner, gave it to Athanasius; not that either of them were incited to any jurisdiction, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> even any precedence, in virtue of it. Among the Latins, Hidore Hispalensis is the first that speaks of archbishops. He distinguishes four orders or degrees in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIERARCHY">hierarchy</a>, viz., patriarchs, archbishops, metropolitans, and bishops. The archbishop, beside the inspection of the bishops and inferior clergy in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> over which he presides, exercises episcopal jurisdiction in his own <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>. He is <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a> of the spiritualities of any vacant see in his province, as the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> is of the temporalities; and exercises ecclesiastical jurisdiction in it. Archbishop He is intitled to present by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAPSE">lapse</a> to all the ecclesiastical livings in the disposal of his diocesan bishop, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not filled within six months. He has likewise a customary <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a>, upon consecrating a bishop, to name a clerk or chaplain to be provided, for by such bishop; in lieu of which it is now usual to accept an option. He is said to be enthroned when vested in the archbishopric; whereas bishops are said to be installed. The archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a> had anciently, viz., till the year 1152, jurisdiction over <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> as well as England, and was styled a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a>, and sometimes alterius orbis <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPA">papa</a>, and orbis Britannici pontifex. Matters were done and recorded in his name thus, Annuntiatus nostris primo, &c. The first archbishop of Canterbury was Austin, appointed by king <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETHELBERT">Ethelbert</a>, on his conversion to Christianity, about the year 598. He was also legatus natus. He even enjoyed some special marks of royalty; as, to be <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of a bishoprick, which he was of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROCHESTER">Rochester</a>; and to make knights, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a> moneys, &c. He is still the first peer of England, and the next to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> family; having precedence of all dukes and all <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> officers of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. It is his privilege, by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, to crown the kings and queens of this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. He may retain and qualify eight chaplains; whereas a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> is by statute allowed only six. He has, by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, the power of probate of wills and testaments, and granting letters of administration. He has also a power to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> licences and dispensations in all <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> formerly sued for in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Rome, and not repugnant to the law of God. He accordingly issues special licences to marry, to hold two livings, &c. and he exercises the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of conferring degrees. He also holds several courts of judicature; as, court of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, court of audience, prerogative court, and court of peculiars. The archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YORK">York</a> has the like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> in his province as the archbishop of Canterbury. He has precedence of all dukes not of the royal blood; and of all officers of state, except the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>. He has also the rights of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNT">count</a> palatine over Hexamshire. The first archbishop of York was <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAULINUS">Paulinus</a>, appointed by Pope Gregory about the year 622. He had formerly jurisdiction over all the bishops of Scotland; but in the year 1470, pope Sextus IV. created the bishop of St Andrew's archbishop and metropolitan of all Scotland. ARCTIUM. For "References at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a>," read "Materia Medica, Catalogue of Simples."

AREIA

Pages 1097-1097

(Encycl.) There is another <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; the holeraeca, which is the true cabbage palm. ARGENTUM VIVUM. For References at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a>, read "Materia Medica, Catalogue of Simples." ARGONAUTIC EXPEDITION. See Thessaly; (Encycl.) This celebrated voyage, which is the first epoch in the Grecian <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> upon which any stress can be laid, was undertaken, according to Archbishop Usher and the authors of the Universal History, 1280 B.C. Dr Blair places it 1263; and Sir <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton and Dr Priestley 936 years before the same <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>; but all chronologers agree in fixing this enterprise near a century before the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>. Dr Bryant rejects the history of the Argonautic expedition as a Grecian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a>, founded indeed on a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>.

ARILLUS

Pages 1097-1098

an improper <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> invented by Linnæus, and defined to be the proper exterior coat <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> covering of the seed, which falls off spontaneously. All seeds are not furnished with an arillus; in many, a dry covering, or scarf-skin, supplies its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. In Jeffamy; <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol11.html#article-HOUND">hound</a>'s tongue, cynoglossum; cucumber; fraxinella, distansus; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STAFF">staff</a>-tree, celastrus; spindle-tree, euonymus; African spiraea, dioica; and the coffee-tree, coffea; it is very conspicuous. In the gecus hound's tongue, four of these arilli, or proper coats, each infolding a single seed, are affixed to the style or pointal; and in this circumstance, says Linnæus, does the essence of the genus consist. In fraxinella, the arillus is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to two seeds. The staff-tree has its seeds only half involved with this cover. The arillus is either Baccatus, succulent, and of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of a berry; as in the spindle tree, euonymus. Cartilagineus, cartilaginous, or grilly; as in the African spiraea, dioica. Coloratus, coloured; as in the staff-tree. Plasticus, endowed with elasticity, for dispersing the seeds; as is remarkable in the African spiraea, dioica, and fraxinella. Scaber, rough and knotty; as in hound's-tongue. Although covered with an arillus, or other dry coat, seeds are said to be naked (semina nuda), when they are not inclosed in any <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of pericarpium or fruit-vessel; as in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALLS">galls</a>, and the labiati or lipped <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> of Tournefort, which correspond to the Didynamia Gynoephermia of Linnæus. Seeds are said to be covered (semina testa) when they are contained in a fruit-vessel, whether <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPSULE">capsule</a>, pod, or pulpy pericarpium, of the apple, berry, or cherry kind. See SEMEN, (Encycl.) This exterior coat of the seed is, by some former writers, styled Calyptra. See CALYPTRA, (Encycl.) The different skins or coverings of the seed, are adapted, say naturalists, for receiving the nutritive juices, and transmitting them within.

ARMSTRONG

Pages 1098-1099

(Dr John), an eminent physician, poet, and miscellaneous writer, was born in Castleton <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROXBURGHSHIRE">Roxburghshire</a>, where his father and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> were ministers; completed his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, where he took his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> in physic, Feb. 4, 1732, with much reputation; and published his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THESIS">thesis</a>, as the forms of that university require; the subject was De tabe purulenta. In 1735 he published a little humourous fugitive pamphlet in 8vo, entitled, An <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> for abridging the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">Study</a> of Physic; to which is added a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIALOGUE">Dialogue</a> betwixt Hygeia, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>, and Pluto, relating to the Practice of Physic, as it is managed by a certain illustrious <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>. As also an Epistle from Ulysses the Perjurer to Joshua <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WARD">Ward</a>, Esq. This piece contains much fun and drollery; in the dialogue, he has caught the very spirit of Lucian. In 1737 he published A Synopsis of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> and Cure of the Venereal Diseases, 8vo. This was soon followed by the Economy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">Love</a>; a poem which has much merit; but, it must be confessed, is too strongly tinctured with the licentiousness of Ovid. It is said, however, that his maturer judgment expanded many of the luxuriances of youthful fancy, in an edition "revised and corrected by the author" in 1768. It appears by one of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> on literary <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, that Mr Millar paid 50 guineas for the copy-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of this poem, which was intended as a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURLESQUE">burlesque</a> on some dictatic writers. It has been observed of Dr Armstrong, that his works have <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> inequalities, some of them being possessed of every requisite to be sought after in the most perfect <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, while others can hardly be considered as superior to the productions of mediocrity. The Art of preserving <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEALTH">Health</a>, his best performance, which was published in 1744, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> transmit his name to posterity as one of the first English writers, has been honoured with the following testimony of a respectable critic. On this <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> we shall also transcribe a beautiful eulogium from an eminent physician *: "Of all the poetical performances on this subject that have come to my <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, Dr Armstrong's Art of preserving Health is by far the best. To quote every charming <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> and beautiful passage of this poem, one must transcribe the whole. We cannot, however, expect new rules, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> was to raise and warm the heart into a compliance with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> precepts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, which he has enforced with great strength and elegance. And, upon the whole, he has convinced us, by his own example, that we ought not to blame antiquity for acknowledging One power of physic, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MELODY">melody</a>, and song." In 1746 Dr Armstrong was appointed one of the physicians to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> for lame and sick <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> behind <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUCKINGHAM">Buckingham</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. In 1751 he published his poem on Benevolence, in folio; and in 1753, "<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">Taste</a>, an epistle to a young Critic." In 1758 appeared, "Sketches, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Essays on various subjects, by Launcelot Temple, Esq., in two parts." In this production which possesses much humour and knowledge of the world, and which had a remarkably rapid <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SALE">sale</a>, he is supposed to have been assisted by Mr Wilkes. In 1760 he had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of being appointed physician to the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> in Germany; where in 1761 he wrote a poem called "<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">Day</a>, an Epistle to John Wilkes of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AYLESBURY">Aylesbury</a>, Esq." In this poem, which is not collected in his works, he wantonly hazarded a reflection on Churchill, which drew on him the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a>-toothed vengeance of that ferocious satirist, whose <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMBALMING">embalming</a> or corrosive <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PEN">pen</a> could deify or lampoon any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>, according as he acquiesced with, or differed from, his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> principles. In 1770 Dr Armstrong published a collection of "Miscellanies in 2 vols;" containing, 1. The Art of preserving Health. 2. Of Benevolence, an Epistle to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUMENES">Eumenes</a>. 3. Taste, an Epistle to a young Critic, 1753. 4. Imitations of Shakepear and Spenser. 5. The Universal Almanac, by Noureddin <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALI">Ali</a>. 6. The Forced <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">Marriage</a>, a tragedy. 7. Sketches." In 1771 he published "A short Ramble through some Parts of France and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, by Launcelot Temple;" and in 1773, in his own name, a quarto pamphlet, under the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Medical Essays, towards the conclusion of which, he accounts for his not having such extensive practice as some of his brethren, from his not being qualified to employ the usual means, from a ticklish state of spirits, and a distempered excess of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol17.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a>. He complains much of the behaviour of some of his brethren, of the herd of critics, and particularly of the reviewers. He died in September 1779; and, to the no small surprise of his friends, left behind him more than 300l. saved out of a very moderate income arising principally from his half pay.

ARUNDO

ASPHODELUS

Pages 1099-1099

(Encycl.) The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a> asphodel is thought to be very noxious to sheep, whenever, through poverty of pasture, they are necessitated to eat it; although they are said to improve much in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> at first, they afterwards die with symptoms of a diseased <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a>. This is the plant of which such wonderful tales have been told by Pauli, Bartholine, and others, of its softening the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of such animals as swallow it; and which they thence called gramin offragium. Horned cattle eat it without any ill effect.

ASSETS

Pages 1099-1099

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, signifies goods sufficient to discharge that burden which is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> upon the executor <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> heir, in satisfying the debts and legacies of the testator or ancestor. Assets are real or personal; where a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> hath lands in fee simple, and dies seised thereof, the lands which come to his heir are assets real; and where he dies possessed of any personal estate, the goods which come to the executors are assets personal. Assets are also divided into assets per decem, and assets inter mains. Assets by decem is where a person is bound in an obligation, and dies seised of lands which descend to the heir, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> shall be assets, and the heir shall be <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> as far as the land to him descended <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> extend. Assets inter mains is when a man indebted makes executors, and leaves them sufficient to pay his debts and legacies; or where some commodity or profit ariseth to them in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of the testator, which are called assets in their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>.

ASTERN

Pages 1099-1099

a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-phrase, used to signify anything at some distance behind the ship; being the opposite of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AHEAD">AHEAD</a>, which signifies the space before her. See AHEAD, (Encycl.) ASTRINGENTS. For no 36, read p. 4479. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">ASTRONOMY</a>. ATMOSPHERE

Pages 1099-1101

(Encycl.) See also AIA in this Appendix.—The lately discovered art of navigating the atmosphere, has ascertained a fact formerly unknown, viz. that in the middle regions of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> most frequently blows in a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> contrary to that below; that there are there also a kind of eddies <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> currents which move in a circular direction. When M. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> ascended by himself, as mentioned under the article Air-Balloon, p. 9019, he was sensible of these currents; and the opposite direction taken by the small globe sent off before their first journey ascertains the latter. In this journey also the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTRICITY">electricity</a> of the upper parts of the atmosphere was the cause of a curious phenomenon, viz. that the flags he carried with him as signals, instead of hanging <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> towards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, erected themselves in the air. The Salubrity of the Atmosphere at different heights and in different places has much engaged the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of philosophers. The air on the tops of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> is generally more salubrious than that in pits. Dense air indeed is always more proper for respiration than such as is more rare; yet the air on mountains, though much more rare, is more free from phlogistic vapours than that of pits. Hence it has been found, that people can live very well on the tops of mountains, where the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BAROMETER">barometer</a> sinks to 15 or 16 inches. M. de Saussure, in his journey upon the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>, having observed the air at the foot, on the middle, and on the summits of various mountains, observes, that the air of the very low plains seems to be the least salubrious; that the air of very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> mountains is neither very pure, nor, upon the whole, seems so fit for the lives of men, as that of a certain height above the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, which he estimates to be about 200 or 300 toises, that is, about 430 or 650 yards. Dr <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">White</a>, in the lxviiiith vol. of the Phil. Trans., giving an account of his experiments on air made at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YORK">York</a>, says, that the atmospherical air was in a very bad state, and indeed in the worst he had ever observed it, the 13th of September 1777; when the barometer stood at 30.30; the thermometer stood at 69°; the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> being calm, clear, and the air dry and sultry, no <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> having fallen for above a fortnight. A slight shock of an earthquake was perceived that <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>. The air of a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a>-room at various times, viz. at night, and in the morning after sleeping in it, has been examined by various persons; and it has been generally found, that after sleeping in it, the air is less pure than at any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>. The air of privies, even in calm weather, has not been found to be so much phlogisticated as might have been expected, notwithstanding its disagreeable smell. From this and other observations, it is thought that the exhalations of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> excrements are very little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> at all injurious, except when they become putrid, or proceed from a diseased body; in which <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> they infect the air very quickly. Dr Ingenhousz, soon after he left <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, sent an account of his experiments made in the year 1779 upon the purity of the air at sea and other parts; which account was read at the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> the 24th of April 1780, and is inserted in the lxixth vol. of the Phil. Trans. His first observations were made on board a vessel in the mouth of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHEERNESS">Sheerness</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARGATE">Margate</a>, where he found that the air was purer than any other sort of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> air he had met with before. He found that the sea air taken farther from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>, viz. between the English <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OSTEND">Ostend</a>, was not so pure as that tried before; yet this inferior purity seems not to take <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> always. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a>'s general observations, deduced from his numerous experiments, are, "That the air at sea, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to it, is in general purer, and fitter for animal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, than the air on the land, though it seems to be subject to some inconsistency in its <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of purity with that..." of the land. "That probably the air <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> be found in general much purer far from the land than near the shore, the former being never subject to be mixed with land air." The Doctor in the same <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> transcribes a journal of experiments, showing the degree of purity of the atmosphere in various places, and under different circumstances; which we shall infer here in an abridged manner, thinking it of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to other experimentors. The method used in those experiments, was to introduce one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of common air into the eudiometer-tube, and then one measure of nitrous air. The moment that these two sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a> came into contact, he agitated the tube in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>-trough, and then measured the diminution, expressing it by hundredth parts of a measure; thus, when he says that such air was found to be 130, it signifies, that after mixing one measure of it with one of nitrous air, the whole mixed and diminished <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> was 130 hundredths of a measure, viz. one measure and 30 hundredths of a measure more. "The different degrees of salubrity of the atmosphere, as I found it in general in my <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> at Southall Green, ten miles from London, from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> to September, lay between 103 and 109. "I was surprised, when upon my return to town to my former lodgings in Pall-Mall <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">Court</a>, I found the common air purer in general in October, than I used to find it in the middle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> in the country; for on the 22d of October, at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> o'clock in the morning, the weather being fair and frosty, I found that one measure of common air, and one of nitrous air, occupied 100 subdivisions in the glass tube, or exactly one measure. That very day, at two o'clock in the afternoon (it being then rainy weather), the air was somewhat altered for the worse. It gave 102. "October the 23d, it being rainy weather, the air gave 102. "October the 24th, the weather being serene, the air at nine o'clock in the morning gave 100. "October the 25th, the sky being cloudy at 11 o'clock in the morning, the air gave 102. At 11 o'clock at night, from five different trials, it gave 105. "October the 26th, the weather being very dark and rainy, the air gave 105, as before." The air at Oltend was found by the Doctor to be generally very good, giving between 94 and 98. At <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRUGES">Bruges</a>, the air taken at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> o'clock at night gave 103. November the 8th, the air at Ghent at three in the afternoon gave 103. November the 12th, the air of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a> at seven o'clock P.M. gave 105½. The next day the air of the lower <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the same <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> gave 106; that of the highest appeared to be purer, as it gave 104; which agrees with the common popular observation. November the 14th, both the air of the highest and that of the lowest part of the city appeared to be of the same goodness, giving 103. The weather was frothy. November the 22d, the air of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a> in the evening gave 109½; the weather being rainy, damp, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a>. November the 23d, the air of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREDA">Breda</a> gave 106. The next day about 11 o'clock the air gave 102; the weather being fair, cold, and inclining to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FROST">frost</a>. At seven o'clock it gave 103. Next day, being the 25th, the air gave 104; the weather being cold and rainy. The 26th it gave 103; the weather being very rainy, cold, and stormy. November the 27th, the air at the Moordyke close to the water gave 101½, the weather being fair and cold, but not frosty. This spot is reckoned very healthy. November the 28th, the air of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROTTERDAM">Rotterdam</a> gave 103; the weather being rainy and cold. November the 29th, the air of Delph gave 103; the weather being stormy and rainy. November the 30th, the air of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a> gave 104; the weather being cold, and the wind northerly. The first of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> the weather underwent a sudden change; the wind becoming southerly and stormy, and the atmosphere becoming very hot. The day after, Fahrenheit's thermometer stood at 54°; and the common air being repeatedly and accurately tried gave 116; and that preserved in a glass phial from the preceding day gave 117; and that gathered close to the sea gave 115. December the 4th, the air of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> gave 103; the weather being rainy, windy, and cold. The day after, the weather continuing nearly the same, the air gave 102. December the 10th, the air of Rotterdam gave 101; the weather being rainy. December the 12th, being in the middle of the water between <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DORT">Dort</a> and the Moordyke, the air gave 109; the weather being remarkably dark, rainy, and windy. December the 13th, the air of Breda in the morning gave 109; the weather continuing as the day before. And in the afternoon, the air gave 106½; the weather having cleared up. December the 16th, the air of the lower part of the city of Antwerp gave 105; that of the higher part, 104; the weather being rainy and temperate. December the 17th, the air of Antwerp gave 107; the weather continuing nearly as in the preceding day. December the 19th, the air of Brussels gave 109; the weather being rainy, windy, and rather warm. December the 21st, the air of Brussels gave 106; the weather being dry and cold. The next day the air and weather <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> the same. December the 23d, the air of Mons gave 104; the weather being rainy and cold. December the 24th, the air near Bouchain gave 104½; the weather being cloudy and cold. December the 25th, the air of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERONNE">Peronne</a> gave 102½; the weather being frothy. December the 26th, the air of Cuvillie gave 103; the weather frothy. December the 27th, the air of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENLIS">Senlis</a> gave 102½; the weather frothy. December the 29th, the air of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> gave 103; the weather frothy. 1780. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> the 8th, the air of Paris gave 100; the weather frothy. January the 13th, the air of Paris gave 98; hard frost. Thus far with Dr Ingenhouz's observations. His <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> was a very portable one, made by Mr Martin, which in reality is the eudiometer-tube and measure as used by Mr Fontana, before he made his last improvement. "The whole of this appa- ratus (says Dr Ingenhouz) was packed up in a box about ten inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, five <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and three and a half high. The glass tube or great measure, which was 16 inches long, and divided into two separate pieces, lay in a small compass, and could be put together by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> screws, adapted to the divided extremities. Instead of a water-trough, such as is used <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a>, I made use of a small round wooden tub, &c." The abbe Fontana, who has made a great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of very accurate experiments upon this subject, gives his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> in the following words. "I have not the least hesitation in affirming, that the experiments made to ascertain the salubrity of the atmospherical air in various places in different countries and situations, mentioned by several authors, are not to be depended upon; because the method they used was far from being exact (A), the elements or ingredients for the experiment were unknown and uncertain, and the results very different from one another. "When all the errors are corrected, it will be found that the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the air of one country and that of another, at different times, is much less than what is commonly believed; and that the great differences found by various observers are owing to the fallacious effects of uncertain methods. This I advance from <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>; for I was in the same <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a>. I found very great differences between the results of the experiments of this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> which ought to have been similar; which diversities I attributed to myself, rather than to the method I then used. At Paris I examined the air of different places at the same time, and especially of those situations where it was most probable to meet with infected air, because those places abounded with putrid substances and impure exhalations; but the differences I observed were very small, and much less than what could have been suspected, for they hardly arrived to one fiftieth of the air in the tube. Having taken the air of the hill called Mount Valerian, at the height of about 500 feet above the level of Paris, and compared it with the air of Paris taken at the same time, and treated alike, I found the former to be hardly one thirtieth better than the latter. "In London I have observed almost the same. The air of Islington and that of London suffered an equal diminution by the mixture of nitrous air; yet the air of Islington is esteemed to be much better. I have examined the air of London taken at different heights, (for instance, in the street, at the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>, and at the top of the adjoining houses), and have found it to be of the same <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>. Having taken the air at the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> gallery of St Paul's cupola, at the height of 313 feet above the ground, and likewise the air of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> gallery, which is 202 feet below the other; and having compared these two quantities of air with that of the street adjoining, I found that there was scarce any sensible difference between them, although taken at such different heights. "In this experiment a circumstance is to be considered, which must have contributed to render the above-mentioned differences more sensible: this is, the agitation of the air of the cupola; for there was felt a pretty brisk wind upon it, which I observed to be stronger and stronger the higher I ascended; whereas in the street, and indeed in all the streets I passed through, there was no sensible wind to be felt. This experiment was made at four in the afternoon, the weather being clear. The quicksilver in the barometer at that time was 28.6 inches high, and Fahrenheit's thermometer stood at 54°." A few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> after, Mr Fontana proceeds thus:— "From this we clearly see, how little the experiments hitherto published about the differences of common air are to be depended upon. In general, I find that the air changes from one time to another; so that the differences between them are far greater than those of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIRS">airs</a> of different countries, or different heights; for instance, I have found that the air of London in the months of September, October, and November, 1778, when treated with the nitrous air, gave II, I, 1,90, and II, II, 2,25, which is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> result of many experiments, which differed very little from each other. The 26th day of November last, I found the air for the first time much better, for it gave II, I, 1,80, and II, II, 2,20; but the 14th of February, 1779, the air gave II, I, 1,69, and II, II, 2,21; from whence it appears, that the air of this 14th of February was better than it had been for six months before. "There can be no doubt of the accuracy of the experiments, because I compared the air taken at different times with that which I had first used in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of September, and which I had preserved in dry glass-bottles accurately stopped." This difference in the purity of the air at different times, Mr Fontana farther remarks, is much greater than the difference between the air of the different places observed by him; notwithstanding this great change, as he observed, and as he was informed by various persons, no particular change of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> in the generality of people, or facility of breathing, was perceived. Mr Fontana lastly concludes with observing, that "Nature is not so partial as we commonly believe. She has not only given us an air almost equally good everywhere, at every time, but has allowed us a certain latitude, or a power of living and being in health in qualities of air which differ to a certain degree. By this I do not mean to deny the existence of certain kinds of noxious air in some particular places; but only say, that, in general, the air is good everywhere, and that the small differences are not to be feared so much as some people would make us believe. Nor do I mean to speak here of those vapours and other bodies which are accidentally joined to the common air in particular places, but do not change its nature and intrinsic <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>. This state of the air cannot be known by the test of nitrous air; and those vapours are to be considered in the same manner as we should consider so many particles of arsenic <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a> in the atmosphere. In this case it is the arsenic, and not the degenerated air, that would kill the animals who ventured to breathe it."
