AURORA

Pages 1102-1103

one of the New <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEBRIDES">Hebrides</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the South <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>, in which Mr Foster supposes the Peak d'Etoile mentioned by Mr Bougainville to be situated. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> is inhabited; but none of its inhabitants came off to visit <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> Cook. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is woody, and the vegetation seemed to be excessively luxuriant. It is about 12 leagues <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, but not above five miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> in any <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a>; lying nearly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and south. The middle lies in S. Lat. 15° 6'. E. Long. 168° 24'. AURUM fulminans. (Encycl.) See Fulminating <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a>.—It has been thought that this substance, which explodes with an astonishing violence, and makes a very sharp report, would produce a far greater effect than <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUN">gun</a>-powder, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it were cheap enough to be used as a substitute for fire-arms. But repeated experiments have shown, that when fulminating gold is confined in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a> of a pistol, in a hollow <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALL">ball</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the like, its effects are much inferior to those of gun-powder; and the reason is, because fulminating gold produces an incomparably less <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> fluid than gun-powder does. The surprising effects produced by it when fulminating in the open <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, according to Mr Cavallo, must be owing to the sudden <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> of the elastic fluid, and not to the quantity of it produced. Bergman says, that the elastic fluid <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> by fulminating gold is scarcely equal to four times the bulk of the fulminating gold. He also says, that half a drachm of fulminating gold, fired in a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> vessel, makes a report hardly audible; and that the elastic fluid it generates, extinguishes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>, is noxious to animals, is not absorbed by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, nor renders lime-water turbid.—These are the characteristic properties of phlogisticated air. BACHELOR. (Encycl.) See also Batchelor, (Encycl.) Knights Bachelor. See Knights Batchelor, (Encycl.) <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BACTRIA">BACTRIA</a>. Marginal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, for Khorasan read Chorasan. BALDNESS. (Encycl.) See also Alopecia (Appendix). BALSAM APPLE. See Momordica, (Encycl.) BAMBOO. See Arundo and Bamboo, (Encycl.) This tree, the illy or illi of the Hortus Malabaricus, grows naturally in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> places, and on the banks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> in both Indies; where it frequently attains a height exceeding even that of the cocoa-tree. The root is not very different from the stem, unless that it is of a whitish <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and consists of several radicles or fibres. From the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> of the main root are emitted small jointed stalks, which again emit others from their joints; and from these, as from so many new roots, arise several stalks joined together; which being planted with their radicles or string-roots, serve to perpetuate the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. These stalks are round, have a green bark; are hard, emit from the joints new branches and twigs, and are armed in the joints themselves with one, two, or more, rigid and acute thorns of an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. It is to be observed, however, that the stalks in question, arising, as we have said, immediately from the root, have attained in their native foil the height of two or three men, and the thickness of almost a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAN">span</a>, before they send forth any lateral branches. These, when young and tender, are nearly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a>, pervious only in the middle by a small tube tube. The older stalks and branches are hollow within, being shut, however, at the joints with a woody partition, and covered internally with a slender whitish membrane that is composed of hard <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> woody filaments. The colour of the stalks, when young, is a brownish green; when older, a shining <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> of white. The leaves are long, narrow, seated on short footstalks, streaked with longitudinal veins, and rough on the edges if rubbed downwards. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> grow in long scaly spikes, which proceed in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers from the joints of the stalks. Rheede mentions a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> prevailing on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Malabar, that the bamboo vegetates till its 60th year; at which <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of its growth, and nearly a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> before the flowers emerge from their scaly covers, the tree is divested of all its leaves; and after it has ceased to flower, immediately dies. This tree or reed is termed by the inhabitants of Ceylon, unaghat, that is, "fever-tree," from an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> generally entertained in that island, that a fever is the certain <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BATHING">bathing</a> in any river into which the flowers or leaves of the bamboo have fallen. By the Arabians it is named tabaxir; as is likewise a milky humour or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> produced in it. The Indians call it mambu; whence vulgarly, and by corruption, its European name of bambu or bamboo. In the island of Madagascar, and particularly in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Galembohou, by the testimony of Flacourt, it is produced in such abundance as to give name to the province, for in those parts it is termed vaula. The size of this tree in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a> is generally so great, that houses are built of it. In the porch of the academical garden at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a> are suspended some fragments, a present of the celebrated Piso, the largest of which exceeds 28, the least 26, feet in length. That they must, however, have been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> that size before they were broken off, appears probable from this circumstance, that the thickness of one extremity scarce differs from that of the other. It is likewise wonderful that so immense a reed should be clothed with so very small leaves; the largest of the dried ones in the collection of Professor Syens at Leyden, mentioned by Rheede in his Hortus Malabaricus, scarcely exceeding a span in length, or the breadth of a finger in width. The stalks, when old, are entirely covered in the cavity with a sort of calyx, which is esteemed useful in the strangury, and to such as are troubled with purulent urine. Bamboo being burnt, affords very fertile ashes, in which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> of all kinds thrive remarkably. Whilst <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>, the stalks emit a very loud <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPLOSION">explosion</a>; the air contained in their cavity being rarefied by the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and desiring a larger space, breaks through the partitions at the joints, and violently seeks a passage whereby to escape. Kempfer relates, in the Amoenitatis Exoticæ, that in a province of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a> called Oomi, which has a flinty bottom, the roots of bamboo luxuriate with such wonderful <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, that, being dug out of the ground and disentangled from the strings which encompass them, they serve, as the stalks with us, for walking-sticks, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called rolang. From this curious reed several conveniences are obtained besides those which have been mentioned. The reader is referred for a more minute detail, to the Mantissa Aromatica of Piso; where, besides a very accurate <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the tabaxir or sugar mentioned above, he <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> also learn, that the tender branches or twigs, particularly those near the root, being macerated in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, afford, with the addition of garlic and the pods of capsicum, a sort of pickle, which is esteemed excellent, and constitutes not the least valuable part of those famous condita commonly termed acbar and atijaar, and well known in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> for exciting the appetite and promoting digestion.

AVIGATO

Pages 1101-1102
or Avocado Pear. See the next article. (A) It is plain that Dr Ingenhouz's method is not implied in this remark; since the Doctor's experiments were made long after, and the method used by him was properly that of Mr Fontana. AVOCADO-Pear. Tree, or Laurus Persea; a species omitted to be described under the article Laurus. (Encycl.) It is a native of the West Indies. In form and thickness the fruit resembles a pear. The pulpy and fleshy part is of a pale green, with little or no consistence when ripe, and melts in the mouth like marrow, which it greatly resembles in taste. The skin is smooth and thin, but of a strong tough substance, and of a beautiful green colour, which does not become yellow till the fruit is perfectly ripe. The fruit, by reason of its softness, may be eaten out of the surrounding skin with a tea-spoon, like jelly and marmalade. It is frequently served up in the West Indies on a plate, with sugar, rose-water, and orange-flowers; most commonly, however, it is mixed with sugar and the juice of limes, which render it extremely palatable. The unripe fruit too is frequently plucked and eaten in thin slices, with pepper and salt. In this stage, the taste of the avocado greatly resembles that of artichokes. Every preparation of this fruit is esteemed highly nourishing; as it warms, exhilarates, and fortifies the stomach.—It is particularly recommended in dysenteries. In the middle of the pulpy part of the fruit lies the nut or seed, which is very large, almost round, of a pale russet colour, a little wrinkled, contains no kernel within it, and whose degree of hardness does not exceed that of a chestnut divested of its skin. This nut, about an hour after it is separated from the fruit, splits of itself into two or three pieces. If committed to the ground in this state, no vegetation ensues, because the embryo of the seed is broken; so that such as would propagate these plants from seed must sow the nuts the moment they are taken out of the pulp, in which case they will begin to germinate in eight or ten days after. The bark and wood of this tree, which rises to a considerable height, are of a greyish colour. The leaves are long, pointed, of a substance like leather, and of a beautiful green colour. The flowers are produced in large knots or clusters at the extremities of the branches, and consist each of six petals disposed in the form of a star, and of a dirty white or yellow colour, with an agreeable odour, which diffuses itself to a considerable distance. The tree begins to bear fruit two years and a half, or at most three years after being planted; and like most of the trees in warm climates, bears twice a year. The buds of the avocado tree are said to be used with success in plasters against the venereal disease. An infusion of them in water, drank in the morning fasting, is strongly recommended for dislodging coagulated blood in the stomach produced by a fall or a severe stroke on that important entrail. "The wild boars in the East Indies (says Labat) eat greedily of the mammees and avigato pears, which give their flesh a luscious and most agreeable flavour."

BAMFF

Pages 1103-1103

(Encycl.) By mistake, this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> was said to have no harbour. The following account is given by Mr Pennant: "It is pleasantly situated on the side of a hill; has several streets; and that with the town-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in it, adorned with a new spire, is very handsome. This place was erected into a borough by virtue of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> from Robert II. dated October 7, 1372, endowing it with the same privileges, and putting it on the same footing with the burgh of Aberdeen; but <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> says it was founded in the reign of Malcolm Canmore. The harbour is very bad, as the entrance at the mouth of the Devon is very uncertain, being often stopped by the shifting of the sands, which are continually changing in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> storms; the pier is therefore placed on the outside. Much salmon is exported from hence. About Troophead some kelp is made; and the adventurers pay the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MANOR">manor</a> £50. per annum for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of collecting the materials."

BANDITTI

Pages 1103-1104

(Encycl.) from the Italian bandito; persons proscripted, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a>, as we call it, outlawed; sometimes denominated bannitti or foris-bannitti. It is also a denomination given to highwaymen or robbers who infest the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> in troops, especially in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, France, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>. Mr Brydone, in his Tour through Sicily, informs us, that in the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a>, called Val Demoni, from the devils that are supposed to inhabit Mount Etna, it has ever been found altogether impracticable to extirpate the banditti; there being numberless caverns and subterraneous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> round that mountain, where no troops could possibly pursue them; besides, they are known to be perfectly determined and resolute, never failing to take a dreadful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> on all who have offended them. Hence the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of Villa-Franca has embraced it, not only as the safest, but likewise as the wisest and most <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> scheme, to become their declared <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> and protector; and such of them as think proper to leave their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> and forests, though perhaps only for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, are sure to meet with good encouragement and a certain protection in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, where they enjoy the most unbounded confidence, which, in no instance, they have ever yet been found to make an improper or a dishonest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of. They are clothed in the prince's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVERY">livery</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> and green, with silver <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LACE">lace</a>; and wear likewise a badge of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> order, which entitles them to universal fear and respect from the people. In some circumstances, these banditti are the most respectable people of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, and have by much the highest and most romantic notions of what they call their point of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>. However criminal they may be with regard to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> in general; yet, with respect to one another, and to every person to whom they have once professed it, they have ever maintained the most unshaken fidelity. The magistrates have often been obliged to protect them, and pay them in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>, as they are known to be perfectly determined and desperate, and so extremely vindictive, that they <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> will certainly put any person to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> that has ever given them <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> cause of provocation. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, it never was known that any person who had put himself under their protection, and showed that he had confidence in them, had cause to repent of it, or was injured by any of them in the most minute trifle; but, on the contrary, they will protect him from impositions of every kind, and scorn to go halves with the landlord, like most other conductors and travelling servants, and will defend him with their lives <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there is occasion. Those of their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> who have thus enlisted themselves in the service of society, are known and respected by the other banditti all over the island; and the persons of those they accompany are ever held sacred. For these reasons, most travellers choose to hire a couple of them from town to town; and may thus travel over the whole island in safety. BANDY-LEGGED. See VALGUS, (Encycl.)

BARILLA

Pages 1104-1104
or BARILHA, the name of a plant cultivated in Spain for its ashes, from which the purest kinds of mineral alkali are obtained. There are four plants, which, in the early part of their growth, bear so strong a resemblance to each other as would deceive any but the farmers and nice observers. These four are, barilla, gazul, (or, as some call it, algazul,) soza, and salicornia or salicor. They are all burnt to ashes; but applied to different uses, as being possessed of different qualities. Some of the rough farmers mix more or less of the three last with the first; and it requires a complete knowledge of the colour, taste, and smell of the ashes to be able to detect their knavery. Barilla is sown afresh every year. Its greatest height above ground is four inches; each root pushes out a vast number of little stalks, which again are subdivided into smaller sprigs resembling samphire; and all together form a large spreading tufted bush. The colour is bright green; as the plant advances towards maturity, this colour vanishes away till it comes at last to be a dull green tinged with brown. Gazul bears the greatest affinity to barilla, both in quality and appearance; the principal difference consists in its growing on a still drier saltier earth, consequently it is impregnated with a stronger salt. It does not rise above two inches out of the ground, spreading out into little tufts. Its sprigs are much flatter and more pulpy than those of barilla, and are still more like samphire. It is sown but once in three, four, or five years, according to the nature of the soil. Soza, when of the same size, has the same appearance as gazul; but in time grows much larger, as its natural soil is a strong salt marsh, where it is to be found in large tufts of sprigs, treble the size of barilla, and of a bright green colour, which it retains to the last. Salicor has a stalk of a deep green colour inclining to red, which last becomes by degrees the colour of the whole plant. From the beginning it grows upright, and much resembles a bush of young rosemary. Its natural soil is on the declivities of hills near the salt marshes, or on the edges of the small drains or channels cut by the husbandmen for the purpose of watering the fields: before it has acquired its full growth, it is very like the barilla of those leafons in which the ground has been dunged before sowing. In those years of manuring, barilla, contrary to its usual nature, comes up with a tinge of red; and when burnt falls far short of its wonted goodness, being bitter, more impregnated with salts than it should be, and raising a blister if applied for a few minutes to the tongue. Barilla contains less salt than the others; when burnt, it runs into a mass resembling a spongy stone, with a faint cast of blue. Gazul, after burning, comes as near barilla in its outward appearance as it does while growing in its vegetable form; but, if broken, the inside is of a deeper and more glossy blue. Soza and salicor are darker, and almost black within, of a heavier consistence, with very little or no sign of sponginess. All these ashes contain a strong alkali; but barilla the best and purest, though not in the greatest quantity. Upon this principle, it is fittest for making glass and bleaching linen; the others are used in making soap. Each of them would whiten linen; but all, except barilla, would burn it. A good crop of barilla impoverishes the land to such a degree, that it cannot bear good barilla a second time, being quite exhausted. For this reason the richer farmers lay manure upon the ground, and let it lie fallow for a season; at the end of which it is sown afresh without any danger, as the weeds that have sprung up in the year of rest have carried off all the pernicious effects of the dung. A proper succession of crops is thus secured by manuring and fallowing the different parts of the farm, each in their turn. The poorer tribe of cultivators cannot pursue the same method for want of capital; and are therefore under the necessity of sowing their lands immediately after manuring, which yields them a profit just sufficient to afford a present scanty subsistence, though the quality and price of their barilla be but trifling. The method used in making barilla is the same as that followed in Britain in burning kelp. The plant as soon as ripe is plucked up and laid in heaps, then set on fire. The salt juices run out below into an hole made in the ground, where they run into a vitrified lump, which is left about a fortnight to cool. An acre may give about a ton.

BAROMETER

Pages 1104-1105

(Encycl.) A considerable improvement on the wheel-barometer† is that of Mr Fitzgerald, F.R.S. It is furnished with two pulleys, each of which turns an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDEX">index</a> on the centre of a graduated circle. The smaller circle is four inches in diameter, and divided into three equal parts, each of which is again subdivided decimally; and the changes corresponding to the rise <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a> from 28 to 31 inches, are marked on the margin of it, as they are on the scales of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> barometers. The larger circle is divided into 300 equal parts; and being about 30 inches in circumference, the index belonging to it <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> mark distinctly the 600th <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of an inch in the rise or fall of the mercury. On the centre of this circle two registers are fixed, which are placed along the index when the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> is adjusted; one of them is carried round with the index, and left behind on its return; so that their distance will determine the limits of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> from one observation to another. Mr Paslemon, an ingenious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, has invented a marine barometer, by twisting the middle part of the common one into a spiral consisting of two revolu- volutions. Thus the impulses which the mercury receives from the motions of the ship are destroyed, by being transmitted in contrary directions. Notwithstanding the amazing pains which Mr de Luc has taken to remove every inaccuracy in the barometer, it is not yet entirely free from <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a>; nor do the observations made by different persons altogether correspond. Considerable improvements have been made by Col. Roy and Sir George Shuckburgh, of which an account is given in the 67th and 68th vols of the Philosophical Transactions. FIRE-BARRELS. See Fire-Ship, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> B, (Encycl.)

BASKERVILLE

Pages 1105-1105

an eminent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>, especially in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>-founding and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>, of the present century. He was born in 1706 at Woverley in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WORCESTERSHIRE">Worcestershire</a>, and was heir to an estate of about 60l. a-year; the whole of which income he allowed to his parents till their deaths. In his early years he conceived a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> for fine <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; and being brought up to no particular profession, he commenced writing <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIRMINGHAM">Birmingham</a> when about 20 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. The improvements in different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> there soon drew his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, and he applied to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a> business, which he carried on for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> with distinguished excellence and success. In 1750 he applied himself to letter-founding, the bringing of which to perfection cost him much labour and expense. In a few years he proceeded to printing; and his first <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> was an edition of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> on <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> quarto, which now sells for three guineas. In a short time he obtained leave from the university of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a> to print a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a> in royal folio, and editions of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">Common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRAYER">Prayer</a> in three sizes; for which he paid a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sum to the university. He afterwards printed Horace, Terence, Catullus, Lucretius, Juvenal, Sallust, and Florus, in royal quarto; Virgil in octavo; and several books in duodecimo. He published likewise some of the English classics. The best testimonies of the merit of these performances are themselves; and Mr Baskerville's name is deservedly ranked among those who, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times, have brought the art of printing to its greatest perfection. Not meeting, however, with that encouragement from the book-sellers which he expected, he set up a letter-foundery for <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SALE">sale</a> a little before his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; which business is now carried on by his widow. He died without issue in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1775.

BASTARD

Pages 1105-1105

(Encycl.) This article contains the state of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> according to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> of England. How it stands in the law of Scotland, see Law, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">Part</a> III. No clxxxii. 3, 4, and clxi. 33. Knights of the Bath, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> order in England, supposed to have been instituted by Richard II. who limited their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> to four; however, his successor Henry IV. increased them to 46. Their motto was Tres in uno, signifying the three theological virtues. This order received its denomination from a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BATHING">bathing</a> before they received the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> spur. It is seldom conferred but at the coronation of kings, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the inauguration of a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YORK">York</a>. They wear a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> ribbon beltwise.—The order of the Bath, after remaining many years extinct, was revived under George I. by a solemn <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> number of knights. BAVINS. See Fire-Ship, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> D, (Encycl.) <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENARES">BENARES</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBSERVATORY">Observatory</a>, (Encycl.) <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">King</a>'s-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENCH">Bench</a>, (Encycl.) See also King's-Bench, (Encycl.)

BERWICK

Pages 1105-1105

(Encycl.) The town of Berwick upon Tweed was originally <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Scotland; and, as such, was for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> reduced by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> Edward I. into the possession of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of England; and, during such its subjection, it received from that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a>, which (after its subsequent cession by Edward Baliol, to be for ever united to the crown and realm of England) was confirmed by king Edward III., with some additions; particularly, that it should be governed by the laws and usages which it enjoyed during the time of king Alexander, that is, before its <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> by Edward I. Its <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> was new-modelled, and put upon an English footing by a charter of king James I. and all its liberties, franchises, and customs, were confirmed in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> by the statutes 22 Edw. IV. c. 8. and 2 Jac. I. c. 28. Though, therefore, it hath some local peculiarities, derived from the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> laws of Scotland; yet it is clearly part of the realm of England, being represented by burgesses in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of commons, and bound by all acts of the British parliament, whether specially named <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> otherwise. And therefore it was (perhaps superfluously) declared by stat. 20 Geo. II. c. 42. that where England only is mentioned in any <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of parliament, the same notwithstanding hath and shall be deemed to comprehend the dominion of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WALES">Wales</a> and town of Berwick upon Tweed. And though certain of the king's writs or proclamations of the courts of Westminster do not usually run into Berwick, any more than the principality of Wales; yet it hath been solemnly adjudged, that all <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a> writs (as those of mandamus, prohibition, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HABEAS_CORPUS">habeas corpus</a>, certiorari, &c.) may issue to Berwick as well as to every other of the dominions of the crown of England, and that indictments and other local matters arising in the town of Berwick may be tried by a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JURY">jury</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEZOAR">BEZOAR</a> MINERAL. Line 2d from the end, for tin, &c. in disrepute, read tin, &c. all now in disrepute.

BIRCH

Pages 1106-1108

(Dr Thomas), an eminent historical and biographical writer, was born in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in 1705. His parents were both of them <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUAKERS">Quakers</a>; and his father, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Birch, was a coffee-mill maker by trade. Thomas being put to school, was indefatigable in his application, and stole many hours from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> to increase his stock of knowledge. By this unremitting diligence, though he had not the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of an university <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, he soon became qualified to take holy orders in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of England, to the surprise of his acquaintance. In 1728 he married the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of the Rev. Mr Cox, to whom he was curate: but his felicity was of short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>, Mrs Birch dying of a puerperal fever in less than 12 months after their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>; an event which he deplores in a very elegant and pathetic poem, preserved in Nichols's Collection. In 1732 he was recommended to the friendship and favour of the late <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> Hardwicke, then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTORNEY_GENERAL">attorney-general</a>; to which noble peer, and to the present <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> of Hardwicke, he was indebted for all his preferments. The first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> he experienced of his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>'s regard, was the living of Ulting in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>, in the gift of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, to which he was presented 1732. In 1734 he was appointed one of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> chaplains to the unfortunate Earl of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KILMARNOCK">Kilmarnock</a>, who was beheaded 1746. Mr Birch was chosen a member of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, Feb. 20. 1734-5; and of the Society of Antiquaries, Dec. 11. 1735; of which he afterwards became <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Before this, the Marischal <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of Aberdeen had conferred on him, by diploma, the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">Master</a> of Arts. In 1743, by the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of Lord Hardwicke, he was presented by the crown to the sinecure rectory of Landewy Wclrey in the county of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PEMBROKE">Pembroke</a>; and in 1743-4 was preferred, in the same manner, to the rectory of Sidington St <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>'s, in the county and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a>. We find no traces of his having taken possession of this living; and indeed it is probable that he quitted it immediately for one more suitable to his inclinations and to his literary engagements, which required his almost constant residence in town; for on the 24th of February 1743-4, he was instituted to the united rectories of St Michael Woodstreet and St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> Staining; and in 1745-6 to the united rectories of St Margaret Pattens and St Gabriel, Fenchurch-street, (by lord chancellor Hardwicke, in whose turn the presentation then was). In <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1752, he was elected one of the secretaries of the Royal Society, in the room of Dr Cromwell Mortimer, deceased. In January 1753 the Marischal College of Aberdeen created him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>; and in that year the same degree was conferred on him by archbishop <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERRING">Herring</a>. He was one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUSTEES">trustees</a> of the British <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MUSEUM">Museum</a>; for which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> he was probably indebted to the present Earl of Hardwicke, as he was for his last preferment, the rectory of Depden in Essex, to which he was inducted Feb. 26. 1761. In the latter <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> he was chaplain to the princess <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMELIA">Amelia</a>. In 1765 he resigned his office of secretary to the Royal Society, and was succeeded by Dr Morton. His <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> declining about this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, he was ordered to ride for the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of it; but being a bad horseman, and going out Jan. 9. 1766, he was unfortunately thrown from his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROAD">road</a> betwixt London and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMPSTEAD">Hampstead</a>, and died on the spot. In the 61st year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> regret of the Doctor's numerous literary friends; and was buried in St Margaret Pattens. Dr Birch had in his lifetime been very generous to his relations; and none that were nearly allied to him being living at his decease, he bequeathed his library of books and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>, with his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> painted in 1735, and all his other pictures and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a> not otherwise disposed of by his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a>, to the British Museum. He likewise left the remainder of his fortune, which amounted to not much more than £500, to be laid out in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>-securities, for the purpose of applying the interest to increase the stipend of the three assistant librarians; thus manifesting at his death, as he hath done during his whole life, his respect for literature, and his desire to promote useful knowledge. To the Royal Society he bequeathed his picture painted by Wills in 1737, being the original of the mezzotinto print done by Fauber in 1741. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> publications were, 1. "The General <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>," tionary, Historical and Critical;" including a new translation of Mr Bayle, and interspersed with several thousand new lives. Dr Birch's associates in this undertaking were, the Rev. John Peter Bernard, Mr John Lockman, and Mr George <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SALE">Sale</a>. The whole <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> was completed in 10 volumes folio. 2. Dr Cudworth's "Intellectual System" (improved from the Latin edition of Mosheim), his discourse on the true notion of the Lord's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUPPER">Supper</a>, and two sermons, with an account of his life and writings, 2 vols 4to, 1743. 3. "The life of the Hon. Robert Boyle, 1744;" prefixed to an edition of that excellent <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>'s works, revised by Dr Birch. 4. "The lives of Illustrious Persons of Great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>," annexed to the engravings of Houbraken and Vertue, 1747—1752. 5. "An Inquiry into the Share which <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. had in the transactions of the Earl of Glamorgan, 1747;" 8vo. 6. An edition of "Spenser's <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FAIRY">Fairy</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a>, 1751;" 3 vols, 4to, with prints from designs by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>. 7. "The Miscellaneous Works of Sir Walter Raleigh;" to which was prefixed the Life of that great, unfortunate, and injured <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>, 1751; 2 vols 8vo. 8. "The Theological, Moral, Dramatic, and Poetical Works of Mrs Catherine Cockburn; with an Account of the Life of that very ingenious Lady, 1751;" 2 vols 8vo. 9. "The Life of the Most Reverend Dr John Tillotson, Lord Archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>. Compiled chiefly from his original Papers and Letters, 1752;" 8vo. 10. "<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a>'s Prose Works, 1753;" 2 vols 4to. 11. "<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of the Reign of Queen <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, from the year 1581 till her death. In which the secret intrigues of her <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>, and the conduct of her favourite Robert Earl of Essex, both at home and abroad, are particularly illustrated. From the original papers of his intimate friend Anthony <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a>, Esq.; and other manuscripts never before published, 1754;" 2 vols 4to. 12. "The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Royal Society of London for improving <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> knowledge, from its first rise. In which the most considerable of those papers, communicated to the Society, which have hitherto not been published, are inserted in their proper order, as a supplement to the Philosophical Transactions, 1756 and 1757;" 4 vols 4to. 13. "The Life of Henry <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, eldest Son of King James I. Compiled chiefly from his own papers and other manuscripts, never before published, 1760;" 8vo. His numerous communications to the Royal Society may be seen in the Philosophical Transactions; and his poetical talents are evident from the verses already referred to.

BLACK-CAP

Pages 1108-1108

in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ornithology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTACILLA">Motacilla</a>, under which article it was omitted to be described. It is a small <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>, scarce weighing half an ounce. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of the head in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>; the hind <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the neck a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> ash-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; the back and coverts of the wings are of a greyish green; the quill-feathers and tail dusky, edged with dull green; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> and upper part of the belly are of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> ash-colour; the vent feathers whitish; the legs of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> colour. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> is distinguished from the male by the spot on the head, which in that is of a dull rust-colour. The black-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a> is a bird of passage, leaving us before winter. It sings very finely; and on that account is called in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a> the mock-nightingale. It has usually a full, sweet, deep, loud wild pipe; yet the strain is of short continuance, and his motions are desultory: but when that bird sits calmly, and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> engages in song, he pours forth very sweet but inward <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MELODY">melody</a>; and expresses <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> variety of sweet and gentle modulations, superior perhaps to those of any of our warblers, the nightingale excepted. The black-cap frequents orchards and gardens. Mr Pennant discovered the nest of this bird in a spruce fir, about two feet from the ground; the outside was composed of the dried stalks of the goose grass; with a little <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> and green moss round the verge; the inside was lined with the fibres of roots, thinly covered with black <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>. There were five eggs of a pale reddish <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, mottled with a deeper colour, and sprinkled with a few dark spots.

BLACK-JACK

Pages 1108-1108

a kind of mineral found in the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-DERBYSHIRE">Derbyshire</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>. It was some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> ago employed in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WALES">Wales</a> for mending the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>; but is now found to answer the purpose of calamine for making bricks.—Mons. Van Swab, in 1738, was the first person who distilled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZINC">zinc</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a>-jack; and it is said that some English manufacturers purchased the secret from him when he was in England; though they might possibly have taken the hint from a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> which he erected for the purpose above mentioned.

BLACKSTONE

Pages 1105-1106

an eminent English lawyer, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1723. His father, Mr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Blackstone, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SILK">silk</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>, citizen, and bowyer of London, died some months before the birth of our author, who was the youngest of four children; and their mother died before he was 12 years old. Even from his birth, the care both of his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> and fortune was kindly undertaken by his maternal uncle Mr Thomas Bigg, an eminent surgeon in London, and afterwards, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his elder brothers, owner of the Chilton estate, which is still enjoyed by that family. In 1730, about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years old, he was put to school at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARTER">Charter</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; and in 1735 was, by the nomination of Sir Robert Walpole, on the recommendation of Charles Wither of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HALL">Hall</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAMPSHIRE">Hampshire</a>, Esq.; his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a> by the mother's side, admitted upon the foundation there. In this excellent seminary he applied himself to every branch of youthful education, with the same assiduity which accompanied his studies through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. His talents and industry rendered him the favourite of his masters, who encouraged and assisted him with the utmost <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>: so that at the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 15 he was at the head of the school, and although so young, was thought well qualified to be removed to the university. He was accordingly entered a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMONER">commoner</a> at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PEMBROKE">Pembroke</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, on the 30th of November 1738, and was the next <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> matriculated. At this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> he was elected to one of the Charter-house exhibitions by the governors of that foundation, to commence from the Michaelmas preceding; but was permitted to continue a scholar there till after the 12th of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>, being the anniversary commemoration of the founder, to give him an opportunity of speaking the customary <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORATION">oration</a> which he had prepared, and which did him much <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>. About this time also he obtained Mr Benson's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a>-medal of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a>, for versifies on that poet. In the February following, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of Pembroke college unanimously elected him to one of Lady Hol- ford's exhibitions for Charter-house scholars in that house. Here he prosecuted his studies with unremitting ardour; and although the classics, and particularly the Greek and Roman poets, were his favourites, they did not entirely engross his attention: logic, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, and the other sciences, were not neglected. At the early age of 20, he compiled a treatise entitled Elements of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, intended for his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> only, and not for publication; but esteemed by those judges who have perused it, in no respect unworthy his maturer judgment and more exercised <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PEN">pen</a>. Having determined on his future <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of life, and made choice of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> for his profession, he was entered in the Middle Temple on the 20th of November 1741. He now found it necessary to quit the more amusing pursuits of his youth, for the severer studies to which he had dedicated himself; and betook himself seriously to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-READING">reading</a> law. He expressed his disagreeable sensations on this occasion in a copy of verses, since published by Doddley in vol. 4th of his miscellanies, intitled The Lawyer's Farewell to his Muse; in which the struggle of his mind is expressed so strongly, so naturally, with such elegance of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> of versification, as must convince every reader that his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> for the muse was too deeply rooted to be laid aside without much reluctance; and that, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had pursued that flowery path, he would perhaps have proved inferior to few of our English poets. Several little fugitive pieces besides this, have at times been communicated by him to his friends; and he left (but not with a view of publication) a small collection of juvenile pieces, both originals and translations, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> with this line from Horace, Nec lusisse pudet, sed non incidere ludum. Some notes on Shakespear, which <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> before his death he communicated to Mr Steevens, and which were inserted by him in his last edition of that author, show how well he understood the meaning, as well as the beauties, of that his favourite among the English poets. In November 1743, he was elected into the society of All-Souls college; and in the November following, he spoke the anniversary speech in commemoration of archbishop Chicheley the founder, and the other benefactors to that house of learning, and was admitted actual fellow. From this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> he divided his time between the Blackstone university and the Temple, where he took chambers in order to attend the courts: in the former he pursued his academical studies, and on the 12th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1745 commenced bachelor of civil law; in the latter he applied himself closely to his profession, both in the hall and in his private studies, and on the 28th of November 1746 was called to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAR">bar</a>. Though he was little known <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> distinguished in Westminster-hall, he was actively employed, during his occasional residence at the university, in attending to its interests, and mingling with and improving its interior concerns. In May 1749, as a small reward for his services, and to give him further opportunities of advancing the interests of the college, Mr Blackstone was appointed <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a> of their manors. And in the same year, on the resignation of his uncle Seymour <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RICHMOND">Richmond</a>, Esq; he was elected recorder of the borough of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALLINGFORD">Wallingford</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BERKSHIRE">Berkshire</a>, and received the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s approbation on the 30th of May. The 26th of April 1750, he commenced <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of civil law, and thereby became a member of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONVOCATION">convocation</a>, which enabled him to extend his views beyond the narrow circle of his own society, to the general benefit of the university at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> 1753, he took the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> of wholly retiring to his fellowship and an academical life, still continuing the practice of his profession as a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> counsel. His Lectures on the Laws of England appears to have been an early and favourite idea; for in the Michaelmas <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a>, immediately after he quitted Westminster-hall, he entered on the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of reading them at Oxford; and we are told by the author of his life, that even at their commencement, such were the expectations formed from the acknowledged abilities of the lecturer, they were attended by a very crowded clas of young men of the first families, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, and hopes; but it was not till the year 1758, that the lectures in the form they now bear were read at the university. Mr Viner having by his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> left not only the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COPYRIGHT">copyright</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABRIDGMENT">abridgment</a>, but other <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> to a considerable amount, to the university of Oxford, to found a professorship, fellowships, and scholarships of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law, he was on the 20th of October 1758 unanimously elected Vinerian professor; and on the 25th of the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> read his first introductory lecture, which he published at the request of the vice-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> and heads of houses, and afterwards prefixed to the first volume of his Commentaries. His lectures had now gained such universal applause, that he was requested by a noble personage who superintended the education of our present sovereign, then <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, to read them to his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Highness; but as he was at that time engaged to a numerous clas of pupils in the university, he thought he could not, consistently with that engagement, comply with this request, and therefore declined it. But he transmitted copies of many of them for the perusal of his royal highness; who, far from being offended at an excuse grounded on so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a>, was pleased to order a handsome gratuity to be presented to him. It is doubtful whether the Commentaries were originally intended for the press; but many imperfect and incorrect copies having got abroad, and a pirated edition

BLACKWALL

Pages 1108-1109

(Anthony, A. M.), a learned author, after completing his academical <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at Emanuel <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, was appointed head <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the free school at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DERBY">Derby</a>, and lecturer of Allhallows there, where he first distinguished himself in the literary world by an edition of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THEOGNIS">Theognis</a>, printed at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in 1706, and was afterwards head master of the free school at Market-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOSWORTH">Bosworth</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEICESTERSHIRE">Leicestershire</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a> whereby he initiated the youth under his care into Latin, was of his own compounding, and so happily fitted for the purpose, that he was prevailed on to make it public, though his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> would not permit him to fix his name to it, because he would not be thought to preferre to other instructors of youth. It is intitled, "A New Latin Grammar; being a short, clear, and easy Introduction of young Scholars to the Knowledge of the Latin Tongue; containing an exact Account of the two first Parts of Grammar." In his "Introduction to the Classics," first published in 1718, 12mo, he displayed the beauties of those admirable writers of antiquity, to the understanding and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> even of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> capacities; and that in so concise and clear a manner, as seemed peculiar to himself. But his greatest and most celebrated <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> was, "The Sacred Classics defended and illustrated; <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a>, An <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> humbly offered towards preserving the Purity, Propriety, and True Eloquence of the Writers of the New <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>," in 2 vols. Mr Blackwall had the felicity to bring up many excellent scholars in his seminaries at Derby and Bosworth; among others, the celebrated Richard Dawes, author of the Miscellanea Critica. A <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> who had been his scholar, being <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CLAPHAM">Clapham</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURREY">Surrey</a>, presented him to that living as a mark of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> and esteem. This happening late in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and Blackwall having occasion to wait upon the bishop of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>, he was somewhat pertly questioned by a young chaplain as to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of his learning. "Boy, (replied the indignant veteran), I have forgot more than ever you knew!" Mr <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">Brown</a> has made a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of experiments on solutions of the different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> precipitated by alkalis impregnated with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHLOGISTON">phlogiston</a> of blood, as in the making of Prussian blue. This lixivium being poured into a solution of silver in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AQUA">aqua</a> fortis, produces a coagulum of a pure <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. The like lixivium made with flesh instead of blood, produces, in this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> coagulum; and simple <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of tartar being used in the same experiment, by way of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> with these lixiviæ, afforded a much whiter sediment. Spirit of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a> being added severally to all the three mixtures, the bloom of the flesh-colour was taken off in the first; but it suffered no other change. In the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, the coagulum was tinged a little blue; and in the third, the whiteness was evidently improved. The bluish tinge in the second case is not wholly to be attributed to the flesh; but perhaps might be owing to an alloy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> in the silver, from which it is seldom entirely freed. The same liquors were made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of to form a precipitate from corrosive sublimate of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a> dissolved in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>: the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which was, that the lixivium with the blood produced a pure <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>; that with flesh, an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> colour; and the simple oil of tartar, a dingy <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>. The addition of spirit of salt afterwards to these made some very odd alterations; for the first changed its yellow into an orange colour, and the second its orange colour to a blue, while the third became without any colour. The blue colour in the lixivium with the flesh, when mixed with this solution, may be accounted for from the vitriol in this <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a>; but it is not so easy to say, why the same vitriol should not have produced also a blue in a lixivium with blood. Copper, when dissolved in aqua fortis, makes the water of a green colour; and on pouring to this the two lixiviæ of blood and of flesh, the coagula are much alike; that is, they are white, tinged with green; but on adding spirit of salt to them, they become of a colour not unlike that of copper before the solution. Oil of tartar gives a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> green solution; and the spirit of salt clears up the liquor, and restores it to its former colour. Bitumen dissolved in aqua fortis, and mixed with a lixivium of blood, produces a milky coagulum, which, after a short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> standing, with the addition of some spirit of salt, becomes of a pale blue. The lixivia of flesh, and of crude salt of tartar, produced both white coagula, which the spirit of salt made no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> in. From these experiments it appears, that not any of these metallic bodies would produce a fine blue colour with the lixivium of the blood; but a solution of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> answers all the experiments that are made with the solution of vitriol, and produces as fine a blue colour as that made in the common way.

BLUE JOHN

Pages 1109-1109

among miners, a kind of mineral which has lately been fabricated into vases and other ornamental figures. It is of the same <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> with the cubical <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAR">spar</a>, with respect to its suitability in the fire. It loses its <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and becomes <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> in moderate <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>: the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of a cubic foot of the bluest kind is 3180 ounces, and that of the least blue is 3140 ounces. This substance began first to be applied to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> about 18 years ago at one of the oldest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-DERBYSHIRE">Derbyshire</a>, called Odin mine, probably from its being dedicated to Odin the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> god of the northern nations, at the foot of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> mountain called Mam Tor in Castleton. Here the greatest quantities are still found; the largest pieces are sold for £1. a ton, the middle-sized for £1., and the least for 50s.

BLUSHING

Pages 1109-1109

a suffusion <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> redness of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a>, excited by a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of shame, on account of consciousness of some failing or imperfection. Blushing is supposed to be produced from a kind of consent or sympathy between several parts of the body, occasioned by the same nerve being extended to them all. Thus the fifth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of nerves being branched from the brain to the eye, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EAR">ear</a>, muscles of the lips, cheeks, palate, tongue, and nose; a thing seen or heard that is shameful affects the cheeks with blushes, driving the blood into the minute vessels thereof; at the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> that it affects the eye and ear. For the same reason it is, as Mr. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DERHAM">Derham</a> observes, that a savoury thing seen or smelt affects the glands and parts of the mouth; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a thing heard be pleasing, it affects the muscles of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAUGHTER">laughter</a>; if melancholy, it exerts itself on the glands of the eyes, and occasions weeping, &c. And to the same cause Dr Willis ascribes the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of killing. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOILING">BOILING</a> FOUNTAIN. See <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ICELAND">ICELAND</a>, and Plate CLVII.

BOLETUS

Pages 1109-1109

(Encycl.) Horned cattle are fond of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> boletus, and eat it greedily; but it is believed that it vitiates the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, and lessens the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of it.

BONES

Pages 1109-1109

(Encycl.) From a discovery made by Mr Scheele, of a method of producing the phosphoric acid in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> from bones, it has been asserted, that this acid is naturally contained in the bones, united with a calcareous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. From many experiments, however, it appears that no acid is naturally contained in calcined bones; nor can the acid of phosphorus be extracted from them but by means of the vitriolic acid: whence it seems probable, that the phosphoric acid in this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> is produced by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of a certain quantity of earth with the vitriolic acid.—With regard to the earth of bones itself, it appears to be very different from the calcareous kind: it is much more soluble in the vitriolic acid, and may be precipitated from that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> any other by means of the caustic volatile alkali, which cannot be done with the calcareous earth.
