BOWYER

Pages 1113-1115

the most learned printer of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">White</a> Friars in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, Dec. 17, 1699. His father, whose name also was William, had been eminent in the same profession; and his maternal grandfather (Isabold Dawks) was employed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> the celebrated Polyglott <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIBLE">bible</a> of bishop Walton. At a proper age, he was placed for grammatical <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> under the care of Mr <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBROSE">Ambrose</a> Bonwicke, a nonjuring clergyman of known piety and learning, who then lived at Headly, near Leatherhead in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURREY">Surrey</a>. Here Mr Bowyer made <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> advances in literature, and a firm <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> commenced between him and his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a>. On the 30th of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1713, the whole <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of the elder Mr Bowyer was destroyed by fire; on which occasion Mr Bonwicke generously undertook the education of his pupil for one year. In 1716, young Mr Bowyer was admitted a sizar at St John's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, where Dr Robert Jenkin was at that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> master. He <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> at the college of Cambridge under the tuition of the reverend Dr John Newcome till <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1722, during which <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> he probably took his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of Bachelor of Arts; and it appears that he was desirous of obtaining a fellowship, though it is not certain that he ever stood a candidate for that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>. Soon after this he had an opportunity of repaying the kindness which Mr Bonwicke had shown him, by officiating some time after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> in the capacity of a schoolmaster for the benefit of his family. Mr Bowyer now entered into the printing-business along with his father. One of the first books which received the benefit of his correction was the complete edition of Selden in three volumes folio by Dr <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAVID">David</a> Wilkins. This edition was begun in 1722, and finished in 1726; and Mr Bowyer's great <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to it appeared in his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> up an epitome of Selden de Synedriis, as he read the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>-sheets. In 1727, he drew up an excellent sketch of William Baxter's Glossary of the Roman Antiquities. This was called "A view of a book entitled Reliquiae Baxterianae. In a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to a friend." A single sheet 8vo. By this first public proof of Mr Bowyer's abilities, Dr Wotton and Mr Clarke were highly pleased; but as it was never published, and very few copies printed, it is very seldom found with the glossary. In 1727 Mr Bowyer lost his mother; on which occasion he received a letter of consolation from Mr Chilhull the learned editor of the Antiquitates Aestatice. In October 1728 he married Miss Ann Prudom, his mother's niece, a very accomplished lady, by whom he had two sons, William and Thomas; the former of whom died an infant, and the latter survived his father. In 1729 Mr Bowyer published a curious treatise, intitled, "A Pattern for young Students in the Uni- Bowyer. University; set forth in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> of Ambrose Bonwicke, some time scholar of St John's College, Cambridge;" but though this treatise was generally ascribed to Mr Bowyer, it was in reality the production of Mr Ambrose Bonwicke the elder. About this time it appears, that Mr Bowyer had written a pamphlet against the Separatists, though neither the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> nor the occasion of it are now remembered. The same year, through the friendship of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">Right</a> Hon. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTHUR">Arthur</a> Ousley, he was appointed printer of the Votes of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">House</a> of Commons; which office he held, under three successive speakers, for near 50 years. In 1731 Mr Bowyer published, and, it is believed, translated, Voltaire's Life of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> XII. This year also his wife died; on which occasion his friends Mr Clarke and Mr Chisholm wrote him very affectionate and Christian letters. He remained a widower till 1747, when he married, a very benevolent and worthy woman, Mrs <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BILL">Bill</a>, by whom he had no children. In 1733 he published a piece in two sheets 4to, intitled, "The Beau and the Academic;" being a translation from a Latin poem recited that year at the Sheldonian <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>; and in 1736 he was admitted into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of Antiquarians, where he became an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> and useful member. In 1737 Mr Bowyer lost his father; and on this occasion Mr Clarke again addressed to him a letter of consolation. In 1742 our author published a translation of Trapp's Latin Lectures on <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>, in which he was assisted by Mr Clarke, though the latter had a contemptible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the performance. In 1749, Mr Bowyer, along with Dr Burton, was virulently attacked by Dr <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">King</a> in a piece intitled "Elogium famae inserviens Jacii Etonensi, five Gigantis:" <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a>, "The praises of Jack Eaton, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called Jack the Giant."—This abuse was probably occasioned by Mr Bowyer's having hinted in conversation some doubts concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a>'s skill in Latin. Our author drew up some strictures in his own <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, which he intended to insert at the conclusion of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> to Montesquieu's Reflections; but by Dr Clarke's advice they were omitted. In 1750, a prefatory critical dissertation and some notes were annexed by our author to Kuster's Treatise De usu verborum mediorum; a new edition of which, with farther improvements, appeared in 1773. He wrote likewise about the same time a Latin preface to Leedes's Veteres poetae citati, &c.—Being soon after employed to print an edition of Col. Bladen's translation of Cæsar's Commentaries, that <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> received considerable improvements from Mr Bowyer's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, with the addition of such notes in it as are signed Typogr. In the subsequent editions of this work, though printed by another person during our author's lifetime, the same <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIGNATURE">signature</a>, though contrary to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECORUM">decorum</a>, and even to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, was still retained. In 1751, he wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> preface to Montesquieu's "Reflections on the rise and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of the Roman Empire;" translated the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIALOGUE">dialogue</a> between Sylla and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>; made several corrections to the work from the Baron's "Spirit of Laws;" and improved it with his own notes. A new edition, with many new notes, was printed in 1759. In 1751 he also published the first translation that ever was made of Rousseau's paradoxical <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORATION">oration</a>, which gained the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> at the academy of Dijon in 1750; and which first announced that singular genius to the attention and admiration of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. On the publication of the third edition of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORRERY">Orrery</a>'s "Remarks on the Life and Writings of Dr Swift," in 1752, Mr Bowyer wrote and printed, but never published, "Two Letters from Dr Bentley in the Shades below, to Lord Orrery in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">Land</a> of thick darkness." The notes signed B, in the ninth quarto volume of Swift's works, are extracted from these Letters. In 1753, he endeavoured to allay the ferment occasioned by the Jew bill; with which view he published, in quarto, "Remarks on the speech made in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, on the bill for permitting persons professing the Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> to be naturalized, so far as prophecies are supposed to be affected by it." This little tract was written with spirit, and well received by those who were superior to narrow prejudices. Its <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> was to show, that whatever <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> reasons might be alleged against the bill, Christianity was in no danger of being prejudiced by the intended protection promised to the Jews. The same year some of Mr Bowyer's notes were annexed to Bishop Clayton's translation of "A Journal from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a> to Mount <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SINAI">Sinai</a> and back again."—In 1754, Mr Bowyer, with a view of lessening his fatigue, entered into <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARTNERSHIP">partnership</a> with a relation; but some disagreement arising, the connection was dissolved in three years. On the death of Mr Richardson in 1761, Mr Bowyer succeeded him as printer to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Society, through the favour of the late <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> of Macclesfield; and, under the friendship of five successive presidents, enjoyed that office till his death. In 1763, Mr Bowyer published an excellent edition of the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, in two vols 12mo. It appeared under the following title: Novum Testamentum Graecum <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> fidem Graecorum folium Codicum MSS. nunc primum impressum, adfuturante Joanne Jacobo Wettenhofer, juxta Sectiones Jo. Alberti Bengelii dicitionis; et nova interpretatione fupius illustratum. Accesse in altero volumine, Emendationes conjecturales virorum doctrinam unumque collectae. This fold with great rapidity: the Conjectural Emendations were well received by the learned, and are thought to be a valuable work. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> and fellows of Harvard college in Cambridge expressed their approbation of this edition in very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> terms. In a letter to Mr Bowyer, written in the year 1767, "This work, (say they), though small in bulk, we esteem as a rich <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> of sacred learning, and of more value than many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> volumes of the commentators." A <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> edition of the Conjectures on the New Testament, with very considerable enlargements, was separately published, in one vol. 8vo, in 1772. Bishop Warburton having censured a passage in the former edition, Mr Bowyer sent him a copy of this book, with a conciliatory letter. Dr Warburton's Divine Legation had received very considerable advantage from Mr Bowyer's corrections; and this even in an edition which was necessarily given to another press. In 1761 he was employed to print his Lordship's Doctrine of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRACE">Grace</a>. A second edition being soon wanted, and Mr Bowyer not having been intrusted with the care of it, he prepared a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of letters to the bishop in his own defence; of which, together with a few he had formerly received from that great writer, he afterwards printed twelve copies, of which ten have since been destroyed. However, there In 1765, at the request of Thomas Hollis, Esq; Mr Bowyer wrote a short Latin preface to Dr Wallis's Grammatica Linguae Anglicane. He wrote also a larger English preface for the same work, which, however, still remains unprinted. In 1766 he entered into partnership with Mr Nichols, who had been trained by him in the profession, and had for several years assisted him in the management of his business. The same year, Mr Bowyer wrote an excellent Latin preface to Joannis Harduini, Jesuïte, ad Centuriam Scriptorum veterum Prolegomena. Juxta Autographum. In 1767 he was appointed to print the Journals of the House of Lords and the Rolls of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">Parliament</a>. This year he printed Mr Clarke's excellent and learned work on "The Connection of the Roman, Saxon, and English Coins;" and wrote some notes upon it, which are interspersed throughout the volume with those of the author. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">Part</a> of the Dissertation on the Roman seferece was likewise Mr Bowyer's production; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDEX">index</a>, which is an uncommonly good one, was drawn up by him entirely. In January 1771 Mr Bowyer lost his second wife, and again received a letter of consolation from his old friend Mr Clarke, who had sent him one almost forty years before on a similar occasion. In the Philosophical Transactions for this year was printed a very ingenious "Inquiry into the Value of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greek and Roman <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">Money</a>," by the late Matthew Raper, Esq. But his opinions not coinciding with those of Mr Bowyer, he printed a small pamphlet, intitled, "Remarks, occasioned by a late Dissertation on the Greek and Roman money." In 1773 three little tracts were published by him, under the title of "Select Discourses. 1. Of the correspondence of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> months with the Julian, from the Latin of Professor Michaelis. 2. Of the Sabbatical years, from the same. 3. Of the years of jubilee, from an anonymous writer in Masson's Histoire Critique de la Republique des Lettres." In 1774 he corrected a new edition of Schrevelius's Greek Lexicon; to which he has added a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of words, distinguished by an asterisk, which he himself had collected in the course of his studies. Considerable additions, still in manuscript, were made by him to the lexicons of Hederic and Buxtorf, the Latin ones of Faber and Littleton, and the English <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a> of Bailey; and he left behind him many other proofs of his critical skill in the learned languages. In 1774 was published, "The Origin of Printing, in two Essays. 1. The substance of Dr Middleton's Dissertation on the Origin of Printing in England. 2. Mr Meerman's Account of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INVENTION">Invention</a> of the Art at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAARLEM">Haarlem</a>, and its progress to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MENTZ">Mentz</a>, with occasional Remarks, and an Appendix." The original idea of this valuable tract, was Mr Bowyer's, but it was completed by Mr Nichols. Although our author, during the last ten years of his life had been afflicted with the palsy and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, he not only preserved a remarkable cheerfulness of temper, but was enabled to support the labour of almost incessant <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-READING">reading</a>; and he regularly corrected the learned works, especially the Greek books, which came from his press. This he continued to do till within a few weeks of his death, which happened in November 1777, when he had nearly completed his 78th year. For more than half a century Mr Bowyer was unrivalled as a learned printer; and many of the most masterly productions of this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> have come from his press. To his literary and professional abilities he added an excellent moral character; and he was particularly distinguished by his inflexible probity, and an uncommon alacrity in relieving the necessitous.

BRAMINS

Pages 1115-1115

(Encycl.) See also <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBSERVATORY">Observatory</a>, (Encycl.) To <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAM">BREAM</a>, to burn off the filth, such as grats, ooze, shells, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-weed, from a ship's bottom, that has gathered to it in a voyage, or by lying <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> in a harbour. This operation is performed by holding kindled furze, faggots, or such materials, to the bottom, so that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> incorporating with the pitch, sulphur, &c. that had formerly covered it, immediately loosens and throws off whatever filth may have adhered to the planks. After this, the bottom is covered anew with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of sulphur, tallow, &c. which not only makes it smooth and slippery, so as to divide the fluid more readily, but also prevents and destroys those <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> which eat through the planks in the course of a voyage. Breaming may be performed either when the ship lies <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGROUND">aground</a> after the tide has ebbed from her, or by docking, or by careening.

BROWN

Pages 1115-1117

a clergyman of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of England, and an ingenious writer, was born at Rothbury in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a> in November 1715. His father John Brown, was a native of Scotland, of the Browns of Colstoun near <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HADDINGTON">Haddington</a>; and at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his son's birth was curate to Dr Thomlinson rector of Rothbury. He was afterwards collated to the vicarage of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WIGTON">Wigton</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>; to which <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> he carried his son, who received the first <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> there. Thence he was removed, in 1732, to the university of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, and entered of St John's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, under the tuition of Dr Tunstall. After taking the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of bachelor of arts with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation (being amongst the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> of wranglers, and his name at the head of the list) he returned to Wigton, and received both deacon's and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>'s orders from Sir George Fleming bishop of Carlisle. Here he was appointed by the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> canon and lectorer of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> church. For some years he lived here in obscurity; and nothing farther is known concerning him, than that in 1739 he went to Cambridge to take his degree of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts. In 1745 he distinguished himself as a volunteer in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, and behaved with great intrepidity at the siege of Carlisle. After the defeat of the rebels, when several of them were tried at the assizes held at Carlisle in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> of 1746, he preached at the cathedral church of that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> two excellent discourses, on the mutual connection between <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> and civil freedom; and between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, tyranny, irreligion, and licentiousness. Mr Brown's <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> cause and to the Whig party procured him the friendship of Dr Oxbaldclton, who was the only person that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to be his friend through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, the peculiarities of Mr Brown's temper, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> some other cause, having produced quarrels with every one else. When Dr Obaldston was advanced to the see of Carlisle, he appointed Mr Brown to be one of his chaplains. It was probably in the early part of his life, and during his residence at Carlisle, that Mr Brown wrote his poem intitled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">Honour</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Viscount Londale. Our author's next poetical production was his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on Satire; and which was of considerable advantage to him both in point of fame and fortune. It was addressed to Dr Warburton; to whom it was so acceptable, that he took Mr Brown into his friendship, and introduced him to Ralph Allen, Esq., of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">Prior</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARK">Park</a>, near Bath, who behaved to him with great generosity, and at whose <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> he resided for some time. In 1751 Mr Brown published his "Essays on the Characteristics of Lord <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHAFTESBURY">Shaftesbury</a>, &c." dedicated to Ralph Allen, Esq. This was received with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> degree of applause, though several persons attempted to answer it. In 1754, our author was promoted by the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Hardwicke to the living of Great Horkeley in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>. In 1755, our author took the degree of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">Divinity</a> at Cambridge. This year he published his tragedy of Barbarossa; which, under the management of Mr Garrick, was acted with considerable applause; but when it came to be published, it was exposed to a variety of strictures and censures. This tragedy introduced our author to the acquaintance of that eminent <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTOR">actor</a>; by whose favour he had a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> tragedy, named Athelstan, represented at Drury-Lane play-house. This was also well received by the public; but did not become so popular as Barbarossa, nor did it preserve so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> the possession of the stage. In 1757 appeared his famous "Estimate of the Manners and Principles of the Times." The reception which this <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> met with from the public was very flattering to his vanity; no fewer than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> editions of it having been printed in little more than a year. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of this performance was to show, that a vain, luxurious, and selfish effeminacy in the higher ranks of life marked the character of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; and to point out the effects and sources of this effeminacy. Several antagonists appeared, some of whom were neither destitute of learning nor ingenuity; though Mr Brown himself asserted that Dr Wallace, a clergyman of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, was the only candid and decent adversary that appeared against him. The testimony given by M. de Voltaire to the effect which the Estimate had on the conduct of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, is very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> to Dr Brown. "When Marshal Richlieu, in 1756, (says that celebrated writer) laid siege to Port <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MAHON">Mahon</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MINORCA">Minorca</a>, the British sent out <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> Byng with a strong naval force, to drive the French fleet off the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, and raise the siege. At this time there appeared a book, entitled An Estimate of the Manners of the Times; of which there was no less than five editions printed off in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in the space of three months. In this treatise the author proves that the English nation was entirely degenerated;—that it was near its ruin;—that its inhabitants were no longer so robust and hardy as in former times;—and that its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> had lost their courage. This work roused the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol17.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a> of the English nation, and produced the following consequences. They attacked, almost at one and the same time, all the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-coasts of France, and her possessions in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>." In 1758, our author published the second volume of his Estimate of the Manners and Principles of the Times; containing additional remarks on the ruling manners and principles, and on the public effects of those manners and principles. The design of this volume was, to retract such mistakes as he thought he had committed; to prove such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> as were affirmed and not proved; to illustrate those particulars which were hinted, but not explained; to reply to such capital objections as had been made to his general system by preceding writers on the same subject; and to display the consequences which might be fairly deduced from his principles, and through a designed brevity were omitted in the first volume. But it unfortunately happened that the Doctor's self-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, which gave too much offence in his first volume, broke out in the second with still greater violence. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this was, that he exposed himself to general censure and dislike; and the prejudices against him occasioned the real excellencies of the work to be very much overlooked. The periodical critics, whom he had gone needlessly out of his way to abuse, treated him with uncommon severity; and such a multitude of antagonists rose against him, so many objections were urged upon him, by friends as well as enemies, that he seems to have been deeply impressed, and to have retired for a while into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. From the country it was that he wrote, in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of letters to a noble friend, "An Explanatory <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFENCE">Defence</a> of the Estimate of the Manners and Principles of the Times; being an Appendix to that Work, occasioned by the clamours lately raised against it among certain Ranks of Men." But while Dr Brown thus distinguished himself as a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> writer, he was advanced to no higher <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> in the church; nay, on some disgust, it is supposed, he resigned his living in Essex; however, in recompense, Dr Obaldston procured him the rectory of St Nicholas in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a> on Tyne. He would probably have received further favours from this prelate, had not the latter died soon after his promotion to the see of London. In 1760 our author published an Additional <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIALOGUE">Dialogue</a> of the Dead, between <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERICLES">Pericles</a> and Aristides; being a sequel to a dialogue of Lord Lyttelton's between Pericles and Colmo. One design of this additional dialogue was to vindicate the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> of Mr Pitt, against whose administration Lord Lyttelton had been supposed to have thrown out some hints. Our author's next publication, in 1663, was "The Cure of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-SAUL">Saul</a>," a sacred ode; which was followed in the same year by "A Dissertation on the Rise, Union, and Power, the Progressions, Separations, and Corruptions of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a> and Music." This is one of the most pleasing of Dr Brown's performances, and abounds with a variety of critical disquisitions. A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of strictures on this piece were published; and the Doctor defended himself in a treatise intitled Remarks on some Observations on Dr Brown's Dissertations on Poetry and Music. In 1764 our author published, in octavo, "The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Rise and Progress of Poetry through its several <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">Species</a>;" which is no more than the substance given in the dissertation abovementioned. The same year Dr Brown pub- lished a volume of sermons, dedicated to his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> Dr Olafsdottson bishop of London; but most, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not all of these, had been separately published, excepting the first three, which were on the subject of education. In the beginning of the year 1765, the Doctor again returned to politics, and published "Thoughts on Civil <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">Liberty</a>, Licentiousness, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACTION">Faction</a>." At the conclusion of this work the author prescribed a code of education, upon which Dr Priestley made remarks at the end of his "Essay on the Course of a Liberal Education for civil and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> Life." The same year he published a sermon "On the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">Female</a> Character and Education," preached on the 16th of May, 1765, before the guardians of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> for deserted female orphans. His last publication was, in 1766, "A <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">Letter</a> to the Rev. Dr Lowth, occasioned by his late Letter to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">Right</a> Reverend Author of the Divine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEGISLATION">Legislation</a> of Moses." This was occasioned by Dr Lowth's having clearly, though indirectly, pointed at Dr Brown as one of the extravagant adulators and defenders of bishop Warburton. Besides these works, Dr Brown published a poem on Liberty, and two or three anonymous pamphlets. At the end of several of his later writings, he advertised his design of publishing "Christian Principles of Legislation," but was prevented from executing it by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; though the work appears to have been completed. We come now to the concluding events of our author's life; concerning which the following is the most authentic intelligence that can be procured. Whilst Dr Dumaresq resided in Russia in the year 1765, to which he had been invited the preceding year to give his advice and assistance for the establishment and regulation of several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> which her Imperial majesty intended to erect, he received a letter from a lady of distinguished character in England, recommending to him Dr Brown as a proper correspondent on this occasion. Dr Dumaresq then wrote a letter to Dr Brown, telling him the occasion of his application, and the difficulties that occurred. He had imagined that nothing more would be wanted of him than what concerned classical learning, and a general foundation for the sciences; as that had been the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> introduction to every kind of useful knowledge in the western parts of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. But on his arrival he found that a much more extensive scheme was required; and such as extended not only to learning properly so called, but also to matters <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> and naval, civil and commercial. But having stated his difficulties in executing this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> to Dr Brown, the latter proposed a scheme still more extensive; and which was no less than a general plan of civilization throughout the whole Russian empire. In this plan, however, though it showed very enlarged <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> and great strength of mind, there were several defects which rendered it, as Dr Brown himself was afterwards convinced, impracticable. He had laid greater stress upon the support, energy, and efficacy of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> power in princes when exerted in a good cause, than <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> would warrant; and he was ready to imagine that the bulk of the Russian nation, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> emerging out of barbarism, was like a tabula rasa, upon which any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> might be written. At last the Doctor's letter was laid before the empress, who was so pleased with it that she immediately invited him to Russia. He accepted the invitation, and procured his Majesty's leave to go: 1000l. were ordered for his expense, and he actually received 200l. But when he was on the point of setting out, an attack of the gout and rheumatism, to which he had been all his lifetime subject, so impaired his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, that his friends dissuaded, and at last succeeded in preventing him from going. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a> was returned, excepting 97l. 6s. which had been expended in necessaries for the intended journey. But though he thus declined the journey, a long letter which he afterwards wrote to the empress, and which does honour to his abilities, shows that he had not abandoned his intention of being serviceable. The affair, however, taken in all its circumstances, did no doubt greatly agitate his mind; and his being obliged at length to give up the journey, must have been no small disappointment to a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> of his sanguine expectations. This disappointment concurring with the general state of his health, and perhaps the recollection of some other failures that had happened, was followed by a dejection of spirits; in consequence of which he put an end to his life on the 23d of September 1766, in the 51st year of his age. On the morning of that <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> came into his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a>-chamber, and asked him what sort of a night he had had? to which he replied, "A pretty good one." The servant having quitted the bedside for a few minutes, heard a noise in the Doctor's throat, which he imagined to be owing to some obstruction occasioned by phlegm. Going to assist his master, he found him speechless, and bleeding profusely, having cut the jugular vein with a razor; and this he had done so effectually, that death speedily ensued. Such was the unhappy end of this ingenious writer; but the manner of it, when some previous circumstances of his life are understood, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> no stain on his character. He had a tendency to insanity in his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>; and from his early life, had been subject at times to some disorder in his brain, at least to melancholy in its excess. Mrs Gilpin of Carlisle, soon after Dr Brown's decease, wrote in the following terms in a letter to a friend. "His distemper was a frenzy, to which he had by fits been long subject; to my own knowledge, above 30 years. Had it not been for Mr Farish frequently, and once for myself, the same event would have happened to him long ago. It was no premeditated purpose in him; for he abhorred the thought of self-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>; and in bitterness of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> expressed his fears to me, that one time or another some ready mischief might present itself to him, at a time when he was wholly deprived of his reason."

BRUCHUS

Pages 1117-1117

(Encycl.) See Plate CCCXIII. BUBONOCELE. For n° 13. read p. 8383, 8422.

BUG

Pages 1117-1118

(Encycl.) Early in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, even in February, the larva of these creatures begins to burst from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EGG">egg</a>; and it is at this season that <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> is so very requisite. The <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a> ought to be stripped of all its furniture; which should be washed, and even boiled, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>; if stuff, it should be hot-pressed. The bedstead should be taken to pieces, dusted, and washed with spirit of wine in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a>; for in those parts the females lay their eggs. This done, the joints, crevices, cavities, &c. should be well filled with the best soft <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOAP">soap</a> mixed with verdigris and Scots snuff. On this substance the larva, if any escape the cleansing, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> BURSERA any, which is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in old houses, creep into the bedstead, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> feed at first, and of course be destroyed: this last will effect the purpose in houses where these <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERMIN">vermin</a> are not so numerous, by repeating the operation every three months.—Professor Kalm mentions, that from repeated trials, he has been convinced that sulphur, if it be properly employed, entirely destroys bugs and their eggs in beds or walls, though they were ten times more numerous than the ants on an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANT">ant</a>-hill. His translator, Dr Forster, adds, that a still more effectual remedy is, to wash all the infected furniture with a solution of arsenic. See further the article Cimicifuga, below.

BURSERA

Pages 1118-1118

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, a genus of the monogynia order, belonging to the hexandria clas of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There is but one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, the gummifera, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUM">gum</a>-elm. This is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> tree. The leaves are pennate, the middle rib five or six inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, with the pinnae set opposite to one another on footstalks half an inch long. The blossoms are succeeded by purple-coloured berries bigger than large peas, hanging in clusters on a stalk of about five inches long, to which each berry is joined by a footstalk of half an inch long. The seed is hard, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, and of a triangular <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, inclosed within a thin <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPSULE">capsule</a>, which divides in three parts, and discharges the seed. This tree produces a large <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of gum, of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and of the consistence of turpentine. It is esteemed a good vulnerary, and is much used for horses. Most of the Bahama <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> abound with these trees.

BUTTERWORT

Pages 1118-1118

(Encycl.) Wherever this plant, called also <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a> fanicle, is found, it is a certain indication of a boggy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>. It has <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> had the reputation of being noxious to sheep. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> people believe that it gives them the rot whenever they eat it, which they <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> not do but from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>. Hence this plant has been called the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> rot. CABBAGE BARK-TREE. Sec Geoffreæa, below.

CABINDA

Pages 1118-1118

the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> port of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Angoy in Loango in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. It is situated at the mouth of a river of the same name about five leagues <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Palmerino, on the north side of the mouth of the river Zaire. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> is very commodious for trade, wooding, and watering. CACHEXY. For <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a> subjoined to Medicine, read, p. 481o. CACTUS. For <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a>, read Cereus. CÆSARIAN OPERATION. For chap. vi. read chap. xv.

CALAMUS

Pages 1118-1118

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, a genus of the monogynia order, belonging to the hexandria clas of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There is but one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, the rotang, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> true <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANE">cane</a>. The stem is without branches, has a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> at top, and is everywhere beset with straight spines. This is the true Indian cane, which is not visible on the outside; but the bark being taken off discovers the smooth stick, which has no marks of spine on the bark, and is exactly like those which the Dutch sell to us; keeping this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> very secret, lest travellers going by should take as many canes out of the woods as they please. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUMATRA">Sumatra</a> is said to be the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where most of these sticks grow. Such are to be chosen as are of a proper growth between two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a>, suitable to the fashionable length of canes as they are then worn: but such are scarce. CALASH. For n° 76. read n° 73.

CALCAREOUS EARTH

Pages 1118-1119

(Encycl.) Though this kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> cannot be vitrified by itself in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of our <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> furnaces, it is remarkable, that by mixing it with argillaceous earth, which is as unvitrifiable as itself, both <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> melt together into glass. To illustrate this, Dr Watson relates the following experiment. "Mix well together equal weights of powdered chalk <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> other calcareous body, and powdered pipe-clay; put the mixture into a crucible. Any where towards the middle of the crucible put two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> pieces; one of pure chalk, the other of pure clay, so that they may not be contiguous to each other, but be everywhere surrounded with the mixture of chalk and clay. Then by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> the whole to a strong <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of heat for a sufficient length of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, it will be found that the mixture has been converted into glass; and upon breaking the vitrified <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, we shall discover the two solid pieces of chalk and clay unvitrified and unaltered in their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, tho' every where surrounded with glass. It is remarkable, that some kinds of calcareous earth, after being deprived of all their fixed <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> by calcination, will regain, upon being exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>, the very same <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> that they lost, while others will not. Dr Watson informs us, that having calcined into lime 204 grains of dove marble, the lime weighed whilst hot 116 grains. This was done on the 6th of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">March</a>; and on the 5th of November following it weighed 203½ grains. As it had been frequently weighed during that <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a>, it is very probable that the half grain had been lost by repeating this operation. A <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> experiment turned out, as accurately as could be expected, the same. Some dry chalk, weighing 120 grains, was reduced by calcination to 68. This quantity of lime increased only to 104 grains; so that 16 parts in 120, or between one seventh and one eighth of its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, were never regained. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a> gives a reason for this defect of increase in the following manner. "The chalk or clunch (says he) of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, is not a pure calcareous earth, but contains a portion of sand; and hence, when a definite weight of this chalk-lime is exposed to the air, it cannot acquire as much increase of weight as the same quantity of purer lime would do; for the sand which is mixed with the lime is of a very different <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> from it, and does not attract any thing from the air." It is difficult, however, on this supposition, to see why the sand should lose any thing by calcination; for as it can regain no air, so it can lose none in the fire. The following is a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of the weight regained by lime made from different materials, according to Dr Watson's experiments. He observes, however, that there is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reason to believe, that the quantity of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> which CAM The same sort of lime can attract from the air, depends very much on the degree of heat with which the lime has been burned. There is a certain definite degree of heat requisite to make the lime attract the greatest possible quantity from the air. When the heat is not sufficient to convert the whole of the substance into lime, then that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> which is not converted into lime will not contribute any thing to the increase of the lime when exposed to the air, inasmuch as it possesses no <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of attracting anything from the air. Our author observes also, that the same effect takes <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> when the heat has been more than sufficient to convert the whole of the substance into lime; for then a partial vitrification takes place. The following substances were changed into lime by being exposed to a very fierce fire for 24 hours. The experiment was made in November 1779; and in three months they had all acquired the greatest increase of weight. The first <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> of the table expresses the increase of weight which a ton of the same substances gained; and the second expresses that which they would have gained, had they been exposed to the fire only for four hours. | Substance | C. q. lb. | C. q. lb. | |-------------------|-----------|-----------| | Sunna marble | 8 | 15 | | Rhomboidal <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAR">spar</a> | 8 | 5 | | Statuary marble | 8 | 0 | | Chalk | 7 | 13 | | Clithero <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a>| 6 | 9 | | Crystalized spar | 6 | 0 |

CALCINATION

Pages 1119-1119

(Encycl.) In <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that the increase of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> in metallic calces is owing to the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADHESION">adhesion</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>, it may be observed, that various metallic calces are in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> soluble in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>; which shows that they have something of a saline <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. Perhaps the elastic, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, whatever it is, which generates the elastic fluids obtained from these calces, renders them so. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CALX">CALX</a> antimonii, is the earthy <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the regulus of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a> when deprived of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHLOGISTON">phlogiston</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PHARMACY">PHARMACY</a>, no 791. By the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of fire, however, the whole of its phlogiston cannot be diffused; though it may be done by the addition of nitre, and the calx become perfectly <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>; but in this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> it cannot be melted into glais, except in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FOCUS">focus</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> mirror. The calx of antimony, perfectly deprived of its phlogiston, has been used in medicine chiefly under the name of diaphoretic antimony; but little regard is now paid to it. CAMPHORA. In marginal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, for no 198, read The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">Table</a>. CAMPVEER. See VEER, (Encycl.) Lighting a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANDLE">Candle</a> by a small spark of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTRICITY">electricity</a>. This method, which is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of Dr Ingenhousz, is recorded in the Phil. Transl. vol. 68. It is done by a small vial, having eight or ten inches of metallic coating, or even less, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with electricity, which may be done at any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the night by a person who has an electric machine in his room. "When I have occasion to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> a candle," says he, "I <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> a small-coated phial, whose knob is bent outwards, so as to hang a little over the body of the phial; then I wrap some loose cotton over the extremity of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> braid <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PIN">pin</a> or a wire, so as to stick moderately fast to its substance. I next roll this extremity of the pin wrapped up with cotton in some fine powder of resin, (which I always keep in readiness upon the table for this purpose, either in a wide-mouthed phial or in a loose <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>); this being done, I apply the extremity of the pin or wire to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> coating of the charged phial, and bring, as quickly as possible, the other extremity wrapped round with cotton to the knob: the powder of resin takes fire, and communicates its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> to the cotton, and both together burn long enough to light a candle. As I do not want more than half a minute to light my candle in this way, I find it a readier method than kindling it by flint and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>, or calling a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>. "I have found, that powder of white or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> resin lights easier than that of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>. "The farina lycopodiis may be used for the same purpose: but it is not so good as the powder of resin, because it does not take fire quite so readily, requiring a stronger spark not to miss; besides, it is soon burnt away. "By <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIPPING">dipping</a> the cotton in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of turpentine, the same effect may be as readily obtained, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> you take a jar somewhat greater in size. This oil <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> inflame so much the readier if you throw a few fine particles of bras upon it. The pin dust is the best for this purpose; but as this oil is scattered about by the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPLOSION">explosion</a>, and when kindled fills the room with much more <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> than the powder of resin, I prefer the last." CANDLE-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOMB">Bomb</a>, a name given to small glass bubbles, having a neck about an inch long, with a very slender bore, by means of which a small <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of water is introduced into them, and the orifice afterwards closed up. This stalk being put through the wick of a burning candle, the vicinity of the flame soon rarifies the water into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STEAM">steam</a>, by the elasticity of which the glass is broken with a loud crack.

CANTHARIS

Pages 1119-1119

(Encycl.) The cantharis noctiluca, which is frequently found in pastures and under juniper trees, shines by night. In <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of winged <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANTHARIDES">cantharides</a> remain all night on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a> and branches of trees, emitting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>; but on the approach of any enemy instantly fly off, and the whole tree seems on fire. This wonderful light, which has no connection either with the culinary <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> electric fire, is placed in the segments of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a> of the insect while it remains alive.

CAOUTCHOUC

Pages 1119-1120

(Encycl.) A method of dissolving this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUM">gum</a> without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETHER">ether</a> is as follows: Take one <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POUND">pound</a> of the spirit of turpentine, and a pound of the gum cut into very small pieces; pour the turpentine into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>-necked matrafs, which must be placed in a sand-bath; throw in the gum, not all at once, but by little and little according as it is perceived to dissolve. When it is entirely dissolved, pour into the matrafs a pint of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> linseed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, or oil of pop- Cardamom pies, rendered deliciatice in the usual manner with lichefelden. Then let the whole boil for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> is finished.—This would make an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">Air</a>-balloons, were it not so expensive on account of the price of the gum. CARDAMOM. For no 210, 211. read The Catalogue of Simples. CAREENING. For plate LXXXIV. read plate LXXXIII.

CAPE COAST

Pages 1121-1122

the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> British settlement on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Guineas in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. The name is thought to be a corruption of Cabo Corso, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Portuguese appellation. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPE">cape</a> is formed by an angular point, washed on the south and east by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, on which stands the English fort. Here the Portuguese settled in 1610, and built the citadel of Cape Coast upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> rock that projects into the sea. A few years afterwards they were dislodged by the Dutch, to whom this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is principally indebted for its strength. In 1664 it was demolished by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">Admiral</a> Holmes. Holmes, and in 1665 the famous Dutch admiral De Ruyter was ordered by the states to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> the insults of the English. With a squadron of 13 men of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> he attacked all the English settlements along the coast, ruined the factories, took, burnt, and sunk all the shipping of the English <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a>; however, after all his efforts, he was baffled in his attempts on Cape Coast. By the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREDA">Breda</a> it was confirmed to the English, and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> granted a new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> in 1672; on which the Company applied all their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the fortifying and rendering it commodious. CHESELDEN

Pages 1120-1121

(William), an eminent anatomist and surgeon, was born at Burrow on the Hill, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEICESTER">Leicester</a>, descended from an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family in the county of Rutland, whose arms and pedigree are in Wright's "<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Rutland." He received the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of his professional skill at Leicester; and married Deborah <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KNIGHT">Knight</a>, a citizen's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, by whom he had one daughter, Williamina Deborah. In 1713 he published his Anatomy of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">Human</a> Body, 1 vol. 8vo; and in 1723, A Treatise on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> Operation for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">Stone</a>. He was one of the earliest of his profession who contributed by his writings to raise it to its present eminence. The following verses were addressed to him in 1733, "on his many dextrous and successful operations:" Oh wondrous Art! (surely given, By the peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> of Heaven, As a new Saviour to mankind, The lame to cure, relieve the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BLIND">blind</a>, And, by the ever happy <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>, To ease, and lengthen human <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>! How dost thou grace that noble art, Which owes to you its noblest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a>? How well deserve the general praise Your universal fame does raise! How <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> your merit, for the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> Conferr'd on you by <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> grace! Well might the care alone be thine, To tend on gracious Caroline, Since all allow your skill divine. No more let France her artists boast, To you but smatterers at most. Their Charité, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Hôtel Dieu, Ne'er <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> such cures as done by you; Aware of this, with utmost speed, Their New Academy decreed You all their honours, and, to grace Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a>, therein give you a place: From such a member they receive A greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> than they give. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a> may you live, and blest the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> With your unerring skill and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, May this ne'er fail, that never warp; And may they both defend to sharp! In the beginning of 1736, he was thus honourably mentioned by Mr Pope: "As soon as I had sent my last <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, I received a most kind one from you, expressing <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> pain for my late illness at Mr Chefelden's. I conclude you was eased of that friendly <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a> in a few days after you had dispatched yours, for mine must have reached you then. I wondered a little at your quare, who Chefelden was. It shews that the truest merit does not travel so far any way as on the wings of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>: he is the most noted and most deserving <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> in the whole profession of chirurgery; and has saved the lives of thousands by his manner of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> for the stone." He appears to have been on terms of the most intimate friendship with Mr Pope, who, frequently, in his Letters to Mr Richardson, talks of dining with Mr Chefelden, who then lived in or near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">Square</a>. In February 1737, Mr Chefelden was appointed surgeon to Chelsea <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOSPITAL">Hospital</a>. As a governor of the Foundling Hospital, he sent a benefaction of 50l. to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>, May 7, 1751, inclosed in a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> with the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>: 'Tis what the happy to the unhappy owe; For what man gives, the gods by him bestow. Pope. He died at Bath, April 11, 1752, of a disorder arising from drinking ale after eating hot buns. Finding himself uneasy, he sent for a physician, who advised vomiting immediately; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the advice had been taken, taken, it was thought his life might have been saved. By his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, he was buried at Chelsea. CHEVERON. For no 23, 24. read p. 3592.

CHINA

Pages 1121-1121

(Encycl.) The immense <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of China, recorded under that article, no 55, falls very far short of that recorded by some late authors. In the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, &c. of the Chinese by the missionaries at Pekin, published at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1780, we find a controversy on this subject between M. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAU">Pau</a> and the ex-judic M. Amiott. The former had published a book, intitled "Philosophical Inquiries concerning the Egyptians and Chinese," in which he <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RATES">rates</a> the population of China much below 82 millions. Amiott is so far from being of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that he estimates their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> at 200 millions. To confirm this estimate, he produces a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> made in 1743, of all that paid taxes in the respective provinces, that is, of all the heads of families; and, on summing up their numbers, he finds 28,516,428 families; in which enumeration, says he, women, children, and domestics, are not reckoned. The Chinese reckon, at an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a>, six to a family. M. Amiott reduces this computation to five, and on this supposition makes the inhabitants of China amount to 142,582,400 souls. But in this number the Missionary comprehends neither the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> mandarins, the inferior ones, nor the literati, nor the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a>, which amount, according to his calculations, to upwards of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> millions; which added to the enumeration abovementioned, make 149,663,000 souls. Fifty millions are nevertheless still wanting to make up the 200 millions at which our Missionary estimates the inhabitants of China. There he finds in the inhabitants of Pekin, which he reckons at two millions, the Manchou Tartars, who live among the Chinese, the tradesmen, the persons employed in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SILK">silk</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, and the populace of the cities, which are not registered. But the computations of M. Amiott are liable to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> difficulties, and are certainly arbitrary and uncertain in several respects. He comprehends in his enumeration districts and provinces that belong to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>, and not to China; and he calculates often from registers of the same districts, that are discordant and contradictory. When it is considered, that the enumerations of the inhabitants of China have been different under different dynasties, as all the emperors did not possess the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of territory,—that the wars with the Tartars often obliging the Chinese to withdraw in great numbers towards the south, rendered certain provinces more populous at one <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> than they were at another,—that the numbers of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, the struggling labourers, and of those that ply on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, cannot be easily computed,—and that many of the registers are evidently arbitrary; we find ourselves disposed to suspend our determination of the controversy between M. Amiott and M. Pau relative to the object now under consideration. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> population had gone on increasing in China, from the third century before the Christian era (which was the period of their rising power), the Chinese might have sent into Tartary numerous colonies, which would have peopled that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> and civilized its inhabitants. But this has not been the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>; and notwithstanding all the pompous relations of the Missionaries, it is certain, that a bad administration,—the extortions and oppressive conduct of civil and military officers,—the revolutions occasioned by the establishment of different dynasties,—famines,—epidemics,—inundations,—wars,—massacres—and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of great ministers, involving their friends and families in ruin, keep population within certain bounds, and hinder it from rising to a pitch that would produce new and fatal revolutions. CHITAU. For Lignum-aloes, read Xylo-aloes.

CHOCOLATE

Pages 1121-1121

(Encycl.) This, according to Linnaeus, is more salutary than either <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TEA">tea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> coffee. There are three methods of preparing it, as practised by the Indians, the Spaniards, and others. The Indians, to one <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POUND">pound</a> of the roasted nuts put half a pound of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> dissolved in rose-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and half a pound of flour of maize or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> corn. The Spaniards, to fix pounds of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a> add three and an half of sugar, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> pods of vanillas, one pound and an half of Indian corn, half a pound of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CINNAMON">cinnamon</a>, fix cloves; one drachm of capicum, and whatsoever is thought requisite of the roucou nut to improve the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, together with ambergrise or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MUSK">musk</a> to give an agreeable scent. In the other and more <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> way, to seventeen pounds of nuts are added ten pounds of sugar, twenty-eight pods of vanillas, one drachm of ambergrise, and fix ounces of cinnamon.

CIMICIFUGA

Pages 1121-1121

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, a genus of the polyandra order, belonging to the dioecia class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. Meillerchmidius, in the Ibis Siberica, gives it the following character and name: *Cimicifuga foetida* with the leaves of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERB">herb</a> Christopher, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> a thyrsis of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> villous seed, the seed-vessel in form of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a>. This whole plant to resembles the actea racemosa, that it is difficult to distinguish them when not in flower; but in the fructification it greatly differs from it, the cimicifuga having four pistils, the actea but one. Jacquin says, that it is a native of the Carpathian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. It has obtained the name of cimicifuga, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> bugbane, both in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>, from its <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of driving away those insects; and the botanists of those parts of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> which are infested by them, have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> desired to naturalise it in their several countries. For <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">Part</a> I. read Part II. CLAVARIA. Par. 2. line 1. For Mr Miller, read Mr <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MULLER">Muller</a>.

CLEPSYDRA
