COCCINELLA

Pages 1122-1122

(Encycl.) Delete the whole article, and read as follows: Coccinella, a genus of insects of the order of coleoptera; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of which are these: The antennae are subclavate; the palpi are longer than the antennae, the last articulation heart-shaped; the body is hemispheric; the thorax and elytra are margined; the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a> is flat. This genus is divided into sections, from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the elytra, and of the spots with which they are adorned. The females, impregnated by the males, deposit their eggs, which turn to small larvae, slow in their progress, and enemies to the plant-louse. Those larvae are frequently found upon leaves of trees covered with plant-<a class="xref" href="../1823/vol0.html#article-LICE">lice</a>. On the point of being metamorphosed, they <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> by the hinder <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of their body, then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> and swell themselves, forming a kind of hook. The skin extends, grows hard; and in a fortnight's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHRYSALIS">chrysalis</a> opens along the back. The insect in its perfect state receives the impressions of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, that gives its elytra a greater <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of consistence. It seldom flies, and cannot keep <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> on the wing. Of all the different larvae of the coccinella, the most curious is the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> hedgehog, a name given it by M. de Reaumur on account of the singularity of its <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, and the tufts of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> which render it remarkable. It feeds its food on the leaves of trees. After a fortnight, it settles on one spot, and, without parting with its fur, turns to a chrysalis; three weeks after which, it becomes a coccinella. The flough appears nowise impaired by its transformation. M. de Reaumur has observed it on a plum-tree. It is likewise found upon the rose-tree. When the coccinellae first arrive at the state of perfection, the colours of their elytra are very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a>, nearly bordering upon white <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> cream colour; and the elytra are very soft and tender, but soon grow hard, and change to very lively brilliant colours. Their eggs are of an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> form, and of the colour of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBER">amber</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COCHINEAL">cochineal</a>-insect, described by mistake under this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> in the Encyclopaedia, belongs to a different genus. See Coccus, below.

COCCUS

Pages 1122-1124

the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COCHINEAL">Cochineal</a>, was by mistake confounded with the Coccinella, (Encycl.) which is a genus belonging to a different order. See Coccinella, above. After "frequent," line 6th of the article Coccus, in Encycl. supply as follows. The most remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> are: 1. The coccus hesperidum, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-GREEN_HOUSE">green-<a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> bug, is oval, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a>, of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, covered with a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a>: It has six legs; with a notch and four bristles at the tail. It infests <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a>-trees, and other similar <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> in green-houses. When young, it runs upon the trees; but afterwards fixes on some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>, where it <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HATCHES">hatches</a> an infinity of eggs, and dies. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> is a very small fly. 2. The coccus phalaridis. The male of this cochinellus is small. Its antennae are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> for its size. The feet and body are of a reddish colour, nearly pink, and sprinkled with a little <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> powder. Its two wings, and the four threads of its tail, are snow white, and of those threads two are longer than the rest. It is to be found upon the species of gramen which Linnaeus calls <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHALARIS">phalaris</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> contrives, along the stalks of that dog-grass, little nests, of a white cottony substance, in which she deposits her eggs. The small threads of her tail are scarcely perceptible. 3. The coccus cacii, or famous Mexican cochineal, (see Cochineal, below), a native of the warm parts of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a> this species is nursed with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> care. It naturally fixes upon the leaves of various kinds of plants. The Indians gather them, put 10 or 12 into little beds made of moss or of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIBRE">fibre</a> of coco; after which they hang them upon the thorns of the plant known under the various names of racket, cardafia, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> fig-tree, opuntia, nopal. There grow great quantities of that plant round their habitations. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GALL">gall</a>-insects give birth to myriads of young ones. They disperse, feed on the juice of the plant, and there produce a fresh <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>. There are three gatherings of them every year. The first is performed by taking off the nests brought and placed upon the plants; the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, by looening the cochineal from off the leaves with pincers; and the third, at the approach of winter, by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off the leaves that are yet loaded with the insects. Those plants remaining green for a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, afford them sustenance. When they have attained their full size, they are taken off by scraping the leaf. This last cochineal is not of so fine a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, because a little of the epiderm of the leaf is blended with it. The Spaniards call it granilla. As soon as the insects are brought together, they are destroyed. The method taken to effect this has great influence upon the colour. It then goes by various names. That which they kill by the gentle <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of ovens, is of an ash-grey or mottled, and is named jaspidea. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the insects are deprived of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> by plunging them with baskets into hot <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, it then goes by the appellation of renegrida, which is not covered over with a white powder. Lastly, it bears the name of negra, if destroyed upon the hot plates that have been used for roasting of maize. By this last <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> it sometimes receives too great a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of heat, from which it turns somewhat <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>. Three pounds of freshly-gathered cochineals weigh but one when dried. The cochineal thus nursed upon cultivated plants, yields a more beautiful colour, and in greater <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, than does the wild. Dried cochineals <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> preserve their colouring particles for ages, as no other insect fixes on them; neither do they ever decay. This valuable insect is used for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a>, where it produces a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> colour of an excellent tincture, in variety of shades. It is made into scarlet and crimson. The English mix it with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUM">gum</a>-lac to dye their cloths. This dye is more expeditions, as good, and cheaper. The cochineal furnishes painters with the most lively colours and most beautiful shades; and the same substance, ground and prepared, produces carmine, which, skillfully laid on over the ladies <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a>, emulates <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. At Constantinople they fell a crape or very fine <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAWN">lawn</a> dyed in cochineal; and the same is imitated at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STRASBOURG">Strasbourg</a>. This lawn, dipped in water, may be used equally with the nacarat-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a> to the same purposes as cochineal, one of which is to give a colour to liquors. It is computed that there are imported yearly into <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, in the course of trade, 880,000 pounds of cochineals. The female cochineal had been long known, and well described, by several naturalists; but the male having been seldom seen, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of this valuable insect has hitherto been very defective. Mr Ellis, being informed that this insect bred in great abundance on the cactus opuntia of Linnæus, in South Carolina and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEORGIA">Georgia</a>, as well as on the cactus coccinellifer in Mexico and Jamaica, obtained from Dr Garden some branches of the former, with the insects upon them. In examining several of these specimens, he at last discovered three or four minute dead flies with white wings; and having moistened them in spirit of wine, and observing them with a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a>, found that they were of a bright red colour, which convinced him that these were the true male insects. Dr Garden, to whom this discovery was communicated, made several observations on the male species. This is very rarely found; so that he imagines there may be 150 or 200 females for one male. The male is much less than the female, more <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>, and better made; and the body of it is of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> red than that of the other. 4. The coccus ilicis, or that forming the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KERMES">kermes</a> grains, inhabits the quercus coccifera of the southern parts of Europe. Mr Hellot of the French Academy of Sciences, in his Art of Dyeing, chap. 12, says it is found in the woods of Vauvert, Vendemen, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NARBONNE">Narbonne</a>; but more abundantly in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, towards Alicante and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VALENCIA">Valencia</a>. It not only abounds in Valencia, but also in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MURCIA">Murcia</a>, Jaen, Cordova, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEVILLE">Seville</a>, Extremadura, la Mancha, Serranias de <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUENCA">Cuenca</a>, and other places. In <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-XIXONA">Xixona</a> and Tierra de Relleu, there is a district called De la Grana, where the people of Valencia first began to gather it, whose example was followed all over Spain. It has some years produced 30,000 dollars (5000l.) to the inhabitants of Xixona. Both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> and moderns seem to have had very confused notions concerning the origin and nature of the kermes; some considering it as a fruit, without a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> knowledge of the tree which produced it; others taking it for an excrescence formed by the puncture of a particular fly, the same as the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> gall observed upon oaks. Tournefort was of this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Marigliani, and Dr Nobile a physician of Montpelier, made experiments and observations, with a view of further discoveries; but did not perfectly succeed. Two other physicians at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIX">Aix</a> in Provence, Dr Emeric and Dr Garidel, applied themselves about the same time, and with greater success; having finally discovered that the kermes is in reality nothing else but the body of an insect transformed into a grain, berry, or husk, according to the course of nature. The progress of this transformation must be considered at three different seasons. In the first stage, at the beginning of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, an animalcule, no larger than a grain of millet, scarce able to crawl, is perceived flickering to the branches of the tree, where it fixes itself, and soon becomes immovable; at this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> it grows the most, appears to swell and thrive with the sustenance it draws in by degrees. This state of rest seems to have deceived the curious observer, it then resembling an excrescence of the bark; during this period of its growth, it appears to be covered with a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, extending over its whole frame like a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NET">net</a>, and adhering to the bark: its <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> is convex, not unlike a small floe; in such parts as are not quite hidden by this soft garment, many bright specks are perceived of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> colour, as well as stripes running across the body from one space to another. At the second stage, in April, its growth is completed, its shape is then round, and about the size of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEA">pea</a>: it has then acquired more strength, and its down is changed into dust, and seems to be nothing but a husk or a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPSULE">capsule</a>, full of a reddish juice not unlike discoloured blood. Its third stage is towards the end of May, a little sooner or later, according to the warmth of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>. The husk appears replete with small eggs, less than the seed of a poppy. These are properly ranged under the belly of the insect, progressively placed in the nest of down that covers its body, which it withdraws in proportion to the number of eggs: after this <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> is performed, it soon dies, though it still adheres to its position, rendering a further <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to its progeny, and shielding them from the inclemency of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, or the hostile attacks of an enemy. In a good season they multiply exceedingly, having from 1800 to 2000 eggs, which produce the same number of animalcules. When observed with the microscope in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> or August, we find, that what appeared as dust, are so many eggs or open capsules, as white as snow, out of each of which issues a gold-coloured animalcule, of the shape of a cockroach, with two horns, six feet, and a forked tail. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a> and Provence the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> are employed to gather the kermes, the women letting their nails grow for that purpose, in order to pick them off with greater facility. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of lopping off the boughs is very injudicious, as by this means they destroy the next year's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a>. Some women will gather two or three pounds a-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>; the great point being to know the places where they are most likely to be found in any quantity, and to gather them early with the morning-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEW">dew</a>, as the leaves are more pliable and tender at that time, than after they have been dried and parched by the rays of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>: strong dews will occasionally make them <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> from the trees sooner than usual: when the proper season passes, they fall off of themselves, and become food for birds, particularly doves. Sometimes there will be a second production, which is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> of a less size with a fainter tinge. The first is generally found adhering to the bark, as well as on the branches and stalks; the second is principally on the leaves, as the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> choose that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> where the nutritious juice preserves itself the longest, is most abundant, and can be most easily devoured in the short time that remains of their existence, the bark being then drier and harder than the leaves. Those who buy the kermes to send to foreign parts spread it on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, taking care to sprinkle it with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, to kill the worms that are within, which produces a red dust, which in Spain is separated from the husk. Cocculus husk. Then they let it dry, passing it through a sieve, and make it up into bags. In the middle of each, its proportion of red dust, put in a little <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> bag, also belongs to the buyer; and then it is ready for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a>, being always in demand on the African <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a>. The people of Hinojos, Bonares, Villalba, and other parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Seville, dry it on mats in the sun, stirring it about, and separating the red dust, which is the finest part, and being mixed with vinegar goes by the name of pastel. The same is done with the husks; but these have but half the value of the dust. The kermes of Spain is preferred on the coast of Barbary, on account of its goodness. The people of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TUNIS">Tunis</a> mix it with that of Tetuan, for dyeing those scarlet caps so much used in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>. The Tunisians export every year above 150,000 dozen of these caps, which yields to the Dey a revenue of 150,000 hard dollars (33,750l.) per annum for duties; so that, exclusive of the uses and advantages of kermes in medicine, it appears to be a very valuable branch of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> in Spain. 5. The cocculus polonicus. See Cocculus Polonicus.

COCHINEAL

Pages 1124-1124
or COCHINEEL, a drug used by the dyers, &c. for giving red colours, especially crimsons and scarlets, and for making carmine; and likewise in medicine as a cardiac, cordial, sudorific, alexipharmic, and febrifuge. The cochineal, in the state in which it is brought to us, is in small bodies of an irregular figure, usually convex, and ridged and furrowed on one side, and concave on the other. The colour of the body is a purplish grey, powdered over with a sort of white dust. All that the world knew of it for a long time was, that it was gathered from certain plants in Mexico; and therefore it was naturally supposed to be a seed, till in the year 1692 Father Plumer gave Pomet an account of its being an animal. And this, though then disregarded, has been confirmed by subsequent observations. Indeed, to determine the point, we have now the means in our own hands, even in this part of the world. —We need only moisten and soak in water, or in vinegar, a number of cochineals till they are swelled and distended, to know that every one is the more or less perfect body of an insect; the most imperfect and mutilated specimens always show the rings of the body; and from observing others, it will be easy to find the number and disposition of the legs; parts, or even whole ones, being left on several, and often complete pairs. In this way the legs, antennae, and proboscis, may be discovered. See Cocculus above.

COCKBURNE

Pages 1124-1125

a most accomplished lady and celebrated writer, was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAVID">David</a> Trotter, a native of Scotland, and a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-commander in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. She was born in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, Aug. 16, 1679, and baptized in the Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, according to which she was bred up in her infancy a Protestant; but being a sprightly, ingenious, and beautiful child, she was particularly cared for by some considerable families among the Papists. This favour naturally wrought a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of such friends; and entering into an intimacy with them as she grew up, she became an easy conquest to their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, in which she <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> many years. In Cockburn the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> her genius ripened apace, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> forth proofs of her talents for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, even before she had passed her childhood. In her 17th year she produced a tragedy called Agnes de Castro, which was acted in 1695. This performance, and some verses addressed to Mr Congreve upon his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOURNING">Mourning</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDE">Bride</a> in 1697, brought her into the acquaintance of that <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>. Thus encouraged in her first attempt, her muse brought upon the stage three plays more; before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Mr Dryden in 1701, to whose <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> she joined with several other ladies in paying a tribute of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>. However, poetry and dramatic <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> was not the most distinguished of Mrs Trotter's talents; she had a remarkable philosophic turn, and capacity equal to such researches. Mr Locke's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">Human</a> Understanding came out during this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a>; that famous <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> had dressed out logic and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-METAPHYSICS">metaphysics</a> in such a new <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODE">mode</a> as was very agreeable to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEX">sex</a> in general, and particularly engaged the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> and admiration of our young authoresses. She had begun to project a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the essay against some remarks of Dr Burnet of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARTER">Charter</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, which was finished so early as the beginning of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1701. She had but lately passed the 22nd year of her <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; and the masterly way in which the piece was drawn must needs have given singular <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> to her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> champion, who accordingly expressed his satisfaction by a present of books to his fair defendress. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a> sojourns in the neighbourhood of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; these philosophical reveries would naturally <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> a thoughtful mind to that subject; and taking into her consideration the tenets of her present faith, she began to discover their indefensible grounds; she therefore resolved to renounce it, and published a vindication of her change in 1707; and returning to the established church of Scotland, she changed her condition likewise the next year, 1708, and was married to Mr Cockburne, a learned divine of that church. The duties of a wife and mother called Mrs Cockburne from her books and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PEN">pen</a> many years; and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> cares engaging her attention, we hear nothing of her as a writer till 1726, when her zeal for Mr Locke's opinions drew her again into public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. She exercised her pen afterwards as occasion offered; and in 1739 she entered into the controversy concerning the foundation of moral duty and obligation. In that controversy she wrote two treatises, the first of which she transmitted in manuscript to Mr afterwards Dr Warburton, the late bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a>, who published it, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> of his own, in 1747. Mrs Cockburne survived this publication two years only. She died in 1749, and was interred at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a> Horley, near her husband, who died the year before her, with this short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> upon the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>, "Let their works praise them in the gates," Prov. xxx. 31. Her works were collected and published in 1751, in two volumes 8vo, with an account of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> prefixed.—This collection is an incontestible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the author's genius. But her abilities as a writer <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> not be seen without attending to the peculiar circumstances in which her writings were produced: her early youth, for instance, when she wrote some; her very advanced age, and ill state of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, when she drew up others; the uneasy situation of her fortune during during the whole course of her life; and an interval of near 20 years, in the vigour of it, spent in the cares of a family, without the least leisure for <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-READING">reading</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a>; after which, with a mind so long diverted and encumbered, resuming her studies, she instantly recovered its entire powers; and, in the hours of relaxation from domestic employments, pursued to the utmost limits some of the deepest researches the human understanding is capable of. Her character is that of a most uncommon lady, no less celebrated for her <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> in her younger years, than for her genius and accomplishments. She was small of stature, but had a remarkable liveliness in her eyes, and a delicacy of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a> which continued to her death. COCKROACH. See BLATTa. (Encycl.) COINING. For Plate LXXXIV. read Plate LXXXII. COINS. (Encycl.) p. 261, middle of col. 2. The harper there mentioned has been disused for a century past. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">Money</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">Table</a>.—For ninepence, read 11s. 3½d.; and for "½ of ours, or 15s." read 18s. 5½d.

COLLINSON

Pages 1125-1125

an eminent naturalist and antiquarian, descended of an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family, was born on the paternal estate called Hugal-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HALL">Hall</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Height of Hugal, near Windermere lake, in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of Staveley, about ten miles from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KENDAL">Kendal</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WESTMORELAND">Westmoreland</a>. Whilst a youth he discovered his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. He began early to make a collection of dried specimens of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, and had access to the best gardens at that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> in the neighbourhood of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. He became early acquainted with the most eminent naturalists of his time; the Drs <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DERHAM">Derham</a>, Woodward, Dale, Lloyd, and Sloane, were amongst his friends. Among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> variety of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> which form that superb collection, now (by the wise disposition of Sir Hans and the munificence of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>) the British <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MUSEUM">Museum</a>, small was the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of those with whose history Mr Collinson was not well acquainted; he being one of those few who visited Sir Hans at all times familiarly; their inclinations and pursuits in respect to natural history being the same, a firm friendship had nearly been established between them. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Collinson was elected a fellow of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> on the 12th of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>, 1728; and perhaps was one of the most diligent and useful members, not only in supplying them with many curious observations himself, but in promoting and preserving a most extensive correspondence with learned and ingenious foreigners, in all countries, and on every useful subject. Besides his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to natural history, he minutely every striking hint that occurred either in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-READING">reading</a> or conversation; and from this source he derived much information, as there were very few men of learning and ingenuity who were not of his acquaintance at home; and most foreigners of eminence in natural history, or in arts and sciences, were recommended to his notice and friendship. His diligence and economy of time was such, that though he never appeared to be in a hurry, he maintained an extensive correspondence with great punctuality; acquainting the learned and ingenious in distant parts of the globe, with the discoveries and improvements in natural history in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and receiving the like information from the most eminent persons in almost every other. His correspondence with the ingenious Cadwallader Colden, Esq; of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEW_YORK">New <a c</a>lass="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YORK">York</a>, and the justly celebrated Dr Franklin of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILADELPHIA">Philadelphia</a>, furnish instances of the benefit resulting from his attention to all improvements. The latter of these gentlemen communicated his first essays on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTRICITY">electricity</a> to Mr Collinson, in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of letters, which were then published, and have been reprinted in a late edition of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a>'s ingenious discoveries and improvements. Perhaps, in some future <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, the account procured of the management of sheep in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, published in the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">Gentleman</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGAZINE">Magazine</a> for May and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1764, may not be considered among the least of the benefits accruing from his extensive and inquisitive correspondence. His conversation, cheerful and usefully entertaining, rendered his acquaintance much desired by those who had a relish for natural history, or were studious in cultivating rural improvements; and secured him the intimate friendship of some of the most eminent personages in this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, as distinguished by their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HORTICULTURE">horticulture</a>, as by their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>. He was the first who introduced the great variety of seeds and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>, which are now the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> ornaments of every garden; and it was owing to his indefatigable industry, that so many persons of the first distinction are now enabled to behold groves transplanted from the Western continent flourishing so luxuriantly in their several domains, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they were already become indigenous to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. He had some correspondents in almost every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, some in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, and even at Pekin; who all transmitted to him the most valuable seeds they could collect, in return for the treasures of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. The great Linnaeus, during his residence in England, contracted an intimate friendship with Mr Collinson, which was reciprocally increased by a multitude of good offices, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to the last. Besides his attachment to natural history, he was very conversant in the antiquities of our own country, having been elected a member of the Society of Antiquaries April 7th, 1737; and he supplied them often with many curious articles of intelligence and observations, respecting both our own and other countries. He died in 1768, leaving behind him many materials for the improvement of natural history.

COLUBER NAJA

Pages 1125-1125
or Cobra de Capello, a very deadly kind of serpent in the East Indies. The root of the lignum colubrinum (ophiorrhiza) is said to have been pointed out to the Indians as an antidote against the bite of this serpent by the viverra ichneumon, a creature which fights with this serpent, and cures itself by eating of this plant when wounded. The Indians, when bit, instantly chew it, swallow the juice, and apply the masticated root to the puncture. COMPASS. For Navigation, Sect. i. 15. read p. 5359, par. 15.

COMPASSES

Pages 1125-1126
PROPORTIONAL, are those whose joint lies between the points terminating each leg; they are either simple or compound. In the former sort CCCXIII, the centre is fixed, so that one pair of these serves only for one proportion. Compound proportional Compasses consist of two branches, each pointed at either end with steel: the length of the branches is cut through, for a cursor to slide up and down; in the middle of which cursor is a screw, Compasses, screw, serving to join the branches, and to fix them at any point required. On the one leg are divisions, serving to divide lines into any number of equal parts, for reducing of figures, &c. On the other are numbers, for inscribing any regular polygon in a circle proposed. The use of the first is easy. Suppose, v.gr., a right line required to be divided into three equal parts; push the cursor till the screw be just on the figure 3; where fixing it, take the length of the given line between the longest part of the legs: the distance between the two shortest will be one-third of the given line. In the same manner may the line be divided into any other number of parts. For the use of the line of polygons. Suppose, v.gr., a pentagon required to be inscribed in a circle; push the cursor till the middle of the screw be against 5; the number of sides in a pentagon; between the shortest parts of the legs take the diameter of the circle: the legs thus opened, the distance between the points of the longest parts will be the side of the pentagon to be inscribed in the circle. And thus for a figure of any other number of sides. Proportional Compasses with the sector lines. The structure of these is so like that of the common proportional compasses, only a little nicer, that it needs no particular description. The lines on the first face are the line of lines, marked lines; it is divided into 100 equal parts, every tenth numbered; and the line of chords, which goes to 60°, is marked chords. On the other face are a line of lines to 90°, and a line of tangents to 45°. On the other side are the tangents from 45° to 71° 34′; on the other, secants from 0° to 70° 30′. For the use of these compasses. 1. To divide a line into any number of equal parts less than 100: Divide 100 by the number of parts required; slip the cursor till the line on the sliding dovetail be against the quotient on the line of lines; then, the whole line being taken between the points of the compasses most remote from the centre, the aperture of the other will show the division required. 2. A right line given, supposed to be divided into 100 parts, to take any number of those parts: slip the line on the sliding dovetail to the number of parts required; the whole line being taken between the points farthest from the centre, the aperture of the other two will include the number of divisions required. 3. The radius being given, to find the chord of any arch under 60°: slip the line on the sliding dovetail to the degrees required on the line of chords; the radius being taken between the points farthest from the centre of the cursor, the aperture of the other line will be the chord required, provided the number of degrees be greater than 29; if it be less, the aperture taken from the radius will leave the chord required. 4. If the chord of an arch under 60° be given, and the radius required; slip the line on the dovetail to the degrees given on the line of chords; the given chord being taken between the two points next the cursor, the aperture of the other will be the radius required. 5. The radius being given, to find the sine of any number of degrees: slip the line on the dovetail to the degree on the line of lines whose sine is required; the radius taken between the points furthest from the cursor, the aperture of the other will give the sine of the angle required; but if the sine sought be less than 30°, the difference of the apertures of the opposite points will be the sine required. 6. The radius being given, to find the tangent of any number of degrees under 71°: if the tangent required be under 26° 30′, then slip the line on the dovetail to the degree proposed on the tangent line; the radius taken between the points farthest from the cursor, the aperture of the others will be the tangent of the degrees required; if the tangent required be above 26° 30′, but under 45°, the line on the cursor must be slipped to the degrees given on the tangent line; then the radius being taken between the points furthest from the cursor, the aperture of the others will be the tangent. If the tangent required be greater than 45°, but less than 56° 20′, slip the notch on the tangent side of the turned cheek to the degree 0 in the tangent line on the side of the compass; the radius taken between the points farthest from the cursor, the difference between the aperture of the other and these added together, will be the tangent required. Thus, for the tangents of other degrees under 71°. After the like manner may the secant of any number of degrees under 71° be found. Mr Heath, a mathematical-instrument maker in London, constructed a pair of proportional compasses in 1746, with a curious and useful contrivance for preventing the shorter legs from changing their position when these compasses were used. It consisted of a small beam soldered to a screw, and running parallel to the leg of the compasses, nearly of the length of the groove: in this beam a slit was made, which admitted of a sliding-nut, the other end of which fell into a hole in the bottom of the screw belonging to the great nut of the compasses. The screw-pin of the beam passed through an adjuster, by means of which the mark on the slider might be brought exactly to any division. But the proportional compasses have been much out of use since the invention of the sector.

COMUS

Pages 1126-1126

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>, the god of jollity <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> festivity. There is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reason to believe he was the Chammos of the Moabites; Bel-Phegor, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAAL">Baal</a> Peor, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIAPUS">Priapus</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>. He is represented under the appearance of a young <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>, with an inflamed <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> countenance, his head inclined, and crowned with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>; his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> drowsy; leaning on a huntsman's spear in his left <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and holding an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a> torch in his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>. His statue was placed at the chamber doors of newly married persons; his pedestal crowned with flowers.

CONCEPTION

Pages 1126-1127

in medicine, denotes the first formation of the embryo, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> fetus, in the womb. Conception is no other than such a concurrence and commixture of the prolific seed of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> with that of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a>, in the cavity of the uterus, as immediately produces an embryo. The symptoms of conception or pregnancy are, when, in a few days after the conjugal <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a>, a small pain is perceived about the navel, and is attended with some gentle convulsions in the bottom of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a>; and within one, two, three, or even four months, the menses cease to flow, or prove in less <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> than usual. Upon the first failure of this kind, kind, the woman begins to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNT">count</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of her weeks, without taking any notice of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> before elapsed; after this, or between the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> or third months, but generally about the third, the motions of the embryo become perceivable to the mother; who hereupon becomes troubled with a nausea, vomiting, loathing, longing, &c. About this time the breasts begin to swell, grow hard and painful, and contain a little <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILK">milk</a>; the nipples also become larger, firmer, and darker coloured, a livid circle appearing round them: the eyes seem sunk and hollow. During the two first months of pregnancy, the woman grows thinner and slenderer; the abdomen being also depressed; though it afterwards dilates, and grows gradually larger. The manner wherein conception is effected is thus laid <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> writers. In the superficies of the ovaries of women, there are found little pellucid spherules, consisting of two concentric membranes filled with a lymphatic humour, and connected to the surface of the ovaries, underneath the tegument, by a thick <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CALIX">calix</a>, contiguous to the extremities of the minute ramifications of the Fallopian tubes. These spherules, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of venery, grow, swell, raise and dilate the membrane of the ovary into the form of papillae; till, the head propending from the stalk, it is at length separated from it; leaving behind it a hollow cicatrix in the broken membrane of the ovary; which, however, soon grows up again. Now, these spherules, while still adhering to the ovary, fetuses have been frequently found; whence it appears, that these are a kind of ova, or eggs, deriving their structure from the vessels of the ovary, and their liquor from the humours prepared therein. Hence it appears, that the Fallopian tubes being swelled and stiffened by the act of venery, with their mucular fimbriae, like fingers, may embrace the ovaries, compress them, and by that compression expand their own mouths: and thus the eggs, now mature, and detached as before, may be forced into their cavities, and thence conveyed into the cavity of the uterus; where they may either be cherished and retained, as when they meet with the male seed; or, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they want that, again expelled. Hence the phenomena of false conceptions, abortions, fetuses found in the cavity of the abdomen, the Fallopian tubes, &c. For in coition, the male seed, abounding with living animalcules, agitated with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> force, a brisk <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and probably with a great quantity of animal-spirits, is violently impelled through the mouth of the uterus, which on this occasion is opener, and through the valves of the neck of the uterus, which on this occasion are laxer than ordinary, into the uterus itself; which now, in like manner, becomes more <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>, turgid, hot, inflamed, and moistened with the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLUX">flux</a> of its lymph and spirits, by means of the titillation excited in the nervous papillae by the attrition against the rugae of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VAGINA">vagina</a>. The semen thus disposed in the uterus, is retained, heated, and agitated, by the convulsive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> of the uterus itself; till meeting with the ova, the finest and most animated <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> enters through the dilated pores of the membranula of the ovum, now become glandulous; is there retained, nourished, dilated; grows to its umbilicus, or navel; stifies the other less lively animalcules; and thus is conception effected. Hence it appears, that conception may happen in any part where the semen meets with an ovum: thus, whether it be carried through the Fallopian tube to the ovary, and there <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> upon the ovum; or whether it meet with it in some recess of the tube itself; or, lastly, whether it join it in the cavity of the uterus, it may still have the same effect, as it appears from observation actually to have done. But it is probable, that conception is then most perfect when the two, viz. the semen and ovum, are carried at the same time into the uterus, and there mixed, &c. Other anatomists choose to suppose the male-seed taken up, before it arrives in the uterus, by the veins which open into the vagina, &c. and thus mixed with the blood; by which, in the course of circulation, it is carried, duly prepared, into the ovary, to impregnate the eggs. It has been advanced by several writers, that women may possibly conceive in their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>, and be with child without any knowledge of the occasion of it. As ridiculous and absurd as this doctrine may appear to the generality of the world, no less an author than Geffil has thought it worthy a particular dissertation.
