AND OTHERS (marked Encycl.) further explained <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> improved; TOGETHER WITH Corrections of Errors and of Wrong References. A. ABATEMENT. For n° 12, l. read p. 3587. art. 2. par. ult.

COOK

Pages 1127-1129

a late celebrated navigator, was born at Marton, a village about four miles from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AYTON">Ayton</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YORK">York</a>, and christened there, as appears from the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-REGISTER">register</a>, November 3, 1728. His father formerly used to be employed as a fisherman, and sometimes as a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>-labourer; and his son divided his early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> between the lowest duties in husbandry and the little school-learning which could be afforded him. He afterwards lived with a grocer in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>: but not liking his situation, he bound himself an apprentice to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of a collier trading from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; with whom he might have <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>, had not the want of seamen in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> occasioned his removal into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of his sovereign before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of his indentures. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> which intervened between this and his being raised to be a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>-officer, was not passed in such a manner as to render it worthy of any detail. He soon acquired all the requisites which belonged to his profession; and deported himself so much to the satisfaction of his superiors, that he received a commission as <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> on the first day of April 1760; and soon after gave a specimen of those abilities which recommended him to the commands which he executed so highly to his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>. In the year 1765 he was with Sir William Burnaby on the Jamaica station; and that officer having occasion to send dispatches to the governor of Yucatan, relative to the logwood cutters in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">Bay</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONDURAS">Honduras</a>, lieutenant Cook was selected for that employment; and he performed it in a manner which intitled him to the approbation of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>. A relation of this voyage and journey was published in the year 1769, under the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of "Remarks on a Passage from the River Balice, in the Bay of Honduras, to Merida, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Yucatan in the Spanish West Indies, by Lieutenant Cook," in an 8vo pamphlet. To a perfect knowledge of all the duties belonging to a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-life, Mr Cook had added a great skill in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>. In the year 1767, the Royal <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> resolved, that it would be proper to send persons into some <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of of the South Seas, to observe the transit of the planet Venus over the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>'s disk; and by a memorial delivered to his majesty, they recommended the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of Marquesas de Mendos, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> those of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROTTERDAM">Rotterdam</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, as the properest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> then known for making such observation. To this memorial a favourable answer was returned; and the Endeavour, a ship built for the coal-trade, was put in commission, and the command of her given to lieutenant Cook. But before the vessel was ready to sail, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> Wallis returned from his voyage, and pointed out Otaheite as a place more proper for the purpose of the expedition than either of those mentioned by the Royal Society. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> was approved of; and our navigator was appointed by that learned body, with Mr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Green, to observe the transit. On this occasion lieutenant Cook was promoted to be captain, and his commission bore <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DATE">date</a> the 25th of May 1768. He immediately hoisted the pennant, and took command of the ship; in which he sailed <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the river on the 30th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>. In this voyage he was accompanied by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Banks, Esq.; and Dr Solander; and on 12th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1771 returned to England, after having been absent almost three years. The narrative of this expedition was written by Dr Hawkesworth. Soon after captain Cook's return to England, it was resolved to equip two ships to complete the discovery of the southern hemisphere. It had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> been a prevailing idea, that the unexplored part contained another continent. To ascertain the fact was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> object of this expedition; and that nothing might be omitted that could tend to facilitate the enterprise, two ships were provided, furnished with every necessary which could promote the success of the undertaking. The first of these ships was called the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RESOLUTION">Resolution</a>, under the command of captain Cook; the other the Adventure, commanded by captain Furneaux. Both of them sailed from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPTFORD">Deptford</a> on the 9th of April 1772, and arrived at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> of Good Hope on the 30th of October. They departed from thence on the 22nd of November; and from that time until the 17th of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1773, continued endeavouring to discover the continent, when they were obliged to relinquish the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, observing the whole sea covered with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ICE">ice</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of S.E. round by the south to west. They then proceeded into the South Seas, and made many other discoveries, and returned to the Cape of Good Hope on the 21st of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1774, and from thence to England on the 14th of July; having, during three years and eighteen days (in which time the voyage was performed), lost but one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> by sickness in captain Cook's ship; although he had navigated throughout all the climates from 52° <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to 71° south, with a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of 118 men. The relation of this voyage was given to the public by captain Cook himself, and by Mr George Forster, son of Dr Forster, who had been appointed by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> to accompany him for the purpose of making observations on such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> productions as might be found in the course of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>. That published by captain Cook has generally been ascribed to a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of great eminence in the literary world; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the testimony of one who was on board the ship, and who made an extract from the journal in its rude uncorrected state, may be relied on, there seems no reason to ascribe the merit of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> to any other person than him whose name it goes under. The want of success which attended captain Cook's attempt to discover a southern continent, did not discourage another <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> being resolved on, which had been recommended some time before. This was no other than the finding out a north-west passage, which some had conceived to be a practicable scheme. The dangers which our navigator had twice braved, would have exempted him from being solicited a third time to venture his person in unknown countries, amongst desart islands, inhospitable climates, and in the midst of savages; but, on his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> being asked concerning the person who would be most proper to execute this design, he once more relinquished the quiet and comforts of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> life, to engage in scenes of turbulence and confusion, of difficulty and danger. His intrepid spirit and inquisitive mind induced him again to offer his services; and they were accepted without hesitation. The manner in which he had departed himself on former occasions, left no room to suppose that a fitter man could be selected. He prepared for his departure with the utmost alacrity, and actually sailed in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of July 1776. A few months after his departure from England, notwithstanding he was then absent, the Royal Society voted him Sir Godfrey Copley's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>-medal, as a reward for the account which he had transmitted to that body, of the method taken to preserve the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> of the crew of his ship; and Sir John Pringle, in his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORATION">oration</a> of 30th November, pronounced an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> eulogium upon him. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> testimony to the merit of our gallant commander, never came to his knowledge.—While his friends were waiting with the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> solicitude for tidings concerning him, and the whole <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a> expressed an anxious impatience to be informed of his success, advice was received from captain Clerke, in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> dated at Kamchatka, the 8th day of June 1779; from which, and from other accounts, we learn, "That captain Cook, after he had passed the Cape of Good Hope, had continued his course along <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-VAN_DIEMEN_S_LAND">Van Diemen's <a c</a>lass="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">Land</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-NEW_ZEALAND">New <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>. He arrived happily in August 1777 at the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Otaheite, where he landed Omiah, a native of the island, in perfect health: That since the last voyage of captain Cook to that island, the Spaniards had been there twice, and staid some months, and their ships had left all sorts of birds and domestic animals, but only of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; so that they received the cows and the she-goats that captain Cook brought with great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. He left that island in the month of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> following; and after having made several new discoveries in the South Sea, he arrived in the month of March 1778 on the coasts of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, situated in the south of Kamchatka. A leak being discovered in captain Cook's ship the Resolution, and finding a very stormy sea, he was obliged to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a> in a bay in that part of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a>. After having repaired his own ship, they both put to sea; and sailing along the coast, they at last distinctly discovered the strait between <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> and America. The two parts of the world presented only, at that height of latitude, a low barren land without any shelter, and a sea of a very very middling depth. They continued their route till they perceived distinctly the American coast extending to the north-east. He then thought himself arrived near to the bounds of his wishes; but when he came to 70° 45' Lat. and 180° of Long. (probably reckoning from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a>), he met with impenetrable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of ice, which obliged him to turn towards the south. He <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> anchor near the island Unalaska, whence his letter is dated. He fixes that island in 53° 55' Lat. and 192° 30' Long., consequently giving that island a more western and southern position than is in the new general chart of Russia. "As he then found himself to the east of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SANDWICH">Sandwich</a> Island, which <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> had passed in his voyage, he reasonably thought he must meet with other islands; he therefore failed again, in order to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the autumn and the winter in a more temperate <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>. He actually discovered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> other islands, which appeared to him extremely fertile, and where the inhabitants had raised <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>-walls upon the heights for their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. He cast anchor at one of these islands, named Owyhee, in the gulph of Caracah-Cossa, and treated very amicably with the natives, who paid him almost divine honours. After he had refreshed his people, one of whom only had died in the voyage, and two others had fallen sick, he was already got under sail, when a furious storm hurt his mizen-mast, which obliged him to return to the gulph to repair it. The islanders became every day more bold, and most clearly demonstrated their inclination for theft; which went so far as to steal one of his boats. Captain Cook, willing to seek <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> for this robbery, went on shore with his lieutenant, and ten or twelve of his crew. He advanced towards a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> body of the inhabitants, who always paid him great respect, and accosted their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>. Whilst the negociation was carrying on, the influence of one of the islanders, who was in the throng, obliged him to fire on him with his musket, loaded only with small-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>, which did not even penetrate the mat with which he was covered. The Indians began then to be enraged; and when the lieutenant had at length fired and killed his man, the whole troop fell on the body; and as soon as the sailors had discharged their pieces, they did not give them time to load again, but killed captain Cook and four of his people, forcing the others, partly wounded, to make their escape under the favour of the fire of their pinnace. "This fatal event happened on the 14th February 1779. A <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> was then called of the officers, to determine whether their commander's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> should not be revenged in an exemplary manner; but it was thought most advisable to keep on the defensive until the mast was repaired. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time captain Clerke made friends with the savages, and quitted the island to return to Kamchatka, where he wintered in Port Awatscha, from the 1st of January that year till the month of June, and then sailed to discover (as he writes word) more exactly the islands between Kamchatka and America." Captain Cook was a married man, and left several children behind him. On each of these his majesty has settled a pension of 25l. a-year, and 200l. a-year on his widow. It is remarkable, if true as reported, that captain Cook was godfather to his wife; and at the very time she was christened, declared that he had determined on the union which afterwards took place between them. Few men have been more regretted than captain Cook. He possessed all the qualities which could insure the esteem of mankind. To the most undaunted courage he added a most persevering resolution. He acquired the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of his seamen, as well by the soft as by stern virtues; being equally gentle and humane as he was commanding and intrepid. Without being possessed of much literature, or cultivating letters, he acquitted himself with credit even where the talents of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> were required. No man seemed so well formed for enterprizes such as he was engaged in. He was fond of the pursuit, and sacrificed every consideration to them. He owed his rise entirely to his merit; and retained the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> of his early state after he had risen beyond the expectations of his friends, and equal to his own. COPPERPLATE. See ENGRAVING, (Encycl.)

CORAL

Pages 1129-1130

(Encycl.) The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and origin of coral has <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> been a subject of much dispute. Some have supposed that it is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; others a plant; and it has been almost universally believed that it was soft while in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, but grew hard on being taken out of it. But Boccone examined coral in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, before it was taken up into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and invariably found it hard, except at its extremities, whence, by pressing it, flowed a small <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of milky fluid, already taken notice of. We may therefore infer, that there is more of imagination than of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> in the name gorgonium, which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> gave to coral, and designed to show that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEDUSA">Medusa</a>'s head did not convert objects into stone, more surely than coral became petrified as soon as it appeared in the air. M. de Peyssonnel of Marfeilles, has, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of experiments and observations from about the year 1720 to 1750, introduced a new system with respect to the nature and production of coral, and similar marine substances. Those bodies, which the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNT">count</a> de Marfaghi imagined to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, this ingenious naturalist discovered to be insects inhabiting the coral; for upon taking branches of it out of the water, the flowers, which proceeded from a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> answering to the holes that pierced the bark, and the radiation of which resembled the flower of the olive-tree, entered into the bark and disappeared; but upon being again restored to the water, they were some hours after perceptible. These flowers spread on white <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> lost their transparency, and became <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> as they dried. The holes in the bark correspond to small cavities upon the substance of the coral; and when the bark is removed, there may be seen an infinite quantity of little tubes connecting the bark with the inner substance, besides a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> number of small glands adhering to them; and from these tubes and glands the milky juice of coral flows forth: the holes in the bark are the openings through which the insects that form these substances for their habitation come forth; and those cavities which are partly in the bark and partly in the substance, are the cells which they inhabit. The organs of the animal are contained in the tubes, and the glandules are the extremities of its feet, and the milky liquor is the blood and juice of. of the animal, which are more <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> less abundant in proportion to its <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> and vigour. When the insects are dead, they corrupt, and communicate to the water the smell of putrid fish. This juice or liquor runs along the furrows perceived upon the proper fulbitude or body of coral, and stopping by little and little becomes fixed and hard, and is changed into stone; and being stopped in the bark, causes the coral to increase proportionally and in every <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>. In forming coral, and other marine productions of this class, the animal labours like those of the tectaceous kind, each according to his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; and their productions vary according to their several forms, magnitudes, and colours. The coral insect, or polype, M. Peyronnel observes, expands itself in water, and contracts itself in air, or when it is touched with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> in water, or acid liquors are poured upon it; and he actually <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> these insects move their claws or legs, and expand themselves; when the sea-water containing coral was placed near the fire, and keep them in their expanded state when separated from the coral in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> water. Broken branches of coral have been observed to fasten themselves to other branches, and have <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to grow; and this is the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>, when they are connected with detached pieces of rock and other substances, from which no nourishment could be derived. The coral insects in their cells, not having been injured, continue their operations; and as they draw no nourishment from the stone of the coral, they are able to increase in a detached and separate state. Coral was found to be equally red in the sea as out of it; and it was more shining when <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> taken out of the water, than even when it is polished; and the bark by being dried becomes somewhat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a>. M. Peyronnel found that it grows in different directions, sometimes perpendicularly downwards, sometimes horizontally, and sometimes upwards; and in the caverns of the sea, open to every exposure. This system was little regarded, though first communicated to the Academy of Sciences at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1727, till Mr Trembley's discovery of the fresh-water polype; but since that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, it has been confirmed by the observations of M. Bernard de Jussieu on the sea-coasts of Normandy, and those of M. de Reaumur near <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROCHELLE">Rochelle</a>. M. Donati of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURIN">Turin</a> has also adopted the same <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>, viz. that coral is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of animals of the polype kind; and instead of representing the polype beds and cells which they contain as the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> of polypes, he thinks it more just to say, that coral and other coralline bodies have the same relation to the polypes united to them, that there is between the shell of a snail and the snail itself, or the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of an animal and the animal itself. The same system has also been excellently illustrated and established by Mr Ellis, in answer to the objections of Dr Baiter of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>, and Dr Pallas of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a>, who still refer corallines to the vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. There are properly but three kinds of coral; red, white, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>: the black is the rarest, and most esteemed; but the red was formerly used in medicine. It must be chosen thick, smooth, and shining, and of a beautiful red, not covered with any tartarous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. However, this substance is now scarce ever prescribed by any intelligent practitioner.

CORALLINES

Pages 1130-1130

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, were formerly reckoned a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, and Mr Tournefort enumerates 36 <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of them; but in the Linnaean system they belong to the class of zoophytes, and are defined by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> naturalists to be submarine plant-like bodies, that consist of many slender finely divided and jointed branches, resembling some species of moss; <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> animals growing in the form of plants, having their stems fixed to other bodies; these stems are composed of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPILLARY">capillary</a> tubes, whose extremities <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through a calcareous crust, and open into pores on the surface. The branches are often jointed, and always subdivided into smaller branches, which are either loose and unconnected, or joined as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they were glued together. They are distinguished from plants by their texture and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a>; they also yield in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a> a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of volatile <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>; and their smell, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>, resembles that of burnt horns and other animal substances. Many of the corallines seem to consist of a single tube, containing a single <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> animal. Every branch emitted contains an offspring of this parent dependent upon it, and yet capable of producing its like in the emission of a new branch. Others consist of many such tubes united, rising up together, and encircling the deserted tubes of their progenitors, whose exuviae become the substratum of a rising <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>. Mr Ellis distributes corallines into the vesiculated, tubular, celliferous, and articulated kinds. Vesiculated corallines are distinguished by their horny hollow ramifications; most of them are furnished with little denticles on their branches, like leaves on mosses; and at certain seasons of the year they are furnished with small bodies like bladders, proceeding from their stems and branches, and differing in form according to the different species. Their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, when dry, is of a yellowish or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, and their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a>. They are found adhering to rocks, shells, and fucuses, by small root-like tubes: they recover their form in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, after having been dried; and when put into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, they cause no effervescence. See Plate CCCXV. fig. 1, a which represents the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-tamarisk in its natural size, and A in which the denticles are magnified. Fig. 2, b, B, is the sea-cypress; fig. 3, c, d, CD, the small climbing coralline with well-shaped cups. Tubular corallines are composed of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of simple tubes, growing up nearly together; or of such branched ones as have neither denticles nor vesicles. These are horny and elastic like the former, and recover their original form in water. Some of them appear wrinkled like the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>-pipe, and others like the intestines of small animals. See fig. 4, E. Celliferous corallines are those which appear, when magnified, to be fine thin cells, the habitations of small animals connected together, and disposed in a variety of elegant forms like branches. These effervescence with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>. See fig. 5, f and F. Articulated corallines consist of short pieces of a stony or cretaceous brittle <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, whose surface is covered with pores or cells, which are joined by a tough, membranous, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a> substance, composed of many small tubes of the like nature compacted together. The stony <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> is soluble in vinegar, and the other part remains entire. See Plate CCCXVI. fig. 1. See the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> and drawings of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> variety of

CORYPHA

Pages 1131-1131

Mountain-Palm, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Cabbage-Tree, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>; a genus of the order of palmæ, belonging to the monocota clas of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There is only one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, the umbracula, a native of the West Indies, where it is said to rise to the height of 150 and 200 feet. It is by some authors called the palmetto <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a>; and well, says Hughes in his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Barbadoes, may it be called royal, since neither the tall cedars of Lebanon, nor any of the trees of the forest, are equal to it in height, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, or proportion. It is generally as straight as an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARROW">arrow</a>; near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> it is about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> feet in circumference, but tapers as it ascends. The bark is of an ash-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, till within 25 or 30 feet of the extremity of the tree; when it alters at once to a deep <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-green, which continues to the top. Upon removing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> leaves, or branches, which surround the top of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> a little way above the beginning of the green bark <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned, what is called the cabbage is discovered lying in many thin, snow-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, brittle flakes, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> resembling an almond, but sweeter. This substance, which cannot be procured without destroying the tree, is boiled, and eaten with mutton by the inhabitants of the West Indies, in the same manner as turnips and cabbage are with us; it is likewise pickled, and sent to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, where it is esteemed an exquisite delicacy. In the pith of the trunk of the cabbage-palms, when felled, there breeds a kind of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>, or grubs, which are eaten and esteemed a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> delicacy by the French of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARTINICO">Martinico</a>, St Domingo, and the adjoining <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. These worms, says father Labat, are about two inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and of the thickness of one's finger; the head is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, and attached to the body without any distinction of neck. Their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">table</a> is as follows: They are strung on wooden skewers before a fire, and as soon as heated, are rubbed over with rapsings of crust, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NUTMEG">nutmeg</a>; this powder absorbs all the fat, which during the cookery would otherwise escape; when properly roasted they are served up with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CITRON">citron</a> sauce. These worms being exposed for some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, are said to yield an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> which is of great efficacy in the piles. The oil in question, says Labat, is never to be heated before its application to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> affected; as repeated experiments have evinced that its spirit is totally diffused by the fire. COURTS of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONSCIENCE">CONSCIENCE</a>. See Courts of REQUESTS, (Encycl.)

CRADLE

Pages 1131-1131

CREST

Pages 1131-1131

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERALDRY">heraldry</a>. For n° 49, read p. 3608. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CRICETUS">CRICETUS</a>. See MUS, (Encycl.)

CRICKET

Pages 1131-1132

(Encycl.) Crickets are thought to be ruminating animals, and certainly are furnished with several different stomachs. In medicine they are believed to be diuretic, and less dangerous than <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANTHARIDES">cantharides</a>; CUL Crimen rides; for which intention they are dried and powdered, and given in doses from 12 grains to a scruple. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> cricket only flies from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, as many other insects do; it feeds almost on everything. The males only chirp; and their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONOTONY">monotony</a>, however disagreeable to some people, is pleasant enough to their own females, for it is the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>; and it is continual, night and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>, except in very <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. They become habituated to bear all kinds of noise; but the field cricket is very timorous, and chirps only in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the finest days of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. CRIMEN FALSI. See Falsi Crimen, (Encycl.) <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRUSADES">CRUSADES</a>. See Croisades, (Encycl.)

CULEX

Pages 1132-1132

the gnat; a genus of insects belonging to the order of diptera. The mouth is formed by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a> sheath, including bristles pointed like stings. The antennae of the males are filiform; those of the females feathered. There are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. These insects, too well known by the severe punctures they inflict, and the itchings thence arising, afford a most interesting <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. Before they turn to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> insects, they have been in some manner fishes, under two different forms. You may observe in stagnating waters, from the beginning of May till winter, small grubs with their heads downwards, their hinder-parts on the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>; from which <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> arises sideways a kind of vent-hole, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> small hollow tube like a funnel, and this is the organ of respiration. The head is armed with hooks, that serve to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> on insects and bits of grass on which it feeds. On the sides are placed four small fins, by the help of which the insect swims about, and dives to the bottom. These larvae retain their form during a fortnight or three weeks, after which <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> they turn to chrysalids. All the parts of the winged insect are distinguishable through the outward robe that shrouds them. The chrysalids are rolled up into spirals. The situation and shape of the windpipe is then altered; it consists of two tubes near the head, which occupy the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the stigmata, through which the winged insect is one <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> to breathe. These chrysalids, constantly on the surface of the water in order to draw breath, abstain now from eating; but upon the least <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> are seen to unroll themselves, and plunge to the bottom, by means of little paddles situated at their hinder-part. After three or four days strict fasting, they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> to the state of gnats. A moment before, water was its element; but now, become an aerial insect, he can no longer exist in it. He swells his head, and bursts his inclosure. The robe he lately wore turns to a ship, of which the insect is the mast and sail. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> at the instant the gnat displays his wings there arises a breeze, it proves to him a dreadful hurricane; the water gets into the ship, and the insect, who is not yet loosed from it, sinks and is lost. But in calm <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, the gnat forsakes his slough, dries himself, flies into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, seeks to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PUMP">pump</a> the alimentary juice of leaves, or the blood of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> and beasts. The sting which our naked eye discovers, is but a tube, containing five or six spicula of exquisite minuteness; some dentated at their extremity like the head of an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARROW">arrow</a>, others sharp-edged like razors. These spicula introduced into the veins, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> as pump-suckers, into which the blood ascends by reason of the smallness of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPILLARY">capillary</a> tubes. The insect injects a small <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of liquor into the wound, by which the blood becomes more fluid, and is seen through the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a> passing through those spicula. The animal swells, grows <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>, and does not quit its hold till it has gorged itself. The liquor it has injected, causes by its fermenting, that disagreeable itching which we <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>; and which may be removed by volatile alkali, or by scratching the part newly stung, and washing it with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> water; for later, the venous ferments, and you would only increase the tumour and the itching. Rubbing one's self at night with fuller's-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> and water, lessens the pain and inflammation. Gnats perform their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COPULATION">copulation</a> in the air. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> deposits her eggs on the water; by the help of her moveable hinder part and her legs, placing them one by the side of another in the form of a little <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOAT">boat</a>. This vessel, composed of two or three hundred eggs, swims on the water for two or three days, after which they are hatched. If storm arises, the boats are sunk. Every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> there is a fresh progeny of these insects. Were they not devoured by swallows, other birds, and by several carnivorous insects, the air would be darkened by them. Gnats in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, however troublesome they may be, do not make us feel them so severely as the musketo-flies (culex pipiens) do in foreign parts. In the day-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> or at night they come into the houses; and when the people are gone to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a> they begin their disagreeable humming, approach always nearer to the bed, and at last suck up so much blood that they can hardly fly away. Their bite causes blisters in people of a delicate complection. When the weather has been cool for some days, the mosquitoes disappear; but when it changes again, and especially after a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, they gather frequently in such quantities about the houses, that their numbers are astonishing. In sultry evenings they accompany the cattle in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> swarms, from the woods to the houses or to town; and when they are drove before the houses, the gnats fly in wherever they can. In the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, they are so numerous in some places, that the air seems to be quite full of them, especially near swamps and stagnate waters, such as the river Morris in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEW_JERSEY">New <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERSEY">Jersey</a>. The inhabitants therefore make a fire before their houses to expel these disagreeable guests by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>.

CULLODEN

Pages 1132-1133

a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in Scotland within two miles of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INVERNESS">Inverness</a>, chiefly remarkable for a complete victory gained over the rebels on the 16th of April 1746. That <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, commanded by the late <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>, began their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">march</a> from Nairn, formed into five <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of three battalions each; headed by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>-general Hulke on the left, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> Semple on the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, and brigadier Mordaunt in the centre; flanked by the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> under the generals Hawley and Bland, who at the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> covered the cannon on the right and left. In this order they marched about eight miles, when a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DETACHMENT">detachment</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGSTON">Kingston</a>'s horse, and of the Highlanders, having advanced before the rest of the army, discovered the van of the rebels commanded by the young pretender. Both armies immediately formed in the order and numbers, shown in the annexed scheme. About two in the afternoon the rebels began to cannonade the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s army; but their <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a> being ill served, did little execution; while the fire from their enemies was severely felt, and occasioned <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> disorder. The rebels then made a push at the right wing of the royal army, in order to draw the troops forward; but finding themselves disappointed, they turned their whole force on the left; falling chiefly on Barrall's and Monro's regiments, where they attempted to flank the king's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRONT">front</a>-line. But this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> also was defeated by the advancing of Wolfe's regiment, while in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time the cannon kept playing upon them with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARTRIDGE">cartridge</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>. General Hawley, with some Highlanders, had opened a passage through some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>-walls to the right for the horse which advanced on that side; while the horse on the king's right wheeled off upon their left, dispersed their body of reserve, and met in the centre of their front-line in their rear; when being repulsed in the front, and great numbers of them cut off, the rebels fell into very great confusion. A dreadful carnage was made by the cavalry on their backs; however, some <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the foot still preferred their order; but the King's horse, from the reserve, galloped up briskly, and falling on the fugitives, did terrible execution. A total defeat instantly took place, with the loss of 2500 killed, wounded, and prisoners, on the part of the rebels; while the royalists lost not above 200. The young pretender had his horse shot under him during the engagement; and after the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> retired to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACTOR">factor</a> of lord Lovat, about ten miles from Inverness, where he died that night. Next day he set out for Fort-Augustus, from whence he pursued his journey through wild defairs with great difficulty and distress, till at last he safely reached France, as related under the article <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, no. 418. CURCULIO

Pages 1133-1133

(Encycl.) These insects are divided into the following families. 1. Those which have the rostrum longer than the thorax, and whose thighs are simple. 2. Those which have the rostrum longer than the thorax, and the thighs thicker and made for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAPING">leaping</a>. 3. Those which have the rostrum longer than the thorax, and the thighs dentated. 4. Those which have dentated thighs, and a rostrum shorter than the thorax. 5. Those whose thighs are without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> spines, and the rostrum shorter than the thorax. The larvae of the curculiones differ not from those of most coleopterous insects. They bear a resemblance to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> soft <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>. They are provided anteriorly with six fleshy legs, and their head is likewise fleshy. But the places where these larvae dwell, and their transformations, afford some singularities. Some <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of them, that are dreaded for the mischief they do in granaries, find means to introduce themselves, while yet small, into grains of corn, and there make their abode. It is very difficult to discover them, as they <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> concealed within the grain. There they grow at leisure, enlarging their dwelling-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> as they grow, at the expense...

DAEMON

Pages 1133-1134

(Encycl.) This word is by some derived from the Greek δαιμων, "knowing, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> intelligent;" by some from δαιμονιστης, "to distribute." Either of these derivations agrees with the office ascribed to daemons by the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> heathens, as the spirits intrusted with the inspection and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of mankind. According to the philosophers, daemons held a middle <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a> between the celestial gods and men on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and carried on all intercourse between them; conveying the addresses of men to the gods, and divine benefits to men. Many were of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that the celestial divinities did not concern themselves with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> affairs, but left the management of them entirely to these subaltern deities. Hence they became the objects of worship, though those who were more immediately so were the spirits of men who were thought to have become daemons or deities after departing from their bodies. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HESIOD">Hesiod</a> and other poets who have written concerning the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> or traditions on which the public <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> was founded, assert, that the men of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, who were very good, became daemons after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, and dispensers of good things to mankind. In this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, according to some, the word daemon (though constantly translated <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a>) is also frequently taken in Scripture, both in the Old and New <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>. Besides the two foregoing kinds of daemons, the fathers as well as philosophers asserted the existence of another, viz. such as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONGRESS">congress</a> of superior beings with women; and in the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> of the fathers, these were the worst of all.

DAMPS

Pages 1134-1134

(Encycl.) Among the other uses to which <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPHLOGISTICATED">dephlogisticated</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> might be applied, Mr. Cavallio reckons that of securing people from the dangerous effects of damps in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, and other subterraneous places. "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> bladder," says he, "into which a solution of lime in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> is introduced, be filled with dephlogisticated air, and a small wooden <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> glass pipe be adapted to its neck, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> may hold that pipe in his mouth, and may breathe the dephlogisticated air; and thus equipped he may enter into these subterranean places, amidst the various <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a> contained in them. A large bladder of dephlogisticated air <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> serve for above a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, which is a length of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> sufficient for various purposes; besides, if longer time is required to be spent in these places, a person may have two or more bladders of dephlogisticated air along with him, and may shift as soon as the air of one is contaminated. Without the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of any more complicated <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a>, the bladders full of dephlogisticated air may be kept stopped by putting corks...

DEFORMITY

Pages 1135-1135

(Encycl.) Deformity is either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> moral. These are both referred by Mr Hutchison to an internal <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>; and our perceptions of them, as he supposes, arises from an original arbitrary structure of our own minds, by which certain objects, when observed, are rendered the occasions of certain sensations and affections. That many objects give no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> to our sense, is obvious. Many are certainly void of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>; but then, says this author, there is no form which seems necessarily disagreeable of itself, when we dread no other evil from it, and compare it with nothing better of the kind. Many objects are naturally displeasing and distasteful to our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> senses, as well as others pleasing and agreeable; as smells, tastes, and some separate sounds: but with regard to our sense of beauty, no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of objects which give not unpleasant simple <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>, seems positively unpleasant or painful of itself, had we never observed any thing better of the same kind. Had there been a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the form which we now denominate ugly or deformed, and had we never seen or expected greater beauty, we should have received no disgust from it; though the pleasure would not have been so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> in this form as in those we now admire. Our sense of beauty seems designed to give us positive pleasure; but not positive pain or disgust, any farther than what arises from disappointment. There are indeed many faces which, at first view, are apt to raise dislike. But this is generally not from any positive deformity; but either from want of expected beauty, or from the carrying some natural indications of morally bad dispositions, which we all acquire a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of discerning in countenances, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIRS">airs</a>, and gestures. That this is not occasioned by any form positively disagreeing, appears hence, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a>, upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> acquaintance, we are sure of finding sweetness of temper, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>, and cheerfulness, though the bodily form continues, it shall give us no disgust. There are horrors raised by some objects, which are only the effect of fear for ourselves, or compassion towards others, when either reason, or some foolish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a> of ideas, makes us apprehend danger; and not the effect of anything in the form itself. For we find, that most of those objects which excite horror at first, when <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> or reason has removed the fear, may become the occasion of pleasure. The casual conjunction of ideas gives us disgust, where there is nothing disagreeable in the form itself. And this, in effect, is the cause of most of our fantastic aversions to the figures of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> animals, &c. Thus <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a> of all kinds, and many insects, really beautiful enough, are beheld with aversion by many people, who have got some accidental ideas of mischief associated to them. A similar reasoning is applied to our perception of moral beauty and deformity. Inquiry into the original of our Ideas of Beauty and Virtue, p. 381. But it is more <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> to distinguish between the sentiments of delight or disgust, excited in us by beautiful or deformed objects, which are effects of some causes, deformity and the natural and real qualities of the perceived objects by which they are produced. There are objects, says an excellent writer, which have a natural aptitude to please or offend, or between which and the contemplating mind there is a necessary <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONGRUITY">congruity</a> or incongruity; and though the actual perception of the understanding, and consequent feeling of the heart, in contemplating the actions and affections of moral agents, may exist in very different degrees, on account of the incidental obstructions arising from bodily indisposition, mental prejudices and biases, and the association of ideas; yet, to every rational mind properly disposed, morally good actions must for ever be acceptable, and can never of themselves offend; and morally evil actions must for ever be disagreeable, and can never of themselves please. What is <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> in actions and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> is beautiful and amiable, and gives pleasure; what is wrong is deformed and odious, and excites disgust: right and pleasure, wrong and pain, are as distinct as cause and effect. It is no less absurd to maintain, that the perception of virtue is nothing distinct from the reception of the pleasure resulting from it, than to infer, with some metaphysicians, that solidity, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, are only particular modes of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a>, because attended, whenever they are perceived, with some sensations of sight or touch. Thus does this author show, that moral beauty and deformity are real qualities of certain actions; in which consists their aptitude to please or disgust. With respect to natural beauty, he observes, that uniformity amidst variety pleases, because of the natures of variety and uniformity, which are such, that, whenever united, they are adapted to please every free unbiased mind that discerns them. He accounts for the pleasure they afford, without referring them to an arbitrary internal sense, by the following circumstances that attend them. They are more easily comprehended by the mind; order and symmetry give things their stability and strength, and subversion to any valuable purpose; regularity and order <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> art and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>. Disorder and confusion, whence deformity arises, denote only the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEGATION">negation</a> of regularity and order; or any arrangement and disposition of things, which are not according to a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, rule, or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, and prove not design. These are not positively displeasing; except where we previously expected order, or where <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMPOTENCE">impotence</a> or want of skill appear, and the contriver has either failed of his design or executed it ill. See on this subject Dr Price's Review of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> Questions and Difficulties in Morals, ch. ii. p. 245. See an admirable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on bodily Deformity, by Mr Hay, in the Fugitive Pieces, vol. i. p. 93. &c.

DODD

Pages 1135-1136

an unfortunate dissenting English divine, eldest son of the Rev. William Dodd, many years <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOURNE">Bourne</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a>, was born May 29, 1729. He was sent, at the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 16, to the university of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>; and admitted, in the year 1745, a fellow of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLARE">Clare</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HALL">Hall</a>. In 1749-50 he took the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of B.A. with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, being upon that occasion occasion in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> of wranglers. Leaving the university, he imprudently married a Miss <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> Perkins in 1751, was ordained a deacon the same year, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> in 1753, and soon became a celebrated and popular preacher. His first preferment was the rectoryship of West-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAM">Ham</a>. In 1754 he was also chosen lecturer of St Olave's, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HART">Hart</a>-Street; and in 1757 took the degree of M.A. at Cambridge. On the foundation of the Magdalen <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOSPITAL">Hospital</a> in 1758, he was a strenuous supporter of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>, and soon after became preacher at the chapel of it. By the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> of Bishop Squire, he in 1763 obtained a prebend of Brecon, and by the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of some <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>-friends procured himself to be appointed one of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s chaplains; soon after which, he had the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of the present <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Chesterfield committed to his care. In 1766, he went to Cambridge, and took the degree of LL.D. At this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, the estimation in which he was held by the world was sufficient to give him expectations of preferment, and hopes of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> and honours; and these he might probably have acquired, had he possessed a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> portion of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>. But, impatient of his situation, and eager for advancement, he rashly fell upon means, which in the end were the occasion of his ruin. On the living of St George, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">Square</a>, becoming vacant, he wrote an anonymous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>'s lady, offering 3000 guineas <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> by her assistance he was promoted to it. This being traced to him, complaint was immediately made to the king, and Dr Dodd was dismissed with disgrace from his office of chaplain. From this period he lived Anecdotes of neglected, if not despised; and his extravagance still Bowyer, &c., continuing, he became involved in difficulties, which tempted him to forge a bond from his late pupil <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> Chesterfield, Feb. 4, 1777, for 4200l. which he actually received: but being detected, he was tried at the Old Bailey, found guilty, and received <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; and, in spite of every application for mercy, was executed at Tyburn, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 27, 1777. Dr Dodd was a voluminous writer, and possessed considerable abilities, with little judgment and much vanity. An accurate list of his various writings is prefixed to his "Thoughts in Prison," ed. 1781.

DODONIAN

Pages 1136-1136

(Encycl.) The origin and occasion of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> we have from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, who observes it was founded on this, that σύλλας, which in the Thessalian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> signifies a pigeon, does likewise signify a witch, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> prophetess. But what is more extraordinary is, another <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> among the poets, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the very oaks of the forest of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DODONA">Dodona</a> spoke, and delivered <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-ORACLES">oracles</a>. This fable is easily deduced from the former; the pigeons in the oaks being supposed to speak, it was no <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> flight of poetical fancy, to introduce the trees themselves speaking, &c. The fountain of Dodona was in the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> naturalists assure us, it had a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of rekindling torches, &c., when newly extinguished. This, no doubt, it did, by means of some sulphureous fumes exhaling from it; as we still find a fountain in Dauphine, called the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> fountain, do. It is also said to have extinguished lighted torches; which is no great miracle, since plunging them into a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the sulphur was too dense, or into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, must have that effect.

DUNSTAFFNAGE

Pages 1136-1136

a castle situated in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SKYE">Skye</a>, said to have been founded by Ewin a Pictish monarch, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with Julius Caesar, naming it after himself, Evonium. In fact, the founder is unknown; but it is certainly of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity, and the first seat of the Pictish and Scottish princes. In this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> preserved the famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALLADIUM">Palladium</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>; brought, says <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEGEND">legend</a>, out of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, where it was first used as a seat of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> by Gathetus, coeval with Moses. It <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> here as the coronation-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> till the reign of Kenneth II. who removed it to Scone, in order to secure his reign; for according to the inscription, Ni fallat fatum, Scotti quoque locum Invenient lapidem, regnare tenentur ibidem. The castle is <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>; the inside only 87 feet; partly ruinous, partly habitable. At three of the corners are round towers; one of them projects very little. The entrance is towards the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a> at present by a staircase, in old times probably by a draw-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, which fell from a little gate-way. The masonry appears very <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>; the tops battlemented. This pile is seated on a rock, whose sides have been pared to render it precipitous, and to make it conform to the shape of the castle. In 1307, this castle was possessed by Alexander Macdougal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of Argyle, a friend to the English; but was that year reduced by Robert Bruce, when Macdougal sued for peace with that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, and was received into favour. We find, about the year 1455, this to have been a residence of the lords of the isles; for here James last <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Douglas, after his defeat in Annandale, fled to Donald, the regulus of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and prevailed on him to take arms and carry on a plundering <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> against his monarch James II. At a small distance from the castle is a ruined chapel, once an elegant <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>; and at one end an inclosure, a family-cemetery. Opposite to these is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> precipice, ending abrupt and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> suddenly toward the south-east. A person concealed in the recesses of the rock, a little beyond the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a>, surprises friends stationed at some distance beneath the precipice, with a very remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECHO">echo</a> of any word, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> even <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>, he pronounces; which reaches the last distinctly and unbroken. The repetition is single, but remarkably clear.

EAR-ACH

Pages 1136-1138

in medicine. This disorder affects the concha, and the whole meatus auditorius. It is attended with inflammation, tumours, puncture, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EROSION">erosion</a>, tension, pollution, and a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. Extraneous bodies falling into the meatus auditorius, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> whatever excites pain in other parts, may cause it here. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the wax may be faulty, and be a cause; but the most frequent causes are <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a>; sometimes an acid serum is secreted in the glands of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EAR">ear</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the pain is violent, it seldom fails to bring on a fever, which is early attended with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> restlessness; and a delirium, fainting, and often convulsions, are the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>: for the membrane that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> the ear is exquisitely sensible, and fully stored with nerves; besides, membranes which adhere to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BONES">bones</a> have a more than ordinary <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol17.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a>. In the beginning, whilst the pain is not very considerable, a little warm olive-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> dropped into the ear <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> often relieve. If cold is the cause, keep the head Motherby's warm. If there is inflammation and tumour, which Med. Diet. will be known by the throbbing pain, a suppuration may be encouraged by cataplasms applied warm on the outer ear; but if the state of suppuration is not manifestly near, endeavour by bleeding, purging, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIETETICS">dietetics</a> applied to the ear, to remove the inflammation and pain. If <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> heat was the cause, bleed, and give daily a moderate dose of Glauber's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a> as a purge, until the pain abates, or until there is reason to suspect a suppuration; an opiate may be given at night when the pain is violent. When acid discharges are the cause, inject a warm infusion of poppy-heads in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>. When living insects have crept into the ear, blow the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a> therein, and then pour in warm oil. If purulent <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> discharges itself, inject tepid water, mixed with a little <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOAP">soap</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a> of roses. Besides the above-mentioned, blisters behind the ears, bladders of warm water laid on the affected ear, and the pediluvium, are occasionally useful. **EAU DE CARMES.** For n° 571, read n° 569. **EAU DE LUCA.** Dele <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, n° 671. **ECSTASY.** See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTASY">EXTASY</a>, (Encycl.) **EDDOES.** For ARUM PERGRINUM, read ARUM ESCULENTUM. **<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">EDUCATION</a>,** (Encycl.) The follies of a too delicate education are well expressed in that device of an ape; which by over caring and hugging its young ones, strangles them; with this motto, complectando necat. Octavius Ferrarius has a very good Latin treatise on the subject of education, intitled <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIRON">CHIRON</a>, the name of the centaur who was <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACHILLES">Achilles</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a>. Mr Locke's excellent treatise of education is known to every body. Quintilian employs the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of his first book in inquiring whether a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> education be preferable, i.e. whether it be better to bring up one's children at home, or send them to the colleges and public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>. After urging all that can be said on either side, he concludes for a college or school education. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of education, whether it be domestic or collegiate, should be suited to the station and views of parents, and to the genius of their children; and it is also <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to consult their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> and inclination.
