It is of great importance, that those who are destined to occupy superior stations in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, should enjoy the benefits of an enlarged and liberal education; that they should be furnished with every substantial and ornamental <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCOMPLISHMENT">accomplishment</a>; and those that are intended for any particular profession or employment, should be principally directed to those studies which are appropriated to their respective views; and in every <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the morals of youth should be a primary object. Though the municipal laws of most countries have made no provision for constraining a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> to bestow a proper education on his children; yet in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, they are under peculiar restrictions in our own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Some of these restrictions, as they affect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">protestants</a> who dissent from the religion of the state, may be thought both impolitic and injurious, and have, therefore, lately been considerably relaxed; but those which are to prevent the progress of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPERY">popery</a>, are prudent and necessary. Thus, if any person sends a child under his care beyond the seas, to be instructed in any Popish college, &c. in the principles of the Popish religion, or shall contribute towards his maintenance, he shall forfeit one hundred pounds, besides the disabilities incurred by the child so sent, (1 Jac. I. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 4. and 3 Jac. I. cap. 5. 11 and 12 W. III. cap. 4.) and both shall be incapable of suing in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a>, of being executor or administrator, of enjoying any legacy or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a> of gift, or of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> any office in the realm; and he shall forfeit all his goods and chattels, and likewise all his real estate for life, 3 Car. I. cap. 2. **EFFLORESCENCE,** (Encycl.) Besides the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CRYSTALLIZATION">crystallization</a> of salts, all of them have the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of appearing in the form of an efflorescence, or small saline spiculae, when mixed with any thick substance, particularly lime. Whatever salt happens to be made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of, there is little or no <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in the efflorescence. Thus, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a> very much salted, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-salt shoots in the form of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> spiculae, though the sea-salt itself never shoots but in the form of cubical crystals. In like manner Glauber's salt will appear in the form of an efflorescence, as well as the fossile alkali, &c. nor will the form of the crystals of the efflorescence be perceptibly different from those of sea-salt. The efflorescences which we see very <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> upon walls are in general Glauber's salt. In some <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> (but seldom in such efflorescences as we have examined), they are composed of fossile alkali. The reason of these differences is not known. In almost all cases of this kind there seems to be a real growth of salt. On one spot of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a> wall about two feet <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, which we observed particularly, this growth was very evident. The produce was a true Glauber's salt; and by frequently taking off the efflorescence, eight ounces were procured; nor did the prolific virtue of the wall seem to be in the least impaired by the waste. **<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTRICITY">ELECTRICITY</a>,** p. 2673, col. 1. line 8. for <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BISMUTH">Bismuth</a>, read <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZINC">Zinc</a>.—P. 2701, col. 1. line 4. for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THUNDER">Thunder</a>, read <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LIGHTNING">Lightning</a>. **ELECTUARY.** For 883, read 893. **ELEGY.** Marginal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, for n° 62, read p. 631. **ELEMI,** (Encycl.) See also BURSERA, in this Appendix. **<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMBALMING">EMBALMING</a>,** (Encycl.) See also <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, § XX. (Encycl.) **EMULSION.** Marginal note, for 910 read 922. **ENGLAND.** P. 2769, marginal note 45. for Henry II. read Henry III. **ENTOMOLOGY.**

ENTOMOLOGY

Pages 1138-1144

the science of insects, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a> which treats of insects. Whoever is desirous of attaining a systematic knowledge of insects, ought primarily to be solicitous about acquiring the terms made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of in the science, that so he may be able rightly to denominate every part of an insect. The student is first to know what an insect is, lest he mistake hippocampi, and other amphibious animals, for them, as was formerly done; or confound them with the vermes, which Linnaeus first distinguished from insects, and which differ as essentially from them as the class <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MAMMALIA">mammalia</a> do from birds. Every insect is furnished with a head, antennae, and feet, of all which the vermes are destitute. All insects have six or more feet; they respire through pores placed on the sides of their bodies, and which are termed spiracula; their skin is externally hard, and serves them instead of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BONES">bones</a>, of which they have internally none. From this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a>, the acus marina is evidently no insect. But the antennae placed on the fore-part of the head, constitute the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> distinction. These are jointed and moveable in every part, in which they differ from the horns of other animals: they are organs conveying some kind of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>; but we have no more idea of what this kind of sense is, than a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> has, who, without eyes, attempts to determine the particular <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the rays of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> on the retina of the eye, or to explain the changes which from thence take <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> mind. That they are the organs of some kind of sense, is apparent from their perpetually moving them. them forward; yet the hard crust with which they are invested, and their shortness in flies and other insects, would induce one to believe them not to be the organs of touch: Mr Barbut supposes them to constitute or contain the organs of hearing. That they are tubular, and filled with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and some kind of humour, appears from the antennae of butterflies immersed in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>.—To come now to the terms of the art. A knowledge of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> parts of the body is first to be established; which, after the method of anatomists, we divide into head, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a>, and extremities. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">Sect</a>. I. External parts of the Body. I. CAPUT, the Head. This part in insects without brain. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the brain and spinal marrow consists in the former being a medullary part organized. We do not deny the existence of a medullary thread in the heads of insects, but we never could discover it to be organized: hence the hippopotamus equina, or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> fly, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> live, run, nay even copulate, after being deprived of its head; so fay nothing of many others which are capable of living a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> while in the same situation. As they are not apparently furnished with ears, they have been apprehended incapable of hearing; as we can no more conceive that sense to exist without ears, than vision without eyes. That they are nevertheless susceptible of any shrill or loud noise, as well as fishes, is indisputable; but it has been supposed to be in a manner different from that of hearing. Mr Barbut, however, supposes them to possess this sense in a very distinct manner. Many insects, he observes, are well known to be endowed with the power of uttering sounds, such as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> beetles, the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEE">bee</a>, wasp, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> fly, gnat, &c. The sphinx <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATROPOS">atropos</a> squeaks, when hurt, nearly as loud as a mouse. Now, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> insects are endowed with the power of uttering sounds, it certainly must be for some purpose. As they vary their cry occasionally, it must certainly be designed either to give notice of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> or pain, or some affection in the creature who possesses it. "The knowledge of their sounds (says our author) is undoubtedly confined to their tribe, and is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> intelligible to them only; saving when violence obliges the animal to exert the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> in distress, craving compassion; then all animals understand the dolorous cry. For instance, attack a bee or wasp near the hive or nest, or a few of them: the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of that assault will be, the animal or animals, by a different tone of voice, will express his or their disapprobation or pain; that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> is known to the hive to be plaintive, and that their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> or brethren require their assistance; and the offending party seldom escapes with impunity. Now, if they had not the sense of hearing, they could not have known the danger their brother or brethren were in by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> of their tone." Another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>, which he reckons still more decisive, was taken from an observation made by himself a large spider in St James's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARK">park</a>. This creature had made a very large web on a wooden railing; and was, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of observation, on one of the rails at a considerable distance from the place where a large fly entangled itself. Nevertheless, the moment the fly was entangled, the spider became sensible of it; though, from the situation of the rail, he could not possibly have seen it. In this, however, Mr Barbut might possibly be deceived; because the spider was perhaps alarmed by the tremulous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the threads, occasioned by the fluttering of the fly; which he might well know how to distinguish from their vibration by the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>. The organ of hearing, in our author's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, is situated in the antennae; both from their situation in the part of the head most favourable to such organs, their inward structure being moveable, the ears of most inferior animals being so. He has never considered the antennae as either offensive or defensive, but has observed them to be endowed with an exquisite sense of feeling; that the animal appeared to be in agony when its antennae were pinched; and that it takes care to avoid the touching any hard substance with them roughly. "This tenderness in the organ of hearing (says he) is common to all animals; and insects seem to be particularly tender in these parts by quickly withdrawing them from the touch." Our author further observes, that the antennae of all insects are composed of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> varying in size, form, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. Those who are chiefly confined to live under water have their antennae in general shorter than those who live on <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>. Some who roam at large in the air, have them long and slender. They are all hollow, and are rendered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a> by the joints, which are very visible in the horns of the crab and lobster. This hollowness, in our author's opinion, is to receive the sound communicated to the extremities of the antennae by the repercussion of the air affected by any noise, and convey it, by means of the joints, from one to another, till it arrives in that lessened <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of tone best suited to the timid nature of the animal. In this circumstance there may be many variations in point of perfection in those organs: the strength, utility, and degree of power in receiving sound being proportioned to the necessities of the animals, different in their nature and requisites. In most animals, the entrance to the auricular organ is patulous; but in this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> the animal would suffer <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> inconvenience from such an organisation, as the organ would often be clogged with dirt, &c. It has also appeared dubious if they have the sense of smell, no organ being found in them adapted to that purpose: and although it was evident they had a perception of agreeable and fetid effluvia, it was thought to be in a manner altogether unknown to us. Mr Barbut is of opinion that the organs of smell reside in the palpi or feelers. Many insects have four and some six, two of which are in general cheliform, in order to assist the insect in conveying its food to its mouth. It may be likewise observed, that the palpi are in continual motion; the animal thrusting them into every kind of putrid or other <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, as a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOG">hog</a> would do his nose, smelling and searching after food. Insects which apparently do not possess palpi or spiral tongues, have undoubtedly some organ concealed within the mouth analogous to them in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a> and utility; the fleshy protocolla of the fly is thrust into every substance in which the animal expects to find food; and when it is extended, nearly in the middle are situated, in our author's opinion, two upright palpi, which, no doubt, perform in their turn some office, perhaps that of smell. Many insects have no tongue, nor make any sound with their mouth; but for this purpose some use their feet, others their wings, and others <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> with which they are naturally furnished. **Eyes.** Most insects have two; but the gyranus has four, the scorpion six, the spider eight, and the scolopendra three. They have no eye-brows, but the external tunic of their eyes is hard and transparent like a watch-glass; their eyes have no external motion, unless it be in the crab. They consist for the most part of one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LENS">lens</a> only; but in those of the butterfly, dipteræ, and many of the beetles, they are more numerous. Pugett discovered 17,325 lenses in the cornea of a butterfly, and Liedewenhoek 800 in a fly. **Antennæ.** Of these there are in general two (unless four are allowed to some kind of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CRABS">crabs</a>), and placed on the fore-part of the head: they are peculiar to insects; and are plainly distinguishable from the tentacles of the vermes, in being crustaceous; and from the palpi of insects, which are more numerous, placed near the mouth, and are sometimes wanting. As the antennæ are of great moment in distinguishing the various kinds of insects, we shall enumerate and explain the several different forms of them. *Setaceæ,* are those which grow gradually <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAPER">taper</a> towards the extremity. *Filiformes,* such as are of the same thickness throughout. *Moniliformes,* are filiform, like the preceding, but consist of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of round knobs, like a necklace of beads. *Clavatae,* such as gradually increase in size toward the extremity. *Capitatae,* are clavatae, but have the extremity somewhat round. *Filiformes,* are capitatae; but have the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPITULUM">capitulum</a>, or knob, divided longitudinally into three or four parts, or laminae, as in the scarabæi. *Perfoliatae,* are also capitatae; but have the capitulum horizontally divided, as in the dermestes. *Petiolatae,* so called from their similitude to a comb, tho' they more properly resemble a feather, as in the moths and elateres. This is most obvious in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a>. *Aristatae,* such as have a lateral <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, which is either naked or furnished with lesser hairs, as in the fly: *Brevioriæ,* those which are shorter than the body; *Longioriæ,* those which are longer than the body; *Mediocris,* those which are of the same length with the body; all three of which varieties are distinguishable in the cerambyces. **Palpi,** or *Feelers,* resemble filiform, articulated, moveable antennæ. They are most <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> four in number, sometimes six; they are sufficiently distinguished from antennæ, in being naked, short, and always placed at the mouth. **Os,** the *Mouth,* is generally placed in the anterior part of the head, extending somewhat downwards. In some insects, it is placed under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, as in the chermes, coccus, cancer (crab), and curculio. **Rostrum,** or *Proboscis,* is the mouth drawn out to a rigid point: in many of the hemiptera clasps it is bent downward toward the breast and belly, as in the cicada, nepa, notoneæta, cimex (bug), aphid, and remarkably so in some curculiones. **Maxillæ,** the *Jaws,* are two in number, sometimes four, and at other times more; they are placed horizontally; the inner edge of them in some insects is <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERRATED">serrated</a>, or furnished with little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>. **Lingua,** the *Tongue,* in some insects is taper and spiral, as in the butterfly; in others it is fleshy, resembling a proboscis, and tubular, as in the fly. **Labium superius,** the *upper Lip,* is situated above the jaws; as in the scarabæus and gryllus. **Stemmata,** or *Crowns,* are three smooth hemispheric dots, placed generally on the top of the head; as in most of the hymenoptera, and others. **II. TRUNCUS,** the *Trunk,* is that part which comprehends the breast or thorax; it is situated between the head and abdomen; and has the legs inserted into it, that its parts may be distinctly determined. It is divided into thorax, scutellum, and sternum. **Thorax,** the *Thorax,* is the back part of the breast; and is very various in its shape. It is called *dentatus,* when its sides are armed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>; *spinosus,* when its back is furnished with them, as in the cerambyx; and *marginatus,* when its margin is laterally dilated, as in the rhinpa and caelida. **Scutellum,** or *Escutcheon,* is the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POSTERIOR">posterior</a> part of the thorax: it is frequently triangular; and appears to be divided from the thorax by an intervening future, as in most of the coleoptera. **Sternum,** the *Sternum,* is situated on the inferior part of the thorax; it is pointed behind in the elateres, and bifid in some of the dytiscæ. **III. ABDOMEN,** the *Abdomen* is in most insects distinct from the thorax; it is the posterior part of the body of the insect; and is composed of a number of annular segments, which serve occasionally to lengthen or shorten it, and to contain the organs of chylification, &c. **Spiracula,** are little holes or pores, placed singly on each side of every segment of the abdomen: through these the insect breathes; and if <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> be applied to stop them up, it proves fatal to most of them. **Tergum,** the *Back,* is the superior part of the abdomen. **Venter,** the *Belly,* is the inferior part. **Anus,** is the posterior part of the abdomen, perforated for the evacuation of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXCREMENT">excrement</a>. This part also frequently contains the organs of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>. **IV. ARTUS,** the *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">Limbs</a> or Extremities,* are the various instruments of motion. **Pedes,** the *Legs,* are generally fix. There is an exception to this, however, in the clasps Aptera, many of which have eight; as acari (mites), phalangii, most of the aranei, (spiders) scorpiones, (scorpions) and cancri (crabs.) The oniscus has 14, and the Iuli and scolopendri still more. The first <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> of the leg, which is generally thick-set, is called *femur:* the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, which is generally of the same size throughout, *tibia:* the third, which is jointed, is distinguished by the name of *<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TARSUS">tarsus</a>:* and the last, which in most insects is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a>, by that of *unguis.* The legs of insects, in general, are named from the various motions they produce: *Cursoria,* from that of running, which are the most numerous; &c. saltatorii, from that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAPING">leaping</a>; natatorii, from that of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a>, &c.—In the saltatorii, the thighs are remarkably large, by which means they are able to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a> to a considerable distance, as in the gryllus, (grasshopper), &c. In those of the Natatorii, the feet are flat, and edged with hairs, which answer the purpose of oars in assisting them to swim, as in the dytiscus.—Muticii, are such feet as have no claws.—Chelæ, or claws, are the fore-feet enlarged towards their extremities, each of which is furnished with two lesser claws, which <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> like a thumb and finger; as in the crab. Alæ, Wings, the instruments which enable them to fly. These are membranous, and undivided, except in the instance of the phalænae alucitæ, in which they are in part divided. Most insects have four; the diptera-clas, and the coccus, however, have two only. The wing is divided into its superior and inferior surfaces; its anterior part in a butterfly, is that towards the anterior margin, or next to the head; its posterior part, that towards the anus; its exterior part, that towards the outer edge; and the interior, that next the abdomen. They are called plicatilæ, when they are folded at the time the insect is at rest, as in the wasp; opposite to these are the planæ, which are incapable of being folded. Erectæ, such as have their superior surfaces brought in contact when the insect is at rest; as in the cimicæ, libellula puella and virgo, and papilionæ (butterflies). Patentæ, which remain horizontally extended when the insect is at rest; as in the phalænae geometræ, and most of the libellulæ. Incumbentæ, such as cover horizontally the superior part of the abdomen when the insect is at rest. Deflexæ, are incumbentæ, but not horizontally, the outer edges declining toward the sides. Reversæ, are deflexæ, with this addition, that the edge of the inferior wings projects from under the anterior part of the superior ones. Dentatae, in which the edge is serrated, or scoloped. Caudatae, in which one or more projections in the hinder wings are extended into processes. Reticulatae, when the vessels of the wings put on the appearance of network, as in the hemerobius perla; the two anterior wings generally become superior, and the posterior ones inferior, in moths, when their wings are closed; but the anterior wings are called primary, and the inferior ones secondary, in butterflies, as they cannot with propriety be called inferior when the wings are erect. Coloræ, the colours, these are self-apparent: but according to their several shapes, they take the different names of punctæ, dots; maculae, spots; fasciæ, bands, which frequently run across and sometimes surround the edge of the wings; Strigæ, streaks, which are very slender fasciæ; and linearæ, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, which are longitudinally extended. Ocellus, is a round spot, containing a lesser spot of a different <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> in its centre. Stigmata, another <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> lately introduced by Linnaeus, signifies the spot, or <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANASTOMOSIS">anastomosis</a>, in the middle of the wing near the anterior margin; it is conspicuous in most of the hymenoptera and neuroptera, and even in the coleoptera. The single or double kidney-shaped spot, situated in the same part of the anterior wings, and frequently occurring in the phalænae paganae, is distinguished likewise by the name of stigma. Elytra (in the singular number elytron.) The upper wings, which are of a hard substance, in some degree resembling <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, and which in most insects are of a very hard texture, but in others flexible, are called elytra; their superior surface is generally convex, their inferior one concave. When the insect flies, they are extended; and shut when it rests, closing together, and forming a longitudinal furrow <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the middle of the back, as in the coleoptera. They are of various shapes. Abbreviata, when shorter than the abdomen. Truncata, when shorter than the abdomen, and terminating in a transverse line. Rafiflizata, when of equal or greater length than the abdomen, and terminating in a transverse line. Serata, when the exterior margin towards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APEX">apex</a> is notched or serrated, as in some of the buprestes. Spinosa, when their surface is covered with sharp points or pricks. Scabra, when their surface is so uneven as to grate against the fingers. Striata, when marked with slender longitudinal furrows. Percata, when with elevated longitudinal sulci or ridges. Sulcata, when these ridges are concave. Hemelytra, when the superior wings are of a middle substance between leather and membrane; either totally so, as in the grylli; or partially so, as in the cimices, nepæ, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTO">noto</a>-neæ: These are commonly distinguished by the name hemiptera. Halteræ, poifers, (a term also introduced by Linnaeus), are little heads placed on a stalk or peduncle, most frequently under a little arched <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>. They are found only in the clas diptera, and appear to be nothing more than the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of the hinder wings. Cauda, the Tail, in most insects is, Simplex, simple, capable of being extended, and again drawn back at pleasure. In the crab and scorpion, however, it is Elongata, elongated, or lengthened out. Setacea, brittle-shaped, or taper; as in the raphidia. Trifota, consisting of three brittles; as in the ephemerae. Furcata, being forked, as in the podura. Forcipata, resembling a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of forceps; as in the forcipula. Foliata, resembling a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>; as in the blatta, grylli, and some <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of cancri. Telifera, such as are armed with a dart or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a>; as in the scorpion and panorpæ. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACULEUS">Aculeus</a>, an instrument with which they wound, and at the same time instill a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POISON">poison</a>; with such the bee, wasp, scorpion, &c. are furnished. Explanation of Plate CCCXVIII. upper Compartment. Fig. 1. Antennæ pectinate, or feather'd; as in the phalænae, moths. 2. Perfoliatae, or perforated; as in the dermestes and dytiscus. 3. Fissiles, or fissile, divided into la- minæ at the extremity, as in the scarabæi, beetles. 4. Antennæ clavatæ, or club-shaped, as in the papilio, butterfly. 5. —— moniliformes, like a necklace of beads; as in the chrysonemæ. 6. —— setacæ, setaceous, or bristle-shaped; as in many of the phalææ. 7. —— arista, furnished with a lateral hair, as in the fly. 8. Caput, the head. b Palpi, or feelers. c Antennæ, or horns. d Oculi, the eyes. e Thorax. f Scutellum, or escutcheon. g Pectus, or breast. h Sternum, or breast-bone. i Abdomen, and its segments. k Anus. l Elytra, or shells. m Membranous wings. n Pedes, or feet, which are natatorii. 10. o Femur, or thigh. p Tibia, or leg. q Tarsus, or foot. r Unguis, or claw. 11. a The anterior part of the wing. b The posterior part. c The exterior part. d The interior part. e The margin. f The disk, or middle. g Oculus, or eye. 22, 13, 14, 15. Represent the insect in its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EGG">egg</a>, caterpillar, pupa, and perfect state. Sect. II. Of the Sexes of Insects. The same difference of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEX">sex</a> exists in insects as in other animals, and they even appear more disposed to increase their species than other animals; many of them, when become perfect, seeming to be created for no other purpose but to propagate their species. Thus the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SILK">silk</a>-worm, when it arrives at its perfect or moth-state, is incapable of eating, and can hardly fly: it endeavours only to propagate its species; after which the male immediately dies, and the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> as soon as she has deposited her eggs. In many insects, the male and female are with difficulty distinguished; and in some they differ so widely, that an unskilful person might easily take the male and female of the same insect for different species; as for instance, in the phalææ humuli, pinaria, rufilata; each sex of which differs in colour. This unlikeness is still more apparent in some insects, in which the male has wings and the female none; as in the coccus, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-LAMPRIS">lampris</a>, phalææ antiqua, brumata, lichenella. And as most insects remain a long while in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COPULATION">copulation</a>, as we may see in the tipula and silk-worm, the winged males fly with the wingless females, and carry them about from one place to another; as in the phalææ antiqua. It is, however, no certain rule, that when one insect of the same species is found to have wings, and the other to be without, the former must necessarily be the male, and the latter the female. The aphides, for instance, are an exception; and besides these, individuals of both sexes, and of the same species, are found without wings, as the carabi majores, tenebriones, meloæ, cimices. The gryllus pedetris is likewise destitute of wings; and might have passed for a gryllus in its pupa state, had it not been seen in copulation; for it is well known that no insect can propagate its species till it arrives at its last or perfect state. "Plaguea infectior genitalia sua intra annum habent abscindita, et penes solitarios, sed nonnulla penem habent bifidum: Cancri autem et Aranei geminos, quem admodum nonnulla <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMPHIBIA">amphibia</a>, et quod mirandum in loco alieno, ut Cancer, sub basi caudæ. Araneus mas palpos habet clavatos, qui penes sunt, juxta os utrinque unicum, quae clave lexum nec speciem distinguunt; et femina vulvas suas habet in abdomine juxta pectus. Heic vero si unquam vere dixeris, "Res plena timoris amor;" si enim proceris in auspiciis accederitis, femina ipsum devorat; quod etiam fit, si non statim se retraxerit. Libellula femina genitalia suum sub apice gerit cauda, et mas sub pectori; adeo ut cum mas collum formæ na forcipæ cauda arripit, illa candam suam pectori ejus adpliceret, sicque peculiari ratione connexæ violent." Besides those of the male and female, a third sex exists in some insects which we call <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEUTER">neuter</a>: As these have not the distinguishing parts of either sex, they may be considered as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUNUCHS">eunuchs</a> or infertile. We know of no instance of this kind in any other class of animals, nor in vegetables, except in the class Syngenesiae, and in the Opulus. This kind of sex is only found among those insects which form themselves into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a>, as bees, wasps, and ants; and here these kind of eunuchs are real slaves, as on them lies the whole business of the economy; while those of the other sex are idle, only employing themselves in the increase of the family. Each family of Bees has one female only (called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>), many males, and an almost innumerable <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of neuters. Of those, the neuters (whose antennæ have 11 joints) do the working part; they extract and collect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a> and wax, build up the cells, keep watch, and do a variety of other things. The males, whose antennæ consist of 15 joints, do no <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>; they serve the female once, and that at the expense of their lives; they may be considered in the light of a set of parasites, or cicidæi; but as soon as their business of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-IMPREGNATION">impregnation</a> is over, they are expelled by their servants the neuters, who now shake off the yoke, but yet pay all due respect to their common mother the queen. The same economy nearly takes place in Wasps, where the young females, which are impregnated in the autumn, live through the winter, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> propagate their species; but the queen, together with all the males, perish in the winter. Among Ants, the neuters form a hill in the shape of a cone, that the water may run off it, and place those which are in the pupa state on that side of it which is least exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. At a considerable distance from these are found the habitations of the males and females, to whom the most ready obedience is yielded by the neuters, till a new offspring succeeds, and then they oblige them to quit their habitations. But those ants which live entirely under ground, ground, provide better for themselves in this respect: for a little before their nuptials, they quit their habitation of their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCORD">accord</a>, and after swarming in the manner of bees, they copulate in the air; and each retiring to some new habitation, founds a new family. No hermaphrodites have as yet been discovered among insects. There is something very singular, however, in the propagation of the aphides. A female aphis once impregnated, can produce young, which will continue to produce others without any fresh impregnation, even to the fifth progeny; afterwards a new impregnation must take place. See Aphis, (En-cycl.) The male insects, like male hawks, are always smaller than the females. In the propagation of their species they are remarkably careful; so that it is with the greatest difficulty that flies are kept from depositing their eggs on fresh meat, the cabbage butterfly from laying them on cabbage, and other insects from depositing them in the several places peculiar to each. The scarabaeus pilarius and carnifex, are deserving of our <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, as they afford a mutual assistance to each other: for when the female has laid her eggs in a little <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALL">ball</a> of dung, the males, with their feet, which are axiform, assist the female to roll it to some suitable place; as <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> and Pliny formerly, and Loefling has lately observed. It is very wonderful to observe, that in the coccus and oniscus, the female has no sooner brought forth her young, than she is devoured by it; and that the sphex should be able so readily to kill the caterpillar of a moth, then <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURY">bury</a> it in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and there deposited her eggs in it. Nor can we without admiration behold the same species of aphis, which was viviparous in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, become oviparous in the autumn. Almost innumerable examples might be brought of the singularities in the eggs of insects; we shall, however, only mention those of the hemerobius, which are deposited on a footstalk; those of the phalena neutria, which are placed regularly in a ring round the branch of some tree; and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> eggs of the blatta. Sect. III. Metamorphoses of Insects. There are no insects, except those of the aptera class, but what are continually undergoing some transformation. Insects change first from the (ovum) egg, into the (larva) caterpillar or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGGOT">maggot</a>; then into the (pupa) <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHRYSALIS">chrysalis</a>; and lastly into the (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMAGO">imago</a>) fly or perfect state. During each of these changes, their appearance differs as much as night and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>. The insect, as soon as it came out of the egg, was by former entomologists called eruca; but as this is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a> with the botanic name fimbrium, it was changed by Linnaeus for the term larva, a name expressive of the insect's being, in this state, as it were masked, having its true appearance concealed. Under this mask or skin the entire insect, such as it afterwards appears when perfect, lies concealed, enveloped only in its tender wings, and putting on a soft and pulpy appearance; inasmuch that Swammerdam was able to demonstrate the butterfly with its wings to exist in a caterpillar, though it bore but a faint resemblance to its future perfection. The insect, therefore, in this state, undergoes no other alteration but the change of its skin. The larva are, for the most part, larger than the insect when perfect, and are very voracious. The caterpillar of the cabbage-butterfly eats double what it would seem to require from its size; but its growth is not adequate to its voracity. Pupa. The insect in this state was formerly called chrysalis, or aurelia: but as the appearance of gilding is confined to a few butterflies only, the term of pupa has been adopted in its stead; because the lepidoptera, especially, resemble an infant in twaddling clothes; and in this state all, except those of the hemiptera clas, take no nourishment. Imago, is the third state. This name is given by Linnæus to this third change, in which the insect appears in its proper shape and colours; and as it undergoes no more transformations, it is called perfect. In this state it flies, is capable of propagating its species, and receives true antennæ; which before, in most insects, were scarce apparent. As the shape of the Pupa is different, in different classes of insects, it assumes different names; thus it is called Coarctata, when it is round, and as it were turned, without the least resemblance of the structure of the insect; as in the diptera, Obteta, when it consists as it were of two parts, one of which surrounds the head and thorax, and the other the abdomen. Incompletea, when they have wings and feet, but are not capable of moving them; as in most of the hymenoptera. Semicompleta, in which they walk or run, but have only the rudiments of wings. Completa, in which they immediately obtain the perfect form of the insect, without undergoing any more change; as in those of the aptera clas, except only the flea. The <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a> bug also belongs to this clas. The spider undergoes frequent transformations, though only in the colour of its skin. The crustaceous insects, as crabs, lobsters, &c. yearly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> their shells, as their growth would otherwise be impeded. The scolopendri, when young, have fewer feet than when they are full grown. All insects, as soon as they undergo the third change, are arrived at their full growth; nor do we find any difference in the size of the same species of insect in the same countries, unless during its caterpillar state, it has not had a sufficiency of proper food. Sect. IV. Classification of Insects. As insects are endowed with the various powers of creeping, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLYING">flying</a>, and swimming, there is scarce any place, however remote and obscure, in which they are not to be found. The great confusion which appeared to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> to arise from their number, made them never dream of reducing them to any system. Swammerdam, that indefatigable inquirer into nature, observed that their metamorphoses were divided by nature into several states or orders. Their external appearance also carried with it some mark of distinction; so that entomologists called all those of the coleoptera clas, Scarabæi (beetles); those of the lepidoptera clas, Papiliones; and those of the hymenoptera clas that had two wings only, Muscae (flies); those of the same clas that had four wings, were called Apes (bees). No far- farther progress was made in the systematic part of this science till the time of Linnæus. He was the first that undertook to determine the genera, and assign them their proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, in the *Systema Naturae*; and thus reduced this science to a systematic form. This system, in subsequent editions, was considerably enriched and amended by him, insomuch that the science of insects now shines forth in its full lustre. He it was who first instituted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> orders, and reduced them into genera by expressive names; determined an infinite number of species in the *Fauna Suecica*, and *Musæum Reginæ*; collected with incredible pains the synonymous names of the various authors who had written on them; and lastly, added their descriptions, and the places in which they were to be found. So that the system of this illustrious author will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> any person, without the assistance of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, for the most part, easily to ascertain the name of any insect he may meet with. Before his time scarce any more than 200 insects were known; whereas, in the last edition of his system, he has determined the names of nearly 3000 distinct species. **Classes.** The Linnean classes of insects are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>; as enumerated in Zoology, and under the article Insects, (Encycl.) which see. **Orders.** These classes are again subdivided into different orders; for which see the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> Zoology and Insect, (Encycl.) and Plate CLIV. **Genera.** To insert here the characters of all the different genera which may be found in Linnæus's *Syst. Nat.* would be unnecessary. It will be sufficient to enumerate some new genera mentioned by the most <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> systematic writers, that, by being acquainted with the subtile distinctions on which they are built, the student may avoid running into confusion. It is among the moderns only that genera of this kind are to be met with, and new names given them. To remove this difficulty, we shall first enumerate the names of those authors which are synonymous with those of Linnæus. **New Genera of authors synonymous with those of Linnæus.** | Linnaeus's Names | Names of other Authors | |------------------|------------------------| | Lucanus | Platyceror | | Hister | Attelabus | | Byrrhus | Anthrenus Cifela | | Mylabris | Laria Scop. | | Attelabus | Clerus | | Silpha | Pelitis | | Bruchus | Mylabris | | Ptinus | Byrrhus | | Chrysomela | Galericula | | Hilpa | Crioforis | | Cantharis | Cicindela | | Buprestis | Cucujus | | Carabus | Buprestis | | Myrmeleon | Formicaleo | | Sirex | Urocerot | **New genera of authors.** | Copris. Scarabæus absque scutello | | Bystricius. Dermestes capecinus | | Cifela. Byrrhus Pilula | | Rhinomancer. Attelabus rostro producto fere Curculionis | | Anthribus. Silpha | These genera appear to be in a great <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> like those which were introduced into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a> by the followers of Riviœus. Paying too little regard to nature, they disunited natural genera, on account of the most trifling distinctions. This made their continuance in the science of very short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>; our business here is not to suppose, but to examine, what nature will allow of, and what she will not. Knowledge of this kind, built on opinion only, will not stand. We are therefore to look into the science with great accuracy; and the larva of the insect, its manner of changing, and other things of moment, are to be known, before we presume to form a new genus. Coining of new names, and changing of one old one for another, has been the source of the greatest confusion. Thus, in order to reduce the cicindela and carabus to the same genus, buprestis has been adopted for the generic name; but as that genus had long ago received a very different application, it was changed for that of cucujus. Again, that the officinal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANTHARIDES">cantharides</a> might be ranged among the cerambyces, the cantharides have been removed from the genus of meloë (to which they naturally belong), and referred to the genus of cicindela, obtaining thus a new name. And so of many others. Thus also, to mention no more, how needless and rash was it to separate the acridium and locusta from the genus of gryllus, the crabro from the tenthredines, and the mylabris from the necydalis! **Trivial Names.** The trivial names placed under their respective genera will occasion little or no controversy; they are current like <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, and of the same utility as the proper names of men, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> or Paul, &c. Insects living on vegetables should receive their names from the particular <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> on which they mostly feed, as they are preferable to all others. Thus the names of the phalena morti, &c. are excellent; and when we are able to give such to insects, the old ones are to be dif-

EPACTS

Pages 1144-1146

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a>, the excesses of the solar <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> above the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SYNODICAL">synodical</a> month, and of the solar year above the lunar year of twelve synodical months; <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> of several solar months above as many synodical months, and several solar years above as many dozen of synodical months. The epacts, then, are either annual or menstrual. Menstrual epacts are the excesses of the civil or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a> month above the lunar month. Suppose, e.g., it were new-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a> on the 1st <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>; since the lunar month is 29 days \(12^h\ 44'\ 3''\), and the month of January contains 31 days, the menstrual epact is 1 day \(11^h\ 15'\ 57''\). Annual epacts are the excesses of the solar year above the lunar. Hence, as the Julian solar year is 365 days \(6^h\), and the Julian lunar year 354 days \(8^h\ 48'\ 36''\), the annual epact <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> be 10 days \(21^h\ 11'\ 22''\); that is, nearly 11 days. Consequently the epact of 2 years is 22 days; of 3 years, 33 days; or rather 31, since 30 days make an embolismic or intercalary month. Thus the epact of 4 years is 14 days, and so of the rest; and thus, every 19th year, the epact becomes 30 or 0; consequently the 20th year the epact is 11 again; and so the cycle of epacts expires with the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, or lunar cycle of 19 years, and begins with the same, as in the following <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">table</a>: | <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a>. Numb. | Epacts. | Gold. Numb. | Epacts. | Gold. Numb. | Epacts. | |------------|---------|------------|---------|------------|---------| | 1 | XI | 7 | XVII | 13 | XXIII | | 2 | XII | 8 | XVIII | 14 | IV | | 3 | III | 9 | IX | 15 | XV | | 4 | XIV | 10 | XX | 16 | XXVI | | 5 | XXV | 11 | I | 17 | VIII | | 6 | VI | 12 | XII | 18 | XIX | | | | | | 19 | XXX | Again, as the new moons are the same, that is, as they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> on the same day every 19 years, so the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the lunar and solar years is the same every 19 years. And because the said difference is always to be added to the lunar year, in order to adjust or make it equal to the solar year; hence the said difference respectively belonging to each year of the moon's cycle is called the epact of the said year, that is, the number to be added to the said year, to make it equal to the solar year; the word being formed from the Greek \(\tau\)α\(\omega\), induco, intercalo. Upon this mutual respect between the cycle of the moon and the cycle of the epacts, is founded this rule. Ephemeris, for finding the Julian epact, belonging to any year of the moon's cycle. Multiply the year given of the moon's cycle into 11; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the product be less than 30, it is the epact sought; if the product be greater than 30, divide it by 30, and the remainder of the dividend is the epact. For instance, I would know the epact for the year 1712, which is the third year of the moon's cycle. Therefore 3 is the epact for 1712; for $11 \times 3 = 33$, and 33 being divided by 30, there is left 3 of the dividend for the epact. But the difference of the Julian and Gregorian years being equal to the excess of the solar above the lunar year, or 11 days, it happens that the Gregorian epact for one year is the same with the Julian epact for the preceding year.

EPHEMERA

Pages 1146-1146

(Encycl.) These flies, who take their name from the shortness of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, are distinguished into several <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. Some live several days, others do not take flight till the setting of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, and live not to see the rising of that luminary. Some exist but one <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, others but half that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>; in which short <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> they comply with the call of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. A peculiarity observed, incident to themselves alone. They have to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> off one flough more, an operation which sometimes takes 24 hours to complete. To bring this about, they cling fast to a tree. The ephemerae, before they flutter in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, have in some manner been fishes. They remain in the states of larva and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHRYSALIS">chrysalis</a> for one, two, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> three years. The chrysalis only differs from the larva by there being observable on its back <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> for wings. Both have on their sides small fringes of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, which, when put into <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, serve them as fins. Nothing can be more curious than the plying of those little oars in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>. Their <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a> is terminated, as well as in their state of flies, by three threads. These larva scoop themselves out dwellings in the banks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>; and they are small tubes made like siphons, the one serving for an entrance, the other affording them an outlet. The banks of some rivers are often perforated with them. When the waters decrease, they dig fresh holes lower <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, in order to enjoy their element the water. The season and hour when the chrysalids of the different species of the ephemerae turn into flies, maintain a kind of regularity. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, the rise or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of the waters, accelerate, however, or postpone their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FINAL">final</a> display. The ephemerae of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a> appear in the air two hours before sunset. These flies are hatched almost all at the same instant in such numbers as to darken the air. The most early of those on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARNE">Marne</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a> in France do not begin to fly till two hours after the setting of the sun, towards the middle of August. They are seen fluttering and sporting on the brink of their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>. The glare of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> attracts them, round which they perform a thousand circles with amazing regularity. Their coming together for the purpose of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> can only be surmised, the shortness of their life requiring that all its functions should be proportionable in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>. Some naturalists have been of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that the males impregnated the eggs after the manner of fishes. The females, by the help of the threads of their tail and the flapping of their wings, support themselves on the surface of the water, and in that almost upright situation drop their eggs in clusters. One single <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> lay 700 or 800 eggs, which sink to the bottom. The larvae that escape from the voraciousness of the fishes, set about the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of habitations to shelter them from every kind of danger. When the flies have propagated, they are seen to die and fall by heaps. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> and water are strewed with them to a considerable thickness. The fishermen consider these multitudes of destroyed insects as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANNA">manna</a> for the fishes.

EPHORI

Pages 1146-1146

(Encycl.) Some authors deny that the ephori were established by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LYCURGUS">Lycurgus</a>, dating their origin 130 years after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a>. Thus Plutarch, in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> of Cleomenes, ascribes their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> to Theopompus <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPARTA">Sparta</a>; which is also confirmed by the authority of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>. **EPIC.** For <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>, chap. ii, read <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">Part</a> II, chap. i.

EPILOBIUM

Pages 1146-1146

(Encycl.) An infusion of the leaves of the anguillifolium, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> roebay willow-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERB">herb</a>, has an intoxicating <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, as the inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KAMTSCHATKA">Kamtschatka</a> have learned. These people also eat the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> young shoots which creep under the ground, and have a sort of ale brewed from the dried pitch of it. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> of the seeds has been lately manufactured by mixing it with cotton or beaver's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>. **EPITHEM.** For 1015, read 1026.

ERYTHRINA

Pages 1146-1146

(Encycl.) Of the wood of this tree the inhabitants of Malabar make sheaths for swords and knives. They <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the same, together with the bark, in washing a sort of garment which they call saraffas; and make of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, the confection carlyl. The leaves pulverized and boiled with the mature nux Indica, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> coco-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a>, consume venereal buboes, and ease pains in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BONES">bones</a>; bruised and applied to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, they cure the cephalaea and ulcers; mixed with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> called jagra, they mitigate pains in the belly, especially in women; and the same effect follows from the use of the bark levigated with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, or swallowing the kernel stripped of its <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> pellicle. The juice of the leaves taken with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> sergelim, mitigates venereal pains; drank with an infusion of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, it stops fluxes; made into a cataplasm with the leaves of beteleira, it destroys <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> in old ulcers; and worked with oil, it cures the plica and itching.

ESCHARA

Pages 1146-1147

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of coralline, &c., the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of which are these: they are of a stony <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> coral-like <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a>, and resemble a woven cloth in their texture; and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a> informs us, that they consist of arrangements of very small cells, whose surfaces appear much in that form. Linnaeus makes it a species of millepora, in the class of lithophytes. See Plate CCCXVI. fig. 9: 10. The narrow-leaved hornwrack, fig. 9. divides as it rises, into narrow leaves made up of regular rows of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>-shaped cells placed alternately by each other, and opposite to an equal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> on the other side of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>, like an honeycomb: from these leaves proceed other still smaller foliaceous ramifications, many of which seem to be connected at the lower <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> by tubuli; as in the corallines; by which means they can ply to and fro more freely in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>.—E. Gives the natural appearance of this coralline. E represents two leaves with their tubuli and cells magnified. E 1 is a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECTION">section</a> of one of the leaves at E, showing the partition and inner form of their cells. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>-leaved hornwrack, fig. 10. when fresh taken out of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a> is of a spongy soft texture and smells very filthy; but when it has lain for some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> on the shore, it becomes stiff and horny, like some sort of withered leaves. Both surfaces, when examined by glasses, appear to be covered with cells; and, when a piece of it is cut across, one may discover the thin membrane that serves as a base to the cells of each surface. The form of the cells is very remarkable, each one being arched at the top, and contracted a little at the lower part of the sides to make way for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> of the two next adjoining cells; so that by this particular <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> no room is lost. The entrance of the cells is immediately under the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> of each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CELL">cell</a>, and the walls of the cells seem to be fortified with spines. Jussieu discovered small polypes extending themselves out of these cells, which he has described in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> of the Academy of Sciences 1742.—F. Gives the natural appearance of a leafy branch of this coralline. F is a part of a leaf magnified to show the superficial <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the cells, and the manner in which they are disposed. F 1 shows a cross section of a leaf, and discovers the several partitions of the cells. At the entrance of many of the cells a small telescopical body like a bivalve shell is discovered: F 2, the figure of the cell, with the shell in it; it is of a transparent <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBER">amber</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, so clear that one may see the dead animal through it, represented by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> spot.

ESCHEAT

Pages 1146-1146

(Encycl.) Escheat is one of the consequences of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a> in chivalry. See Feudal System, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KNIGHT">Knight</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">Service</a>, and Tenure. It is the determination of the tenure, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of the mutual bond between the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> and tenant, from the extinction of the blood of the latter by either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> or civil means: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he died without heirs of his blood, or if his blood was corrupted and stained by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TREASON">treason</a> or felony; whereby every inheritable <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> was entirely blotted out and abolished. In such <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> escheated or fell back to the lord of the fee; that is, the tenure was determined by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> of the original condition, expressed or implied in the feudal donation. In the one <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>, there were no heirs subsisting of the blood of the first feudatory or purchaser, to which heirs alone the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEUD">feud</a> extended: in the other, the tenant, by perpetrating an atrocious crime, showed that he was no longer to be trusted as a vassal, having forgotten his duty as a subject; and therefore forfeited his feud, which he held under the implied condition that he should not be a traitor or a felon. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which in both cases was, that the gift,

ESTRAY

Pages 1147-1147
or STRAY, signifies any tame beast, as sheep, oxen, swine, and horses, or swans, found within a lordship, and not owned by any man; in which case being cried, according to law, in the church, and two market towns adjoining, if it be not claimed by the owner within a year and a day, it becomes the lord's of the soil where found. If the owner claims it within the year and day, he must pay the charges of finding, keeping, and proclaiming them; and he may seize it, without telling the marks, or proving his property, which may be done at the trial if contested. If the beast stray within the year to another lordship, the first lord cannot retake it. An stray must be fed and kept, uninjured, and without labour, till it is reclaimed, or the limited time expires.

EXERCISE

Pages 1147-1147

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> affairs, (Encycl.) See also Words of Command, (Encycl.)

EYE

Pages 1147-1147

(Encycl.) A new-born child shall be observed, perhaps, never to keep its eyes fixed on any one object, but continually changing from one to another, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> you put your <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> before them, the child <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> not wink. Hence some have thought, that new-born <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a> have no sight: but this is a mistake; and the true reason why their eyes are in perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> is, that they have not yet acquired the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of examining one thing at once with their eyes: their not winking at the approach of the hand, arises from their want of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> how easily their eyes may be hurt; but in a few days they get the habit of winking, so that afterwards their eyes do it spontaneously at the approach of danger.—See a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the eye and its adjacent parts, by J. Warner. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">Artificial</a> eyes are made of concave plates of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> glass, and are stained so as to resemble the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> eye. They must, when fixed in the orbit, be taken out and cleaned every night, and replaced in the morning. If no more of a diseased eye is removed than what is preternaturally projected, or if enough is left to preserve the muscles unhurt, the artificial eye will have a little motion from the muscles that remain. If the eye does not fit well, it irritates and inflames the other eye; in which <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> lay it aside, until one can be had that fits better.

FARTHING

Pages 1147-1147

a small English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, amounting to one-fourth of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENNY">penny</a>. It was anciently called fourthing, as being the fourth of the integer <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> penny. Farthing of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a>, a coin used in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> times, containing in value the fourth <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of a noble, or 20d. silver. It is mentioned in the stat. 9 Hen. V. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 7, where it is enacted, that there shall be good and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the noble, half-noble, and farthing of gold. Farthing of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">Land</a> seems to differ from Farding-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAL">deal</a>. For in a survey-book of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MANOR">manor</a> of West-Hapton in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, there is an entry thus: A. B. holds six farthings of land at 126l. per ann. So that the farthing of land must have been a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, far more than a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOD">rood</a>.

FAWKES

Pages 1147-1148

an ingenious poet, had his school-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEEDS">Leeds</a>; from whence he was transplanted to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, where he took the degrees in arts. Entering early into holy orders, he settled first at Bramham in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, near the elegant seat of that name (Mr Lane's). which he celebrated in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> in 1745, in a 410 pamphlet anonymous. His first poetical publications were "Gawen Douglas's <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCRIPTION">Description</a> of May and Winter modernized." Removing afterwards to the curacy of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROYDON">Croydon</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURREY">Surrey</a>, he recommended himself to the notice of... FEOFFMENT. Archbishop <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERRING">Herring</a>, then resident there on account of his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, to whom besides other pieces he addressed an Ode on his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> in 1754, printed in Mr Doddley's Collection. In <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRACE">Grace</a> collated him in 1755 to the vicarage of Orpington with St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> Cray, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>; and Mr Fawkes lamented his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> in 1757 in a pathetic Elegy (styled Aurelius, first printed with his Grace's "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">Seven</a> Sermons," in 1763). He married about the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> Miss Parrier of Leeds. In April 1774, by the late Dr Plumptree's favour, he exchanged his vicarage for the rectory of Hayes. He was also one of the chaplains to the Princess Dowager of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>. He published a volume of Poems by subscription in 8vo, 1761; the "Poetical <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CALENDAR">Calendar</a>, 1763;" and "Poetical <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGAZINE">Magazine</a>, 1764," in conjunction with Mr Woty; "<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARTRIDGE">Partridge</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a>, an Eclogue, to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">Honourable</a> Cha. Yorke, 1797;" 4to, and a "Family <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>," with notes, in 4to, a compilation. But his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> strength lay in translation, in which, since Pope, few have equaled him. Witness his fragments of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MENANDER">Menander</a> (in his Poems); his "Works of Anacreon, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SAPPHO">Sappho</a>, Bion, Moschus, and Musaeus," 12mo, 1760; his "Idylls of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THEOCRITUS">Theocritus</a>," by subscription, 8vo, 1767; and his "Argonautics of Apollonius Rhodius," by subscription also, (a posthumous publication, completed by the Reverend Mr Meen of Emanuel College, Cambridge), 8vo, 1780. He died August 26, 1777.

FEOFFMENT

Pages 1148-1148

(Encycl.) A substantive derived from the verb, to enfeoff, seofare <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> insefudare, "to give one a feoff;" and therefore fefment is properly donatione feudii. It is the most <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> method of conveyance, the most solemn and public, and therefore the most easily remembered and proved. And it may properly be defined, the gift of any corporeal hereditament to another. He that so gives, or enfeoffs, is called the seoffer; and the person enfeoffed is denominated the seoffee. This is plainly derived from, or is indeed itself the very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of, the ancient feudal donation; for though it may be performed by the word "enfeoff" or "<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRANT">grant</a>," yet the aptest word of fefment is "do or dedi." And it is still directed and governed by the same feudal rules; insomuch that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> rule relating to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> and effect of the feudal grant, tenor est qui legem dat feudo, is in other words become the maxim of our <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> with relation to fefments, modus legem dat donationi. And therefore as in pure feudal donations the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a>, from whom the fend moved, must expressly limit and declare the continuance or <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of estate which he meant to confer, ne quis plus donatse praesumatur, quam in donatione exprerit; i.e., <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> one grants by fefment lands or tenements to another, and limits or expresses no estate, the grantee (due ceremonies of law being performed) hath barely an estate for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. For, as the personal abilities of the seoffee were originally presumed to be the immediate or principal inducements to the fefment, the seoffer's estate ought to be confined to his person and subsist only for his life; unless the seoffer, by express provision in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of the estate, hath given it a longer continuance. These express <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> are indeed generally made: for this was for ages the only conveyance, whereby our <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> were wont to create an estate in fee-simple, by giving the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> to the seoffee, to hold to him and his heirs for ever; though it serves equally well to convey any other estate of freehold.

FERETTO

Pages 1148-1148

(Encycl.) Another way of making feretto is as follows.
