Make a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of stratifications of plates of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> vitriol alternately in a crucible; which <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> of the glafs <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a> near the eye; and let it stand there three days; then take it out, and make a new stratification with more fresh vitriol; calcine again as before. Repeat this operation five times, and a most valuable feretto <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> be obtained.

FICUS

Pages 1148-1148

(Encycl.) That <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the fig-tree, which for many ages was so enigmatical, and which nothing but the doctrine of the sexes of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> has completely cleared up, namely, the husbandry <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> caprification, as it is called, is more particularly worthy of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, not only as a singular phenomenon in itself, but as it has furnished one of the most convincing proofs of the reality of the sexes of plants. Our limits <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> not allow us to detail this subject; in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> it is this: It is now known, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> of the fig-tree are situated within a pulpy receptacle, which we call the fig, or fruit of this tree; of these receptacles, in the wild fig-tree, some have <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> flowers only, and others have male and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a>, both distinct, though placed in the same receptacle. In the garden, or cultivated fig, these are found to contain only female flowers; which are fecundated by means of a kind of gnat bred in the fruit of the wild fig-trees, which pierces that of the cultivated, in order to deposit its eggs within; at the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> diffusing within the receptacle the farina of the male flowers. Without this operation the fruit may <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIPEN">ripen</a>, but no effective seeds are produced: hence the garden fig can only be propagated by layers and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CUTTINGS">cuttings</a>, in those countries where the wild fig is not known. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of this ripening the fruit, in the oriental countries, is not left to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, but is managed with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> art, and different degrees of dexterity, so as to reward the skilful husbandman with a much larger increase of fruit than would otherwise be produced. A tree of the same size, which, in Provence, where caprification is not practised, may produce about 25 pounds of fruit, will, by that art, in the Grecian <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, bring ten times that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>.

FINE-DRAWING

Pages 1148-1149

The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> is particularly used for a rent <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> hole happening in the dressing or preparing of a piece of cloth, artfully sewed up or mended with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SILK">silk</a>. All fine-drawings are reputed defects or blemishes, and ought to be allowed for in the price o the piece.—Hence, M. Savary establishes it as a rule, which is certainly founded on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a>, that every <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MANUFACTURER">manufacturer</a> mark the fine drawings of his cloths with a piece of packthread tied to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a>; to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> the draper to the spot; and that the draper apprize the taylor or other person to whom he sells it of the same, that he may not come to damage in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a>; there being instances of drapers condemned to take back their cloth, when cut to pieces, for omitting to mention the fine-drawings and other flaws. On this occasion M. Savary extols the procedure of an English merchant, who sending a piece of cloth damaged in one spot, to his correspondent at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, put a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> in the damaged <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, to make up the damage.—But as this example is perhaps the only one of its kind, that author recommends it to the merchant or draper to unfold all the pieces entirely as they come to him; to discover the fine-drawings and other flaws, in order to make the clothier accountable for them.

FINGAL

Pages 1149-1150
king of Morven, or ancient Caledonia. He flourished in the third century; and according to the Irish histories died in the year 283, although there is some reason from Ossian's poems for placing his death a few years latter. Fingal was descended in all probability from those Celtic tribes who were the first inhabitants of Britain. Tradition, and the poems of Ossian, give him a long line of royal ancestors, such as Combal, Trenmor, Trathal, &c., who had all reigned over the same territory. Whether this territory was bounded by the Caledonian forest, or extended somewhat farther to the south, towards the Roman province, is uncertain; but there is no doubt of its having extended over all the north and west Highlands, comprehending the Hebrides, whose petty chiefs were all subject to the king of Morven. His principal place of residence was Selma, which was probably in the neighbourhood of Glenco, supposed to be the Cona of Ossian; though some imagine it to have been in Strath-Conan in Moray. The truth seems to be, that as Fingal and his people lived by hunting, they often shifted their habitation. Hence, in all parts of the Highlands we find, in the names of places, buildings, &c., such monuments as justify their several claims for the honour of Fingal's residence. Fingal acquired great fame by his prowess in arms. He made many successful incursions into the Roman province, from whence he carried away those spoils which his son so often mentions under the names of the wine of the stranger, and the wax of the stranger. By sea we find him frequently making voyages to Scandinavia, the Orkneys, and Ireland; called by Ossian Lochlin, Inisflore, and Ullin. Several of these expeditions were celebrated by his son in epic poems, of which two only remain, Fingal and Temora. In the last of these poems, we find Fingal fighting together with his grandson Oscar. How long he lived afterwards is uncertain. He is said to have died a natural death; and therefore none of his son's poems relate to this event, though it is occasionally mentioned in many of them. "Did thy beauty last, O Ryno? Stood the strength of car-borne Oscar? Fingal himself passed away; and the halls of his fathers have forgot his steps. The blast of the north opens thy gates, O king, and I behold thee sitting on mist, dimly gleaming in all thine arms. Thy form now is not the terror of the valiant; but like a watery cloud, when we see the stars behind it, with their weeping eyes. Thy shield is like the aged moon; thy sword vapour half kindled with fire. Dim and feeble is the chief who travelled in brightness before.—But thy steps are on the winds of the desert, and the storms darken in thy hand. Thou takest the sun in thy wrath, and hidest him in thy clouds. The sons of little men are afraid, and a thousand showers descend."—Berrathon. "The character of Fingal is perhaps the most perfect that was ever drawn by a poet, for we may boldly defy all the writers of antiquity to show us any hero equal to Fingal. Throughout the whole of Ossian's works, he is presented to us in all that variety of lights which give the full display of a character. In him concur almost all the qualities that can ennoble human nature; that can either make us admire the hero, or love the man. He is not only unconquerable in war, but he makes his people happy by his wisdom in the days of peace. He is truly the father of his people. He is known by the epithet of "Fingal of the mild look," and distinguished on every occasion by humanity and generosity. He is merciful to his foes, full of affection to his children, full of concern about his friends, and never mentions Agandecca, his first love, without the utmost tenderness. He is the universal protector of the distressed; none ever went sad from Fingal.—'O Oscar! bend the strong in arms, but spare the feeble hand. Be thou a stream of many tides against the foes of thy people; but like the gale that moves the grass to those who ask thine aid; so Trenmor lived; such Trathal was; and such has Fingal been. My arm was the support of the injured; the weak relied behind the lightning of my steel.' These were the maxims of true heroism, to which he formed his grandson. His fame is represented as everywhere spread; the greatest heroes acknowledge his superiority; his enemies tremble at his name; and the highest encomiums that can be bestowed on one whom the poet would most exalt, is to say, That his soul was like the soul of Fingal. Wherever he appears, we behold the hero. The objects he pursues are always great; to bend the proud, to protect the injured, to defend his friends, to overcome his enemies by generosity more than by force. "Some strokes of human imperfection and frailty are what usually give us the most clear view and the most sensible impression of a character, because they present to us a man such as we have seen; they recall known features of human nature. When poets go beyond this range, and attempt to describe a faultless hero, they, for the most part, set before us a sort of vague undistinguishable character, such as the imagination cannot lay hold of, or realize itself as the object of affection. But Fingal, though exhibited without any of the common human failings, is nevertheless a real man; a character which touches and interests every reader." Dr Blair. We may observe, that Fingal appears to have been no less a poet than a warrior; at least in all those passages ascribed to him in the poems of his son, there is a grandeur and loftiness that elevates them above the common style even of Ossian. The following passage from the poem of Carthon may be taken as a speci- men of Fingal's poetry.—"Raise, ye bards," said the mighty Fingal, "the praise of unhappy Moina. Call her ghost, with your songs, to our hills; that she may rest with the fair of Morven, the sunbeams of other days, and the delight of heroes of old.—I have seen the walls of Balclutha, but they were defoliate. The fire had refounded in the halls; and the voice of the people is heard no more. The stream of Clutha was removed from its place by the fall of the walla. The thistle shook, there, its lonely head: the moos whiskled to the wind. The fox looked out from the windows; the rank grass of the wall waved round his head. Defoliate is the dwelling of Moina: silence is in the house of her fathers. Raise the song of mourning, O bards, over the land of strangers. They have but fallen before us; for, one day we must fall.—Why dost thou build the hall, son of the winged days? Thou lookest from thy towers to-day; yet a few years, and the blast of the distant comes; it howls in thy empty court, and whistles round thy half-worn shield.—And let the blast of the distant come! We shall be renowned in our day. The mark of my arm shall be in the battle, and my name in the song of bards. Raise the song; send round the shell; and let joy be heard in my hall. When thou, sun of heaven, shalt fail; if thou shalt fail, thou mighty light! if thy brightness is for a season, like Fingal; our fame shall survive thy beams." Such was the joy of Fingal in the day of his joy. His thousand bards leaned forward from their seats, to hear the voice of the king. It was like the music of the harp on the gale of the spring. Lovely were thy thoughts, O Fingal! Why had not Ossian the strength of thy soul? But thou standest alone, my father; and who can equal the king of Morven?"

FIRE

Pages 1150-1151

Method of securing Buildings against it.— Dr Hales proposes to check the progress of fires by covering the floors of the adjoining houses with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. The proposal is founded on an experiment which he made with a fir-board half an inch thick, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of which he covered with an inch depth of damp garden mould, and then lighted a fire on the surface of the mould: though the fire was kept up by blowing, it was two hours before the board was burnt through, and the earth prevented it from flaming. The thicker the earth is laid on the floors, the better: however, Dr Hales apprehends that the depth of an inch <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> gen- erally be sufficient; and he recommends to lay a deeper covering on the stairs, because the fire com- monly ascends by them with the greatest velocity. Mr <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HARTLEY">Hartley</a> made several trials in the years 1775 and 1776, in order to evince the efficacy of a method which he had invented for restraining the spread of fire in buildings. For this purpose thin <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> plates are well nailed to the tops of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOISTS">joists</a>, &c. the edges of the sides and ends being lapped over, folded together, and hammered <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>. Partitions, stairs, and floors, may be defended in the same manner; and plates applied to one side have been found sufficient. The plates are so thin as not to prevent the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> from being nailed in the joists, in the same manner as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> this preventative were not used; they are kept from rust by being painted <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> varnished with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> and turpentine. The expense of this addition, when extended through a whole <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, is estimated at about 5 per cent. Mr Hartley has a patent for this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> has voted a sum of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a> towards defraying the ex- pense of his numerous experiments. The same preven- tative may also be applied to ships, furniture, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MAHON">Mahon</a> has also discovered and published a very simple and effectual method of securing every kind of building against all danger of fire. This method he has divided into three parts, viz. under-flooring, extra- lathing, and inter-securing. The method of underflooring is either single or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a>: In single underflooring, a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> strong lath of oak or fir, about one-fourth of an inch thick, should be nailed against each side of every joist, and of every main tim- ber, supporting the floor which is to be secured. Other similar laths are then to be nailed along the whole length of the joists, with their ends butting against each other. The top of each of these laths or fillets ought to be at 1½ inch below the top of the joists or timbers against which they are nailed; and they will thus form a sort of small ledge on each side of all the joists. These fillets are to be well bedded in a rough <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a> here- after mentioned, when they are nailed on, so that there may be no <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> between them and the joists; and the same plaster ought to be spread with a trowel upon the tops of all the fillets, and along the sides of that part of the joists which is between the top of the fillets and the upper edge of the joists. In order to fill up the intervals between the joists that support the floor, short pieces of common laths, whose length is equal to the width of these intervals, should be laid in the con- trary <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> to the joists, and close together in a row, so as to touch one another: their ends must rest upon the fillets, and they ought to be well bedded in the rough plaster, but are not to be fastened with nails. They must then be covered with one thick coat of the rough plaster, which is to be spread over them to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the tops of the joists; and in a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> or two this plaster should be trowelled over close to the sides of the joists, without covering the tops of the joists with it. In the method of double-flooring, the fillets and short pieces of laths are applied in the manner already described; but the coat of rough plaster ought to be little more than half as thick as that in the former method. Whilst this rough plaster is laid on, some more of the short pieces of laths above-mentioned must be laid in the intervals between the joists upon the first coat, and be dipped deep in it. They should be laid as close as possible to each other, and in the same di- rection with the first layer of short laths. Over this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> layer of short laths there must be spread another coat of rough plaster, which should be trowelled level with the tops of the joists without rising above them. The rough plaster may be made of coarse lime and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>; or instead of hair, hay chopped to about three inches in length may be substituted with advantage. One <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of common rough sand, two <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> of slacked lime, and three measures of chopped hay, will form in general a very good proportion, when suffi- ciently <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> up together in the manner of common <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>. The hay should be put in after the two other ingredients are well beat up together with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>. This plaster should be made stiff; and when the floor- ing boards are required to be laid <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> very soon, a fourth or fifth part of quicklime in powder, formed by dropping a small <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of water on the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a> a little while before it is used, and well mixed with this rough plaster, will cause it to dry very fast. If any cracks appear in the rough plaster-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> near the joists when it is thoroughly dry, they ought to be closed by washing them over with a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a> wet with mortar-wash; this wash may be prepared by putting two measures of quicklime, and one of common sand, in a pail, and stirring the mixture with water till the water becomes of the consistence of a thin jelly. Before the flooring boards are laid, a small quantity of very dry common sand should be strewed over the plaster-work, and struck smooth with an hollow rule, moved in the direction of the joists, so that it may <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> rounding between each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of joists. The plaster-work and sand should be perfectly dry before the boards are laid, for fear of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DRY_ROT">dry rot</a>. The method of under-flooring may be successfully applied to a wooden stair-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>; but no sand is to be laid upon the rough plaster-work. The method of extra-lathing may be applied to ceiling joists, to sloping roofs, and to wooden partitions. The third method, which is that of inter-securing, is very similar to that of under-flooring; but no sand is afterwards to be laid upon it. Inter-securing is applicable to the same parts of a building as the method of extra-lathing, but it is seldom necessary. Lord Mahon has made several experiments in order to demonstrate the efficacy of these methods. In most houses it is only necessary to secure the floors; and the extra-expense of under-flooring, including all materials, is only about <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> pence per <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> yard, and with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of quicklime a little more. The extra-expense of extra-lathing is no more than six pence per square yard for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> side-walls and partitions; but for the ceiling about nine pence per square yard. But in most houses no extra-lathing is necessary. Fire-Eater. We have a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of mountebanks who have procured the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> and wonder of the public by eating fire, walking on fire, washing their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> in melted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and the like tricks. The most celebrated of these was our countryman Richardson, much talked of abroad. His secret, as related in the Journal des Savans, of the year 1680, consisted in a pure spirit of sulphur, wherewith he rubbed his hands, and the parts that were to touch the fire; which <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> and cauterising the epidermis, hardened and enabled the skin to resist the fire. Indeed, this is no new thing: Amb. Pare assures us he had tried it on himself, that after washing the hands in urine, and with unguentum aureum, one may safely wash them in melted lead. He adds also, that by washing his hands in the juice of onions he could bear a hot shovel on them while it melted <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-LARD">lard</a>. FLATUS. For <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a> subjuncted to Medicine, read Medicine, n° 364.

FLAX-PLANT

Pages 1151-1154

(Phormium tenax, Forst.) is a name which we may give to a plant that serves the inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-NEW_ZEALAND">New <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a> instead of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>. Of this plant there are two sorts; the leaves of both resemble those of flags, but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> are smaller, and their clusters more numerous; in one kind they are <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, and in the other a deep <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>. Of the leaves of these <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, with very little <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a>, they make all their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> apparel, and also their strings, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, and cordage, for every purpose; which are so much stronger than anything we can make with hemp, that they <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> not bear a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a>. From the same plant, by another preparation, they draw <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> slender fibres, which shine like <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, and are as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> as snow: of these, which are very strong, they make their finest cloths; and of the leaves, without any other preparation than splitting them into proper breadths, and tying the strips together, they make their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>-nets, some of which are of an enormous size. The seeds of this valuable plant have been brought over into England; but, upon <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, appeared to have lost their vegetating power. The filamentous parts of different vegetables have been employed in different countries for the same mechanic uses as hemp and flax among us. <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUTREFACTION">Putrefaction</a>, and in some <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> alkaline lixivias, destroy the pulpy <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> fleshy <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, and leave the tough filaments entire. By curiously putrefying the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> of a plant in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, we obtain the fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a> fibres, which constituted the basis of the ribs and minute veins, and which form as it were a skeleton of the leaf. In Madagascar, different kinds of cloth are prepared from the filaments of the bark of certain trees boiled in strong ley; and some of these cloths are very fine, and approach to the softness of silk, but in durability come short of cotton: others are coarser and stronger, and last thrice as long as cotton; and of these filaments they make sails and cordage to their vessels. The stalks of nettles are sometimes used for like purposes, even in France; and Sir Hans Sloane relates, in one of his letters to Mr Ray, that he has been informed by several, that muslin and calico, and most of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> linens, are made of nettles. A strong kind of cloth is said to be prepared; in some of the provinces of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, of hop-stalks; and in the Transactions of the Swedish Academy for 1750, we have an account of an experiment relating to this subject: A <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the stalks was gathered in autumn, which was equal in bulk to a quantity of flax sufficient to yield a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POUND">pound</a> after preparation. The stalks were put into water, and kept covered with it during the winter. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">March</a> they were taken out, dried in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STOVE">stove</a>, and dressed as flax. The prepared filaments weighed nearly a pound, and proved fine, soft, and white; they were spun and wove into six ells of fine strong cloth. Unless the stalks are fully rotted, which will take much longer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> than flax, the woody <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> will not separate, and the cloth will prove neither white nor fine. FLETCHER (Andrew) of Salton, a celebrated Scots patriot and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> writer, was descended from an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family who trace their origin to one of the followers of William the Conqueror. He was the son of Sir Robert Fletcher of Salton and Innerpeffer, and born in the year 1650. The tuition of our author was committed by his father, on his deathbed, to Mr. (afterwards Bishop) Burnet, then his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>-minister; by whose care he received a pious, learned, and polite <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>. Endowed with uncommon genius, and possessed of virtues and abilities peculiarly fitted to the times in which he lived, Mr Fletcher quickly shone forth the ornament of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and the champion of its freedom. Having in the course of his classical studies Fletcher studies and historical <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-READING">reading</a> been impressed with an enthusiastic admiration both of ancient and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> republics, he had early contracted an ardent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, and an aversion to arbitrary rule. Hence his spirit the more readily took alarm at certain <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">Second</a>. Being <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> of the shire for <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LOTHIAN">Lothian</a> to that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> where the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YORK">York</a> was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a>, he openly opposed the designs of that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BILL">bill</a> of accession. He had a share with <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> viscount Stair in framing the test, by which the duke of York complained that he lost Scotland. On these accounts, he became peculiarly obnoxious to the duke; and was at last obliged to flee to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, to avoid the fatal consequences of prosecutions which on various pretences were commenced against him: being cited before the privy-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> and judiciary courts, and not appearing, he was declared traitor, and his estate confiscated. In Holland he and Mr Baillie of Jerifwood were the only persons whom the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Argyle consulted concerning the designs which were then in agitation. In 1681 they came over to England, in order to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a> matters with their party in that country; and were the only two who were intrusted so far as to be admitted to the secrets of lord Russell's council of six. Mr Fletcher managed his part of the negociation with so much <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>, that administration could find no <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRETEXT">pretext</a> for seizing him: nor could they fix upon him those <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> on account of which Mr Baillie was condemned; to whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> let it be remembered, that although offered a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> on condition of his accusing his friend, he persisted in rejecting the proposal with indignation. Mr Fletcher having joined the duke of Monmouth upon his landing, received a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> command under him. But the duke was deprived of his services on the following occasion, as related by Sir John Dalrymple. Being sent upon an expedition, and not esteeming "times of danger to be times of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>," he had feigned for his own riding the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> of a country <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> [the mayor of Lynne] which stood ready equipt for its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a>. The master, hearing this, ran in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> to Fletcher, gave him opprobrious <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, shook his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANE">cane</a>, and attempted to strike. Fletcher, though rigid in the duties of morality, yet having been accustomed to foreign services both by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>, in which he had acquired <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of the honour of a soldier and a gentleman, and of the affront of a cane, pulled out his pistol, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> him dead on the spot. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> was unpopular in countries where such refinements were not understood. A clamour was raised against it among the people of the country: in a body, they waited upon the duke with their complaints; and he was forced to desire the only soldier, and almost the only <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> of parts, in his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, to abandon him. With Fletcher all Monmouth's chances of success in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> left him." But, in a manuscript memoir belonging to the family, we have the following notice concerning Mr Fletcher's connection with Monmouth, in which his separation from that prince is very differently accounted for: "To lord Marischal Mr Fletcher explained the motives which induced him first to join, and afterwards abandon, the duke of Monmouth. The former he ascribed to the duke's maiming in Scotland relating to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and in England to liberty. For the latter he accounted by the disgust produced in his own mind and that of his associates, when the duke declared himself <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>, and broke <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> with all who embarked with him on his principles. He complained heavily of the account <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> given of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the mayor of Lynne; and mentioned to Lord Marischal, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the contrary, that he did not leave the duke till he came to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TAUNTON">Taunton</a>, where he was proclaimed king, several weeks after the death of the mayor of Lynne." Seeing all the efforts of himself and his friends in favour of liberty frustrated at Taunton, he endeavoured to secure his own personal freedom by taking his passage in the first ship bound to a foreign country. It was his misfortune to land in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; where he was immediately arrested, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> into prison, and guarded by three different bands of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, till a vessel should be prepared to carry him a victim in chains to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. But on the morning before the ship could sail, whilst he looked pensively through the bars that fenced the window of his room, he was hailed by a venerable personage who made signs to speak with him. The prison-doors he found open, and whilst his friendly conductor waved to him to follow him, he passed through three different guards of soldiers all fast asleep. Without being permitted to offer his thanks to his deliverer, he found himself obliged to prosecute with all speed the journey, in which he was directed by a person concerning whom he could never collect any information; and in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a> he proceeded in safety through Spain. He felt a peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> in relating to his friends instances of the care of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> which he had experienced during his exile; and entertained them often with narratives of this kind, which he always mingled with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> reflections. Of these, another may be here mentioned. Happening in the evening to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the skirt of a wood at a few miles distance from a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> where he intended to lodge, he came to a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> met. After he had entered upon the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROAD">road</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, he was accosted by a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> of a respectable <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, who warned him to turn back, and take the road on the left; for that in the other there was danger which he could not escape <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to proceed. After which she suddenly retired into the wood, out of which she had issued no less unexpectedly. Having arrived at the city, the inhabitants were soon after alarmed by an account of the robbery and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> of several travellers who that evening had fallen into the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of a banditti upon the very way in which he had intended to travel. From these and other instances of preservation from dangers, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> of his mind, habituated from his infancy to an intercourse with heaven, led him to conclude that he was in a peculiar manner the care of Providence; and that in critical <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> his understanding received its <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> from a supernatural impulse. During his exile, he maintained a frequent and extensive correspondence with the friends of liberty at home; and he partly employed himself in making a curious collection of books, which compose the best private library in Scotland. But his genius also prompted him to engage in more <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> employments. He repaired to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, and served several campaigns as a volunteer under the duke of Lorraine with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation. At length, understanding that the great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> then projecting in Holland, and upon the issue of which he considered the liberties of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> to be suspended, had attained a considerable degree of maturity, he hastened thither; where his counsels and addresses were of eminent <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. He came over with king William; and in zeal, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>, penetration, and political skill, proved inferior to none of the leaders in the Revolution. Such, however, was his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGNANIMITY">magnanimity</a>, that from a survey of K. William's papers it appears, that while others laboured to turn this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> event to the emolument of themselves and the aggrandisement of their family, Mr Fletcher asked nothing. His estate had been forfeited, and his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> abandoned to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>; his fortune was greatly shattered, and his family reduced to circumstances of distress. Nothing was given him in recompence of all his sufferings. On the contrary, he, together with the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAMILTON">Hamilton</a>, was distinguished by marks of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> and ministerial dislike. Still, whatever private resentment he might entertain, it appeared that his ruling principle was the good of his country; and that to this grand object of his heart he was willing to sacrifice all private resentments. For when, in 1692, the abdicated king meditated an invasion, Mr Fletcher addressed a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> (preferred in Sir John Dalrymple's Collection) to the duke of Hamilton, in which every argument is employed with skill and energy to engage his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRACE">Grace</a> to forget his injuries, and in the present crisis to employ the extensive influence and authority he then possessed in the cause of freedom and of his country. This letter produced its full effect; and the duke returned to his duty, from which he had in part declined. To follow our author through all the mazes of his political <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> subsequent to the Revolution, is beyond our purpose, and would exceed our limits. One or two circumstances more shall therefore suffice. Being elected a member for the parliament 1683, he showed an uniform zeal for the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of his country. The thought of England's domineering over Scotland was what his generous <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> could not endure. The indignities and opprobrium which Scotland lay under galled him to the heart; so that in his learned and elaborate discourses, he exposed them with undaunted courage and pathetic eloquence.—In that great event, the Union, he performed essential service. He got the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of security passed, which declared that the two crowns should not pass to the same head till Scotland was secured in her liberties civil and religious. Therefore lord Godolphin was forced into the Union, to avoid a civil war after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEMISE">demise</a>. Although Mr Fletcher disapproved of some of the articles, and indeed of the whole frame of the Union; as the act of security was his own <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, he had all the merit of that important transaction. We must not omit mentioning, that in the ardour of his political <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAREER">career</a> Mr Fletcher forgot not the interests of the place that gave him birth. He esteemed the education of youth one of the noblest objects of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. On this subject he wrote a treatise, still extant, most characteristic of himself; and he established at Salton a foundation for the same purpose, of great utility while it lasted. This great man died at London in 1716, aged 66. His remains were conveyed to Scotland, and deposited in the family vault at Salton. That Mr Fletcher received neither honours nor emoluments from king William, may perhaps be in part attributed to himself; a circumstance, however, which must add greatly to the lustre of his character. His uncompromising virtue, and the sternness of his principles, were ill calculated to conciliate courtly favour. He was too zealous an adherent of the liberties of the people, that he was too jealous of the growing power of all princes; in whom he thought ambition so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>, that he was not for trusting the best of kings with the power which ill ones might make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of against their subjects: he was of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that all princes were made by, and for the benefit of, the people; and that they should have no power but that of doing good. This, which made him oppose king Charles and invade king James, led him also to oppose the giving so much power to king William, whom he would never serve after his establishment. So we are told by the author of Short political <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">Characters</a>, a MS. in the library of the late T. Rawlinson, Esq.—Mr Lockhart, in his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a>, p. 72, expresses a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> that his aversion to the English and to the Union was so great, that, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> to them, he was inclined to side with the abdicated family: "But (adds he) as that was a subject not fit to be entered upon with him, this is only a conjecture from some innuendos I have heard him make: but so far is certain, he liked, commended, and conversed with high-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> Tories, more than any other set of men; acknowledging them to be the best countrymen, and of most honour, integrity, and ingenuity." It seems difficult to reconcile this with Mr Fletcher's avowed principles and the general tenor of his conduct. May we suppose, that chagrin, if not at the neglect or the ill treatment which he had himself received from government since the Revolution, yet at the public measures relating to his native country, might have occasioned him to relent in his sentiments with regard to the exiled family?—In the family-memoirs already quoted, we are informed, That "Lord Marischal held Mr Fletcher's character in high admiration;" and that, "when governor of Neufchatel, where Rousseau resided about the year 1766, he prevailed with this very extraordinary genius to write the life of a man whose character and actions he wished to have transmitted to posterity with advantage. For this purpose, his lordship applied to an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> relation of Mr Fletcher's for materials, which by him were transmitted to lord Marischall: but the design failed through Rousseau's desultory and capricious disposition." This anecdote must appear incompatible with the known loyalty and attachments of the Earl Marischal, unless we suppose him to have been privy to some such sentiments of Mr Fletcher, as those alluded to by Mr Lockhart: for how could we suppose him anxious to promote a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, in which the task would be to celebrate principles diametrically opposite to his own, and to applaud actions subversive of that royal family in whose cause he had ventured his life, and forfeited his fortune, and forgone his country!—But however these circumstances may be reconciled,—as the integrity, disinterestedness, and public spirit of Mr Fletcher, have been universally acknowledged, there is reason to believe, that all his sentiments and actions were were founded in honour, and that he never once pursued a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> further than he judged it to be for the interest of his country. Mr Fletcher was master of the English, Latin, Greek, French, and Italian languages; and well versed in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the civil <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and all kinds of learning. In his travels, he had not only acquired considerable knowledge in the art of war, but also became versed in the respective interests of the several princes and states of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. In private life, he was affable to his friends, and free from all manner of vice. He had a penetrating, clear, and lively <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a>; but is said to have been too much wedded to opinions, and impatient of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a>.—He possessed an uncommon elevation of mind, accompanied with a warmth of temper, which would suffer him to brook from no <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a> among men, nor in any place, an indignity. Of this he exhibited a singular proof in the Scots parliament. The Earl of Stair, secretary of state and minister for Scotland, having in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of debate used an improper <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> against Mr Fletcher, he seized him by his robe, and inflicted upon public and immediate satisfaction. His Lordship was obliged instantly to beg his pardon in presence of parliament. Mr Fletcher was by far the finest speaker in the parliament of Scotland: the earl of Stair alone rivalled him. The latter was famed for a splendid, the former for a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> and nervous eloquence. He formed his style on the models of antiquity; and the small volume of his works, Sir John Dalrymple observes, tho' imperfectly collected, is one of the very few classical compositions in the English language. FLOS masculus, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, a flower which contains the stamen, reckoned by the sexalists the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> organ of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>; but not the stigma or female organ. All the plants of the clas diecea Linnaeus have male and female flowers upon different roots: those of the clas monoceca bear flowers of different sexes on the same root. The plants, therefore, of the former are only male and female; those of the latter are androgynous; that is, contain a mixture of both male and female flowers.

FOSSILS

Pages 1154-1154

(Encycl.) The adventitious <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> extraneous fossils, or those which include the subterraneous exuviae of different <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> animals, and even vegetables, as shells, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, leaves, stalks, &c. which are found buried in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> abundance in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, have employed the curiosity of several of our latest naturalists, who have each their several system to account for the surprising appearances of petrified sea-fishes, in places far more remote from the sea, and on the tops of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>; shells in the middle of quarries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; and of elephants teeth, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of divers animals, peculiar to the southern climates, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> only growing in the east, found fossil in our northern and western parts. See Plate CCCXVII. Some <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> have these shells, &c. to be real <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and stone plants, formed after the usual manner of other figured stones; of which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> is our learned Dr Lister. Another opinion is, that these fossil shells, with all other foreign bodies found within the earth, as bones, trees, plants, &c. were buried therein at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the universal deluge; and that, having been penetrated either by the bituminous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> abounding chiefly in watery places, or by the salts of the earth, they have been preserved entire, and sometimes petrified. Others think, that those shells, found at the tops of the highest mountains, could never have been carried thither by the waters, even of the deluge; inasmuch as most of these aquatic animals, on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of their shells, always remain at the bottom of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and never move but <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> along the ground. They imagine, that a year's continuance of the waters of the deluge, intermixed with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a> waters of the sea, upon the surface of the earth, might well give occasion to the production of shells of diverse kinds in different climates; and that the universal saltness of the water was the real cause of their resemblance to the sea-shells, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> formed daily by the retention of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> water produce different kinds. Others think, that the waters of the sea, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, with those which fell from heaven, turned the whole surface of the earth upside <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a>; after the same manner as the waters of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LOIRE">Loire</a>, and other rivers, which roll in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> bottom, overturn all their sands, and even the earth itself, in their swellings and inundations; and that in this general subversion, the shells came to be interred here, fishes there, trees there, &c. But nobody has set this system in a better <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> than Dr Woodward, in his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Earth. That author, pursuing and improving the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a> of Dr Burnet, maintains the whole <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of earth, with every thing belonging thereto, to have been so broken and dissolved at the time of the deluge, that a new earth was then formed in the bosom of the water, consisting of different <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STRATA">strata</a>, or beds of terrestrial matter, ranged over each other usually according to the order of their specific gravities. By this means, plants, animals, and especially fishes and shells, not yet dissolved among the rest, remained mixed and blended among the mineral and fossil matters; which preserved them, or at least assumed and retained their figures and impressions either indentedly, or in relievo.

FOTHERGILL

Pages 1154-1155

a late eminent physician, was born in 1712, at Wentley-dale in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>. His father had been bred to the profession of husbandry, and occupied a small estate of his own in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a> was the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> of five children (four sons and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>), and received his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> in the seminary belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUAKERS">Quakers</a>; and afterwards served his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> to one Mr Bartlett an apothecary at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRADFORD">Bradford</a>. From thence he removed to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and became a pupil of Dr (afterwards Sir Edward) Wilmot, at St Thomas's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOSPITAL">Hospital</a>. He then went to the university of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, where he took his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> in 1736. From Edinburgh he went to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>; whence, after a short stay, he returned to London, and began to practise physic about the year 1740, in a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">White</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HART">hart</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">Court</a>, Lombard-street, where he resided during the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and acquired most of his fortune. In 1744 he was admitted a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LICENTIATE">licentiate</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of physicians in London; and in 1754 a fellow of that of Edinburgh, to which he was a considerable benefactor. He afterwards became a member of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Medical <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, ris, and a member both of the Royal and Antiquarian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOCIETIES">Societies</a>. He <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> his practice with unremitting <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> and success, till his illness, during the two last years of his life, obliged him to give up a considerable part of it. The disorder which hastened his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, was a scirrhus of the prostate gland, and an obstruction in the bladder, in which were found two quarts of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> after his decease. This had been gradually coming upon him for six years, by reason of his delicacy, which made him unwilling to alight often from his carriage; and when, after his temporary <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> from it the year before he died, he submitted to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> relief in his carriage, it was too late. He died in his house in Harpur-street, Dec. 26. 1780. Dr Fothergill, besides his attention to medicine, had imbibed an early <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, which was improved by his friend Mr Collinson. He was for many years a valuable contributor to the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">Gentleman</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGAZINE">Magazine</a>; which, in return, considerably assisted his rising fame. His observations on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">Weather</a> and Diseases were begun in 1751, and continued monthly for some years. He did not add to the medical art any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> valuable improvements. His pamphlet on the Ulcerous Sore Throat is in every respect the best of his performances, and owes much of its merit to the information of the late Drs Leatherland and Sylvester. It was first printed in 1748, on the reappearance of that fatal disorder, which, in 1739, had carried off the two sons of Mr Pelham. At the expense of Dr Fothergill also was made and published a new translation of the whole <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>, by Anthony Perrier a Quaker, who, by his own industry, acquired a knowledge of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, Greek, and Latin languages. This publication is said to have cost the Doctor not less than 2000l. It appeared in 1764 in two vols folio; and in 1780 was published an edition of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAN">Dean</a> Percy's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KEY">Key</a> to the New <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, adapted to the use of a seminary of young Quakers at Ackworth, near <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEEDS">Leeds</a> in Yorkshire. This was founded in 1778 by the society, who purchased by subscription, in which Dr Fothergill's name stood foremost, the house and estate of 30 acres possessed by the Foundling Hospital, but which they found inconvenient for their purpose on account of distance. The Doctor first projected this on the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of a smaller <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> of the same kind at Gildersome. He also endowed it handsomely by his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a>. It now contains above 300 children of both sexes, who are fed and instructed. The fortune acquired by Dr Fothergill was immense; and, taking all things together, the computation cannot be less than 80,000l. His business, when in full practice, was valued at 7000l. a-year. In the influenza of 1775 and 1776, he is said to have had 60 patients daily on his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a>, and his profit was estimated at 8000l.—When the infirmities of old <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> obliged him to relax his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> attention to business, he quitted his house in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and resided in Harpur-street, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">Red</a>-lion <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">Square</a>. He also furnished himself with a pleasant retreat at Upton, which he used to visit on Saturdays during the winter, and sometimes more frequently in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. For several years before his death he was accustomed to retire in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> to Lea-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HALL">Hall</a>, a pleasant estate in the neighbourhood of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MIDDLEWICH">Middlewich</a>, which he rented from Sir John <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEICESTER">Leicester</a>. He generally resided at this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> till the latter end of September; and while here took no fees, but used to go once a-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> to an inn at Middlewich, and prescribe gratis to all who applied to him. Dr Fothergill's character was excellent. A transaction, indeed, with regard to one Dr Leeds gave occasion to some of his enemies to blame him; but how unjustly, has been abundantly shown by his biographers, Dr Elliot and Dr Lettsome. Dr Fothergill wrote a considerable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of Tracts, which are now collected into one vol. &c., by Dr Elliot. He sometimes wrote in the newspapers, and is said to have been the author of more than 100 letters in the Gazetteer concerning the New Pavement.

FRAXINELLA

Pages 1155-1155

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>. See DICTAMNUS (Encycl.)—It is remarkable of this odoriferous plant, that, when in full blossom, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> which surrounds it in a still night, may be inflamed by the approach of a lighted <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a>. Dr Watson doubts whether this inflammability proceeds from an inflammable air which is exhaled by the plant, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> from some of the finer parts of the essential <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of the plant being dissolved in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> atmospherical air. The latter is the most probable supposition; for were it the pure inflammable air, as Mr Cavalli observes, it would, on account of its small specific gravity, leave the plant as soon as it was produced. Common air acquires the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of becoming inflammable, by being transmitted through several essential oils.

FRENUM

Pages 1155-1155

in anatomy, the same with the ligamentum annulare, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> annular ligament.—This name is given to a ligament on each ankle and each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WRIST">wrist</a>, and this more on account of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> than their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. They <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIDLE">bridle</a> the tendons of the muscles which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through them.

FROST

Pages 1155-1156

(Encycl.) The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> power of frost on vegetables is a thing insufficiently known; but the differences between the frosts of a severe winter, and those which happen in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> mornings, in their effects on <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> and trees, were never perfectly explained, till by M. Du Hamel and Buffon in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> Academy. The frosts of severe winters are much more terrible than those of the spring, as they bring on a privation of all the products of the tenderer <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the vegetable world; but then they are not frequent, such winters happening perhaps but once in an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; and the frosts of the spring are in reality greater injuries to us than these, as they are every year repeated. In regard to trees, the great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> is this, that the frosts of severe winters affect even their wood, their trunks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> branches; whereas those of the spring have only power to hurt the buds. The winter frosts happening at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> when most of the trees in our woods and gardens have neither leaves, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, nor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> upon them, and have their buds so hard as to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> against slight injuries of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, especially <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the preceding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> has not been too wet; in this state, if there are no unlucky circumstances attending, the generality of trees bear moderate winters very well; but hard frosts, which happen late in the winter, cause very great injuries even to those trees which they do not utterly destroy. These are, 1. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a> cracks following the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the fibres. 2. Parcels of dead wood inclosed round with wood yet in a living state. And, 3. That di- flemperature which the foresters call the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> blea, which is a perfect circle of blea, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> soft <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> wood, which, when the tree is afterwards felled, is found cov- ered by a circle of hard and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> wood. The opinions of authors about the expositions of trees to the different <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, have been very differ- ent, and most of them grounded on no rational foun- dation. Many are of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that the effects of frost are most violently felt on those trees which are exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>; and others think the south or the west the most strongly affected by them. There is no doubt but the north exposure is subject to the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a>. It does not, however, follow from this, that the injury must be always greatest on the trees expo- sed to the north in frosts: on the contrary, there are abundant proofs that it is on the south side that trees are generally more injured by frost: and it is plain from repeated experiments, that there are particular accidents, under which a more moderate frost may do more injury to vegetables, than the most severe one which happens to them under more favourable circum- stances. It is plain from the accounts of the injuries trees re- ceived by the frosts in 1709, that the greatest of all were owing to repeated false thaws, succeeded by repeated new frosts. But the frosts of the spring-season furnish abundantly more numerous examples of this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>; and some experiments made by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> de Buffon, at large in his own woods, prove incontrovertibly, that it is not the severest cold, or most fixed frost, that does the greatest injury to vegetables. This is an observation directly opposite to the com- mon opinion; yet it is not the least true, nor is it any way discordant to reason. We find by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of experiments, that humidity is the thing that makes frost fatal to vegetables; and therefore every thing that can occasion humidity in them, exposes them to these injuries, and every thing that can prevent or take off an over proportion of humidity in them, every thing that can dry them, though with ever so increas- ed a cold, must prevent or preserve them from these injuries. Numerous experiments and observations tend to prove this. It is well known that vegetables al- ways feel the frost very desperately in low places where there are fogs. The plants which stand by a river side are frequently found destroyed by the spring and au- tumnal frosts, while those of the same <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, which stand in a drier <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, suffer little, or perhaps not at all by them; and the low and wet parts of forests are well known to produce worse wood than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and drier. The coppice wood in wet and low parts of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> woods, though it push out more vigorously at first than that of other places, yet never comes to so good a growth; for the frost of the spring killing these early top-shoots, obliges the lower part of the trees to throw out lateral branches: and the same thing happens in a greater or lesser <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> to the cop- pice wood that grows under cover of larger trees in great forests; for here the vapours not being carried off either by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, stagnate and freeze, and in the same manner destroy the young shoots, as the fogs of marshy places. It is a general observation also, that the frost is never hurtful to the late shoots of the vine, or to the flower-buds of trees, except when it follows heavy dews, or a long rainy season, and then it never fails to do great mischief, tho' it be ever so slight. The frost is always observed to be more mischievous in its consequences on newly cultivated ground than in other places; and this is because the vapors which continually arise from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, find an easier passage from those places than from others. Trees also which have been newly cut, suffer more than others by the spring frosts, which is owing to their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a> out more vigorously. Frosts also do more damage on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> grounds, than on the tougher and firmer soils, suppos- ing both equally dry; and this seems partly owing to their being more early in their productions, and par- tly to their lax texture suffering a greater <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of vapors to transpire. It also has been frequently observed, that the side- shoots of trees are more subject to perish by the spring frosts than those from the top; and M. Buffon, who examined into this with great accuracy, always found the effects of the spring frosts much greater near the ground than elsewhere. The shoots within a foot of the ground quickly perished by them; those which stood at two or three feet high, bore them much bet- ter; and those at four feet and upwards frequently re- mained wholly unhurt, while the lower ones were entirely destroyed. There are a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of observations, which have pro- ved beyond all doubt, that it is not the hard frosts which do much hurt plants, as those frosts, that less severe, which happen when they are full of moisture; and this clearly explains the account of all the great damages done by the severe frosts being on the south side of the trees which are affected by them, tho' that side has been plainly all the while less cold than the north. Great damage is also done to the western sides of trees and plantations, when after a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> with a west wind the wind turns about to the north at sun-set, as is frequently the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, or when an east wind blows upon a thick fog before sun-rising.

FUCUS

Pages 1156-1159

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, a genus of the order of algae, belonging to the cryptogamia class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. The most remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> are, 1. The ferratus, ferrated fucus, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-wrack. This is frequent at all seasons of the year upon the rocks at low- <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> mark, but produces its seeds in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> and August. It consists of a flat, radical, and dichotomous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>, about two feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>; the branches half an inch wide, ferrated on the edges with dents of unequal size, and at unequal distances, having a flat-stalk or rib divided like the leaf, and running in the middle of it through all its various ramifications. A small species of coralline, called by Linnaeus Sertularia pumila, frequently creeps along the leaf. All the species of fucus afford a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of impure alkaline <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>; but this much less than some others, eight ounces of the ashes yielding only three of fixed salt. The Dutch cover their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CRABS">crabs</a> and lob- sters with this fucus to keep them alive and moist; and prefer it to any other, as being destitute of those mucous vesicles with which some of the rest abound, and which would sooner ferment and become putrid. 2. The vesiculofus, bladder fucus, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> sea-wrack, or sea-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WARE">ware</a>. It grows in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> abundance on the sea-rocks about low-water mark; producing its fructifications in July and August. It has the same <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and sub- stance flance as the foregoing; but differs from it in the following respects: The edges of the leaf have no serratures, but are quite entire. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISC">disc</a> or surface are immersed hollow, spherical, or oval <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>-bladders, hairy within, growing generally in pairs, but often single in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> of the branches, which are most probably air-bladders, destined to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUOY">buoy</a> up the plant in the water. Lastly, on the summits or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> segments of the leaves, appear tumid vesicles about three <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of an inch long, sometimes oval and in pairs, sometimes single and bifid, with a clear viscid mucus interpenetrated with downy hairs.—This species is an excellent manure for <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>; for which purpose it is often applied in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> parts of Scotland and other countries. In the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JURA">Jura</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SKYE">Skye</a> it frequently serves as a winter-food for cattle, which regularly come <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the shores at the receds of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TIDES">tides</a> to seek for it.
