And sometimes even the flags have been observed, after a storm, to descend from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> to the sea-sides to feed upon this plant. Linnaeus informs us, that the inhabitants of Gothland in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> boil this fucus in water, and mixing therewith a little coarse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> or flour feed their hogs with it; for which reason they call the plant svintang. And in Scania, he says, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> people cover their cottages with it, and sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> it for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>. In Jura, and some other of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEBRIDES">Hebrides</a>, the inhabitants dry their cheeses without salt, by covering them with the ashes of this plant; which abounds with such quantity of salts, that from five ounces of the ashes may be procured two ounces and a half of fixed alkaline salts, that is, half of their whole <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. But the most beneficial use to which the fucus vesiculosus is applied, in the way of economy, is in making pot-ash or kelp, a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> much practised in the western isles. There is great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in the goodness and price of this commodity, and much care and skill required in properly making it. That is esteemed the best which is hardest, finest grain'd, and free from sand or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. The price of kelp in Jura is 3l. 10s. per ton, and about 40 or 50 tons are exported annually from that <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. So great a value is set upon this fucus by the inhabitants of that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, that they have sometimes thought it worth their while to roll fragments of rocks and huge <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a> into the sea, in order to invite the growth of it. Its virtues in the medical way have been much celebrated by Dr Russel, in his Dissertation concerning the use of Sea-water in the Diseases of the Glands. He found the saponaceous liquor or mucus in the vesicles of this plant to be an excellent reolvent, extremely serviceable in dispersing all scrofulous and seropulous swellings of the glands. He recommends the patient to rub the tumour with these vesicles bruised in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> till the mucus has thoroughly penetrated the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a>, and afterwards to wash with sea-water. Or otherwise, to gather two pounds of the tumid vesicles, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of July, when they are full of mucus, and infuse them in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-QUART">quart</a> of sea-water, in a glaas vessel, for the space of 15 days, when the liquor <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> have acquired nearly the consistence of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>. Then strain it off through a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> cloth, and rub this liquor with the hand, as before, three or four times a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> upon any hard or seropulous swellings, washing, the parts afterwards with sea-water, and nothing can be more efficacious to disperse them. Even scirrhosities, he says, in women's breasts, have been dispelled by this treatment. The same author, by calcining the plant in the open air, made a very <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> salt powder, which he called vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a>; a medicine much in use as a reolvent and deoblituent, and recommended also as an excellent dentifrice, to correct the scrofulous laxity of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUMS">gums</a>, and take off the foulness of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>. 3. The plicatus, matted, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a>-grass fucus, grows on the sea-shores in many places both of Scotland and England. It is generally about three or four, but sometimes six inches long. Its colour, after being exposed to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and air, yellowish, or auburn. Its substance pellucid, tough, and horny, so as to bear a strong resemblance to what the anglers call Indian grass, that is, the tendrils issuing from the ovary of the dog-fish. 4. The palmatus, palmated, or sweet fucus, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called dulce, or dills. This grows plentifully on the sea-coasts of Scotland, and the adjoining islands. Its substance is membranaceous, thin, and pellucid; the colour <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>, sometimes green with a little mixture of red; its length generally about five or six inches, but varies from three inches to a foot; its manner of growth fan-shaped, or gradually dilated from the base upwards. Its divisions extremely various. The inhabitants both of Scotland and England take <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> in eating this plant, without expecting any medical virtues from it. The inhabitants of the Archipelago also are fond of this plant, as we learn from Steller. They sometimes eat it raw, but esteem it most when added to ragouts, oglios, &c. to which it gives a red colour; and, dissolving, renders them thick and gelatinous. In the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of Skye it is sometimes used in fevers to promote a sweat, being boiled in water with the addition of a little <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>. In this manner it also frequently purges. The dried leaves, infused in water, exhale the scent of violets. 5. The esculentus, eatable fucus, or bladder-locks, commonly called tangle in Scotland, is likewise a native of the British shores. It is commonly about four feet long, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> or eight inches wide, but is sometimes found three yards or more in length, and a foot in width. Small specimens are not above a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUBIT">cubit</a> long, and two inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. The substance is thin, membranaceous, and pellucid; the colour green or olive. The root consists of tough, cartilaginous fibres. The stalk is about six inches long, and half an inch wide, nearly <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, and pinnated in the middle, between the root and origin of the leaf, with ten or a dozen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of thick, cartilaginous, oval-obtuse, foliaceous ligaments, each about two inches long, and crowded together. The leaf is of an oval-lanceolate, or long elliptic form, simple and undivided, waved on the edges, and widely ribbed in the middle from bottom to top, the stalk running through its whole length, and standing out on both sides of the leaf. This fucus is eaten in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> both by men and cattle. Its proper season is in the month of September, when it is in greatest perfection. The membranous part is rejected, and the stalk only is eaten. It is recommended in the disorder called a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PICA">pica</a>, to strengthen the stomach and restore the appetite. 6. The fucarina, sweet fucus, or sea-belt, is very common on the sea-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a>. The substance of this is cartilaginous and leathery; and the leaf is quite ribbed. By these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> it is distinguished from the preceding, to which it is nearly allied. It consists only of one simple, linear, elliptic leaf, of a tawny green colour, about five feet long, and three inches wide, in its full-grown state; but varies so exceedingly as to be found from a foot to four yards in length. The ordinary length of the stalk is two inches, but it varies even to a foot. The root is composed of branched fibres, which adhere to the stones like claws. This plant is often infested with the furtaria ciliata. The inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ICELAND">Iceland</a> make a kind of pottage of this fucus; <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> it in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, and eating it with a spoon. They also soak it in fresh water, dry it in the sun, and then lay it up in wooden vessels, where in a short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> it is covered with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> efflorescence of sea-salt, which has a sweet <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> like <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>. This they eat with butter; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> taken in too great a quantity, the salt is apt to irritate the bowels and bring on a purging. Their cattle feed and get fat upon this plant, both in its recent and dry state; but their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> acquires a bad flavour. It is sometimes eaten by the common people on the coast of England, being boiled as a pot-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERB">herb</a>. 7. The ciliatus, ciliated, or ligulatus fucus, is found on the shores of Jona and other places, but is not common. The colour of this is red, the substance membranous and pellucid, without rib or nerve; the ordinary height of the whole plant about four or five inches. It is variable in its appearance, according to the different stages of its growth. This fucus is eaten by the Scotch and Irish promiscuously with the fucus palmatus or dilfe. 8. The pinnatisidus, jagged fucus, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>-dilfe, is frequent on sea-rocks which are covered by the tides, both on the eastern and western coasts. It is of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> olive-colour, often tinged with red. The substance is cartilaginous, but yet tender and transparent; the height about two or three inches. This fucus has a hot taste in the mouth, and is therefore called pepper-dilfe by the people in Scotland, who frequently eat it as a salad in the same manner they do the fucus palmatus. 9. The placanium, or pectinated fucus, is frequent on the sea-rocks, and in basins of water left by the recedes of the tides. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> colour is a most beautiful bright red or purple, but is often variegated with white or yellow. Its substance is cartilaginous, but extremely thin, delicate, and transparent. Its height commonly about three or four inches. The stalk is compressed, about half a line in diameter, erect, but waved in its growth, and divided almost from the base into many widely expanded branches. These primary branches are very long, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a>, exactly like the stalk, and subdivided into alternate secondary branches, which are again frequently compounded in like manner, and these divisions decorated with subulate teeth growing in alternate rows, curiously pectinated or finely toothed on the upper side like a comb, the smallest of these teeth scarcely visible to the naked eye. The fructifications are minute spherical capsules, or smooth dark-red globules, scattered without order on the sides of the branches; generally sessile, but some few of them supported on short peduncles. This fucus, on account of its elegant colours and fine divisions, is the species most admired by the ladies who are fond of pictures and mimic landscapes composed of marine vegetables. 10. The filum, thread-fucus, or sea-laces, is found on the sea-rocks, and waving under the water like long strings, frequent on many parts of the coast. The substance of this is opaque and cartilaginous, but not difficult to be broken. The colour, when recent, a dull olive-green; when dry, fulvous, or nearly black; and when exposed for some time on the shores to the sun and air, it becomes yellow, straw-coloured, or white. It consists only of a simple, unbranched, naked, cylindrical stalk, three or four yards long, more or less, from the size of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> fiddle-string to that of a thick whip-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CORD">cord</a>; smallest at the base and summit; smooth on the outside, full of mucus within; often twisted, and always intercepted by numerous transverse diaphragms, visible when the plant is held between the eye and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. The fructifications have not yet been discovered; but from the transverse septa in its structure, it is reasonable to suppose this plant to belong rather to the genus of conferva than that of fucus. The stalks, skinned when half dry and twisted, acquire to considerable <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of strength and toughness, that we were informed the Highlanders sometimes used them for the same intentions as Indian grass. 11. The giganteus, or gigantic fucus, is a native of the Straits Le Maire; and grows on rocky ground, which in those countries is distinguished from sand or ooze. ooze by the enormous length of the sea-weeds that grow upon it. The leaves are four feet long, and some of the stalks, though not thicker than a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s thumb, are 120. Mr Banks and Dr Solander found over some of them which were 84 feet long; and as they made a very acute <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> with the bottom, they were thought to be at least one half longer.

FULGORA

Pages 1159-1159

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a>, a genus of insects belonging to the order of hemiptera; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of which are. The frons, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> fore-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the head, is drawn extended and empty. The antennae are seated below the eyes, having two articulations, whereof the exterior is larger, and of a globular form. The rostrum is inflected, or bent inwards under the body. The feet are made for walking. There are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, the most remarkable of which is the lanternae. See <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANTERN">Lantern</a>-Fly, (Encycl.) and Plate CCCXIII.

FUNGI

Pages 1159-1159

(Encycl.) The piperatus, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>-agric, though the most acid and suspicious of the whole tribe, is eaten in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities by the Russians. They fill <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> vessels with them in the autumn, season or pickle them with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, and eat them in the ensuing <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LENT">Lent</a>. But as the free <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of these and others of the genus has frequently been attended with fatal consequences, it may not be amiss in this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, once for all, to admonish the reader of the general <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and dangerous qualities of them; which we cannot do better than in the words of the great and ingenious Haller. "All fungi are crude in their nature, of speedy growth and sudden decay. They <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> up, arrive at maturity, and perish in a few days, most of them dissolving away in a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> corrupted liquor, of a fetid nauseous smell. They are the food of snails, beetles, flies, maggots, and the nidus where they deposit their young. "The Russians indeed devour almost every <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, even those which other nations esteem the most poisonous, such as the agaricus muiarius, piperatus, &c.; but all of them are a doubtful and suspicious food, and the most innocent have proved sometimes prejudicial. "By <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a> it is found, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> parts of eight in their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> are watery. They yield by fire a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> spirit like hartshorn, a yellow empyreumatic <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and a dry, volatile, crystalline salt; so that their nature is evidently alkaline, extremely prone to corruption. "Their fibres are tough and very difficult to digest, swelling in the stomach like a sponge; so that there are instances of their remaining undigested for three days before their bad effects have appeared. The maladies they occasion are, a swelling of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a>, restlessness, heartburns, vomitings, colics, difficult breathings, hiccoughs, melancholy, diarrhoeas accompanied with a tenesmus, and gangrenes. To which dreadful complaints the acrimonious <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of some fungi bring on, besides, inflammations in the mouth, with bloody lotions and bloody stools. Lastly, it is certain that some species have an intoxicating quality, followed often by deliriums, tremblings, watchings, faintings, apoplexies, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> sweats, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> itself. Some have fancied that skilful cookery would deprive them of their bad effects, and that oils would heal their noxious qualities; but these are fatal deceits, not to be trusted. "To persons suffering from eating any species of fungi, the most approved and speedy remedy is to use emetics and cathartics."

FURIA

Pages 1159-1159

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a>, a genus of insects belonging to the order of vermes zoophyta. There is but one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, viz. the infernalis. This has a linear smooth body ciliated on each side, with reflexed feelers prehended to its body. In <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FINLAND">Finland</a>, Bothnia, and the northern provinces of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, it was not unfrequently that people were seized with a pungent pain, confined to a point, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> other exposed <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the body, which presently increased to a most excruciating <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, and hath sometimes been suddenly fatal. This disorder was more particularly observed in Finland, especially about boggy and marshy places, and always in autumn. At length it was discovered that this pain instantly succeeded somewhat that dropped out of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and in a moment penetrated and buried itself in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>. The Finlanders had tried variety of applications to no purpose, until at length a poultice of curds or cheese was found the most effectual in easing the pain; and the event confirmed that the insect was allured by this application to leave the flesh; as, on its removal, this worm, no longer than the sixth of an inch, was found in it, and thus the cause of this painful <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> explained. But by what means this creature is raised into the air, is as yet unknown.

GARDENS

Pages 1159-1160

in antiquity, gardens raised on <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEBUCHADNEZZAR">Nebuchadnezzar</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a>, in order to gratify his wife Amytis, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASTYAGES">Astyages</a> king of Media. Q. Curtius makes them equal in height to the walls of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>, viz. 50 feet. They contained a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> of 400 feet on every side, and were carried up into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> in several terraces laid above one another, and the ascent from terraces to terraces was by stairs 10 feet wide. The arches sustaining the whole pile were raised above one another, and it was strengthened by a wall, surrounding it on every side, of 22 feet in thickness. The floors of each of the terraces were laid in the following manner: on the top of the arches were first laid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> flat <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a> 16 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and 4 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and over them was a layer of reed mixed with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of bitumen, over which were two rows of bricks closely cemented together by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a>, and over all were laid thick sheets of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>; and lastly, upon the lead was laid the mould of the garden. The mould <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> was of such a depth as to admit the largest trees to take root and grow; and it was covered with various kinds of trees, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>. flowers. In the upper terraces there was an aqueduct or engine, whereby <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> was drawn up out of the river for watering the whole garden.

GAS

Pages 1160-1160

(Encycl.) The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of aerial vapours <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> gases, is a subject which has drawn the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of the curious, though little can be known with precision. What can be known with any <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> is drawn entirely from the effects of latent <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> upon terrestrial bodies. By means of this element almost all substances become for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> aeriform; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they do not constantly remain so, it is because of their inability to absorb the heat in a permanent manner. From <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a>, however, we must be apt to conclude, that those aerial <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a> which continue permanently <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> are formed in like manner by the union of a vast <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of latent heat with some small portion of terrestrial <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, in such a manner that they cannot afterwards be separated, at least so easily as the latent heat of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> aqueous or other vapours is absorbed. This <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> be in some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> confirmed by the two following considerations. 1. There is no kind of aerial vapour which does not expand by heat to a very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> degree. Terrestrial bodies, whose texture is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a>, expand but little by heat. These, we know, are formed of a great quantity of inactive matter, together with a very fine invisible fluid with which their pores are filled. The expansion probably takes <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> by means of an agitation in this fluid excited by heat. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">Air</a> is exceedingly expansible; whence its terrestrial particles are probably few in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, while the quantity of fluid interposed betwixt them is very great. 2. All kinds of air seem to be produced from some terrestrial matter and heat, at least heat in some way or other seems to be concerned in the formation of all that are yet known. In the first <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> published by Dr Priestley for making <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPHLOGISTICATED">dephlogisticated</a> air, a violent heat was employed. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">Oil</a> of vitriol poured on <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> was afterwards found to yield dephlogisticated air also: but the red-lead had been previously subjected to a strong heat; and, even in the very <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of producing the air, a great degree of heat is spontaneously <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a>. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> processes for producing dephlogisticated air, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, and consequently his heat, in some degree is necessary for its formation. Besides, all the different <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIRS">airs</a> or gases we know, fixed air, inflammable, nitrous, marine acid, vitriolic acid, fluor acid, vegetable acid, phlogisticated airs, &c. are every one of them produced from terrestrial materials. In these materials we know that an invisible fluid, the same with elementary heat or fire, is continually acting; whence it is exceedingly probable that all of these vapours are nothing else than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a> of the two.

GAUBIUS

Pages 1160-1160

a celebrated physician of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, studied under the illustrious Boerhaave; and became so much the favourite of his professor, that he resigned the chemical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> in his favour. He taught at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a> with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> applause for 40 years. In the year 1775 he laid <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> his office, as being no longer able to support the fatigues of it. He was succeeded by John <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAVID">David</a> Hahn, then professor at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>. His reputation was extended all over <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> by several valuable publications, particularly by his Institutiones Pathologiae Medicinalis, and his Adversaria, which have contributed not a little to the improvement both of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> and practice of medi- cine. He died at Leyden 29th November 1780, in General Gentoo's 76th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENERATION">GENERATION</a> OF INSECTS. The world is now generally convinced, that insects are not bred of corruption, but ex ovo; though the contrary was believed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, because of the vast numbers that were sometimes hatched, as it were at once, and because they could not discern the particular manner of their propagation. Malpighi, Swammerdam, and Redi, have abundantly disproved the doctrine of equivocal generation, as well as the chimerical transformation of the caterpillar into the butterfly, and other the like metamorphoses; and have shown, that all the members of the butterfly were originally inclosed under the skin <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> nympha of the caterpillar, as the parts of a plant are in the seed. Insects take particular care to deposit their eggs or seed in such places where they may have a sufficient incubation, and where the young, when hatched, may have the benefit of proper food till they become able to shift for themselves. Those whose food is in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, lay their eggs in the water; those to whom <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> is a proper food, in flesh; and those to whom the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> or leaves of vegetables are food, are accordingly deposited, some in this fruit, some in that tree, and some in one plant, and some in another; but constantly the same kind in the same tree or plant. As for others that require a more constant and greater <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of warmth, they are provided by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> animal with some <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in or about the body of other animals; some in the feathers of birds, some in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> of beasts; some in the scales of fishes, some in the nose, some in the flesh, nay, some in the bowels and inmost recesses of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> and other creatures. And as for others, to whom none of those methods are proper, the parents make them nests by perforation in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, in woods, in combs, and the like; carrying in and feeding up <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> that serve both for the production of their young, and for their food, when produced. In flies, butterflies, &c. it is observed, there is a kind of gluten, by which the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> fastens her eggs to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> buds of trees, &c. so that the rains cannot wash them off. These eggs <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> not be hurt by the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FROST">frost</a>.

GENTOOS

Pages 1160-1162

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> acceptation of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a>, denote the professors of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of the bramins <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> brachmans, who inhabit the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> called Hindoostan, in the East Indies, from the word Shan, a "region," and hind or hindoo; which Ferishteh, as we learn from <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLONEL">colonel</a> Dow's translation of his history, supposes to have been a son of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAM">Ham</a> the son of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NOAH">Noah</a>. It is observed, however, that Hindoo is not the name by which the inhabitants originally styled themselves; but, according to the idiom of the shanansrit which they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, jumboosep, from jumboo, a "jackall," an animal common in their country; and deep, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> portion of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> surrounded by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; or bhertekhant, from khunt, i.e. a "continent," and bherrhut, the name of one of the first <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> rajas. It is also to be observed, that they have assumed the name of Hindoos only since the era of the Tartar <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, to distinguish themselves from their conquerors the Mussulmen. The term Gentoo or Gent, in the Shanansrit dialect, denotes animal in general, and in its more confined <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> mankind, and is never never appropriated particularly to such as follow the doctrines of Brhima. These are divided into four <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> tribes, each of which has its own separate appellation; but they have no common or collective term that comprehends the whole <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a> under the idea affixed by the Europeans to the word Gentoo. Mr Halhed, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> to his translation of the Code of Gentoo Laws, conjectures, that the Portuguese, on their first arrival in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, hearing the word frequently in the mouths of the natives, as applied to mankind in general, might adopt it for the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> appellation of the Indians themselves, or perhaps their bigotry might force from the word Gentoo a fanciful allusion to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENTILE">Gentile</a> or Pagan. The Hindoos, or Gentooes, vie with the Chinese as to the antiquity of their nation. They reckon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> of the world by four jagues, or distinct ages: the first is the Suttee jague, or <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of purity, which is said to have lasted about 3,200,000 years; during which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> was 100,000 years, and his stature 21 cubits: the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, the Tirah jague, or the age in which one-third of mankind were reprobate; which consisted of 2,400,000 years, when men lived to the age of 10,000 years: the third, the Dwapar jague, in which half of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RACE">race</a> became depraved; which endured to 600,000 years, when mens lives were reduced to 1000 years: and fourthly, the Collee jague, in which all mankind were corrupted, or rather diminished, which the word collee imports. This is the present era, which they suppose <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> subsist for 400,000 years, of which near 5000 are already past; and mans life in this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> is limited to 100 years. It is supposed by many authors, that most of the Gentoo shasters, or scriptures, were composed about the beginning of the collee jague; but an objection occurs against this supposition, viz. that the shasters take no notice of the deluge; to which the bramins reply, that all their scriptures were written before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Noah, and the deluge never extended to Hindoostan. Nevertheless, it appears from the shasters themselves, that they claim a much higher antiquity than this; instances of which are recited by Mr Halhed. The doctrine of transmigration is one of the distinguishing tenets of the Gentooes. With regard to this subject, it is their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, according to Mr Holwell, that those souls which have attained to a certain <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of purity, either by the innocence of their manners or the severity of their mortifications, are removed to regions of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> proportioned to their respective merits; but that those who cannot so far surmount the prevalence of bad example, and the powerful degeneracy of the times, as to deserve such a promotion, are condemned to undergo continual <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANIMATION">animation</a> of successive animal forms, until, at the stated period, another renovation of the four jagues shall commence, upon the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of the present. They imagine six different spheres above this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; the highest of which, called suttee, is the residence of Brhima and his particular favourites. This sphere is also the habitation of those men who have never uttered a falsehood, and of those women who have voluntarily burned themselves with their husbands; the propriety of which practice is expressly enjoined in the code of the Gentoo laws. This code, printed by the East-India <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a> in 1776, is a very curious collection of Hindoo <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JURISPRUDENCE">jurisprudence</a>, which was selected by the most experienced pundits or lawyers, from curious originals in the Sanscrit <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, who were employed for this purpose from May 1773 to February 1775; afterwards translated into the Persian idiom, and then into the English language, by Mr Halhed. The several institutes contained in this collection are interwoven with the religion of the Gentooes, and revered as of the highest authority. The curious reader will discover an astonishing similarity between the institutes of this code and many of the ordinances of the Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>; between the character of the bramins or priests, and the Levites; and between the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of the scape-goat under the Mosaic dispensation, and a Gentoo ceremony called the affrumentum jugi, in which a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> answers the purpose of the goat. Many obsolete customs and usages alluded to in many parts of the Old <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, may also receive illustration from the institutes of this code. It appears from the code, that the bramins, who are the priests and legislators of the country, have resigned all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXECUTIVE_POWER">executive power</a> into the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> or tribe; and no bramin has been properly capable of the magistracy since the time of the suttee jague. The only privilege of importance which they have appropriated to themselves, is an exemption from all <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> punishment: they may be degraded, branded, imprisoned for life, or sent into perpetual exile; but it is everywhere expressly ordained, that a bramin shall not be put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> on any account whatsoever. We have already observed, that the Hindoos are divided into four great and original tribes, which, according to the Gentoo <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, proceeded from the four different members of Brhima, the supposed immediate <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGENT">agent</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> under the spirit of the Almighty. These tribes are the bramins, which proceed from his mouth, and whose office is to pray, read, and instruct; the Chehteree, which proceed from his arms, whose office is to draw the bow, to fight, and to govern; the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BICE">Bice</a>, proceeding from the belly or thighs, who are to provide the necessaries of life by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> and traffic; and the Sooder, from the feet, which are ordained to labour, serve, and travel. Few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, says the translator of the Gentoo code, have expressed themselves with a more becoming reverence of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> and impartial designs of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> in all its works, or with a more extensive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> towards all their fellow-creatures of every profession, than the Gentooes. It is indeed an article of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> among the bramins, that God's all-merciful power would not have permitted such a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of different religions, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had not found a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> in beholding their varieties. GEOFFREÆA, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, a genus of the decandra order, belonging to the diadelphia clas of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There is only one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, viz. the cabbage-bark tree. The wood of this tree is used in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>; but it is chiefly valued for its bark, which is administered in different forms, viz. in decoctions, syrup, powder, and extract, as an anthelmintic medicine. From this medical <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> it is also called the worm-bark tree. The decoction made by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> an ounce of the bark in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-QUART">quart</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, is mostly used in Jamaica; and it seldom fails to perform every thing that can be expected from an anthelmintic medicine, by destroying <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a> worms in the intestines, and bringing them away in great quantities. This bark is externally of a grey <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and internally <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> and furrowed; its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, when fresh, is mucilaginous and sweet; and its smell, which it retains in the decoction, disagreeable. Dr Wright of Jamaica recommends it as a very valuable remedy. GEOGRAPHY. At no. 33. dele Plate CXVI. fig. 2. on the margin; and at the end of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECTION">section</a> add, "See Plate XLVIII. fig. 2. and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, p. 802." GILLICRANKY. See KILICRANKY, (Encycl.)

GLOSSOPETRA

Pages 1162-1162
or GLOTTOPETRA, in href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural history, a kind of extraneous fossil, somewhat in form of a serpent's tongue; frequently found in the island of Malta, and divers other parts. See Plate CCCXVII. The vulgar notion is, that they are the tongues of serpents petrified; and hence their name, which is a compound of ἀγκών, "tongue," and ἄρξα, "stone." Hence also their traditional virtue in curing the bites of serpents. The general opinion of naturalists is, that they are the teeth of fishes, left at land by the waters of the deluge, and since petrified. The several sizes of the teeth of the same species, and those of the several different species of sharks, afford a vast variety of these fossil substances. Their usual colours are black, bluish, whitish, yellowish, or brown; and in shape they usually approach to a triangular figure. Some of them are simple; others are tricuspidate, having a small point on each side of the large one; many of them are quite straight; but they are frequently found crooked, and bent in all directions; many of them are serrated on their edges, and others have them plain; some are undulated on their edges, and slightly serrated on these undulations. They differ also in size as much as in figure; the larger being four or five inches long, and the smaller less than a quarter of an inch. They are most usually found with us in the strata of blue clay, though sometimes also in other sublances, and are frequent in the clay-pits of Richmond and other places. They are very frequent also in Germany, but nowhere so plentiful as in the island of Malta. The Germans attribute many virtues to these fossil teeth; they call them cordials, sudorifics, and alexipharmics; and the people of Malta, where they are extremely plentiful, hang them about their children's necks to promote dentition. They may possibly be of as much service this way as an anodyne necklace; and if suspended in such a manner that the child can get them to its mouth, may, by their hardness and smoothness, be of the same use as a piece of coral.

GORDON

Pages 1162-1162

an excellent draughtsman, and a good Grecian, who resided many years in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, visited most parts of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and had also travelled into France, Germany, &c. was secretary to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> for Encouragement of Learning; and afterwards to the Egyptian Club, composed of gentlemen who had visited <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> (viz. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SANDWICH">Sandwich</a>, Dr Shaw, Dr Pococke, &c.) He succeeded Dr Stukely as secretary to the Antiquarian Society, which office he resigned in 1741 to Mr <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Ames. He went to Carolina with governor Glen, where, besides a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>, he had several offices, such as <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, &c.; and died a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the peace, leaving a handsome estate to his family. He published, 1. "Itinerarium Septentrionale, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> a Journey through most parts of the Counties of Scotland, in two parts, with 66 copperplates, Lond. 1726," folio. 2. "Additions and Corrections, by way of Supplement, to the Itinerarium Septentrionale; containing several Dissertations on, and Descriptions of, Roman Antiquities, discovered in Scotland since publishing the said Itinerary. Together with Observations on other <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Monuments found in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">North</a> of England, never before published. Lond. 1732," folio. 3. "The Lives of Pope Alexander VI. and his son Cesare Borgia, comprehending the wars in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> VIII. and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> XII. kings of France; and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> Transactions and Revolutions in Italy, from the year 1492 to the year 1516. 4. "A compleat <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the ancient Amphitheatres, more particularly regarding the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a> of these Buildings, and in particular that of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERONA">Verona</a>, by the marquis Scipio Maffei; translated from the Italian, 1730," 8vo. afterwards enlarged in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> edition. 5. "An <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> towards explaining the hieroglyphical figures on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COFFIN">Coffin</a> of the ancient Mummy belonging to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> William Lethieller. Lond. 1737," folio, with cuts. 6. "Twenty-five plates of all the Egyptian Mummies, and other Egyptian Antiquities in England," about 1739, folio.

GORDONIA

Pages 1162-1162

lobolly-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, a genus of the polyandra order, belonging to the monodelphia clas of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. This is a tall and very straight tree, with a regular pyramidal head. Its leaves are shaped like those of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> bay, but <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERRATED">serrated</a>. It begins to blossom in May, and continues bringing forth its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. The flowers are fixed to foot-stalks, four <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> five inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>; are monopetalous, divided into five segments, encompassing a tuft of stamens headed with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> apices; which flowers, in November, are succeeded by a conic capsula having a divided calyx. The capsula, when ripe, opens, and divides into five sections, disclosing many small half-winged seeds. This tree retains its leaves all the year, and grows only in wet places, and usually in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>. The wood is somewhat soft; yet Mr Catesby mentions his having seen some beautiful tables made of it. It grows in Carolina, but not in any of the more northern colonies.

GORGONIA

Pages 1162-1163

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a name given by some writers to coral, on occasion of its supposed change from a soft substance to an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, on being brought out of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>; but this is known now to be a fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, coral being as hard while growing, to the rocks as when it has been ever so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> out of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. The gorgonite are a genus of zoophytes, which formerly were called ceratophytonis, and are known in English by the names of sea fans, sea-feathers, and sea-whips. Dr Linnaeus and Dr Pallas consider them as of a mixed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> in their growth, between animals and vegetables; but Mr Ellis has clearly proved that they are true animals of the polype kind, growing up in a branched form resembling a shrub, and in no <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> vegetable. They differ from the fresh-water polype in many of its qualities, and particularly in producing from its own substance a hard and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> support, serving many of the purposes of the bone in other animals. This is formed by a concreting juice thrown out from a peculiar set of longitudinal <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> tubes, running along the internal surface of the fleshy part; in the coats of these tubes are a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of small orifices, through which the osseous liquor exudes, and, concreting, forms the layers of that part of the hard annular circles which some, judging from the consistence rather than the texture, have erroneously denominated wood. The surface of the gorgonia is composed of a kind of scales, so well adapted to each other as to serve for defense from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> injuries; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a>, as some have called it, the bark or cortex, consists of proper muscles and tendons for extending the openings of their cells, for sending forth from thence their polype suckers in search of food, and for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> them in suddenly and contracting the sphincter muscles of these starry cells, in order to secure these tender parts from danger; and also of proper secretory ducts, to furnish and deposit the osseous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> that forms the stem and branches as well as the base of the bone. Mr Ellis affirms, that there are ovaries in these animals, and thinks it very probable that many of them are viviparous.

GRASS

Pages 1163-1165

(Encycl.) By grasses are meant all those <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> which have a round, jointed, and hollow stem, surrounded at each <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> with a single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, narrow, and pointed, and whose seeds are contained in chaffy husks. It appears by this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a>, which is Ray's, that all the kinds of grain, as wheat, oats, barley, &c., are properly grasses; and that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, the hop, &c., clovers are not grasses, though so frequently called by that name. Culmiferous grasses might be divided into two general classes for the purposes of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a>, that it might be of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> for him to attend to; viz. 1st, Those which, like the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> annual kinds of corn, run chiefly to seed-stalks; the leaves gradually decaying as they advance towards perfection, and become totally withered <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> off entirely when the seeds are ripe. Rye-grass belongs to this class in the strictest <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>. To it likewise may be assigned the vernal-grass, dogs-tail-grass, and fine bent-grass. 2ndly, Those whose leaves continue to advance even after the seed-stalks are formed, and retain their verdure and succulence during the whole season, as is the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> with the fescue and poa tribe of grasses, whose leaves are as green and succulent when the seeds are ripe and the flower-stalks fading, as at any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>. "It is wonderful, Mr Stillingfleet remarks, to see how long mankind has neglected to make a proper advantage of plants of such importance, and which, in almost every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, are the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> food of cattle. The farmer, for want of distinguishing and selecting grasses for seed, fills his pastures either with weeds or bad or improper grasses; when, by making a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> choice, after some trials, he might be sure of the best grass, and in the greatest abundance that his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> admits of. At present, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a farmer wants to lay <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> his land to grass, what does he do? he either takes his seeds indiscriminately from his own foul hay-rick, or sends to his next neighbour for a supply. By this means, besides a certain mixture of all sorts of rubbish, which must necessarily happen, if he chances to have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> proportion of good seeds, it is not unlikely but that what he intends for dry land may come from moist, where it grew naturally, and the contrary. This is such a slovenly method of proceeding, as one would think could not possibly prevail universally: yet this is the case as to all grasses except the darnel-grass, and what is known in some few counties by the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a> grass; and this latter instance is owing, I believe, more to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> than any care of the husbandman. Now, would the farmer be at the pains of separating once in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> half a pint or a pint of the different kinds of grass-seeds, and take care to sow them separately, in a very little time he would have wherewithal to stock his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FARM">farm</a> properly, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of each soil, and might at the same time spread these seeds separately over the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, by supplying the seed-shops. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of grasses fit for the farmer is, I believe, small, perhaps half a dozen or half a score are all he need to cultivate; and how small the trouble would be of such a task, and how <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> the benefit, must be obvious to every one at first sight. Would not any one be looked on as wild who should sow wheat, barley, oats, rye, peas, beans, vetches, buck-wheat, turnips, and weeds of all sorts together? yet how is it much less absurd to do what is <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> in relation to grasses? Does it not import the farmer to have good hay and grass in plenty? and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> cattle thrive equally on all sorts of food? We know the contrary. Horses will scarcely eat hay that will do well enough for oxen and cows. Sheep are particularly fond of one sort of grass, and fatten upon it faster than any other, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, if we may give <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> to Linnaeus. And may they not do the same in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>? How shall we know till we have tried?" As the generality of farmers know scarce any of the grasses by name, and as without such knowledge little improvement can be made in this branch of husbandry, we have on Plate CCCXIX. given figures of those sorts which have been recommended as the most profitable, viz. 1. Hordeum murinum, Rye-grass vulg. [Rye-grass proprius is the secale vulgatum. Perennial darnel, lolium perenne, is also, in some counties of England, improperly called rye-grass.] 2. Festuca rubra, Purple Fescue-grass. See <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a>, no. 52. 3. Festuca ovina, Sheep's <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DITTO">ditto</a>. See Agriculture, no. 54. 4. Holcus lanatus, Creeping Soft-grass. See Agriculture, no. 57. 5. Alopecurus bulbosus, Bulbous Foxtail-grass, is recommended by Mr Anderson, as promising on some occasions to afford a valuable pasture-grass. It seems chiefly, he observes, to delight in a moist soil, and therefore promises to be only fit for a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEADOW">meadow</a> pasture-grass. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> that first recommended it to his notice, was the unusual firmness that its matted roots gave to the surface of the ground, naturally soft and moist, in which it grew; which seemed to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> that it might be of use upon such soils, chiefly in preventing them from being much poached by the feet of cattle which might pasture upon them. Muddy soils especially are so much hurt by poaching, that anything that promises to be of use in preventing it deserves to be attended to. 6. Poa pratensis, Great Meadow-grass, seems to approach in many respects to the nature of the purple-fescue; only that its leaves are broader, and not near so long; being only about a foot or 16 inches at their greatest length. Like it, it produces few feed-stalks and many leaves, and is an abiding plant. 7. Poa compressa, Creeping Meadow-grass, according to Mr Anderson, seems to be the most valuable grass of any of this genus. Its leaves are firm and succulent, of a dark Saxon-green <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; and grow so <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> upon one another, as to form the richest pile of pasture-grass. The flower-stalks, if suffered to grow, appear in sufficient quantities; but the growth of these does not prevent the growth of the leaves, both advancing together during the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>; and when the stalks fade, the leaves continue as green as before. Its leaves are much larger and more abundant than the common meadow-grass, Poa trivialis, and therefore it better deserves to be cultivated. 8. Anthoxanthum odoratum, Vernal Grass, grows very <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> on dry hills, and likewise on found rich meadow-land. It is one of the earliest grasses we have; and from its being found on such kinds of pastures as sheep are fond of, and from whence excellent mutton comes, it is most likely to be a good grass for sheep-pastures. It gives a grateful odour to hay. It is very easy to gather, as it sheds its seeds upon the least rubbing. 9. Cynosurus cristatus, Crested Dog's-tail Grass. Mr Stillingfleet imagines this grass to be proper for parks, from his having known one, where it abounds, that is famous for excellent venison. He recommends it also, from <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, as good for sheep; the best mutton he ever tasted, next to that which comes from hills where the purple and sheeps fescue, the fine bent, and the silver <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> grasses abound, having been from sheep fed with it. He adds, that it makes a very fine turf upon dry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> or chalky soils; but unless swept over with the scythe, its flowering-stems will look <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>; which is the case of all grasses which are not fed on by variety of animals. For that some animals will eat the flowering-stems is evident by commons, where scarcely any parts of grasses appear but the radical leaves. 10. Stipa pennata, Cock's-tail or Feather Grass. 11. Agrostis capillaris, Fine Bent, is recommended by Mr Stillingfleet, from his having always found it in great plenty on the best sheep-pastures, in the different counties of England that are remarkable for good mutton. 12. Areia flexuosa, Mountain Hair. 13. Caryophyllus, Silver Hair. The same may be said of these two grasses as of the preceding one. 14. Festuca filiformis, Flote Fescue. In a piece published in the Amoenitates Academicae, vol. 3. intitled Planta Eculenta, we are informed, that "the seeds of this grass are gathered yearly in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, and from thence carried into Germany, and sometimes into Sweden, and sold under the name of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANNA">manna</a> seeds. These are much used at the tables of the great, on account of their nourishing quality and agreeable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. It is wonderful, (adds the author), that amongst us these seeds have hitherto been neglected, since they are so easily collected and cleansed." There is a clammy nes on the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EAR">ear</a> of the flote-fescue, when the seeds are ripe, that tastes like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>; and for this reason perhaps they are called manna seeds. Linnaeus (Flor. Suec. art. 95.) says that the bran of this grass will cure horses troubled with botts, if kept from drinking for some hours. Concerning this grass we have the following information by Mr Stillingfleet. "Mr <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAN">Dean</a>, a very sensible farmer at Ruffcomb, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BERKSHIRE">Berkshire</a>, assured me that a field, always lying under <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, of about four acres, that was occupied by his father when he was a boy, was covered with a kind of grass, that maintained five farm-horses in good heart from April to the end of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a>, without giving them any other kind of food, and that it yielded more than they could eat. He, at my desire, brought me some of the grass, which proved to be the flote-fescue with a mixture of the marsh-bent; whether this last contributes much towards furnishing so good pasture for horses, I cannot say. They both throw out roots at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> of the stalks, and therefore likely to grow to a great length. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDEX">index</a> of dubious plants at the end of Ray's Synopsis, there is mention made of a grass under the name of gramen caninum supinum-longiflum, growing not far from <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SALISBURY">Salisbury</a>, 24 feet long. This must by its length be a grass with a creeping stalk; and that there is a grass in Wiltshire growing in watery meadows, so valuable, that an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACRE">acre</a> of it lets from 10 to 12 pounds, I have been informed by several persons. These circumstances incline me to think it must be the flote-fescue; but whatever grass it be, it certainly must deserve to be inquired after." 15. Alopecurus pratensis, Meadow Foxtail. Linnaeus says that this is a proper grass to sow on grounds that have been drained—Mr Stillingfleet was informed, that the best hay which comes to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a> is from the meadows where this grass abounds. It is scarce in many parts of England, particularly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEREFORDSHIRE">Herefordshire</a>, Berkshire, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>. It might be gathered at almost any time of the year from hay-ricks, as it does not shed its seeds without rubbing, which is the case of but few grasses. It is amongst the most grateful of all grasses to cattle. 16. Poa annua, Annual Meadow Grass. "This grass (says Mr Stillingfleet) makes the finest of turfs. It grows everywhere by way sides, and on rich found commons. It is called in some parts the Suffolk grass. I have seen whole fields of it in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">High</a> Suffolk without any mixture of other grasses; and as some of the best <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a> we have in London comes from that country, it is most likely to be the best grass for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAIRY">dairy</a>. I have seen a whole <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARK">park</a> in Suffolk covered with this grass; but whether it affords good venison, I cannot tell, having never tasted of any from it. I should rather think not, and that the best pasture for sheep is also the best for deer. However, this wants <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>. I remarked on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALVERN">Malvern</a>-hill something particular in relation to this grass. A walk that was made there for the convenience of the water-drinkers, in less than a year was covered in many places with it, though I could not find one single plant of it besides in any <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the hill. This was no doubt owing to the frequent treading, which above all things makes this grass flourish; and therefore it is evident that rolling must be very serviceable to it. "It has been objected, that this grass is not free from..." Harmattan, a very extraordinary kind of <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> and fog on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>, of which an account, taken from Dr Lind's works, is given under the article Medicine, p. 4657, col. 2. An account remarkably different, however, from that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a>, may be seen in the Philosophical Transactions, vol. lxxi. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">Heat</a>, (Encycl.) See also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHLOGISTON">Phlogiston</a>, (Encycl.) <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEBRIDES">Hebrides</a>. P. 3556. col. 2. line 2. for Mulk read <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MULL">Mull</a>. Hedge-nettle, the Flacrys sylvatica. Horses abominate this plant. Cows, notwithstanding its fetid smell, will eat it; and Gunner says it undoubtedly increases their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILK">milk</a> greatly. Hedge-Sparrow, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTACILLA">Motacilla</a>, omitted under that article. Its head is of a deep brown, mixed with ash-colour; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a> marked with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> spots of dirty white; the back and coverts of the wings are dusky, edged with reddish brown; the quill-feathers and tail dusky; the rump brown, tinged with green; the throat and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> are of a dull ash-colour; the belly of a dirty white; the sides, thighs, and vent-feathers are of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> tawny brown; the legs of a dull <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>-colour.—This <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> frequents low hedges, especially those of gardens. It makes its nest in some small bush, and lays four or five eggs of a fine pale-blue colour; during the breeding season it has a remarkable flirt with its wings. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> has a short but very sweet plaintive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, which it begins with the first frosty mornings, and continues till a little time in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>. This is the motacilla modularis of Linnaeus; the bird which he supposes to be our hedge-sparrow, and describes under the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of motacilla curruca, differs in colours of plumage as well as eggs. Heir-Looms, (Encycl.) See Heir-Looms, (Encycl.) <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HELMET">Helmet</a>. For Plate CXLVIII. read CLVIII. Hemerobius, (Encycl.) This insect takes the name of hemerobius from the shortness of its life, which, however, continues several days. In the state of larva it is a great devourer of plant-<a class="xref" href="../1823/vol0.html#article-LICE">lice</a>, for which it has had bestowed upon it the appellation of lion of the plant-lice. The hemerobii, even after their transformation, preserve their carnivorous inclination. Not satisfied with making <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> upon the plant-lice, who tamely let themselves be devoured, they do not spare each other. The eggs of this insect are borne upon small pedicels, which are nothing but a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUM">gum</a> spun out by the hemerobius by raising up the hinder-part of its <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a>, and by that means the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EGG">egg</a> remains fastened to the upper part of the thread. Those eggs are deposited upon leaves, and set in the form of bunches. They have been taken for parasitic plants. The larva, when hatched, finds there its food in the midst of plant-lice. In 15 or 16 days it has attained to its full growth. With its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a>-wheel at its tail, it makes itself a small, round, white, silky cocoon, of a close texture. In summer, at the end of three weeks, the hemerobius issues forth with its wings; but when the cocoon has not been spun till autumn, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHRYSALIS">chrysalis</a> remains in it the whole winter, and does not undergo its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FINAL">final</a> metamorphosis till the ensuing spring. The flight of this insect is heavy; some species have an excrementitious smell. One goes by the name of the water-hemerobius, because it lives mostly at the water-side. Hemskerck (Egbert), called the Old, a celebrated Flemish painter of drolls and conversations, of whom, though so universally known, we have no information as to the time in which he flourished, or the school in which he was taught. Though the taste of his compositions is but low, yet it ought to be considered that he took his subjects from nature; from persons in the meanest occupations, whose dress, actions, and manners, could not furnish the imagination with any <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of elegance: and to express their passions and undigested humours, seems to have been the utmost of his ambition. By frequenting <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>, merry-meetings, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GAMING">gaming</a>-houses, and inns, he acquired a surprising power of connecting humorous circumstances; he designed and drew correctly, and his pictures have a strong effect from his accurate management of the chiaro obscuro. Some of his pictures have suffered from unskillful cleaners, and many things are sold as his which dishonour him; but his genuine works, well preserved, have a clearness and force equal to any of the Flemish artists. Hemskerck (Egbert), called the Young, was the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Grebber, but imitated the manner of Brouwer and of the elder Hemskerck. He was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAARLEM">Haarlem</a> in 1645, but settled at London, where for a long time his works were exceedingly esteemed, tho' they are now much sunk in their value. He had a whimsical imagination, and delighted in composing uncommon and fanciful subjects; such as the temptation of St Anthony, nocturnal intercourse of witches and spectres, enchantments, &c. which he executed with a free <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> and a spirited touch. It was customary with him to introduce his own <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a> among the conversations he designed; and for that purpose had a small looking-glass placed near his cafe. He died in 1704. Herbalry. P. 3593. col. 2. for 19 argent, read 20 argent. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERB">Herb</a>-Robert. This plant is in great reputation with some farmers on account of its prevailing virtues against staling of blood, and the bloody-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLUX">flux</a> in cattle; in which <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> it is said to be the best among a great variety of means commonly used on these occasions.

HERIOT

Pages 1165-1166

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, a customary tribute of goods and chattels, payable to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of the fee on the decease of the owner of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TENURE">TENURE</a>, (Encycl.) Heriot is of two sorts—viz. 1. Heriot-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, where heriots have been paid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> out of mind by custom, after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of a tenant for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. In some places, there is a customary <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, as 10 <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> 20 shillings in lieu of a heriot, by which the lord and tenant are both bound, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it be an indisputably <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> custom; but a new composition of this sort <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> not bind the representatives of either party. 2. Heriot-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, when a tenant holds by such service to pay heriot at the time of his death; which service is expressed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a> of feoffment.—For this latter the lord shall disfrain; and for the other he shall feine, and not disfrain. If the lord purchase <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the tenancy, heriot-service is extinguished; but it is not so of heriot-custom.

HERNANDIA

Pages 1166-1166

(Encycl.) The sonora is a native of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JAVA">Java</a>, and other parts of the East Indies.
