It affords a sure antidote against <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POISON">poison</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> you either put its small roots on the wounds <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> eat them; as was discovered to Rumphius by a captive woman in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> between the people of Macasar and the Dutch in the year 1667. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> of the former always carry this root about them, as a remedy against wounds with poisonous arrows. The leaves of this tree are thick and smooth. Another tree like this, which likewise grew here, had not such thick and smooth leaves. HINDOOS. See GENTOOS in this APPENDIX. HIRUNDO. P. 3647. col. 2. dele l. 4.

HOLOTHURIA

Pages 1166-1166

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a>, a genus belonging to the order of vermes <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MOLLUSCA">mollusca</a>. There are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, all inhabitants of the ocean. The physalis, called by the Dutch beantyser, by Dampier cutters, and by the English sailors <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>-of-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>, has a half-round body, stands directly upwards, has many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and many short tentacles, is slimy, transparent, somewhat bluish, shines in dark nights, is poisonous, and so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> that it <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> scarce sink in Spanish brandy. Beyond the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> they are small; in the ocean they are larger and very numerous, especially in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">March</a>.

HOOKE

Pages 1166-1167

author of an esteemed <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMAN_HISTORY">Roman <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and other performances.—Of this learned <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> the earliest particulars to be met with are furnished by himself, in the following modest but manly <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, dated Oct. 7, 1722: "My <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>, the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> I had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to wait upon your Lordship since your coming to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, your lordship had the goodness to ask me, what way of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> I was then engaged in; a certain mauvais honte hindered me at that time from giving a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> answer. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> is, my lord, I cannot be said at present to be in any form of life, but rather to live extempore. The late epidemic distemper seized me, I endeavoured to be rich, imagined for a while that I was, and am in some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> happy to find myself at this instant but <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> worth nothing. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> your Lordship, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> any of your numerous friends, have need of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>, with the bare qualifications of being able to read and write, and to be honest, I shall gladly undertake any employments your Lordship shall not think me unworthy of. I have been taught, my lord, that neither a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a>, nor his self-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>, is an equal judge of what is fit for him; and I shall endeavour to remember, that it is not the short <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> we <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a>, but the manner of our performance, which gains or loses us the applause of him who is finally to decide of all <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> actions. My lord, I am just now employed in translating from the French, a History of the Life of the late archbishop of Cambrey; and I was thinking to beg the honour of your lordship's name to protect a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> have so much need of it. The original is not yet published. 'Tis written by the author of the "Discourse upon Epic <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>," in the new edition of Telemaque. As there are some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> in the book of a particular <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, I dare not solicit your lordship to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> me the favour I have mentioned, till you first have perused it. The whole is short, and pretty fairly transcribed. If your lordship could find a spare <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> to look it over, I would wait upon your lordship with it, as it may possibly be no unpleasing entertainment. I should humbly ask your lordship's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> for so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> an address in a season of so much business. But when should I be able to find a time in which your lordship's goodnese is not employed? I am, with perfect respect and duty, my lord, your lordship's most obliged, most faithful, and most obedient humble servant, NATHANIEL HOOKE." The translation here spoken of was afterwards printed in 12mo, 1723. From this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, Mr Hooke enjoyed the confidence and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> of men not less distinguished by virtue than by titles. In 1725 he published a translation of Ramfay's Travels of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CYRUS">Cyrus</a>, in 4to; in 1733 he revised a translation of "The History of the Conquest of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a> by the Spaniards, by Thomas Townend, Esq;" printed in 2 vols Svo; and in the same year he published in 4to, the first volume of "The Roman History, from the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of Rome to the ruin of the Commonwealth; illustrated with maps and other plates." In the dedication to this volume, Mr Hooke took the opportunity of "publicly testifying his just esteem for a worthy friend, to whom he had been long and much obliged," by telling Mr Pope, that the displaying of his name at the head of those sheets was "like the hanging out a splendid sign, to catch the traveller's eye, and entice him to make <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of the entertainment the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> affords. But," he proceeds, "when I can write under my sign, that Mr Pope has been here, and was content, who will question the goodnes of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>?" The volume is introduced by "Remarks on the History of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">Seven</a> Roman Kings, occasioned by Sir <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton's objections to the supposed 244 years <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> state of Rome." His nervous <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PEN">pen</a> was next employed in digesting "An Account of the conduct of the Dowager-duchess of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARLBOROUGH">Marlborough</a>, from her first coming to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">Court</a> to the Year 1710. In a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">Letter</a> from herself to Lord ——. 1742." 8vo. His reward on this occasion was considerable; and the reputation he acquired by the performance much greater. The circumstances of this transaction are thus related by Dr Maty, in his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of Lord Chesterfield, vol. i. p. 116. "The relish of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Marlborough, being desirous of submitting to posterity her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> conduct, as well as her lord's, applied to the earl of Chesterfield for a proper person to receive her information, and put the memoirs of her life into a proper dress. Mr Hooke was recommended by him for that purpose. He accordingly waited upon the duchess, while she was still in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a>, oppressed by the infirmities of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. But, knowing who he was, she immediately got herself lifted up, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> speaking during six hours. She delivered to him, without any notes, her account, in the most lively as well as the most connected manner. As she was not tired herself, she would have continued longer the business of this first sitting, had not she perceived that Mr Hooke was quite exhausted, and wanted refreshment as well as rest. So eager was she for the completion of the work, that she insisted upon Mr Hooke’s not leaving her house till he had finished it. This was done in a short time; and her <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRACE">Grace</a> was so well pleased with the performance, that she complimented the author with a present of £500l., a sum which far exceeded his expectations. As soon as he was free, and permitted to quit the house of his benefactress, he hastened to the earl, to thank him for his favour, and communicated to him his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a>. The perturbation of mind he was under, occasioned by the strong <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of his obligation, plainly appeared in his flattery out his acknowledgments; and he, who had succeeded so well as the interpreter of her Grace’s sentiments, could scarcely utter his own.” The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> volume of his “Roman History” appeared in 1745; when Mr Hooke embraced the fair occasion of congratulating his worthy friend the earl of Marchmont, on “that true <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>, the consenting praise of the honest and the wife,” which his lordship had so early acquired. To the second volume Mr Hooke added “The Capitoline Marbles, or Consular Calendars, an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Monument accidentally discovered at Rome in the year 1545, during the Pontificate of Paul III.” In 1758 Mr Hooke published “Observations on I. The Answer of M. l’Abbe de Vertot to the late earl of Stanhope’s Inquiry concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENATE">Senate</a> of ancient Rome: dated <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>, 1719. II. A Dissertation upon the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">Constitution</a> of the Roman Senate, by a Gentleman: published in 1743. III. A Treatise on the Roman Senate, by Dr Conyers Middleton: published in 1747. IV. An <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on the Roman Senate, by Dr Thomas Chapman: published in 1750;” which he with great propriety <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> to Mr Speaker Onslow. The third volume of Mr Hooke’s “Roman History,” to the end of the Gallic <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>, was printed under his inspection before his last illness; but did not appear till after his death, which happened in 1764. The fourth and last volume was published in 1771. Mr Hooke left two sons; of whom one is a divine of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of England; the other, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of the Sorbonne, and professor of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a> in that illustrious seminary.

HOPE

Pages 1167-1168

in ethics, is the desire of some good, attended with a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> of the possibility, at least, of obtaining it, and enlivened with joy, greater <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> less, according to the greater or less <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> of our possessing the object of our hope. Alexander, preparing for his Asian expedition, distributed his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> dominions among his friends; allotting to some villages, to others boroughs, to others cities; and being asked what he had reserved for himself, replied, Hope. HOPS. See Humulus, (Encycl.) The cultivation of hops, which is now so very general, is not in all places equally successful. Very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> hop-grounds <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> for 20 years successively appear with the most promising verdure, yet produce nothing. When the fructification in an early state contracts a mouldiness, it withers and is destroyed. It is then infected by the aphides, who produce on it what is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEW">dew</a>; but the plant must first be in a sickly state before it is infected with these insects. Into this situation it is reduced by the caterpillar of the phalena humuli or other moth, which feeds on its roots; a circumstance of which the cultivators of this plant are generally ignorant, though some of them have discovered that a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> hop will be infected by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> a sickly one near it, when they transplant the roots from a hop-ground that is thus attacked to one that is perfectly healthy. The hop grows naturally among <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a> and fragments of rocks, where it is never damaged by the honey-dew. The reason is, that the caterpillar abovementioned, cannot in such a foil penetrate to its roots; and therefore, those who cultivate this plant ought to cover the ground with stones. HUMMING-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIRD">BIRD</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TROCHILUS">Trochilus</a>, (Encycl.) We have the following pleasing account of this little animal in professor Kalm’s Travels into <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> applies to the trochilus colubris. Its plumage is most beautifully coloured, most of its feathers being green, some grey, and others forming a shining <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> round its neck; the tail glows with fine feathers, changing from green into a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. These birds come here (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENNSYLVANIA">Pennsylvania</a>) in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, about the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> when it begins to grow very warm, and make their nests in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>; but towards autumn, they retreat again into the more southern countries of America. They subsist barely upon the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NECTAR">nectar</a>, or sweet juice of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, contained in that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> which botanists call the nectarium, and which they suck up with their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> bills. Of all the flowers, they like those most which have a long tube; and they are observed to flutter chiefly about the impatiens noli tangere, and the monarda with crimson flowers. An inhabitant of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is sure to have a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of these beautiful and agreeable little birds before his windows all the summer long, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he takes care to plant a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a> with all sorts of fine flowers under them. The flowers of the above-mentioned monarda grow verticillated, that is, at different distances they surround the stalk, as the flowers of our mint (<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MENTHA">mentha</a>), <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BASTARD">bastard</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a> (galeopsis), mother-wort (leonturus), and dead nettle (lamium). It is therefore diverting to see them putting their bills into every flower in the circle. As soon as they have sucked the juice of one flower, they flutter to the next. One that has not seen them would hardly believe in how short a space of time they have had their tongues in all the flowers of a plant, which when large, and with a long tube, the little bird, by putting its head into them, looks as if it crept with half its body into them. “During their sucking the juice out of the flowers, they never <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> on it, but flutter continually like bees, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> their feet backwards, and move their wings so quick, that they are hardly visible. During this fluttering, they make a humming like bees, or like that which is occasioned by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> of a little wheel. After they have thus, without resting, fluttered for a while, they fly to a neighbouring tree or <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POST">post</a>, and resume their vigour again. They then re- HUN Hamming, turn to their humming and sucking. When several of them were on the same bed, there was always a violent <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a> between them, in meeting each other at the same flower (for envy was likewise predominant among these little creatures), and they attacked with such impetuosity, that it would seem as if the strongest would pierce its antagonist through and through with its long <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BILL">bill</a>. During the fight, they seem to stand in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>, keeping themselves up by the incredibly swift <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of their wings. When the windows towards the garden are open, they pursue each other into the rooms, fight a little, and flutter away again. Sometimes they come to a flower which is withering, and has no more juice in it; they then, in a fit of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGER">anger</a>, pluck it off and throw it on the ground, that it may not mislead them for the future. If a garden contains a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> number of these little birds, they are seen to pluck off the flowers in such quantities, that the ground is quite covered with them, and it seems as if this proceeded from a motion of envy. "Commonly you hear no other sound than their humming; but when they fly against each other in the air, they make a chirping noise like a sparrow or chicken. They are so small, that one would easily mistake them for great humble-bees or butterflies; and their flight resembles that of the former, and is incredibly swift. They have never been observed to feed on insects or fruit; the nectar of flowers seems therefore to be their only food. Several people have caught some humming-birds, on account of their singular <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, and have put them into cages, where they died for want of a proper food. However, Mr Bartram has kept a couple of them for several weeks together, by feeding them with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> in which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> had been dissolved; and I am of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that it would not be difficult to keep them all winter in a hot-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. "The humming-bird always builds its nest in the middle of a branch of a tree; and it is so small, that it cannot be seen from the ground, but he who intends to see it must get up to the branch. For this reason it is looked upon as a great rarity if a nest is accidentally found, especially as the trees in summer have so thick a foliage. The nest is quite round, and consists in the inside of a brownish and quite soft <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, which seems to have been collected from the leaves of the great mullen or verbasum thapsus, which are often found covered with a soft <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> of this colour, and the plant is plentiful here: other materials, however, are often used, as <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, hemp, moss, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, or such like soft substances. The outside of the nest has a coating of green moss, such as is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> on old pales, or enclosures, and on trees; the inner diameter of the nest is hardly a geometrical inch at the top, and its depth half an inch; they are said to lay two eggs, each of the size of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEA">pea</a>."

HUNTER

Pages 1168-1169

a celebrated anatomist, was a native of Kilberge in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LANARK">Lanark</a> in Scotland. Being designed by his father for the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, he was sent, at a proper <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of Glasgow; but having spent five years in regular academical attendance there, he began to feel strong objections to theological studies; and happening to become acquainted with Dr <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CULLEN">Cullen</a>, who was at that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> established in practice at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAMILTON">Hamilton</a>, he was persuaded to apply himself to physic. Dr Cullen's Hunter, friendship made it easy to obtain his father's consent. He was taken into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, where he spent two of the happiest years of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. In Scotland (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we except <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>) there is not that distinction between the branches of physic that prevails in England. The physicians generally dispense their own medicines, and likewise practise <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a>. Dr Cullen, though an enthusiastic cultivator of physic and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, had always a dislike to the surgical <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of his practice. It was therefore agreed between him and Mr Hunter, that the latter should go first to the college at Edinburgh, and then to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, in order to see the practice of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, and improve himself in anatomy and surgery, and that at his return to Hamilton a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARTNERSHIP">partnership</a> should take <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> between them. Mr Hunter brought with him to London a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of introduction to his countryman Dr James Douglas, at that time in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> reputation as a physician and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>-midwife, and well known by his "Treatise on the Muscles," and other works. Dr Douglas advised him to attend St George's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOSPITAL">Hospital</a>, and Dr Nichols's lectures, as a perpetual pupil, for the opportunity of learning all his arts in making anatomical preparations. At the end of the season, when he was preparing to set out on his return to Hamilton, Dr Douglas persuaded him to change his proposed <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>; to assist him in his anatomical pursuits; to accompany his son, at that time a student in physic, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>; and afterwards to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> in London, and to teach anatomy. Mr Hunter communicated this proposal, and the arguments which Dr Douglas had used, to Dr Cullen; who, thinking it a fairer prospect, with his usual generosity readily gave his consent. After the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> Dr Douglas, Mr Hunter began to teach anatomy in London. His easy, agreeable manner of lecturing, the new and clear <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of view in which he placed the different parts of his subject, added to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> and elegance of his preparations, drew to him a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> number of pupils. He soon became eminent in his profession, and enriched the art with many important discoveries. In <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> about 1747, Mr Hunter was admitted a member of the Surgeon's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>. His anatomical reputation soon procured him an extensive practice, particularly in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MIDWIFERY">midwifery</a>; and when he came to be established, the university of Glasgow complimented him with the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of M.D. In 1756 he was admitted a member of the College of Physicians; and soon afterwards was elected F.R.S. having made himself known by an ingenious <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> "on the Structure of Cartilages," published in the Phil. Trans. so early as 1743. He since, at different times, communicated several other valuable papers to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. When the present <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> became pregnant, Dr Hunter was consulted, and at the same time honoured with the appointment of physician-extraordinary to her majesty. When the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Academy of Arts was founded, he was nominated professor of anatomy to that <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>; and lately, upon the death of one of the eight foreign associates of the Academy of Sciences at Paris, he was elected to supply the vacancy. To consider him as a teacher, is to view him in his most amiable character: perspicuity, unaffected <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>, and a desire of being useful, were his peculiar characteristics; and, and, of all others, he was most happy in blending the utile with the dulce, by introducing apposite and pleasing stories to illustrate and enliven the more abstruse and jejune parts of anatomy; thus fixing the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of the volatile and the giddy, and enriching the minds of all with useful knowledge. Employed as Dr Hunter had been, for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of years, by persons of the highest <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and consulted as an anatomist in difficult <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of surgery by all ranks of people and from every part of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, his gains must have been immense; and he employed them in a manner of all others the most liberal, the improvement of science. Having never married, and being averse to ostentation and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a>, he always conducted his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> expenses on a plan adapted to his profession; and his accumulated fees were expended in erecting and furnishing a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a>, which, considered in every point of view, is certainly not to be equalled in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. It is unnecessary to say anything of the anatomical varieties it contains, because it <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> be easily conceived, that a person of the Doctor's disposition, who had spent near half a century in the pursuit of a favourite object, must have amassed everything that is curious and valuable on that subject. But the specimens of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-COMPARATIVE_ANATOMY">comparative anatomy</a> form only a small part of the Hunterian Museum. The collection of scarce and valuable books is to be equalled only by royal <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a>; and his cabinet of medals, particularly Greek and Roman, is far more valuable than the Imperial collection at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a>. The expense of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> his house and museum in Windmill-street, and furnishing the latter, is said to have approached near to 100,000l. His plates of the gravid uterus, and his other publications, sufficiently evince his profound knowledge and unwearied industry; and the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of his Greek coins his boundless munificence. It is much to be feared that the other works he had in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> at the time of his death are left too incomplete for the public eye. His museum, the most comprehensive and select of any individual's in Europe, was left for thirty years to his sister's son, Mr Bailey. If during the above-mentioned <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of 30 years Mr Bailey should die, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of the museum for the remainder of the period devolves to Mr Cruikshank. At the conclusion of the period of 30 years, the entire museum, without any participation or entail whatever, is bequeathed to the university of Glasgow. The sum of 4000l. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a> is left, with the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> from time to time growing on it, for the support and augmentation of the collection. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, Mr John Hunter, the surgeon, on account of some <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between them, is not named in the will. The executors are, Dr Pitcairn, Mr Coombe apothecary (the Doctor's learned coadjutor in his literary labours), and Dr Fordyce of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>-street; to each of whom Dr Hunter has left a legacy of 20l. a-year, during the period in which they will be executing the purposes of the will. Making a pecuniary estimate of the museum in question, 70,000l. is said to be the sum it is worth. Besides that, the Doctor was possessed of above 20,000l. in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a>; the bulk of which is given to Mr Bailey. We are credibly informed, that the Doctor formerly applied to the ministers of this country to allot him a piece of ground, on which he might build a museum, that he would engage to leave endowed for the public <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. His request, however, was not complied with; and he then purchased the premises in Great Windmill-street, where he built his museum and spacious habitation. He died 30th April 1783, of the gout in his stomach.

HYDRA

Pages 1169-1169

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a>, a genus of the order of zoophyta, belonging to the class of vermes. There are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, known by the general name of polypes. See POLYP, in this Appendix.

HYDROCEPHALUS INTERNUM

Pages 1169-1169

(Encycl.) See MEDICINE, no 370. 438. Besides the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>, there recommended as effectual in this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, formerly so fatal, a surprising instance of the efficacy of the vapour-bath is given in the 8th volume of the Medical Commentaries. The instance, however, is singular, and the medicine ought to be often repeated with success before much confidence is put in it.

ICHNEUMON

Pages 1169-1170

(Encycl.) One distinguishing and striking character of these <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of flies is the almost continual agitation of their antennae. The name of ichneumon has been applied to them from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> they do us by destroying caterpillars, plant-<a class="xref" href="../1823/vol0.html#article-LICE">lice</a>, and other insects, as the ichneumon <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> mantouette destroys the crocodiles. The variety to be found in the species of ichneumons is prodigious; among the smaller species, there are males who perform their amorous preludes in the most passionate and gallant manner. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POSTERIOR">posterior</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the females is armed with a whimple, visible in some species, nowise discoverable in others; and that <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, though so fine, is able to penetrate through <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a>: the structure of it is more easily seen in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>-whimpled fly. The food of the family to be produced by this fly is the larva of wasps or mason-bees; for it is sooner espies one of those nests, but it fixes on it with its whimple, and bores through the mortar of which it is built. The whimple itself, of an admirable structure, consists of three pieces: two collateral ones, hollowed out into a gutter, serve as a sheath, and contain a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a>, Ichneumon solid, dentated stem, along which runs a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROOVE">groove</a> that conveys the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EGG">egg</a> from the animal, who supports the whimble with its hinder legs, lest it should <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a>; and by a variety of movements, which it dexterously performs, it bores through the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, and deposits one or more eggs, according to the size of the ichneumon, though the largest drop but one or two. Some agglutinate their eggs upon caterpillars; others penetrate through the caterpillar's eggs, though very hard, and deposit their own on the inside. When the larva is hatched, its head is so situated, that it pierces the caterpillar, and penetrates to its very entrails. These larvae <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PUMP">pump</a> out the nutritious juices of the caterpillar, without attacking the vital parts of the creature; who appears healthy, and even sometimes transforms itself to a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHRYSALIS">chrysalis</a>. It is not uncommon to see these caterpillars fixed upon trees, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they were fitting upon their eggs, and it is afterwards discovered that the larvae, which were within their bodies, have spun their threads, with which, as with cords, the caterpillars are fastened <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and so perish miserably. The ichneumons performed special service in the years 1731 and 1732; by multiplying in the same proportion as did the caterpillars, their larvae destroyed more of them than could be effected by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> industry. Those larvae, when on the point of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> into chrysalids, spin a silky cocoon. Nothing is more surprising and singular, than to see these cocoons <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a>, when placed on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">table</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. Plant-lice, the larvae of the curculions, spiders' eggs, are also sometimes the cradle of the ichneumon-fly. Carcasses of plant-lice, void of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, are often found on rose-tree leaves: they are the habitation of a small larva, which, after having eaten up the entrails, destroys the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> and inward economy of the plant-louse, performs its metamorphose under shelter of the pellicle which enfolds it, contrives itself a small circular outlet, and falls forth into open <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>. There are ichneumons in the woods, who dare attack spiders, run them through with their sting, tear them to pieces, and thus avenge the whole <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a> of flies of so formidable a foe: others, destitute of wings, (and those are females) deposit their eggs in spiders' nests. The ichneumon of the bedeguar (or sweet-briar sponge), and that of the rose-tree, perhaps only deposit their eggs in those places, because they find other insects on which they feed. The genus of the ichneumon flies, might with propriety be termed a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RACE">race</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> cannibals.

ICHTHYOLOGY

Pages 1170-1170

(Encycl.) The most judicious arrangement of this branch of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a> seems to be that of Mr Pennant, who distributes fish into three divisions; Cetaceous, Cartilaginous, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONY">Bony</a>. Div. I. **CETACEOUS FISH**; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of which are the following: No gills; an orifice on the top of the head, through which they breathe and eject <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>; a flat <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> tail; exemplified in Plate CCXVIII. (lower compartment), fig. 1, by the Beaked Whale, borrowed from Dale's Hist. Harw. 411. Tab. xiv.—This <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> comprehends three genera; the Whale, Cachalot, and Dolphin. Div. II. **CARTILAGINOUS FISH**; the characters of which are: Breathing through certain apertures, generally placed on each side the neck; but in some instances beneath, in some above, and from one to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> on each <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a>, except in the pipe-fish, which has only one; the muscles supported by cartilages instead of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BONES">bones</a>. Example, the Picked Dog-fish, fig. 2. a, The lateral apertures.—The genera are, the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-LAMPREY">Lamprey</a>, Skate, Shark, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FISHING">Fishing</a>-frog, Sturgeon, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">Sun</a>-fish, Lump-fish, Pipe-fish. Div. III. **BONY FISH**, includes those whose muscles are supported by bones or spines, which breathe thro' gills covered or guarded by thin bony plates, open on the side, and dilatable by means of a certain row of bones on their lower part, each separated by a thin web; which bones are called the radii branchiologii, or the gill covering rays. The tails of all the fish that form this division are placed in a situation perpendicular to the body; and this is an invariable character. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> sections of the Bony Fish into Apodail, Thoracic, Jugular, and Abdominal, he copies from Linnaeus: who founds this system on a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of the ventral fins to the feet of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>-animals or reptiles; and either from the want of them, or their particular situation in respect to the other fins, establishes his sections.—In order to render them perfectly intelligible, it is necessary to refer to those several organs of movement, and some other parts, in a perfect fish, or one taken out of the three last sections. In fig. 4. (the Haddock), a, is the pectoral fins; b, ventral fins; c, anal fins; d, caudal <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIN">fin</a>, or the tail; e, e, dorsal fins; f, bony plates that cover the gills; g, branchiostegal rays and their membranes; h, lateral or side line. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">Sect</a>. 1. **APODAL**: The most imperfect, wanting the ventral fins; illustrated by the Conger, fig. 3. This also expresses the union of the dorsal and anal fins with the tail, as is found in some few fish.—Genera: The Eel, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WOLF">Wolf</a>-fish, Launce, Morris, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWORD">Sword</a>-fish. Sect. 2. **JUGULAR**: The ventral fins b, placed before the pectoral fins a, as in the Haddock, fig. 4.—Genera: The Dragonet, Weever, Codlith, Blenny. Sect. 3. **THORACIC**: The ventral fins a, placed beneath the pectoral fins b, as in the Father Lasher, fig. 5.—Genera: The Goby, Bull-head, Doree, Flounder, Gilt-head, Wrasse, Perch, Stickleback, Mackrel, Surmullet, Gurnard. Sect. 4. **ABDOMINAL**: The ventral fins placed behind the pectoral fins, as in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MINNOW">Minnow</a>, fig. 6.—Genera: The Loche, Salmon, Pike, Argentine, Athene, Mullet, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLYING">Flying</a> fish, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERRING">Herring</a>, Carp.

IDEAS

Pages 1170-1173

(Encycl.) The origin of ideas has been a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> disputed among philosophers. The <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol14.html#article-PERIPATETICS">Peripatetics</a> maintain, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> objects emit <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> which resemble them all around; and that these species, striking on our senses, are by them transmitted to the understanding; and that, being material and sensible, they are rendered intelligible by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> intellect; and are at length received by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PASSIVE">passive</a>. Others are of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that our souls have of themselves the power of producing ideas of things we would think upon; and that they are excited to produce them by the impressions which objects make on the body, tho' these impressions are not images in any respect like the objects that occasioned them. And in this, say they, it is, that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> is made after the image of God, and that he partakes of his power; for as God made all things out of nothing, and can reduce them to nothing when he pleases, so man can create as many ideas as he pleases, and annihilate them when he has done. Others Others maintain, that the mind has no occasion for any thing beside itself to perceive objects; and that, by considering itself, and its own perfections, it is able to discover all things that are without. Others, with Des Cartes, hold, that our ideas were created and born along with us. Malebranche, and his followers, assert, that God has in himself the ideas of all the beings he has created; that thus he sees all things, in considering his own perfections, to which they correspond; and that, as he is intimately united to our souls, by his presence, our mind sees and perceives things in him which represent created beings; and that it is thus we come by all our ideas. He adds, that though we see all sensible and material things in God, yet that we have not our sensations in him. When we perceive any sensible object, in our perception is included both a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a> and a pure idea. The sensation is a modification of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, and it is God who causes it in us; but for the idea joined with the sensation, it is in God; and it is in him that we see it. The Cartesians distinguish three kinds of ideas. The first, innate; such, they say, is that we have of God, as of a Being infinitely perfect. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, adventitious; which the mind receives in proportion as bodily objects present themselves to our senses: such is the idea of body, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, &c. The third, according to these philosophers, are factitious; which are those which the mind forms, by uniting and assembling, the ideas which it already had; and these are called complex. But Mr Locke seems to have put this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> out of dispute; having made it appear, that all our ideas are owing to our senses; and that all innate, created, and factitious ideas, are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> chimeras. Our mind, he shows, has not absolutely any ideas besides those presented to it by the senses, and those which it forms by its own operations on those others which the senses furnish; so that a man, destitute of one of his senses, would never have any idea belonging to that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>; and, supposing him destitute of all the senses, he would never have any idea at all: external objects having no other way of producing ideas in him, but by means of sensation, he would have no idea, not even of reflection; because, in wanting all sensation, he wants that which would excite in him the operations of his mind, which are the objects of his reflection. It is plain, therefore, there is no innate idea; no general <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> first principle, inherent in the soul, and created with it; no immediate object of the mind, before it had perceived external objects by means of the senses, and reflected on that perception. Those ideas only seem to be innate, because we find we have them as soon as we come to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of reason; but they are, in effect, what we formed from the ideas wherewith the mind was insensibly filled by the senses. Thus, when the mind is employed about sensible objects, it comes by the ideas of bitter, sweet, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, hard, &c. which we call sensation; and, when employed about its own operations, perceiving and reflecting on them, as employed about the ideas before got by sensation, we get the ideas of perception, thinking, doubting, willing, &c. which we call inward sensation, or reflection; and these two, viz. external material things as the objects of sensation, and the operations of our own minds as the objects of reflection, are the only originals whence all our ideas have their rise. When we have considered these, and their several modes and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a>, we shall find, that they contain our whole stock of ideas, infomuch that the understanding does not seem to have the least glimmering of any ideas, that it did not receive from one of those sources. And thus far the mind appears merely passive, as not having it in its power to choose whether it <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> have these first beginnings, or materials of knowledge, or not. For the objects of sense will obtrude their ideas upon the mind; and the operations of the mind will not let us be without some (however obscure) notion of them. The origin of our ideas and notions is a perplexed question, and not at all cleared up by the labours of metaphysicians. As to ideas of sense, some philosophers have pretended, that bodies acting or pressing upon our nerves, or putting the animal-spirits in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, produce sensations; but as the motion communicated to the nerves or spirits has nothing in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> either with the thing or body moving, or with the idea excited in the mind, and that we do not conceive the least relation between the motion of the nerves or spirits and the production of an idea; to say that the motion of, or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> upon, the nerves or animal-spirits is the cause of ideas, is explaining nothing at all. The species emitted by objects, and the formation of ideas by the soul itself, are not more clear. As to innate ideas, it is true indeed, that the arguments of those who maintain them, have been refuted by Mr Locke; but when he goes farther, and denies innate ideas, his arguments have been thought by some not to be conclusive. Dr Price, in his Inquiry into the Original of our Ideas, has taken occasion to remark, that the system of Mr Locke, which attributes all our ideas to sensation and reflection, is materially defective; for, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> by sensation we understand the effects arising from the impressions made on our minds by external objects, and by reflection the notice which the mind takes of its own operations, it will be impossible to drive some of the most important of our ideas from them. This excellent reasoner observes, that the power within us that understands, the intuition of the mind, or the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> in it that discerns truth, that views, compares, and judges of all ideas and things, is a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of new simple ideas, or original, primary, and uncompounded perceptions of the mind. To this source he refers our ideas of the impenetrability and vis inertiae of matter, substance, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>, space, infinity, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>, contingency, possibility, impossibility, power, causation, &c. all our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> ideas, and also our ideas of moral <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> and wrong, and of moral obligation. It is, he says, of the essence of these ideas to imply something true or false of an object, and that they by no means denote the manner in which we are affected by it; so that they cannot with any propriety be referred to that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of our <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, which has been distinguished by the appellation of sense. Accordingly, our ideas may be divided, first, into those implying nothing real without the mind, or nothing real and true besides its own affections and passions; to which class we may refer the immediate effects of impressions on the bodily senses. senses, without supposing any previous ideas; as all tastes, smells, colours, &c.; and those that arise upon occasion only of other ideas; as the effects in us of considering, order, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>, the beauties of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, &c. Secondly, into those which are images of something distinct from sensation, or which imply real, independent of existence and truth; which may be subdivided into such as denote the real properties of external objects, and the actions and passions of the mind; and those which are derived immediately from intelligence. By the notices conveyed to the mind through the organs of the body, or its observation of the necessary attendants and concomitants of certain sensations and impressions, it perceives the figure, ex- tension, motion, and other primary qualities of mate- rial substances; by contemplating itself, it perceives the properties of spiritual substances, volition, conscious- ness, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, &c. To all these ideas it is essential that they have real, certain, invariable archetypes, ac- tually existing, to which they are referred, and to which they are conformable. These ideas again be- come objects or archetypes to the intellective faculty; from whence arises a new set of ideas, which are the perceptions of this faculty, and represent not the mind’s own affections, but necessary truth. Antecedently to these, whatever other ideas we may be furnished with, nothing is understood; whatever feeds or subjects of knowledge may be in the mind, nothing is known. The system of Mr Locke, with regard to the origin of our ideas, has lately been attacked by Dr Reid and others; and it has been <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> as the foundation of universal scepticism. Dr Reid objects to every sys- tem which supposes that the mind receives images of things from without by means of the senses, because sensations bear no resemblance to bodies, or any of their qualities. With regard to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a>, figure, mo- tion, &c., he says, if they are not ideas of sensation, nor like to any sensation, then the ideal system is a rope of sand, and all the laboured arguments of the sceptical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> against a material world, and a- gainst the existence of every thing but impressions and ideas, proceed upon a false <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>. To this ob- jection it has been replied, that ideas are only in a figurative sense the images of external things; that certain impressions are conveyed to the mind by means of the organs of sense, and their corresponding nerves, between which, and the sensations existing in the mind, there is a real and necessary, though at present an unknown connection; and that the same reasoning would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> him to deny that sounds are produced by bodies striking against one another, because he can perceive no proper resemblance between the cause and the effect. Dr Reid farther objects to the notion generally re- ceived among philosophers, that the images of exter- nal objects are conveyed by the organs of sense to the brain, and there perceived by the mind. But from this objection it might be inferred, that the whole sys- tem of our senses, nerves, and brain, is of no real use whatever; because it is impossible to say how they <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> upon the mind, or the mind upon them. It is also objected, that Mr Locke’s <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of i- deas into those of sensation, and those of reflection, is contrary to all the rules of logic; because the second member of the division includes the first. For can we, says he, form clear and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> notions of our sensations any other way than by reflection? Sensation is an op- eration of the mind, of which we are conscious, and we get the notion of it by reflecting upon that which we are conscious of. In like manner, doubting and be- lieving are operations of the mind, whereof we are conscious, and we get the notion of them by reflecting upon what we are conscious of. The ideas of sensation, therefore, are ideas of reflection, as much as the ideas of doubting or believing, or any other idea whatso- ever. But it has been alleged, that the author con- founds the ideas of sensation with the idea of sensation itself, which is, without doubt, of the same class with the ideas of doubting, &c., as Mr Locke would have allowed. But the ideas belonging to the class of sen- sation do not require any scientific knowledge of that power, or any reflection upon it. If this were the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>, brute animals, having no proper ideas of reflection, could have no ideas of sensation; and the case would be the same with the bulk of mankind. In another <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, Dr Reid acknowledges, that <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> beings may have ideas of mere sensation some time before they <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIS">dis</a>- cover any power of reflection, and that this power may discover itself and come into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> afterwards. Dr Beattie, Dr Oswald, and others, have pursued and extended the same kind of reasoning against the principles of Mr Locke; and alleged, that Berkeley’s reasoning against the existence of a material world, and Hume’s reasoning against the existence both of soul and body, are deduced from Locke’s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a>, and the Principia of Des Cartes. In opposition to this system, Dr Reid, and those who have adopted his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THEORY">theory</a>, have recourse to cer- <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAIN">tain</a> instinctive principles; alleging that our perceptions necessarily imply the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> of the present existence of external objects; and that the real, separate, and in- dependent existence of matter, is believed, not because it can be proved by argument, but because the consti- tution of our <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> is such, and we must believe it; and that we cannot, in our own minds, separate the belief of external objects from our sensations. How- ever, it has been urged by an ingenious writer, that Mr Locke’s doctrine is not so favourable to Mr Ber- keley’s theory as Dr Reid’s; and that a system which attributes our primary mental operations to mere con- stitution and feeling, is more favourable to scepticism than that in the room of which it is substituted. Ac- cording to Mr Hume’s system, all perceptions are ei- ther impressions or ideas, and it is not possible for us to much as to conceive any thing specifically different from ideas and impressions; and since all ideas are co- pied from impressions, we can, therefore, have no idea or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a> of any thing of which we have not received an impression. No man can have any idea of power or energy, because he has never received any impression of it; and for the same reason no man can have any idea of self. What we call a mind is no- thing but a bundle or collection of different per- ceptions, which succeed each other with inconceivable rapidity, and are in a perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLUX">flux</a> and movement. There is properly, says Mr Hume, no simplicity in the mind at one time, nor identity at different times, whatever <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> propensity we may have to imagine that simplicity and identity. They are the successive perceptions only that constitute the mind; so that there is nothing in the universe but impressions and ideas; all possible perceptions being comprehended in those two classes. Consequently, this philosophy, excluding body and mind, admits of no existence whatsoever, not even of a percipient being to be the subject of these perceptions. To the same purpose Dr Reid observes, that, according to Mr Locke's system, ideas being the only objects of thought, and having no existence but when we are conscious of them, it necessarily follows, that there is no object of our thought which can have a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> and permanent existence. Body and spirit, cause and effect, time and space, to which we were wont to ascribe an existence independent of our thought, are all turned out of existence by this short <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DILEMMA">dilemma</a>. Either these things are ideas of sensation or reflection, or they are not; if they are ideas of sensation or reflection, they can have no existence but when we are conscious of them; if they are not ideas of sensation or reflection, they are words without any meaning. To which we shall only reply, that we have the same reason to believe, that mind exists as that body exists; since it is only by that name that we distinguish the subject of certain powers or properties, of which we are conscious, as perception, memory, will, &c. and we have just the same reason to believe the identity of an idea as that of any external body, or that of our own minds. Those who wish to be farther acquainted with the controversy relating to the nature and origin of our ideas, must be referred to Hume's Treatise of Human Nature, vol. i. p. 123, &c. 282, &c. 434, &c. Reid's Inquiry into the Human Mind, passim. Beattie's Essay on Truth, part ii. chap. 2. Priestley's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXAMINATION">Examination</a> of Reid, Beattie, &c. passim.

INEBRIANTS

Pages 1173-1173

are defined to be such things as affect the nerves in a particular and agreeable manner, and through them alter and disturb the functions of the mind. They are properly divided into native and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a>; the former chiefly in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among the oriental and other nations, the latter principally throughout <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> Inebriants are, 1. Opium; in use all over the east, and of which the Turks, through <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, swallow a drachm. 2. Peganum harmala, Syrian rue. The seeds are sold in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> for this purpose; and with these, as Bellonius relates, the Turkish <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Soliman kept himself intoxicated. 3. Maslac of the Turks, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> bangue of the Persians; prepared from the dust of the maleflower of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, or from the leaves. 4. Bangue of the Indians, from the leaves of the hibiscus sabdariffa. 5. Seeds of various <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the datura, or thorny apple. 6. Pinang, or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BETEL">betel</a> of the Indians. 7. Roots of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> henbane. 8. The hyoscyamus physaloides. 9. Berries of the deadly nightshade. 10. Leaves of millfoil, are used by the Dalecarlians to render their beer intoxicating. 11. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">Tobacco</a>, and several others less material are mentioned; such as clary, laffron, and darnel. Artificial Inebriants, are fermented liquors from farinaceous feeds; wines, and spirits drawn by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a>. With these is ranked the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NECTAR">nectar</a> of the gods, and the anodyne medicine of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called nepenthe; and the spells by which Medea and Circe produced their enchantments. INFORMATION. Line penult, formade, read <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODE">mode</a>.

INJECTION

Pages 1173-1173
or INJECTING, in surgery, the Injection, throwing in some liquor or medicine into a vein opened by incision. This practice, and that of transfusion, or the conveying the arterial blood of one man, or other animal, into another, were once greatly practised, but are now laid aside. The method of injecting is this: A vein is to be opened in the arm with a lancet as in bleeding, and the small pipe of a syringe being introduced at the orifice, the liquor intended to be mixed with the blood, and contained for that purpose in the body of the syringe, is to be forcibly injected, or thrown into the vein upwards, or toward the heart; which done, the orifice is to be secured with compresses and bandage, as in bleeding. The bold experiment of injecting medicated liquors into the human veins was first made in the hospital at Danzig. One of the patients was a hulky robust soldier dangerously infected with the venereal disease, so that he had exostoses on the bones of his arms. While the liquor, (two drachms of a laxative medicine,) was passing into the vein of his arms, he complained of great pain in his elbows, and the valves of the vein swelled visibly, that it was necessary to stroke them up with a finger towards the patient's shoulders. In four hours after, it began to operate by stool, and continued to do so till next day; so that the patient had in all five stools from it. The disease disappeared without any other remedy. A married woman of 35 years of age, and a young woman of 20, had both been so grievously afflicted with epileptic fits from their infancy, that little or no hope could be entertained of their cure. Both of them underwent this singular treatment: into their veins were injected a laxative rosin dissolved in an antiepileptical spirit; but what the rosin and spirit were, we are not told. The married woman had several gentle stools some hours after the injection, and also next day; soon after which the disease vanished; the young woman, it is said, cast herself away by going into the air, catching cold, and not observing any diet. It was remarked, that all the three patients vomited frequently and severely soon after the injection. Whether this practice of injecting proper medicines into the blood may not be found of use in apoplexies, quinsies, hydrophobia, &c. is worthy to be tried by repeated experiments. The method of injecting liquors into the blood of living animals is said to be the invention of Sir Christopher Wren. His method was by making ligatures on the veins, and opening them on the side of the ligature towards the heart; then putting into them small syringes or quills fastened to bladders, in the manner of clyster-pipes, containing the matter to be injected. Mr Boyle soon made the experiment upon dogs with infusions of opium and crocus metallorum; all which he circumstantially described in his Usefulness of Experimental Philosophy, part ii. eff. 2. The ingenious Dr Hales made a variety of experiments of this kind on different animals. Many disorders of particular parts are noway curable, unless the parts affected are injected with a proper liquor, by means of a syringe and proper tube. The method of performing this is too obvious to need any directions; but these general cautions are neces-

JAGO

Pages 1169-1169

an ingenious poet, was <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a> of Snitterfield in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARWICKSHIRE">Warwickshire</a>, and rector of Kimcote in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEICESTERSHIRE">Leicestershire</a>. He was the intimate friend and correspondent of Mr Shenstone, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with him at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, and, it is believed, his schoolfellow; was of University <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a>; took the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of M.A. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 9, 1739; was author of several poems in the 4th and 5th volumes of Doddley's Poems; published a sermon, in 1755, on the Causes of Impenitence considered, preached May 4, 1755, at Hartbury in Warwickshire, where he was vicar; on occasion of a conversation said to have passed between one of the inhabitants and an apparition in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-yard there; wrote "Edge-hill," a poem, for which he obtained a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> subscription in 1767; and was also author of "Labour and Genius, 1768;" 4to; of "The Blackbirds," a beautiful elegy in the Adventurer; and of many other ingenious performances. He died May 28, 1781.

KALMIA

Pages 1173-1174

(Encycl.) The two <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> are the la- tifolia and the angustifolia. The first, a most beautiful shrub, rises usually to the height of five <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> six feet, and sometimes twice that height in its native places. The stems of some are as big as the small of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s leg, though generally they are smaller, and covered with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> rough bark. The wood is very <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> grained, heavy, and hard like box. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a> in general are crooked, and grow <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>; but are thick-clothed with stiff smooth leaves of a shin- ing bright green. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> grow in bunches on the tops of the branches, to footstalks of three inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>; they are <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, stained with purplish <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>, con- sisting of one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> in form of a cup divided at the verge into five sections: in the middle is a stamen and 12 sta- <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINA">mina</a>; which, when the flower first opens, appear ly- ing close to the sides of the cup at equal distances, their apices being lodged in ten little hollow cells, which being prominent on the outside, appear as so many little <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TUBERCLES">tubercles</a>. The flowers are succeeded by small round capsules; which when ripe open in five parts, and discharge its small dust like seeds. This plant is a native of Carolina, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>, and other parts of the northern continent of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>; yet are not <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a>, but are found only in particular places: they grow on rocks hanging over rivulets and running streams, and on the sides of barren hills. They blo- om in May, and continue in flower the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. The noxious qualities of this elegant plant lessen that esteem which its <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> claims: for although deer feed on its green leaves with impunity, yet when cattle and sheep, by severe winters deprived of better food, feed on the leaves of these <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many of them die annually. The kalmia angustifolia, rises to the height of a- bout 16 feet, producing evergreen leaves in shape like the lauro-cerasus, but small, and of a shining dark green. The flowers grow in clusters, the buds of which appear in autumn wrapped up in a conic scaly perianthium, on which is lodged a viscid <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, which protects them from the severe <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> in winter. These buds dilating in the following <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> forth into twenty or more monopetalous flowers di- vided into five segments, and set singly on pedicles half an inch long. These flowers, when blown, appear white; but on a near view are of a faint bluish <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, which as the flower decays grow paler. One of the five petals is longer and more concave than the rest, and is blended with purple, green, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> specks, being a viscid matter on the extremities of very fine hairs. The convex side of the same petal is also speck- led with yellowish green. The pointal rises from the centre of the flower, and has its head adorned with scarlet, and surrounded by 10 stamens, whereof three are long and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> short, whose farina issues out at a small round hole at its top. This elegant tree adorns the western and remote parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENNSYLVANIA">Pennsylvania</a>, always growing in the most sterile <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, or on the rocky de- clivities of hills and river-banks, in shady moist places.

KERATOPHYTUM

Pages 1174-1176

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of Gorgonia.—The keratophyta are called the frutices caroloides, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>; and generally known among naturalists by the different appellations of litophyta, li- thoxyla, and keratophyta; epithets tending to convey an idea of their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, which at first view, seems to consist partly of a woody or horny, partly of a stony or calcareous substance, variously disposed with Lampyris, the fire-fly, a genus of insects belonging to the coleoptera order; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of which are: The antennae are filiform; the elytra are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a>; the thorax is flat, of a semiorbicular form, surrounding and concealing the head. The segments of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a> terminate in papillae, which are turned up towards the elytra, and partly fold one over the other. The females in general are apterous. There are 18 species; of which the most remarkable is the noctiluca. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> of this insect is less than the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a>: its head is shaped exactly in the same manner, and covered likewise by the plate of the thorax, only it appears rather longer than that of the female. Both the head and antennae are <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>. The thorax of the male, which is smaller and shorter than that of the female, has the folds and papillae on its sides much less remarkable: but the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> that is found between the two sexes is, that the male is covered with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> elytra, shagreened and marked with two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> longitudinally. The elytra are longer than the abdomen, and under them <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> the wings. The two last rings of the abdomen are not so bright as those of the female, only there appear four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUMINOUS">luminous</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, two upon each of the two last rings. The insect called glow-worm, and which is frequently met with towards evening, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, in woods and meadows, is the female belonging to this species. By the shining <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> which it emits, it attracts the male; a wonderful instance of the divine <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVIDENCE">providence</a>.
