It is apparent that their shining light depends... <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">Language</a> depends on a liquor placed at the lower extremity of the insect, which when in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, the light is more lively and shining, and of a finer green. This light the insect withdraws at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, either by unfolding or contracting itself. As a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> that the light depends on a phosphorous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, you may crush the animal, which, though dead and bruised, leaves a luminous substance on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, that only loses its lustre when dried. The perfect insect flies about during the evening in autumn, and frequents the grally plantations of juniper trees. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">Beauty</a> of Language, p. 4095, col. 2. l. 4. from bottom, for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">Part</a> II. read Part III.

LARVA

Pages 1176-1176

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a name given by Linnaeus to insects in that state called by other writers eruca <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> caterpillar. LARVÆ, in antiquity, derived from the Hetruscan word lar or laris, signifying <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a>, denoted the ghosts of the deceased, considered as wicked and mischievous. Hence is formed the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> larvatus, i.e. larva indutus, or demoniac. The ingenious Mr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FARMER">Farmer</a> urges the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ETYMOLOGY">etymology</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of this term to prove, that the heathen demons were <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> ghosts.

LEASE

Pages 1176-1176

from the French laisser, demittere, "to let," in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEMISE">demise</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> letting of lands, tenements, or hereditaments, unto another for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> of years, or at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a>, for a rent reserved. A lease is either written, called an indenture, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a>-poll, or lease in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>; or by word of mouth, called lease parole. All estates, interests of freehold, or terms for years in lands, &c. not put in writing and signed by the parties, shall have no greater effect than as estates at will; unless it be of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-LEASES">leases</a> not exceeding three years from the making; wherein the rent reserved shall be two-thirds of the value of the things demised. Leases exceeding three years must be made in writing; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the substance of a lease be put in writing, and signed by the parties, though it be not sealed, it shall have the effect of a lease for years, &c. An assignment differs from a lease only in this; that by a lease one grants an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> less than his own, referring to himself a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-REVERSION">reversion</a>; in assignments he parts with the whole <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, and the assignee stands to all intents and purposes in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the assignor. Lease, in Scots law. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TACK">Tack</a>, (Encycl.)

LEPAS

Pages 1176-1176

the acorn, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a>, a genus belonging to the order of vermes testacea. The animal is the triton; the shell is multivalve, unequal, fixed by a stem <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> sessile. There are several <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, of which the most remarkable is the anatifa, consisting of five shells depressed, affixed to a pedicle and in clusters. It adheres to the bottom of ships by its pedicles. The tentacles from its animal are feathered; and have given the old English historians and naturalists the idea of a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>. They ascribed the origin of the barnacle goosel to those shells. See Plate CLIX. fig. 8.

LIBERTY

Pages 1176-1177

physical, is that principle of spontaneity <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> self-determination which constitutes us agents; or which gives us a command over our actions, rendering them properly ours, and not effects of the operation of any foreign cause. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-METAPHYSICS">Metaphysics</a>, (Encycl.) n° 78—80. Without this liberty, or being under a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of always following some <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> different from his own, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> would be a machine acted upon by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, having no principle of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> in himself, or command over events; and therefore incapable of all merit or demerit. Whether man is endued with this kind of liberty or self-determining power, has been a subject of much controversy; it was agitated at the beginning of this century between Leibnitz, Colline, &c. on one side, and Clarke, Jackson, &c. on the other; and has been lately revived by Dr Priestley. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> arguments in favour of liberty, as it is popularly understood, and as it is defined above, are the following. This principle is necessary to constitute man an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGENT">agent</a>. For, as far as it is true of a being that he acts, so far he must himself be the cause of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, and therefore not necessarily determined to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a>; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he has no <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> power over his own actions, i.e. if he be not a free agent, the actions which he performs cannot properly be said to be his own, but must be ascribed to some other power by which he is led on to perform them; as a good clock or watch performs the motions assigned to it by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>. This argument is excellently illustrated by Dr Clarke. Man, says he, either has within himself a principle of action; properly speaking, i.e. a self-moving <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a>, a principle or power of beginning motion; or he has not. If he has within himself such a principle, then he is a free, and not a necessary agent: for every necessary agent is moved necessarily by something else; and then that which moves it, not the thing itself which is moved, is the true and only cause of the action. That any other thing operating upon an agent should efficiently and necessarily produce self-motion in that agent, is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> in terms. If man has not within himself a principle or power of self-motion, then every motion and action of man is chiefly and properly produced by the efficiency of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRINSIC">extrinsic</a> cause; which cause must be either what we usually call the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> or reason upon which a man acts; or else it must be some insensible subtle <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, or some other being or substance making an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> upon him. If the reasons or motives upon which a man acts be the immediate and efficient cause of the action, then either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> notions, such as all reasons and motives are, have a real subsistence, that is, are themselves substances; or else that which has itself no real subsistence can put a body into motion; either of which is manifestly absurd. If insensible subtle matter, or any other being or substance, continually making impression upon a man, be the immediate and efficient cause of his acting; then the motion of that subtle matter or substance must be caused by some other substance, and the motion of that by some other, till at last we arrive at a free agent; and then liberty is a possible thing, and man possibly may have liberty: and if he may possibly have it, then <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> will prove that he probably, nay, that he certainly has it. If we never arrive at any free cause, then there is either in infinitum a progression of motions without any mover, of effects without any cause, of things acted without any agent; which is a manifest contradiction, or else motion exists necessarily of itself. If motion exists necessarily of itself, it must be either with a determination every way, or one certain way: if with a determination every way, this is no motion at all; if with a determination one certain way, then that determination is either necessary, and consequently all other determinations impossible, which is contrary to experience; or else there must be a particular reason of that determination, and so backwards in infinitum; which comes to the forementioned absurdity, of effects existing without any cause. Farther, liberty is the dictate of our own consciousness: we have really the same constant and necessary consciousness of liberty that we have that we think, choose, will, or even exist; and, whatever men may say to the contrary, it is impossible for them in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> to think they have no <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> self-moving powers, and are not the causes of their own volitions, or not to ascribe to themselves what they must be conscious they think and do. Mr Hume, though he denies the reality of liberty, grants we have a feeling of it; that the divine <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> required that we should be so made, as to seem to ourselves free; that the whole <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of things is as if we were free; and that being under a necessity of approving and disapproving actions and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, we are so far under a necessity of believing ourselves and others free. After these concessions, it can hardly be imagined that the constitution of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> should be altogether imposition and deceit. Besides, if man be not, in the strictest <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of the word, a free agent, he can be no moral agent. It is hard to say what virtue and vice, commendation and blame, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a>, if they do not suppose agency, voluntary motion, free-choice, and an absolute dominion over our resolutions. Can we applaud or reproach ourselves for what we were no more the causes of than of our own beings, and what it was no more possible for us to prevent than the returns of the seasons, or the revolutions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>? On the system of necessity, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a> is an inexorable principle: its censures or applause are equally futile and groundless: the approbation of mankind is an insult with regard to those on whom it is bestowed, because they can have no merit; and the reproach of men unjust and cruel, because there can be no demerit and ground of blame. Whatever difficulties, therefore, may attend the nature of that influence which we ascribe to motives, they cannot be the efficient necessitating cause of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> actions: since, on this supposition, there could be but one agent in the universe; who must equally be the author of all the good and evil in the world, and on whom must ultimately be <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> the sin and misery, as well as the virtue and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>, of his creatures. Moreover, it has been urged by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a> of liberty, that if men's determinations and actions flow necessarily from the previous state of their minds and the motives or influences resulting from a nature or condition imposed upon them without their own consent or choice, the idea of responsibility or accountability must vanish, and there can be no propriety or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of rewards or punishments. God cannot reward without virtue, and there can be no virtue without a self-determining power: he cannot punish without guilt, and there can be no guilt when men do what they cannot avoid doing, and when their actions arise from circumstances in which their Creator placed them. It is also equally unjust and useless to threaten <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> or inflict it on men, to prevent crimes, when they are necessarily determined in all their actions. And if men are necessary agents, though we cannot well admit this verbal contradiction, it can be of no use to reason with them, to admonish or treat them; and God must be insincere in his addresses and invitations, and cruel in his requirements and commands. But such is the whole tenor of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a>; and therefore the conclusion is necessary, that man is a free agent, capable of good or evil, and of determining his pursuit of either, from the sole power of his own judgment or will. See on this subject Collins's Inquiry concerning Human Liberty, first printed in 1717. Clarke's Remarks, 1717; and Collection of Papers which passed between Mr Leibnitz and Dr Clarke, in 1715 and 1716. Jackson's Vindication and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFENCE">Defence</a> of Human Liberty, 1730. Price's Review of the principal Questions, &c., in Morals, p. 315, &c., edit. 1758. Priestley's Doctrine of Philosophical Necessity, 1777.—For the objections against liberty, and the arguments in support of necessity, see NECESSITY.

LIEUTAUD

Pages 1177-1177

counsellor of state and first physician at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a> of France, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIX">Aix</a> in Provence, and resided principally there till he took the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of medicine. After this he prosecuted his studies for some years at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTPELLIER">Montpellier</a>. He returned to Aix, where he soon acquired extensive practice, and became eminent for literary abilities. He resided there till the year 1750, when he was invited to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> as physician to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> infirmary at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERSAILLES">Versailles</a>. There he practised with such reputation and success, that he soon arrived at the head of his profession; and in the year 1774, upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of M. Senac, he was appointed archbishop. His extensive engagements in practice did not prevent him from cultivating the science of medicine in all its branches, and from freely communicating to others the result of his own studies. He published many valuable works; among which the following may be accounted the most remarkable, 1. Elementa Philologie. 2. Precis de la Medicine. 3. Pratique Precis de la Matiere Medecale. 4. Essai Anatomique. 5. Synopsis Universa Praxes Medicinae. 6. Historia Anatomico-Medica. He died at Versailles Dec. 8th, 1780, in the 78th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>.

LITHOSTROTION

Pages 1177-1177

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of fossil coral, composed of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and slender columns, sometimes round, sometimes angular, jointed nicely to one another, and of a starry <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> radiated surface at their tops. These are found in considerable quantities in the northern and western parts of this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, sometimes in single, sometimes in complex specimens. See Plate CCCXVII.

LYMINGTON

Pages 1177-1177

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAMPSHIRE">Hampshire</a> in England situated on a hill near the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1.

MACBRIDE

Pages 1177-1179

an eminent physician and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, was descended from an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GALLOWAY">Galloway</a> in Scotland. His grandfather, a clergyman, had settled in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> about the end of the last century, as minister to a Presbyterian <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BELFAST">Belfast</a>; and his father, who followed the same line, was settled at Ballymony in the county of Antrim, where he married, and where our author was born in April 1726. After a proper school-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, and having passed some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> under the tuition of an eminent surgeon in his native <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, he was sent to the university of Glasgow. Having there completed the usual course of academical studies, he came to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> for the further prosecution of medical science. After a short stay here, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> then prevailing between France and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, he was induced to go on board the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> in the station of a surgeon's mate. In the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> he <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> for several years; and after discharging for some time the duties of an assistant, he was raised to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of surgeon. In this situation, he first turned his thoughts towards the discovery of a remedy for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-scurvy. It was not, however, at this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, that either chance <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> reasoning suggested to him the employment of an article, which has since been attended with the most beneficial consequences. Here he had an opportunity only of observing the symptoms, of studying the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and of lamenting the consequences of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>. The termination of the war by the peace of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIX">Aix</a>-la-Chapelle, put a period to Dr Macbride's employment as a naval surgeon. He had now probably obtained much medical knowledge in the school of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>; but he was sensible that he had still much to acquire in that of science. An ardent keenness to mingle in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> had led him from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> of medicine at an earlier period than could have been wished; and an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> desire to found his future practice in the best established principles led him back to them, when a judgment, matured by years, and informed from the observation of facts, rendered him capable of hearing teachers with greater advantage. He returned therefore to Edinburgh, and again entered on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAREER">career</a> of academical pursuits, under the tuition of Dr Monro, and those other teachers, whose abilities raised the name of the medical school at this place. But, not satisfied with the instructions to be had from any one set of professors, the celebrity of the medical teachers in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a> led him also to visit that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. There he particularly became the pupil of those distinguished lecturers, Dr Hunter and Dr Smellie. And while from the former he laboured to acquire an accurate surgical knowledge, from the latter he endeavoured to obtain the true principles of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MIDWIFERY">midwifery</a> considered as a science. At the same time, he was no less industrious in improving himself in the successful practice of both arts by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>. Thus prepared for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of his profession, about the end of the year 1749 he fixed his residence in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a> in the character of surgeon and accoucheur. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> amiable manners, and extensive knowledge of his profession, could alone have been sufficient introductions to practice, he might in a short time have looked for a competent share of business in that capital; but while he had to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a> that objection which very generally arises from youth, his progress was also not a little retarded by an uncommon <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>. Hence for several years he remained almost in a state of obscurity, and was employed by but few people either of rank or fortune. But, if it is to be regretted that for many years his time was not so fully employed in the lucrative <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of his profession as was due to his merit, it ought still to be remembered, that this essentially promoted the cause of science: for by this means his genius and industry were directed to medical researches; and were productive of discoveries which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> transmit his name to latest posterity. These, though some of them might have been successfully turned to his own emolument, were fully communicated to the world in different publications; and he did not show greater ingenuity in making discoveries, than liberality of sentiment in publishing them for the advantage of others.—His first publication, intitled, "Experimental Essays on medical and philosophical Subjects," made its appearance in the year 1764.—These essays are five in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>: 1. On the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a> of alimentary mixture and the digestion of the food. 2. On the nature and properties of fixed <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>. 3. On the different kinds of antiseptics. 4. Of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISSOLVENT">dissolvent</a> power of quicklime. 5. Of the seascurvy. The merit of all these is sufficiently known and acknowledged: but the last of them is unquestionably the most important; the method therein proposed of both the prevention and cure of that dreadful disease the scurvy, having been confirmed by repeated and undeniable observation. Having thus equally distinguished himself as an ingenious philosopher and able practitioner, the world were not now slow in bestowing upon him the tribute of applause to which he was entitled. His name was enrolled with honour in the lists of many learned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a>; and the university, where his studies had first been commenced, were proud to confer upon him the degree of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a> of Medicine. The reputation, however, of being a distinguished author, was to him but a secondary object; and his talents were not confined to the advancement of medicine alone. Having successfully discovered a considerable improvement in the art of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TANNING">tanning</a>, with that spirited generosity which is ever the concomitant of real real worth, he speedily and freely communicated it to the public, by publishing, first, "An account of a new method of tanning;" and afterwards, "Instructions for carrying on the new method of tanning." As a mark of approbation for this liberal conduct, as well as a testimony of respect for his ingenuity, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a>-medals were conferred upon him by the Societies of Arts both in London and Dublin. But his last and most extensive publication was more immediately in the line of his own profession: It is intitled, "A Methodical Introduction to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THEORY">Theory</a> and Practice of Medicine." In that valuable <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> he has given a concise and connected view of the principles and practice of the healing art, as best established by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> reasoning, and confirmed by accurate observation. Most, if not all these publications, not only went through various editions, but were translated into different languages. After the merit of Dr Macbride came to be properly known, the public seemed to show a desire of making compensation for having so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> overlooked it. His employment increased rapidly, that he had more business than he could transact either with ease or safety. This having kept him in perpetual agitation both of body and mind, at last induced an almost total incapacity of sleeping. From this circumstance his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> could not fail to be impaired. In this situation, after accidental exposure to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, he was attacked with a fever, which put an end to his life on the 13th of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1778, in the 53rd year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Those who were his most intimate acquaintance were inclined to believe that his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> was not a little hastened by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> calamities. During his residence in Dublin he was twice married, and was often subjected to that inexpressible distress which must result from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FINAL">final</a> separation in this world from the most intimate and loving friends. By both of his wives he had several children; but none of them survived their father. And on these calamitous events, although he was able to conceal his feelings from the world, yet they gave a severe shock to his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>. After his death, several of the playful trinkets of his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a>, with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIGNATURE">signature</a> of dulces exuviae, were found in his repositories among papers on medical and other important subjects: an incontrovertible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>, that in him at least, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> mind of the philosopher was conjoined with the feeling heart of the affectionate father. But if his abilities were remarkable as a philosopher and physician, if his conduct was exemplary as a husband and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARENT">parent</a>, his manners were no less amiable as a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> and friend. His polite and benevolent conduct, joined to his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for the fine arts, conciliated the affections and esteem of all who knew him. His death was universally and sincerely lamented in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Dublin.

MADREPORA

Pages 1179-1179

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the name of a genus of submarine substances; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of which are, That they are almost of a stony <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a>, resembling the corals, and are usually divided into branches, and pervious by many holes <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> cavities, which are frequently of a stellar <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. In the Linnæan system, this is a genus of lithophyta: The animal that inhabits it is the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEDUSA">medusa</a>; it comprehends 39 <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. According to Donati, the madrepora is like the coral as to its hardness, which is equal to bone or marble; the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> when polished; its surface is lightly wrinkled, and the Madrepora wrinkles run lengthwise of the branches; in the centre there is a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a>, which is often pierced through its whole length by two or three holes. From this cylinder are detached about 17 laminae, which run to the circumference in straight <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>; and are transversely intersected by other laminae, forming many <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> cavities; the cellules, which are composed of these laminae ranged into a circle, are the habitations of little polypes, which are extremely tender animals, generally transparent, and variegated with beautiful colours. M. de Peyssonel observes, that those writers who only considered the figures of submarine substances, denominated that class of them, which seemed pierced with holes, pores; and those, the holes of which were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, they called madrepora. He defines them to be all those marine bodies which are of a stony substance, without either bark or crust, and which have but one apparent opening at each extremity, furnished with rays that proceed from the centre to the circumference. He observes that the body of the animal of the madrepora, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> is so soft that it divides upon the gentlest touch, fills the centre; the head is placed in the middle, and surrounded by several feet or claws, which fill the intervals of the partitions observed in this substance, and are at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> brought to its head, and are furnished with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> papillae. He discovered that its head or centre was lifted up occasionally above the surface, and often contracted and dilated itself like the pupil of the eye: he <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> all its claws moved, as well as its head or centre. When the animals of the madrepora are destroyed, its extremities become white. In the madrepora, he says, the animal occupies the extremity; and the substance is of a stony but more loose texture than the coral. This is formed, like other substances of the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, of a liquor which the animal discharges; and he farther adds, that there are some species of the polype of the madrepora, which are produced singly, and others in clutters.

MAGNOLIA

Pages 1179-1180

(Encycl.) The glauca generally grows in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> swampy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> on wet meadows. The English and Swedes in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENNSYLVANIA">Pennsylvania</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEW_JERSEY">New <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERSEY">Jersey</a> call it beaver tree, because the root of this tree is the dainty of beavers, which are caught by its means. It drops its leaves early in autumn, though some of the young trees kept them all the winter. This tree is seldom found to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Pennsylvania, where it begins to flower about the end of May. The scent of its blossoms is exquisite: for by it you can discover, within three <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of an English <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILE">mile</a>, whether these little trees stand in the neighbourhood, provided the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> be not against it; for the whole <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> is filled with this sweet and pleasant odour. It is beyond <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> agreeable to travel in the woods about that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, especially towards night. They retain their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> for three weeks, and even longer, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the soil on which the trees stand; and during the whole time of their being in blossom, they spread their odoriferous exhalations. The berries likewise look very fine when they are ripe; for they have a rich <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and hang in bunches on slender stalks. The cough and other pectoral diseases are cured by putting the berries into rum or brandy, of which a draught every morning may be taken: the virtues of this remedy were universally extolled, and even praised, for their salutary effects in consumptions. The bark being put into brandy, or boiled in any other liquor, is said not only to ease pectoral diseases, but likewise to be of some <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> against all internal pains and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>; and it was thought that a decoction of it could stop the dysentery. Persons who had caught <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> boiled the branches of the beaver-tree in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and drank it to their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> relief. Kalm.

MALALEUCA

Pages 1179-1179

the CAYPUTI TREE; a genus of the polyandra order, belonging to the polyadelphia class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There is but one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, viz. the leucodendron, a native of the East Indies and South-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">Sea</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. Mr Forster relates that they were found in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of New <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CALEDONIA">Caledonia</a>. They were <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> at the root, but had a bark perfectly <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> and loose, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> narrow leaves like our willows. The leaves are extremely fragrant and aromatic; and Rumphius tells us, that from them the natives of the Moluccas make the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> called cayputi. This oil is commended as a nervous medicine, and as being useful in some cardialgies. The dose is four <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> five drops in some convenient liquor.

MAN-OF-WAR BIRD

Pages 1180-1180

(Pelicanus Aquilus, Lin.) Its <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BILL">bill</a> is more than a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>'s-breadth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and is narrow: the upper jaw is somewhat the longest, with a hook-shaped point; the cere, which is blue, covers the bill from the eyes to the hook-shaped point: the mandibles have no such <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERRATED">serrated</a> incisions (supplying the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>) as are usually found in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-birds: the head is covered with short feathers as far as the eyes, which are pretty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>: the tongue is large, almost trifid at the top; the corner at its bottom is split: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> are naked: the wings consist of three parts, and are very long; of the 22 quill feathers, the first ten are of a considerable length; the two inner <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> contain, besides the coverts, 22 secondary feathers: the outward of the 12 tail-feathers are much longer than the middle ones, which make the tail look like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of scissors. The <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> is about the size of a goose, and is a yard long: the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the whole body, and of the toes, is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>; but the head, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, belly, and fore-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the neck, are of a fine <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>. Its food is fishes, which it takes from others, because it is not forced to catch them itself: the English for this reason call it <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>-of-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>.

MARBELLA

Pages 1180-1180

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, situated at the mouth of the Rio Verde, 30 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of Gibraltar, and 28 south-west of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALAGA">Malaga</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5. 25. N. Lat. 30. 25.

MARINE REMAINS

Pages 1180-1182

a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> used by many authors to express the shells of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-fishes, and parts of crustaceous and other sea-animals, found in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a> at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> depths in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> on the tops of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. Their being lodged in these places, is an evident and unquestionable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the sea's having once been there, since it must have covered those places where it has left its productions. It has been a favourite system with many, and particularly with the late Dr Woodward, that all these marine bodies were brought to the places where they now <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a>, by the waters of the universal deluge; which, as we are informed by holy writ, covered the whole surface of the globe, and even the highest mountains. But though this is a very ready expedient to account for many of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> phenomena, yet there are evident proofs that it cannot have been the cause of all that is attributed to it; and there must necessarily have been some other cause of many of these remains having been placed where we now find them. Neither does the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of some particular authors, that partial inundations of different places have left these marine bodies behind them at the receds of the waters, seem sufficient to account for the multitudes of these remains, many of which we find thrown upon places inaccessible to such floods. Signior Moro has attempted to account for these phenomena on a new <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of reasoning. He observes, that it is the best basis of argument to begin from facts; and that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we can certainly find how some <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of these animal remains come to be deposited at such great distances from their natural residence, we may very rationally conclude, that by the same means, be they what they <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a>, all the rest were also brought thither. He adds, that the earth, once the bottom of the sea, or the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> surface of a plain, may be, and frequently has been, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>, raised up into a mountain by subterranean fires, earthquakes, and volcanoes. He mentions the famous instance of the new <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> raised out of the bottom of the sea near Santorini in the year 1707, which became of a circumference not less than six miles, and of the new mountain raised near Puzzoli in 1538. These, and many other like facts, prove that the origin of mountains and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> may have been such, and that the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> they consist of may have been the same with what was once the bottom of the sea; and that the marine bodies found in these mountains were such as were living, or remaining of living fish at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> when the islands or mountains were so raised above the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> which before covered it. This is no new opinion; but this author has set it in a new and much stronger <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> than it ever had appeared in before, by the instances and examples he has brought in proof of it. Some have been fond of believing that the bodies we call marine remains, were never indeed any parts of living animals, but that they are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> lusii <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> formed in the places where they are found; but Fabius Columna proved this to be an <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a>, showing that the shark's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, or globopterae of the island of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>, when calcined by a strong fire, yielded ashes the same with those from animal-bodies, and by no means of the same nature with those produced from calcined <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. That changes of parts of the bottom of the sea into dry <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>, have often been made, is proved not only from the late known instances, but from the testimonies of Strabo, Pliny, and other writers of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>; and nothing is more obvious to reason, than that in the sudden rise of such parts of the bottom of the sea, all its contents, all the shells, and other hard parts of fishes lying there, would be carried up with it. As some mountains and some islands must have certainly been produced in this manner, it is not impossible but that all of them may have been so; and there is no more than this required to account clearly and evidently for all the vast profusion of marine bodies at land as we find them, without having recourse to the improbable means of the universal deluge, which for many plain reasons cannot have been the cause; or to the effects of particular inundations, which must have been wholly incapable of lodging many of them there. The lodgment of shells in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> of mountains, is better accounted for by this system of Signior Moro than any other; and if it be asked why some mountains afford them in great plenty, and others not at all, it will not be difficult to answer, by observing, that among the mountains of the more known parts of the world, some consist of mere solid rock, and others of various strata of earthy and other matter; that the first of these may be supposed primary or natural mountains, and the others secondary or accidental ones; and that these marine remains are always wanting in the former, and usually are found in the latter, which is a fact greatly favourable to this system. There are many difficulties attending the accounts of all authors of the formation of the earth, and the lodging these bodies in it; nor is this last system without difficulty. The causes here assigned as to the origin of mountains and islands, doubtsless have been so in regard to some, but scarce to all; and the bodies here treated of are so numerous, in some particular places, that scarce any account can solve the difficulty of their being collected together in so strange a manner. **MARITAGIUM,** (Encycl.) In the feudal customs, *maritagium* (as contradistinguished from *matrimonium*) signifies the power which the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a> in chivalry had of disposing of his infant <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WARD">ward</a> in matrimony. For while the infant was in ward, the guardian had the power of tendering him or her a suitable <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATCH">match</a>, without disparagement or inequality: if which the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a> refused, they forfeited the value of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, *valorem maritagii*, to their guardian; that is, so much as a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JURY">jury</a> would assess, or any one would *<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BONA">bona</a> fide* give to the guardian for such an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a>: and if the infants married themselves without the guardian's consent, they forfeited <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the value, *duplicum valorem maritagii*. **MASCULUS FLOS.** See *Flos Masculus* in this Appendix. **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASORA">MASORA</a>,** a term in the Jewish <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, signifying a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>, performed by several learned rabbins, to secure it from any alterations which might otherwise happen. Their work regards merely the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> text; in which they have, first, fixed the true <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-READING">reading</a> by <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-VOWELS">vowels</a> and accents: they have, secondly, numbered not only the chapters and sections, but the verses, words, and letters of the text; and they find in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENTATEUCH">Pentateuch</a> 5245 verses, and in the whole Bible 22206. The masora is called, by the Jews, the hedge or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FENCE">fence</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>, because this enumeration of the verses, &c., is a means of preserving it from being corrupted and altered. They have, thirdly, marked whatever irregularities occur in any of the letters of the Hebrew text; such as the different size of the letters, their various positions and inversions, &c., and they have been fruitful in finding out reasons for these irregularities and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol12.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> in them. They are, fourthly, supposed to be the authors of the Keri and Chetibh, or the marginal corrections of the text in our Hebrew Bibles. The text of the sacred books, it is to be observed, was originally written without any breaks or divisions into chapters or verses, or even into words; so that a whole book, in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> manner, was but one <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> word; of this kind we have still several ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>, both Greek and Latin. In regard, therefore, the sacred writings had undergone an infinite <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of alterations, whence various readings had arisen, and the original was become much mangled and disguised, the Jews had recourse to a canon, which they judged infallible, to fix and ascertain the reading of the Hebrew text; and this rule they call *masora*, "<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>," from *tradidit*, as if this critique were nothing but a tradition which they had received from their forefathers. Accordingly they say, that when God gave the law to Moses at mount <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SINAI">Sinai</a>, he taught him, first, the true reading of it; and, secondly, its true interpretation; and that both these were handed <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORAL">oral</a> tradition, from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> to generation, till at length they were committed to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>. The former of these, viz. the true reading, is the subject of the masora; the latter, or true interpretation, that of the mishna and gemara. According to Elias Levita, they were the Jews of a famous school at Tiberias, about 500 years after Christ, who composed, or at least began, the masora; whence they are called *masorites*, and *maforetic doctors*. Aben <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EZRA">Ezra</a> makes them the authors of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> and accents in the Hebrew text, as we now find it; and which serve for vowels. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of the masorites has been much disputed. Archbishop Usher places them before Jerom; Capel, at the end of the fifth century; father Morin, in the tenth century. Balmage says, that they were not a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, but a succession of men; and that the masora is the work of many grammarians, who, without associating and communicating their notions, composed this collection of criticisms on the Hebrew text. It is urged that there were masorites from the time of Ezra and the men of the great synagogue, to about the year of Christ 1030; and that Ben Asher and Ben Naphtali, who were the best of the profession, and who, according to Balmage, were the inventors of the masora, flourished at this time. Each of these published a copy of the whole Hebrew text, as correct, says Dr Prideaux, as they could make it. The eastern Jews have followed that of Ben Naphtali, and the western that of Ben Asher; and all that has been done since is to copy after them, without making any more corrections or maforetical criticisms. The Arabs have done the same thing by their Koran that the masorites have done by the Bible; nor do the Jews deny their having borrowed this expedient from the Arabs, who first put it in practice in the seventh century. There is a great and little masora printed at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> and at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>, with the Hebrew text, in a different character. Buxtorf has written a maforetic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a>, which he calls *Tiberias*. **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASQUE">MASQUE</a>,** or Mask, a cover for the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a>, contrived with apertures for the eyes and mouth; originally worn chiefly by women of condition, either to preserve their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, or out of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>, to prevent their being known. Poppaea, wife of Nero, is said to be the first inventor of the masque; which she did to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> her complexion from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and weather, as being the most delicate woman, with regard to her person, that has been known. Theatrical masques were in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> both among <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MASQUERADE">Masquerade</a> the Greeks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>: Suidas and Athæneus ascribe <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURES">Measures</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of them to the poet Cherilus, a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> of Thespis; Horace attributes them to Æschylus; but <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> informs us, that the real inventor, and consequently the time of their first introduction and use, were unknown. Brantome observes, that the common use of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> masques was not introduced till towards the end of the 16th century.

MASQUERADE

Pages 1182-1182
or MASCARADE, an assembly of persons masked or disguised, meeting to dance and divert themselves. This was much in use with us, and has been long a very common practice abroad, especially in carnival time. The word comes from the Italian mascarata, and that from the Arabic maschara, which signifies "railery, buffoonery." Granacci, who died in 1543, is said to have been the first inventor of masquerades.

MEASURES

Pages 1182-1183

(Encycl.) It is necessary, for the convenience of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, that an uniformity should be observed in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WEIGHTS_AND_MEASURES">weights and measures</a>, and regulated by proper standards. A foot-rule may be used as a standard for measures of length, a bushel for measures of capacity, and a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POUND">pound</a> for weights. There should be only one authentic standard of each kind, formed of the most durable materials, and kept with all possible care. A sufficient <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of copies, exactly corresponding to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> standard, may be distributed for adjusting the weights and measures that are made for <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. There are several standards of this kind both in England and Scotland. See the article Weights and Measures, (Encycl.) <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> any one of the standards above-mentioned be justly preferred, it <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> serve as a foundation for the others, by which they may be corrected, if inaccurate, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> restored, if entirely lost. For instance, if we have a standard foot, we can easily obtain an inch, and can make a box, which shall contain a cubical inch, and may serve as a standard for measures of capacity. If it be known that a pint contains 100 cubical inches, we may make a vessel five inches <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, and four inches deep, which will contain a pint. If the standard be required in any other form, we may fill this vessel with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and regulate another to contain an equal <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>. Standards for weights may be obtained from the same foundation; for if we know how many inches of water it takes to weigh a pound, we have only to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> that quantity, and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> which balances it may be assumed as the standard of a pound. Again, if the standard of a pound be given, the measure of an inch may be obtained from it: for we may weigh a cubical inch of water, and pour it into a regular vessel; and having noticed how far it is filled, we may make another vessel of like capacity, in the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUBE">cube</a>. The side of this vessel may be assumed as the standard for an inch; and standards for a foot, a pint, or a bushel, may be obtained from it. Water is the most proper substance for regulating standards; for all other bodies differ in weight from others of the same kind; whereas it is found by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-RIVER_WATER">river water</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, and melted snow, and all other kinds, have the same weight; and this uniformly holds in all countries when the water is pure, alike warm, and free from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a> and minerals. Thus, any one standard is sufficient for restoring all the rest. It may further be desired to <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol11.html#article-HIT">hit</a> on some expedient, if possible, for restoring the standards, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> that all of them should ever <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into disorder, or should be forgotten, through the length of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and the vicissitudes of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> affairs. This seems difficult, as no words can convey a precise idea of a foot-rule, or a pound weight. Measures, assumed from the dimensions of the human body, as a foot, a handbreadth, or a pace, must nearly be the same in all ages, unless the size of the human <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RACE">race</a> undergo some change; and therefore, if we know how many square feet a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACRE">acre</a> contained, we may form some judgment of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> which restricted the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of a Roman citizen to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> acres; and this is sufficient to render <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> intelligible; but it is too inaccurate to regulate measures for commercial purposes. The same may be said of standards, deduced from the measure of a barley-corn, or the weight of a grain of wheat. If the distance of two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> be accurately measured and recorded, the nature of the measure used will be preserved in a more permanent manner than by any standard; for if ever that measure fall into disuse, and another be substituted in its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, the distance may be measured again, and the proportion of the standards may be ascertained by comparing the new and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> distances. But the most accurate and unchangeable manner of establishing standards is, by comparing them with the length of pendulums. The longer a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENDULUM">pendulum</a> is, it vibrates the slower; and it must have one precise length in order to vibrate in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a>. The slightest <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in length will occasion a difference in the time; which will become abundantly sensible after a number of vibrations, and will be easily observed if the pendulum be applied to regulate the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of a clock. The length of a pendulum which vibrates seconds in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a> is about 39½ inches, is constantly the same at the same place; but it varies a little with the latitude of the place, being shorter as the latitude is less. Therefore, though all standards of weights and measures were lost, the length of a second pendulum might be found by repeated trials; and if the pendulum be properly divided, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> measure of an inch will be obtained; and from this all other standards may be restored. 1. Measures of length. Lineal measure is regulated by the yard. The use of this measure was established by Henry I. of England, and the standard taken from the length of his own arm. It is divided into 36 inches, and each inch is supposed equal to 3 barleycorns. When used for measuring cloth, it is divided into 4 <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, and each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> subdivided into 4 nails. The English ell is equal to a yard and a quarter, or 45 inches, and is used in measuring linens imported from Germany and the Low-Countries. The Scots ell was established by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAVID">David</a> I. and divided into 37 inches. The standard is kept in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>-chamber of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, and being compared with the English yard, is found to measure 37½ inches; and therefore the Scots inch and foot are larger than the English, in the proportion of 180 to 185; but this difference being so inconsiderable, is seldom attended to in practice. The Scots ell, though forbidden by law, is still used for measuring some coarse commodities, and is the foundation of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>-measure of Scotland. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSEMANSHIP">horsemanship</a> is 4 inches. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAN">span</a> 9 inches. A geometrical pace 5 feet. A fathom, chiefly used in measuring depth, 6 feet. Itinerary measure is regulated by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">Table</a> IX. (see <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARITHMETIC">Arithmetic</a>, p. 655.) both in England and Scotland. The length of the chain is 4 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>, or 22 yards; 80 chains make a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILE">mile</a>. The old Scots computed miles were generally about a mile and a half each. The reel for yarn is 2½ yards, or 10 quarters, in circuit; 120 threads make a cut, 12 cuts make a hank or hank, and 4 hanks make a spindle. 2. Land measure. This, in England, is regulated by Tab. VII. (see Arithmetic, p. 655.). Because the length of a pole is 5 yards and a half, the square of the same contains 30¼ square yards. A square mile contains 640 square acres. In measuring fens and woodlands, 18 feet are generally allowed to the pole, and 21 feet in forest-lands. A hide of land, frequently mentioned in the earlier <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the English history, contained about 100 arable acres; and 5 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a> were esteemed a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a>'s fee. At the time of the Norman conquest, there were 243,600 hides in England. Scots land-measure is founded on the Scots ell, and regulated by Tab. VIII. (See Arithmetic, p. 655.) The proportion between the Scots and English acre, supposing the feet in both measures alike, is as 1369 to 1089, or nearly as 5 to 4. If the difference of the feet be regarded, the proportion is as 10,000 to 7869. The length of the chain for measuring land in Scotland is 24 ells, or 74 feet. A husband-land contains 6 acres of stock and scythe land, that is, of land that may be tilled with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a> or mown with a scythe: 13 acres of arable land make one ox-gang, and 4 ox-gangs make a pound-land of old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. 3. Liquid measure. The English gallon was originally founded on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a> weight. It was appointed that 8 lb. Troy of wheat, gathered from the middle of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EAR">ear</a>, and well dried, should make a gallon. When avordupois weight came into use, another gallon was formed from it in the same manner; which therefore is greater than the former, in the same proportion that the lb. avordupois exceeds the lb. Troy. The wine-gallon is now appointed to contain 231 inches; and a cylindrical vessel, 7 inches diameter and 6 inches deep, which answers almost exactly to that capacity, is also appointed to be a legal wine-gallon. This measure is used for wine, spirits, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, cider, perry, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>. The ale-gallon is appointed to contain 282 inches; and is used in selling malt-liquors of all kinds, and in collecting the revenue of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCISE">excise</a>. Table of Wine Measure. Table of Ale Measure. 2 pints = 1 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-QUART">quart</a> 2 pints = 1 quart 2 quarts = 1 pottle 2 quarts = 1 pottle 3 pottles = 1 gallon 3 pottles = 1 gallon 10 gallons = 1 anker 8 gallons = 1 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIRKIN">firkin</a> ale 18 gallons = 1 runlet 9 gallons = 1 firkin beer 3½ gallons = 1 <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a> 2 firkins = 1 kilderken 4½ gallons = 1 tierce 4 firkins = 1 barrel 2 <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAR">bar</a>. or 2 barrels = 1 hogshead 2 barrels = 1 hd. 63 gallons = 1 butt 84 gallons = 1 puncheon 2 butts = 1 ton 2 hds. = 1 pipe or butt 2 butts = 1 ton The barrel for ale in London is 32 gallons, and the barrel for beer 36 gallons. In all other places of England, the barrel, both for ale and beer, is 36 gallons. For the Scots measures, see Pint, (Encycl.) 4. Dry measure. The standard for measuring corn, salt, coals, and other dry goods, in England, is the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a> gallon, which contains 272½ cubic inches. The bushel contains 8 gallons, or 2178 inches. A cylindrical vessel, 18½ inches diameter, and 8 inches deep, is appointed to be used as a bushel in levying the malt-tax. A vessel of these dimensions is rather less than the Winchester bushel of 8 gallons, for it contains only 2150 inches; though probably there was no difference intended. The denominations of dry measure <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> used, are given in Tab. V. (see Arithmetic, p. 655.) Four quarters corn make a chaldron, 5 quarters make a wey or load, and 10 quarters make a ton. In measuring <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-coal, 5 pecks make a bushel, 9 bushels make a quarter or vat, 4 quarters make a chaldron, and 2½ chaldrons make a score. There was formerly only one measure of capacity in Scotland; and some commodities were heaped, others straited, or measured exactly to the capacity of the standard. The method of heaping was afterwards forbidden, as unequal, and a larger measure appointed for such commodities as that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> had been extended to. The wheat-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIRLOT">firlot</a>, used also for rye, peas, beans, salt, and grass-seeds, contains 21 pints 1 muttonkin, measured by the Stirling jug. The barley-firlot, used also for oats, fruit, and potatoes, contains 31 pints. A different method of regulating the firlot was appointed, from the dimensions of a cylindrical vessel. The diameter for both measures was fixed at 19½ inches, the depth 7½ inches for the wheat-firlot, and 10½ for the barley-firlot. A standard constructed by these measures is rather less than when regulated by the pint; and as it is difficult to make vessels exactly cylindrical, the regulation by the pint has prevailed, and the other method gone into disuse. If the Stirling jug contain 103½ inches, the wheat-firlot will contain 2109 inches; which is more than 2 per cent. larger than the legal malt-bushel of England, and about 1 per cent. larger than the Winchester bushel; and the barley-firlot will contain 3208 inches. The barley-boll is nearly equal to six legal malt bushels. In <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STIRLINGSHIRE">Stirlingshire</a>, 17 pecks are reckoned to the boll: in Invernessshire, 18 pecks: in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AYRSHIRE">Ayrshire</a>, the boll is the same as the English quarter. And the firlots, in many places, are larger than the Linlithgow standard. 40 feet hewn <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> make a load. 50 feet unhewn timber make a load. 32 gallons make a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERRING">herring</a> barrel. 42 gallons make a salmon barrel. 1 cwt. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUN">gun</a>-powder makes a barrel. 256 lb. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOAP">soap</a> make a barrel. 10 dozen candles make a barrel. 12 barrels make a last.

MEDICINE
