The branches which are carried into the solidity of walls do not exceed three feet in depth, and two feet six inches in width nearly: this sort of mine is most excellent to blow up the strongest walls. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of a cubic foot of powder should be 80lb. 1 foot 1 inch <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUBE">cube</a> will weigh 100lb. and 1 foot 2 inches and ½, 150lb. and 200lb. of powder will be 1 foot 5 inches cube; however, there is a diversity in this, according to the quantity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>. If, when the mines are made, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> be found at the bottom of the chamber, planks are laid there, on which the powder is placed either in sacks or barrels, of 100lb. each. The saucisses must have a clear passage to the powder, and be laid in an auger or wooden trough, through all the branches. When the powder is placed in the chamber, the planks are laid to cover it, and others again across these; then one is placed over the top of the chamber, which is shaped for that purpose: between that and those which cover the powder, props are placed, which shore it up; some inclining towards the outside, others to the inside of the wall; all the void spaces being filled with earth, dung, brick, and rough <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. Afterwards planks are placed at the entrance of the chamber, with one across the top, whereon they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUTTRESS">buttress</a> three strong props, whose other ends are likewise propped against another plank situated on the side of the earth in the branch; which props being well fixed between the planks with wedges, the branch should then be filled up to its entrance with the aforementioned materials. The saucisses which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through the side-branches must be exactly the same length with that in the middle, to which they join: the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> which reaches beyond the entrance of the mine is that which conveys the fire to the other three; the saucisses being of equal length, will <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> together. From a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of experiments, it appears, 1. That the force of a mine is always towards the weakest side; so that the disposition of the cham- MOS her of a mine does not at all contribute to determine this effect. 2. That the quantity of powder must be greater or less, in proportion to the greater or less weight of the bodies to be raised, and to their greater or less <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COHESION">cohesion</a>; so that you are to allow for each cubic fathom Of loose earth, - 9 or 10 lb. Firm earth and strong sand, - 11 or 12 Fat clayey earth, - 15 or 16 New masonry, not strongly bound, - 15 or 20 Old masonry, well bound, - 25 or 30 3. That the aperture, or entonnoir of a mine, if rightly charged, is a cone, the diameter of whose base is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the height taken from the centre of the mine. 4. That when the mine has been overcharged, its entonnoir is nearly cylindrical, the diameter of the upper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> not much exceeding that of the chamber. 5. That besides the shock of the powder against the bodies it takes up, it likewise crushes all the earth that borders upon it, both underneath and sidewise. To <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> a mine so as to have the most advantageous effect, the weight of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> to be carried must be known; that is, the solidity of a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> cone, whose base is double the height of the earth over the centre of the mine; thus, having found the solidity of the cone in cubic fathoms, multiply the number of fathoms by the number of pounds of powder necessary for raising the matter it contains; and if the cone contains matters of different weights, take a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> weight between them all, always having regard to their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of cohesion. As to the disposition of mines, there is but one general rule, which is, that the side towards which one would determine the effect be the weakest; but this varies according to occasions and circumstances. The calculation of mines is generally built upon this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>, That the entonnoir of a mine is the frustum of an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a> cone, whose <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALTITUDE">altitude</a> is equal to the radius of the excavation of the mine, and the diameter of the whole lesser base is equal to the line of least-resistance; and though these suppositions are not quite exact, yet the calculations of mines deduced from them have proved successful in practice; for which reason this calculation should be followed, till a better and more simple be found out. M. de Valliere found that the entonnoir of a mine was a paraboloid, which is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROTATION">rotation</a> of a semiparabola about its axis; but as the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between these two is very insignificant in practice, that of the frustum of a cone may be used.

MINERALOGY

Pages 1187-1187

(Encycl.) P. 5065, line 13, from the bottom, for n m v, mark d e f; and line 5, from the bottom, after <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>, supply "mentioned, n° 68."

MOATAZALITES

Pages 1187-1187
or Separatists, a religious sect among the Turks, who deny all forms and qualities in the Divine Being; or who divest God of his attributes. There are two opinions among the Turkish divines concerning God. The first admits metaphysical forms, or attributes; as, that God has wisdom, by which he is wise; power, by which he is powerful; eternity, by which he is eternal, &c. The second allows God to be wise, powerful, eternal; but will not allow any form or quality in God, for fear of admitting a multiplicity. Those who follow this latter opinion are called Moatazalites; they who follow the former, Sephalites. The Moatazalites also believed that the word of God was created in subjecto, as the schoolmen term it, and to consist of letters and sound; copies thereof being written in books to express or imitate the original; they denied absolute predetermination, and affirmed that man is a free agent. This sect is said to have first invented the scholastic divinity, and is subdivided into no less than 20 inferior sects, which mutually brand one another with infidelity.

MORGO

Pages 1187-1187

anciently Amorgos, an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Archipelago, fertile in wine, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and corn. It is well cultivated, and the inhabitants are affable, and generally of the Greek-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. The best parts belong to a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>. The greatest inconvenience in this island is the want of wood. It is 30 miles in circumference. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 26. 15. N. Lat. 36. 30.

MOSES

Pages 1187-1187

(Encycl.) Moses, by the inconsiderate mind, are generally deemed an useless <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> insignificant <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>. That they are not, is evident from hence; that he who made them has made nothing in vain, but on the contrary has pronounced all his works to be very good. Many of their uses we know; that they have many more which we know not, is unquestionable, since there is probably no one thing in the universe of which we dare to assert that we know all their uses. Thus much we are certain of with respect to mosses, that as they flourish most in winter, and at that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> cover the ground with a beautiful green carpet, in many places which would otherwise be otherwise naked, and when little verdure is elsewhere to be seen; so at the same time they shelter and preserve the seeds, roots, gems, and embryo <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> of many vegetables, which would otherwise perish; they furnish materials for birds to build their nests with; they afford a warm winter's retreat for some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a>, such as bears, dormice, and the like, and for numberless insects, which are the food of birds and fishes, and these again the food or delight of men. Many of them grow on rocks and barren places, and rotting away afford the first principles of vegetation to other plants, which could never else have taken root there. Others grow in bogs and marshes, and, by continual increase and decay, fill up and convert them either into fertile pastures, or into <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PEAT">peat</a>-bogs the source of inexhaustible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a> to the polar regions.—They are applicable also to many <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> purposes: the lycopodiums are some of them used in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a> of yarn, and in medicine; the sphagnum and polyptrichum furnish convenient beds for the Laplanders; the hypnume are used in tiling of houses, stopping crevices in walls, packing up of brittle wares and the roots of plants for distant conveyance.—To which may be added, that all in general contribute entertainment and agreeable instruction to the contemplative mind of the naturalist, at a season when few other plants offer themselves to his view.

MULLEIN

Pages 1188-1188

Verbascum, (Encycl.) <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">White</a> mullein has received the name of cow's lungwort, from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation it had formerly among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> people for inveterate coughs among the horned cattle. Parkinson tells us, that in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> it was used in such <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> with great success. It still retains the same <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> in several parts of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>.

MUNDA

Pages 1187-1188

(Encycl.) This <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> was anciently famous for a victory gained by Caesar over the sons of Pompey, who had collected an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> after the defeat of their father at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHARSALIA">Pharsalia</a>. An account of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> was referred from Rome, n° 218, to Munda, but omitted. The Pompeys posted their army advantageously on a rising ground, whereof one side was defended by the city of Munda, and the other by a small river which watered the plain, and by a marsh; so that the enemy could not attack them but in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRONT">front</a>. Caesar likewise drew up his troops with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> art, and having advanced a little way from his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, ordered them to halt, expecting the enemy would abandon their advantageous <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POST">post</a>, and come to meet him. But as they did not stir, Caesar made as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he intended to fortify himself in that post; which induced the young general, who looked upon this as a sign of fear, to advance into the plain, and attack the enemy before they could secure themselves with any works. Pompey's army was by far the most numerous; for it consisted of 13 legions, 6000 <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, and an incredible <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of auxiliaries, among whom were all the forces of Bocchus <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAURITANIA">Mauritania</a>, commanded by his two sons, both youths of great valour and bravery. Caesar had 80 cohorts, three legions, to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, the third, the fifth, and the tenth, and a body of 8000 horse. As the enemy drew near, Caesar betrayed a great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of uneasiness and concern, as if he were doubtful of the success, knowing he was to engage men no way inferior in valour and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> to his own, and commanded by officers who had on many occasions given signal proofs of their bravery and conduct. Cnecius, the elder of the two brothers, was generally looked upon as an able commander; and Labienus, who had revolted, esteemed scarce inferior to Caesar himself. However, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DICTATOR">dictator</a>, desirous to put an end to the civil <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a>, either by his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> that of his rivals, gave the signal for the battle, and fell upon the enemy with his usual vigour and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>. At the first onset, which was dreadful, the auxiliaries on both sides betook themselves to flight, leaving the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> to decide their quarrel by themselves. Then the legionaries engaged, with a fury hardly to be expressed; Caesar's men being encouraged by the hopes of putting an end to all their labours by this battle, and those of Pompey exerting themselves out of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> and despair, since most of them expected no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>, as having been formerly pardoned. Never was victory more obstinately disputed. Caesar's men, who had been always used to conquer, found themselves so vigorously <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> by the enemy's legionaries, that they began to give ground; and though they did not turn their backs, yet it was manifest that shame alone kept them in their posts. All authors agree, that Caesar had never been in so great danger; and he himself, when he came back to his camp, told his friends, that he had often fought for victory, but this was the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> he had ever fought for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Thinking himself abandoned by fortune, which had hitherto favoured him, he had some thoughts of stabbing himself with his own <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, and, by a voluntary death, preventing the disgrace of a defeat; but returning soon to himself, and concluding it would be more to his reputation to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> by the enemy's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> at the head of his troops, than, in a fit of despair, by his own, he dismounted from his horse, and snatching a buckler from one of his legionaries, he threw himself, like a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> in despair, into the midst of the enemy; crying out to his men, Are you not ashamed to deliver your general into the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of boys? At these words, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> of the tenth legion, animated by the example of their general, fell upon the enemy with fresh vigour, and made a dreadful havoc of them. But, in spite of their utmost efforts, Pompey's men still kept their ground, and, though greatly fatigued, returned to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> with equal vigour. Then the Caesarians began to despair of victory; and the dictator, running thro' the ranks of his disheartened legionaries, had much ado to keep them together. The battle had already lasted from the rising to the setting of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, without any considerable advantage on either side. At length a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> accident decided the dispute in favour of the dictator. Bogud, a petty king of Mauritania, had joined Caesar, soon after his arrival in Spain, with some squadrons of Numidian horse; but, in the very beginning of the battle, being terrified at the shouting of the soldiers, intermingled with groans, and the clashing of their arms, he had abandoned his post, and retired with the auxiliaries under his command to a rising ground at a small distance from the enemy's camp. There he <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> the whole <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> an idle spectator of the battle that was fought in the plain. But towards the evening, partly out of shame, and partly out of compassion for his friend Caesar, he resolved to fall upon Pompey's camp; and accordingly flew thither with all the forces he had with him. Labienus, apprised of his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, hastened after him, to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the camp; which Caesar observing, cried to his legionaries, Courage, fellow-soldiers! the victory at length is ours! Labienus flies! This artifice had the desired effect; Caesar's men, believing that Labienus was truly fled, made a last effort, and charged the wing he commanded so briskly, that after a most obstinate dispute they put them to flight. Though the enemy's left wing was thus entirely defeated, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> wing, where the elder Pompey commanded, still kept their ground for some time. Pompey dismounting from his horse, fought on foot like a private man in the first line, till most of his legionaries being killed, he was forced to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> himself by flight from falling into the enemy's hands. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">Part</a> of his troops fled back to their camp, and part took shelter in the city of Munda. The camp was immediately attacked, and taken sword in hand; and as for the city, Caesar, without loss of time, drew a line of circumvallation round it. This victory was gained on the 16th of the calends of April, i.e. according to our way of counting, on the 17th day of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, when the Dionysian festival, or the Liberalia, were celebrated at Rome; the very day, as Plutarch observes, in which Pompey the Great, four years before, had set out for the war. In this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> Pompey lost 30,000 men; among whom were the famous Labienus, Attius Varus, and 3000 Roman knights. Seventeen officers of distinction were taken, and all the enemy's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EAGLES">eagles</a> and ensigns, together with Pompey's falces, which he had assumed as governor of Spain. On Caesar's side only 1000 men were killed, and 500 wounded.

MUSCA

Pages 1188-1189

(Encycl.) Line 1. for gnat, read fly. Flies form one of the most numerous classes of insects. Variety runs through their forms, their structure, their organization, their metamorphoses, their manner of living, propagating their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, and providing for their posterity. Every species is furnished with implements, adapted to its exigencies. What exquisiteness, what proportion, in the several parts that compose the body of a fly! What precision, what mechanism in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>! Some oviparous, others viviparous; which latter have but two young ones at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, whereas the propagation of the former is by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a>. Flies are lascivious, troublesome insects, that put up with every kind of food. When storms impend, they have most <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>, and sting with greatest force. They multiply most in hot moist climates; and so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> was formerly their numbers in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, that there were fly-hunters commissioned to give them <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHASE">chase</a>. The vapour of sulphur <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> arsenic destroys them; and their numbers may be reduced by taking them in phials of honeyed <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, or between boards done over with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>.

MYA MARGARITIFERA

Pages 1189-1189

(Encycl.) Linnæus has made a remarkable discovery relating to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> of pearls in this fish. This must not be confounded with what is called the mother-of-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PEARL">pearl</a> shell; as that belongs to another genus, is a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-shell, and an inhabitant of the warmer countries only. The shell-fish in question is found in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> in all the northern parts of the world; in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> it abounds; it is found in the rivers of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TYRONE">Tyrone</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, and in those of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DONEGAL">Donegal</a>; in Scotland, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DON">Don</a> is said to abound with it; and it is not unfrequent in the rivers of England. This fish <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> bear removal remarkably well; and it is said, that in some places they form reservoirs for the purpose of keeping it, and taking out the pearl, which, in a certain <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, will be again renewed. From observations on the growth of these shells, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of their annular laminae, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> scales, it is supposed the fish will attain a very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; 50 or 60 years are imagined to be a moderate computation. The discovery turned on a method which Linnæus found, of putting these muscles into a state of producing pearls at his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; though the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FINAL">final</a> effect did not take <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> for several years: He says, that in five or six years after the operation the pearl would have acquired the size of a vetch. We are unacquainted with the means by which he accomplished this extraordinary operation; but it was probably published at the time, and considered as important, since it is certain that the author was rewarded with a munificent premium from the States of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> on this account. We regret that we cannot speak more fully on this head; but may observe, that it is probable, from a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> published many years afterwards in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a> Acts, that the method consisted in injuring the shell externally, perhaps by a perforation; as it has been observed, that these concretions in shell-fish are found on the inside, exactly opposite to perforations and injuries made from without by serpulae and other animals.

MYCETITES DISCOIDES

Pages 1189-1189

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a name given by Dr Woodward to those kinds of fossil coraloid bodies which the generality of writers had called, after Dr Plot, porpita. These are usually small, and of a roundish, but flattened <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>; they are hollowed on one side with a sort of umbilicus, and striated on the other; they are found on the ploughed lands in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORDSHIRE">Oxfordshire</a>, and some other of our midland counties, and in other places, buried in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; they are sometimes yellowish, sometimes brownish, and are from the breadth of an inch to a fourth <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> less of that size; when broken, they are usually found to consist of a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAR">spar</a>, not unlike that of which the shelly coats of the echinites, or the lapides indicis, and other spines of echini consist in their fossil state; and in some of them the ridges and striae are thick set with little knobs and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TUBERCLES">tubercles</a>. The basis in some of these is flat, as it is in others rising in form of a circular elevation from the umbilicus, and others have a circular cavity in the same <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>.

NARVA

Pages 1189-1189

a strong town of the Russian empire, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVONIA">Livonia</a>, with a castle, and a harbour. It was taken by the Muscovites from the Danes in 1583, by the Swedes in 1581, and they defeated the Muscovites near it in 1700; but it was retaken by the Russians in 1704, by storm, and the inhabitants sent to Astrachan. It is seated on the river Narva, 95 miles S.W. of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WIBURG">Wiburg</a>, and 172 N.E. of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGA">Riga</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 29. o. N. Lat. 59. 8.

NECESSITY

Pages 1189-1192

(Encycl.) Mr Hobbes, who is said to have been the first who understood and maintained the proper doctrine of philosophical necessity, gives the following account of it in his Leviathan, p. 108. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">Liberty</a> and necessity are consistent; as in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, that hath not the liberty, but a necessity of descending in the channel; so likewise in the actions which men voluntarily do, which, because they proceed from their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a>, proceed from liberty; and yet, because every <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s will, and every desire and inclination, proceedeth from some cause, and that from another cause, in a continual chain (whose first link is in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of God, the first of all causes), proceed from necessity; so that to him who could see the connection of those causes, the necessity of all men's voluntary actions would appear manifest: and therefore God that seeth and dispelleth all things, seeth also, that the liberty of man, in doing what he will, is accompanied with the necessity of doing that which God will, and no more <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> less: for though men may do many things, which God does not command, nor is, therefore, the author of them, yet they can have no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, will, or appetite to any thing, of which appetite God's will is not the cause: and did not his will assure the necessity of man's will, and consequently of all that on man's will dependeth, the liberty of men would be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> and impediment to the omnipotence and liberty of God. Mr Collins, one of the most admired writers on the subject of necessity, has stated the question concerning <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> liberty in the following manner. Man, he says, is a necessary <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGENT">agent</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> all his actions are so determined by the causes preceding each <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, that not one past action could possibly not have come to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>, or have been otherwise than it hath been; nor one future action can possibly not come to pass, or be otherwise than it shall be. But he is a free agent, if he is able, at any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, under the circumstances and causes he then is, to do different things; or, in other words, if he is not unavoidably determined, in every point of time, by the circumstances he is in, and causes he is under, to do that one thing he does, and not possibly to do any other. According to this state of the question, he undertakes to prove, that man is a necessary agent; and that there neither is nor can be such a thing as liberty. 1. He appeals to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>; alleging, that though the vulgar urge this in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of liberty, it is not a proof of it: that many celebrated philosophers and theologians, both <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>, have given definitions of liberty, that are consistent with fate or necessity: that some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> patrons of liberty do, by their concessions in this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, destroy all arguments from experience: that all the actions of men may be ranked under the four heads of perception, judging, willing, and doing as we will; and that experience does not prove any of these to be free; and that experience not only does not prove liberty, but, on the contrary, men may see by experience, that they are necessary agents. It is, says he, matter of experience, that man is ever determined in his willing: we experience perfect necessity: and they, who think liberty a matter of experience, yet allow that the will follows the judgment of the understanding; and that, when two objects are presented to a man's choice, one whereof appears better than the other, he cannot choose the worst. 2. Man is a necessary agent, because all his actions have a beginning; for whatever has a beginning must have a cause, and every cause is a necessary cause; and if any action whatsoever can be done without a cause, then effects and causes have no necessary relation; and consequently, we should not be necessarily determined in any <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> at all. 3. Liberty would not be a perfection, but an imperfection; whereas, on the contrary, necessity is an advantage and a perfection. 4. Liberty is inconsistent with the divine <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PREDESTINATION">predestination</a>; for if God foreknows the existence of any thing, as it depends on its own cause, that existence is no less necessary than if it were the effect of his decrees: for it no less implies a contradiction, that causes should not produce their effects, than that an event should not come to pass which is decreed by God. This last argument for necessity has been urged by a variety of writers; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a> for liberty have felt its force, and endeavoured to obviate it. Some have actually given up the divine predestination; some have allowed the seeming contradiction implied in the foreknowledge of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINGENT">contingent</a> event, and have acknowledged themselves incapable of removing it. Others have endeavoured to reconcile the foreknowledge of God and the liberty of man, by alleging, that there is a great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between God's foreknowledge and his decrees; with regard to the necessity of future events; for God's predestination has no influence at all on our actions: his infallible judgment, concerning contingent truths, does no more alter the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the things, and cause them to be necessary, than our judging <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, at any time, concerning a contingent <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, makes it cease to be contingent; or, than our <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of a present truth is any cause of its being true or present. In the argument, says Dr Clarke, drawn against liberty from the divine predestination, it must not first be supposed that things are in their own nature necessary; but from the divine predestination or power of judging infallibly (which power is as much more extensive and infallible than in man, as the divine nature and understanding are superior to ours) concerning free events, it must be proved, that things otherwise supposed free, will therefore unavoidably become necessary; which can no more be proved, than it can be proved that an action, supposed at this present time to be free, is yet (contrary to the supposition) at the same time necessary; because, in all past time, whether foreknown or not foreknown, it could not, upon that very supposition of its being now freely done, but be future. In another <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, he acknowledges, that, though it is impossible for us to explain distinctly the manner how God can foresee future events without a chain of necessary causes, yet we may form some general notion of it. For, as a man, who has no influence over another person's actions, and yet often perceives beforehand what that other will do; and a wiser and more experienced man will still, with greater <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, foresee what another, whose disposition he is perfectly acquainted with, will in certain circumstances do; and an angel, with still much less <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a>, may have a farther prospect into men's future actions: so it is very reasonable to apprehend, that God, without influencing men's wills by his power, yet by his foresight cannot but have as much more certain a knowledge of future free events than either men or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a> can possibly have, as the perfection of his nature is greater than that of theirs. The certainty of foreknowledge, says this excellent writer, does not cause the certainty of things, but is itself founded on the reality of their existence; nor does it imply any other certainty than such as would be equally in things, tho' there was no foreknowledge; nor again does this certainty of event, in any sort, imply necessity. To the same purpose <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORIGEN">Origen</a> has <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> ago observed, that predestination is not the cause of things future, but their being future is the cause of God's predestination that they will be. It cannot reasonably be disputed, that there is an essential difference between the foreknowledge and permission of events, and the preordination and production of them: and the scheme of necessity seems directly to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> God with being the efficient cause or author of those vices and evils which arise from circumstances and connections of his previous and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> appointment. Indeed, many of the advocates of this scheme will not admit the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> that seems to be fairly deducible from their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>: however, Dr Priestley very candidly allows it. It certainly (says he) sounds harsh to vulgar ears to say, that in all those crimes that men charge themselves with, and reproach themselves for, God is the agent; and that, in such <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, they are in reality no more agents, than a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> is an agent when employed to commit a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>. It does require strength of mind not to flatter at such a conclusion; but then it requires nothing but strength of mind; i.e., such a view view of things as shall carry us beyond first and fallacious appearances. 5. Another argument in favour of necessity is the following: if man was not a necessary agent, determined by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> and pain, there would be no foundation of rewards and punishments, which are the essential supports of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. These would be useless, because if men were free or indifferent to pleasure and pain, they could be no motives to a man to do or forbear any action. 6. Another argument of the same kind is deduced from the nature of morality: for if man was not a necessary agent, determined by pleasure and pain, he would have no notion of morality, or <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> to practise it; and if he were indifferent to pleasure and pain, he would have no rule to go by, and might never judge, will, and practise right. Every act of the will, it is said, is excited by some motive, which motive is the cause of that act; and if volitions are properly the effects of motives, then they are necessarily connected with their motives: whence it is inferred, that volition is necessary, and doth not proceed from any self-determining power in the will. This argument has been illustrated and urged in all its force by many modern writers, from M. Leibnitz to Dr Priestley, the last and most zealous advocate for necessity; and it has often been answered by Dr Clarke and others, who have strenuously maintained, that liberty is perfectly consistent with men acting from a regard to motives. Supposing, says Dr Price, a power of self-determination to exist, it is by no means necessary that it should be exerted without a regard to any end or rule: on the contrary, it can never be exerted without some view or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>. Whoever acts, means to do somewhat. The power of determining ourselves, by the very nature of it, wants an end or rule to guide it; and no probability or certainty of its being exerted agreeably to a rule can have the least tendency to infringe or diminish it. All that should be avoided here is the intolerable absurdity of making our reasons and ends, in acting, the physical causes or efficient causes of action. This is the same with ascribing the action of walking, not to the feet, or the power which moves the feet, but to the eye, which only sees the way. The perception of a reason for acting, or the judgment of the understanding, is no more than seeing the way; it is the eye of the mind which informs and directs; and whatever certainty there may be that a particular determination will follow, such determination will be the self-determination of the mind; and not any change of its state stamped upon it, over which it has no power, and in receiving which, instead of being an agent, it is merely a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PASSIVE">passive</a> subject of agency. Although the views and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of beings may be the occasions of their acting; yet it is a contradiction to make them the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> efficient causes of their actions: so necessary and important is the distinction insisted upon by Dr Clarke, between the operation of physical causes and the influence of moral reasons. Upon the whole, the question concerning liberty is not, Whether the views or ideas of beings influence their actions; but, What is the nature of that influence. If we say, that it is some kind of mechanical or physical efficiency; or, with Dr Priestley, after Hobbes and Leibnitz, that man has no other liberty, in following motives, than water has in running <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> hill, or than the arms of a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>, pressed by weights, have in rising and falling; then it must follow, that man never acts, and it must be folly to applaud or reproach ourselves for our conduct, and there is an end of all moral obligation and accountability. However, the necessarians do not allow these consequences; but, on the contrary, maintain, that the doctrine of the necessary influence of motives upon the mind of man, makes him the proper subject of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>, reward, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>, praise and blame, both in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> and the philosophical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the words; and that the doctrine of self-determination, independently of the influence of motives, entirely disqualifies a man from being the proper subject of them. Mr Edwards, an acute writer on this subject, has endeavoured to prove, that liberty of indifference is not only not necessary to virtue, but utterly inconsistent with it; and that all habits and inclinations, whether virtuous or vicious, are inconsistent with the Arminian notions of liberty and moral agency. And Dr Priestley observes, that the sense of self-reproach and shame is excited by our finding that we have a disposition of mind leading to vice, and on which motives to virtue, in particular cases, have had no influence. If we ask, whence proceeds that disposition, and how it comes to pass that motives to virtue had not a greater influence, we must ultimately ascribe the inefficacy of the one, and the evil tendency of the other, to God, who made us what we are, and placed us in the situation which we occupy. Dr Priestley overcomes this difficulty by alleging, that the distinction between things <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and moral entirely ceases in the scheme of necessity; that the vices of men come under the class of common evils, producing misery for a time, but, like all other evils, in the same great system, ultimately subservient to greater good. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, he says, every thing without distinction may be ascribed to God. However, he acknowledges, that this is a view of moral evil, which, though innocent, and even useful, in speculation, no wise man can or would choose to act upon himself, because our understandings are too limited for the application of such a means of good; though a Being of infinite knowledge may introduce it with the greatest advantage. If there be any foundation for the doctrine of necessity, i.e., if all events arise from preceding situations, and the original situations of all things, together with the laws by which all changes of situation take place, were fixed by the Divine Being, there can be no difference whatever with respect to his causation of one thing more than another; and even whatever takes place in consequence of his withholding his special and extraordinary influence, is as much agreeable to his will as what comes to pass in consequence of the general laws of nature. But our supposing that God is the author of sin, (as by the scheme of necessity he must in fact be the author of all things), by no means implies that he is a sinful being; for it is the disposition of mind and the design which constitute the sinfulness of an action. If therefore his disposition and design be good, what he does is morally good. To the same purpose he observes, that the proper foundation, or rather the ultimate object, of virtue, is general utility; since it consists of such conduct as tends to make intelligent creatures the most truly happy in the whole of their existence; though, with respect to the agent, no action is denominated virtuous that is not voluntary, or that does not proceed from some good motive. And this reasoning he applies to the Deity, who pursues the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of his creatures by such means as are best calculated to secure that end, and which are sanctified by it. And he further adds, that the Deity may adopt some things which he would not have chosen on their own account, but for the sake of other things with which they were necessarily connected. The scriptures, according to this last writer, are favourable to the doctrine of necessity; though he does not think that the sacred writers were, strictly speaking, necessarians, for they were not philosophers: but their habitual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> led them to refer all things to God, without reflecting on the rigorous meaning of their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>: and very probably, had they been interrogated on the subject, they would have appeared not to be apprised of the proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of the necessarian scheme, and would have answered in a manner unfavourable to it. The reader, who is desirous of being farther acquainted with the reasoning of different writers on this subject, may consult the collection of papers between Leibnitz and Clarke, 1717. Collins's Philosophical Inquiry concerning Human Liberty, 1735, 3d Ed. with Clarke's Answer. Edwards on the Freedom of the Will, 8vo. 1775, 4th edit. Priestley's Doctrine of Philosophical Necessity, 8vo, 1777. Correspondence between Dr Price and Dr Priestley, 8vo, 1778. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HARTLEY">Hartley</a>'s Observations on Man, 8vo, 1749. See Liberty, (Append.)

NEREIS

Pages 1192-1192

(Encycl.) The head of this insect is roundish, flattened, with the rostrum extending to a point; tentacula (feelers) two, very short, subulate; eyes, two, prominent, on the sides of the head; body consisting of 23 segments, diminishing toward the tail; the side of every segment has a conical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APEX">apex</a> cut short at the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERTEX">vertex</a>, and denticulated; from which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> a small <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> of hairs, under each pencil a filament resembling a foot, subulate, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a>, unarmed. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">Colour</a>, glaify, pellucid. Length, two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>. Habitation, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-SEA_PLANTS"><a class="</a>xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, as the fuci and algae, which sometimes it leaves, and wanders on the surface of the sea. This insect is frequent in all seasons of the year, but particularly in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, and on the approach of a tempest, when it seems through inquietude to give a much greater <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>; its appearance also is very brilliant when the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> is in the east and south-east <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, and in winter-nights preceded by a warm <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> containing these animacules be kept warm, they retain their light two whole days after they are dead; but in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> lose it in eight hours: <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> and warmth, which increase their vivacity and strength, increase their light also.

NEWTON

Pages 1192-1193

late <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of St Paul's, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, was born on the first of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1704. His father, John Newton, was a considerable brandy and cider merchant, who, by his industry and integrity, having acquired what he thought a competent fortune, left off trade several years before he died. He received the first <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> in the free school of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LITCHFIELD">Litchfield</a>; a school which, the bishop observes with some kind of exultation, had at all times forth several persons of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> and eminence; from bishop Smalridge and Mr Wollaston, to Dr Johnson and Mr Garrick. From Litchfield he was removed to Westminster-school, in 1717, under the care of Dr Freind and Dr Nicoll. During the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> he was at Westminster, there were, he observes, more young men who made a distinguished <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> afterwards in the world, than perhaps at any other <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, either before <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> since. He particularly mentions William Murray, the present <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MANSFIELD">Mansfield</a>, with whom he lived on terms of the highest friendship to the last. He <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> six years at Westminster-school, five of which he passed in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>. He went to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, and entered at Trinity college. Here he constantly resided eight months at least in every year, till he had taken his Bachelor of Arts <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. Soon after he was chosen Fellow of Trinity college, he came to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> in London. As it had been his inclination from a child, and he was also designed for holy orders, he had sufficient time to prepare himself, and composed some sermons, that he might have a stock in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> when he entered on the ministry. His <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> for orders was his fellowship; and he was ordained deacon in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1729, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> in the February following, by bishop Gibbon. At his first setting out in the world, he officiated as curate at St George's, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>; and continued for several years assistant-preacher to Dr Trebeck. His first preferment was that of reader and afternoon-preacher at Grosvenor chapel, in South-Audley street. This introduced him to the family of lord Tyrconnel, to whose son he became <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a>. He continued in this situation for many years, very much at his ease, and on terms of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> intimacy and friendship with lord and lady Tyrconnel, "without so much (says he) as an unkind word or a cool look ever intervening." In the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of 1744, he was, through the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the earl of Bath (who was his great friend and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>, and whose friendship and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> were returned by grateful acknowledgments and the warmest encomiums) presented to the rectory of St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> le Bow; so that he was 40 years old before he obtained any living. At the commencement in 1745, he took his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a>'s degree. In the spring of 1747 he was chosen lecturer of St George's Hanover-square, by a most respectable vestry of noblemen and gentlemen of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> distinction. In August following he married his first wife, the eldest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Dr Trebeck, an unaffected, modest, decent young woman, with whom he lived very happy, in mutual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a>, near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years. In 1749 he published his edition of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a>'s Paradise Lost, which (says he, very modestly) it is hoped hath not been ill received by the public, having, in 1775, gone through eight editions. After the Paradise Lost, it was judged (says he) proper that Dr Newton should also publish the Paradise Regained, and other poems of Milton; but these things he thought detained him from other more material studies, though he had the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> by them more than... Milton did by all his works put together. But his greatest gain (he says) was their first introducing him to the friendship and intimacy of two such men as Bishop Warburton and Dr Jortin, whose works <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> speak for them better than any private commendation. In 1754 he lost his father, at the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 83; and within a few days his wife, at the age of 38. This was the severest <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> he ever underwent, and almost overwhelmed him. At that time he was engaged in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> his Dissertations on the Prophecies; and happy it was for him: for in any affliction he never found a better or more effectual remedy, than plunging deep into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, and fixing his thoughts as intensely as he possibly could upon other subjects. The first volume was published the following winter; but the other did not appear till three years afterwards, as, for the encouragement of his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, he was appointed, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, to preach the Boyle's lecture. The bishop informs us, that 1250 copies of the Dissertations were taken at the first <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a>, and 1000 at every other edition: and "though (says he) some things have been since published upon the same subjects, yet they still hold up their head above <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and having gone through five editions, are ready prepared for another. Abroad, too, their reception hath not been unfavourable, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> accounts from thence may be depended upon." They were translated into the German and Danish languages; and received the warmest encomiums from persons of learning and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a>. In the spring of 1757, he was made prebendary of Westminster, in the room of Dr Green, and promoted to the deanery of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SALISBURY">Salisbury</a>. In October following, he was made sub-almoner to his majesty. This he owed to bishop Gilbert. He married a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> wife in September 1761. She was the widow of the Rev. Mr Hand, and daughter of John lord viscount Lisleburne. In the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> he killed his majesty's hand for his bishopric. In the winter of 1764, Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">Stone</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIMATE">primate</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, died. Mr Grenville sent for bishop Newton, and in the most obliging manner desired his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ACCEPTANCE">acceptance</a> of the primacy. Having maturely weighed the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> in his mind, he declined the offer. In 1768 he was made dean of St Paul's. His ambition was now fully satisfied; and he firmly resolved never to seek or ask for anything more. From this time to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, ill <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> was almost his constant <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a>. It was wonderful that such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, and weak, and slender thread as the bishop's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, should be spun out to such an amazing length. In the autumn of 1781 (usually the most favourable part of the year to him) he laboured under repeated illnesses; and on Saturday the 9th of February 1782, he began to find his breath much affected by the frosts. His complaints grew worse and worse till the Thursday following. He got up at five o'clock, and was placed in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> by the fire; complained to his wife how much he had suffered in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a>, and repeated to himself that portion of the Psalms, "O my God, I cry unto thee in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>-time," &c. &c. About six o'clock he was left by his apothecary in a quiet <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>. Between seven and eight he awoke, and appeared rather more easy, and took a little refreshment. He continued dozing till near <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a>, when he ordered his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> to come and dress him, and help him <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> stairs. As soon as he was dressed, he inquired the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, and bid his servant open the shutter and look at the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIAL">dial</a> of St Paul's. The servant answered, it was upon the stroke of nine. The bishop made an effort to take out his watch, with an intent to set it; but sunk down in his chair, and expired without a sigh, or the least visible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMOTION">emotion</a>, his countenance still retaining the same placid appearance which was so peculiar to him when alive.

NIDDUI

Pages 1193-1193

in the Jewish customs, is used to signify "separated <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> excommunicated." This, according to some, was to be understood of the lesser sort of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXCOMMUNICATION">excommunication</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among the Hebrews. He that had incurred it was to withdraw himself from his relations, at least to the distance of four cubits: it <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> it was not taken off in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, it might be prolonged for 60 or even 90 days: but if, within this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a>, the excommunicated person did not give satisfaction, he fell into the cherem, which was a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> sort of excommunication; and thence into the third sort called shammata, or shema-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TA">ta</a>, the most terrible of all. But Selden has proved that there were only two kinds of excommunication, viz. the greater and less; and that these three terms were used indifferently.

NILOMETER

Pages 1193-1193

a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> built by the side of the river <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NILE">Nile</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, on purpose to show the increase and decrease of the waters of that river. See Indicative Column, (Encycl.) NOUN. See <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, n° 6. (Encycl.)

ODIN

Pages 1193-1194

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>, called also in the dialect of the Anglo-Saxons Woden <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Wodan, a name given by the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Scythians to their supreme god, and assumed, about 70 years before the Christian era, by Sigge, a Scythian <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, who conquered the northern nations, made <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> changes in their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, manners, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, enjoyed great honours, and had even divine honours paid him. According to the account given of this conqueror by Snorro, the ancient historian of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, and his commentator Torfaeus, Odin was a Scythian, who withdrew himself, with many others in his train, by flight, from the vengeance of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, under the conduct of Pompey; and having officiated as <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> in his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, he assumed the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> worship, as well as the civil government, of the nations which he conquered. Having subdued <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, and Norway, he retired to Sweden, where he died. There is nothing certain in this account; but it is probable, that the god, whose prophet or priest this Scythian pretended to be, was named Odin, and that the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of succeeding ages confounded the Deity with his priest, composing out of the attributes of the one, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the other, the character of the northern conqueror. He deluded the people by his enchantments and skill in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGIC">magic</a>; having cut off the head of one Mimer, who in his lifetime was in great reputation for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, he caused it to be embalmed, and persuaded the Scandinavians that he had restored it to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of speech; and he caused it to pronounce whatever... ever <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-ORACLES">oracles</a> he wanted. The Icelandic chronicles represent Odin as the most eloquent and persuasive of men; they ascribe to him the introduction of the art of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> among the Scandinavians, and likewise the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of the Runic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>. He had also the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> to persuade his followers, that he could run over the world in the twinkling of an eye; that he had the direction of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> and tempests; that he could transform himself into all sorts of shapes, could raise the dead, could foretell things to come, deprive his enemies, by enchantment, of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> and vigour, and discover all the treasures concealed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. They add, that by his tender and melodious <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIRS">airs</a>, he could make the plains and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> open and expand with delight; and that the ghouls, thus attracted, would leave their infernal caverns, and stand motionless about him. Nor was he less dreadful and furious in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>; changing himself into the shape of a bear, a wild bull, or a lion, and amidst ranks of enemies committing the most horrible devastation, without receiving any wound himself.

OESTRUS

Pages 1194-1194

(Encycl.) See Plate CCCXXII.—This is one of the most curious genera of insects. They are distinguished into several <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, by reason of the different places wherein they deposit their eggs. Some, instructed by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> that their eggs cannot be hatched but under the skins of living creatures, such as bulls, cows, rein-deer, stags and camels, fix upon them at the instant of laying their eggs. From the hinder-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of their body issues a whimble of wonderful structure. It is a scaly <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a>, composed of four tubes, which draw out like the pieces of a spying-glass; the last is armed with three hooks, and is the gimlet with which the oestrus bore through the tough <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a> of horned cattle. The animal seems to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> no pain from the puncture, unless the insect, plunging too deep, attacks some nervous <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIBRE">fibre</a>; in which <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>, the beast runs about, and becomes furious. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EGG">egg</a> being hatched, the grub feeds on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of the wound. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of its abode forms upon the body of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a> a bunch sometimes above an inch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. When full grown, the larva breaks through the tumor, and slides <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the ground; for doing which it takes the cool of the morning, that it may neither be overpowered by the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>, nor chilled by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> of the night: it then digs itself a burrow, into which it retires. Its skin grows hard, and turns to a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> shell. There it is transformed to a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHRYSALIS">chrysalis</a>, and afterwards to a winged insect. Nature has provided for every exigence: the shell wherein the oestrus is inclosed, is of so strong a texture that it could not make its way out, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> at one of the ends there were not a small <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VALVE">valve</a>, fastened only by a very slight filament. The first push the oestrus makes, the door gives way, the prison opens. The insect wings its way to woods and places frequented by cattle. See Oestrus, and Botts, (Encycl.)

ONONIS

Pages 1194-1194

RESTHARROW; a genus of the decandra order, belonging to the diadelphia class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of different <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; but the most remarkable is the arvensis <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> cammock, growing in barren pastures in several parts of Scotland and England. The stalks recline towards the ground; are tough and branched, and have a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> hairy bark. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> are red, and come out from the axil of the branches. As the plant grows old, the branches are all terminated by a sharp woody spine; in which state several authors, among whom is Dr Withering, have described it as a distinct species. The smooth sort is sometimes pickled as samphire. The whole plant is diuretic, and has been recommended in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JAUNDICE">jaundice</a> and gravel. The plant abounds in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>; whence Mr Hasselquist conjectures (very probably according to Mr Lightfoot) that it is the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THORN">thorn</a> mentioned in the Scripture which the ground produced after the curse. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OPERA">OPERA</a>. For <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>, chap. i. read Poetry, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">Part</a> II. chap. ii.

OPORTO

Pages 1194-1194
or PORTO; a rich, handsome, and considerable town of Portugal, in the province of Entre Douro and Minho, with a bishop's see. It is a place of great importance, and by nature almost impregnable. It is noted for its strong wines; and a large quantity is from thence exported into Britain, whence all red wines that come from Spain or Portugal are called port-wines. It is seated on the declivity of a mountain near the river Duero, which forms an excellent harbour. W. Long. 8° 1'. N. Lat. 41° 0'.

OPPENHEIM

Pages 1194-1194

a town of Germany, in the lower <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALATINATE">palatinate</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a bailiwick of the same name; seated on the declivity of a hill near the Rhine. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8° 20'. N. Lat. 49° 48'.

OPTION

Pages 1194-1194

the power <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of wishing or choosing, or the choice a person makes of anything. When a new suffragan bishop is consecrated, the archbishop of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, by a customary <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a>, claims the collation of the first vacant benefice or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> in that see, according as he shall choose; which choice is called the archbishop's option. But in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> the bishop dies, or is translated before the present incumbent of the promotion chosen by the archbishop shall die or be removed, it is generally supposed that the option is void; insomuch as the greater, singly and by himself, could not convey any <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> beyond the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> of his continuance in that see. And <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the archbishop dies before the avoidance shall happen, the right of filling up the vacancy shall go to his executors or administrators.

OSMUNDA

Pages 1194-1194

MOONWORT, a genus of the order of filices, belonging to the cryptogamia class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are several <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; the most remarkable of which is the regalis, osmund-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> flowering-fern. This is a native of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, growing in putrid marshes. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> is doubly winged, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> bunches of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> at the ends. The root boiled in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> is very slimy; and is used in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to stiffen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> instead of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STARCH">starch</a>. Only some of the leaves bear flowers.

OTALGIA

Pages 1194-1195

(Encycl.) Instead of, "See there, n° 314. and p. 4869." read, See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EAR">Ear</a>-ach, in Appendix. PAINTER'S <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALANCE">BALANCE</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAINTING">PAINTING</a>, n° 18. PALMÆ, PALMS. Under this name Linnæus has arranged several genera, which, although capable of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in separate classes of his system, he has chosen rather, rather, on account of their singular structure, to place apart, in an appendix to the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>.—See Areca, Chamærops, Phoenix, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COCOS">Cocos</a>, &c. (Encycl.) and Corypha, in this Appendix. The same <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> constitute one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> families <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> tribes into which all vegetables are distributed by Linnæus in his Philosophia Botanica. They are defined to be plants with simple stems, which at their summit bear leaves resembling those of the ferns, being a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> and a branch; and whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> and fruit are produced on that particular receptacle or seat called a Spadix, protruded from a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> calyx in form of a sheath or scabbard, termed by Linnæus Spatha. Palmae is likewise the name of the first order in Linnæus's Fragments of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> Method. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, p. 1304.

PARMESAN CHEESE

Pages 1195-1195

a sort of cheese much esteemed among the Italians; so named from the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Parma where it is made, and whence it is conveyed to various parts of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. The excellent pasture-grounds of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> are watered by the Po; and the cows from whose <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILK">milk</a> this cheese is made yield a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of it. Of this cheese there are three sorts; the fromaggio di for- ma, about two palms in diameter, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> eight inches thick; and the fromaggio di ribiòle and di riboloni, which are not so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>. This cheese is of a satiny-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; and the best is kept three or four years.

PARONYCHIA

Pages 1195-1195

the Whitlow, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a>, is an abscess at the end of the fingers. According as it is situated more <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> less deep, it is differently denominated, and divided into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>.
