It begins with a slow heavy pain, attended with a slight pulsation, without swelling, redness, or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>; but soon the pain, heat, and throbbing, are intolerable; the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> grows <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>, the adjoining fingers and the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> swell up; in some <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, a kind of red and inflated streak may be observed, which beginning at the affected part, is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> almost to the elbow; nor is it unusual for the patient to complain of a very sharp pain under the shoulder, and sometimes the whole arm is excessively inflamed and swollen; the patient cannot <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>, the fever, &c., increasing; and sometimes delirium or convulsions follow. 1. When it is seated in the skin or fat, in the back or the fore part of the finger, or under or near the nail, the pain is severe, but ends well. 2. When the periosteum is inflamed or corroded, the pain is tormenting. 3. When the nervous coats of the flexor tendons of the fingers or nerves near them are seized, the worst symptoms attend. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the first kind suppures, it must be opened, and treated as abscesses in general; but the best method of treating the other two species is, on the first, or at furthest the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>, to cut the part where the pain is seated quite to the bone; if this operation is longer deferred, a suppuration <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> come on; in which <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> suppuration should be speedily promoted, and as early a discharge given to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> as possible. As the pain is so considerable as to occasion a fever, and sometimes convulsions, the tinct. theb. may be added to the suppurating applications, and also given in a draught at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>. The second species proves very troublesome, and sometimes ends in a caries of the subjacent bone. The third species is very tedious in the cure, and usually the phalanx on which it is seated, is destroyed.

PARRA

Pages 1195-1195

in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ornithology</a>, a genus of birds belonging to the order of grallæ; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of which are: The <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BILL">bill</a> is tapering and a little obtuse; the nostrils are oval, and situated in the middle of the bill; the forehead is covered with fleshy caruncles, which are lobated; the wings are small, and spinous. There are five <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; of which the most remarkable is the chavaria, which is about the size of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> cock. The Indians in the neighbourhood of Cartagena, who breed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> flocks of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a> that stray in the woods, train up the chavaria to defend them against the numerous birds of prey, no one of which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> dare to encounter it. It is never known to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> the flock, and it returns every evening to roost.

PARTING

Pages 1195-1197

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, an operation by which <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver are separated from each other. As these two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> resist equally well the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of fire and of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, they must therefore be separated by other methods. This separation could not be effected <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they were not soluble by different menstruums. Nitrous acid, marine acid, and sulphur, which cannot dissolve gold, attack silver very easily; and therefore these three agents furnish methods of separating silver from gold, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> of the operation called parting. Parting by nitrous acid is the most convenient, and therefore most used, and even almost the only one employed by goldsmiths and coiners. Wherefore it is called simply parting. That made with the marine acid is only made by cementation, and is known by the name of concentrated parting. Lastly, parting by sulphur is made by fusion, which the chemists call the dry way, and is therefore called dry parting. Parting by Aquafortis. Although parting by aquafortis is easy, as we have said, it cannot however succeed or be very exact, unless we attend to some essential circumstances. 1. The gold and silver must be in a proper proportion; for if the gold was in too <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, the silver would be covered and guarded by it from the action of the acid. Therefore, when assayers do not know the proportion of these two metals in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a> to be operated upon, they discover it by the following method. They have a certain <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEEDLES">needles</a> composed of gold and silver alloyed together in graduated proportions, and the alloy of each <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a> is known by a mark upon it. These are called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>-needles. When assayers want to know nearly the proportion of gold and silver in a mass, they rub this mass upon a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TOUCHSTONE">touchstone</a>, so as to leave a mark upon it. They then make marks upon the touchstone with some of the needles the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of which they think comes nearest to that of the mass. By comparing the marks of these needles with the mark of the mass, they discover nearly the proportion of the gold and silver in the mass. If this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> shows, that in any given mass the silver is not to the gold as three to one, this mass is improper for the operation of parting by aquafortis. In this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>, the quantity of silver necessary to make an alloy of that proportion must be added. This operation is called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTATION">quartation</a>, probably because it reduces the gold to a fourth <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the whole mass. 2. That the parting may be exact, the nitrous acid or aquafortis employed must be very pure, and especially free from mixture of vitriolic and marine <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>. For if this was not attended to, a quantity of silver, proportionate to these two foreign acids would be separated during the solution; and this portion of silver reduced by these acids to vitriol of silver and to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUNA">luna</a> cornea, would remain mingled with the gold, which consequently would not be entirely purified by the operation. When the metallic mass is properly allayed, it is to be reduced to plates, rolled up spirally, called cornets; or to grains. These are to be put into a matras, and upon them a quantity of aquafortis is to be poured, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of which is to that of the silver as three to two: and as the nitrous acid employed for this operation is rather weak, the solution is assisted, especially at first, by the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of a sand-bath, in which the matras is to be placed. When, notwithstanding the heat, no further mark of solution appears, the aquafortis <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with silver is to be decanted. Fresh nitrous acid is to be poured into the matras, stronger than the former, and in less quantity, which must be boiled on the residuous mass, and decanted as the former. Aquafortis must even be boiled a third <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> on the remaining gold, that all the silver may be certainly dissolved. The gold is then to be washed with <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>. This gold is very pure, if the operation has been performed with due <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. It is called gold of parting. No addition of silver is required, if the quantity of silver of the mass is evidently much more considerable than that of the gold: persons who have not proof needles and other <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> to determine the proportion of the alloy, may add to the gold an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDETERMINATE">indeterminate</a> quantity of silver, observing that this quantity be rather too great than too small, and so considerable as to render the mass nearly as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> as silver; for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantity of silver is rather favourable than hurtful to the operation: It has no other inconvenience than an useless expense, as the larger the quantity is of silver, the more aquafortis must be employed. We ought to attend to this fact, that the colour of gold is scarcely perceptible in a mass two-thirds of which is silver and one-third is gold; this colour then must be much less perceptible when the gold is only one-fourth part, or less, of the whole mass. If the quantity of gold exceeds that of the silver, the mass may be exposed to the action of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AQUA">aqua</a> regia, which would be a kind of inverse parting, because the gold is dissolved in that menstruum, and the silver is not, but rather reduced to a luna cornea, which remains in form of a precipitate after the operation. But this method is not much practised, for the following reasons. First, the gold cannot be easily separated from the aqua regia; for if the parting has been made with an aqua regia prepared with sal ammoniac, or if the gold be precipitated by a volatile alkali, this gold has a fulminating <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, and its <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> requires particular operations. If the aqua regia has been made with spirit of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, and the precipitation effected by a fixed alkali, the gold <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> not then be fulminating, but the precipitation will be very slow, and probably incomplete. Secondly, in the parting by aqua regia, the silver is indeed precipitated into a luna cornea, and thus separated; but this separation is not perfect, as a small quantity of luna cornea will always remain dissolved by the acids, if this solution even could be only effected by the superabundant water of these acids. Accordingly the silver is not so accurately separated from the gold by aqua regia, as the gold is from the silver by aqua fortis. The gold, after the parting by aqua fortis, is much more easily collected when it remains in small masses, than when it is reduced to a powder. When the mass has been regularly quartered, that is, when it contains three parts of silver and one part of gold, we must employ, particularly for the first solution, an aqua fortis so weakened that heat is required to assist the solution of the silver: by which means the solution is made gently; and the gold which remains, preserves the form of the small masses before the solution. If the aqua fortis employed were stronger, the parts of the gold would be disunited and reduced to the form of a powder, from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> with which the solution would be made. We may indeed part by aqua fortis a mass containing two parts of silver to one part of gold: but then the aqua fortis must be stronger; and if the solution be not too much hastened, the gold will more easily remain in masses after the operation. In both <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, the gold will be found to be tarnished and blackened, probably from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHLOGISTON">phlogiston</a> of the nitrous acid. Its parts have no <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADHESION">adhesion</a> together, because the silver dissolved from it has left many interstices; and the cornets or grains of this gold will be easily broken, unless they be handled very carefully. To give them more solidity, they are generally put into a test under a muffle and made <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>-hot, during which operation they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> considerably, and their parts are approximated. These pieces of gold are then found to be rendered much more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a>, so that they may be handled without being broken. By this operation also the gold resumes its colour and lustre; and as it generally has the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of cornets, it is called gold in cornets, or grain gold. Essayers avoid melting it, as they choose to preserve this form, which shows that it has been parted. The gold and silver thus operated upon ought to have been previously refined by lead, and freed from all alloy of other metallic matters, so that the gold which remains should be as pure as is possible. However, as this is the only metal which resists the action of aqua fortis, it might be purified by parting from all other metallic substances; but this is not generally done, for several reasons. First, because the refining by lead is more expeditious and convenient for the separation of the gold from the imperfect metals; secondly, because the silver, when afterwards separated from the aqua fortis, is pure; lastly, because most imperfect metals do not remain completely and entirely dissolved in nitrous acid, from the portion of phlogiston which this acid deprives them of, the gold would be found after the parting mixed with the part of these metals which is precipitated. The gold remaining after the parting ought to be well washed, to cleanse it from any of the solution of silver which might adhere to it; and for this purpose distilled led water ought to be used, or at least water the purity of which has been ascertained by its not forming a precipitate with a solution of silver, because such a precipitate would alter the purity of the gold. The silver dissolved in the aquafortis may be separated either by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a>, in which case all the aquafortis is recovered very pure, and fit for another parting; or it may be precipitated by some substance which has a greater <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> than this metal with nitrous acid. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">Copper</a> is generally employed for this purpose at the mint. The solution of silver is put into copper vessels. The aquafortis dissolves the copper, and the silver precipitates. When the silver is all precipitated, the new solution is decanted, which is then a solution of copper. The precipitate is to be well washed, and may be melted into an ingot. It is called parted silver. When this silver has been obtained from a mass which had been refined by lead, and when it has been well washed from the solution of copper, it is very pure. Mr. Cramer observes justly in his Treatise on Effaying, that however accurately the operation of parting has been performed, a small portion of silver always remains united with the gold, if the parting has been made by aquafortis; or a small portion of the gold remains united with the silver, if the parting has been made by aqua regia; and he estimates this small alloy to be from a two hundredth to a hundredth and fiftieth part; which quantity may be considered as nothing for ordinary purposes, but may become sensible in accurate chemical experiments. Chem. Dict. The mass of gold and silver to be quartered, ought previously to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANULATED">granulated</a>; which may be done by melting it in a crucible, and pouring it into a large vessel full of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> water, while at the same time a rapid circular <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> is given to the water by quickly stirring it round with a stick or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BROOM">broom</a>. The vessels generally used for this operation, called parting-glasses, have the form of truncated cones, the bottom being <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> inches wide, the aperture about one or two inches wide, and the height about 12 inches. These glass vessels ought to have been well annealed, and chosen free from flaws; as one of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> inconveniences attending the operation is, that the glasses are apt to crack by exposure to cold, and even when touched by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. Some operators secure their glasses by a coating. For this purpose they spread a mixture of quicklime slaked with beer and whites of eggs upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> cloth, which they wrap round the lower part of the vessel, leaving the upper part uncovered, that they may see the progress of the operation; and over this cloth they apply a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of clay and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>. Schlutter advises to put the parting-glasses containing some water, and supported by treytes, with fire under them. When the heat communicated by the water is too great, it may be diminished by adding cold water, which must be done very carefully by pouring against the sides of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAN">pan</a>, to prevent too sudden an application of cold to the parting-glass. The intention of this contrivance is, that the contents of the glasses, if these should <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a>, may be received by the copper vessel. Into a glass 15 inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and 10 or 12 inches wide at bottom, placed in a copper-pan 12 inches wide at bottom, 15 inches wide at top, and 10 inches high, he usually put about 80 ounces of metal, with twice as much aquafortis. The aquafortis ought to be so strong as to be capable of acting sensibly on silver when cold, but not so strong as to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> violently. If the aquafortis be very strong, however pure, and if the vessels be well closed, a small quantity of the gold will be dissolved along with the silver, which is to be guarded against. Little heat ought to be applied at the beginning, the liquor being apt to swell and rise over the vessel; but when the acid is nearly saturated, the heat may be safely increased. When the solution ceases, which may be known by the discontinuance of the effervescence, or emission of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>-bubbles, the liquor is to be poured off. If any grains appear entire, more aquafortis must be added, that all the silver may be dissolved. If the operation has been performed slowly, the remaining gold will have still the form of distinct masses, which are to receive solidity and colour by fire, in the manner directed by the author of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>. If the operation has been performed hastily, the gold will have the appearance of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> mud or powder, which after five or six washings with pure water must be melted.

PASSIFLORA

Pages 1199-1200
or PASSION-FLOWER, a genus of the pentandria order, belonging to the gynandria class of plants. There are near 30 different species; all of them natives of warm foreign countries, only one of which is sufficiently hardy to succeed well in the open ground here; all the others requiring the shelter of a greenhouse or house, but chiefly the latter. The most remarkable are, 1. The caerulea, or blue-rayed common palmated passion-flower, hath long, slender, shrubby, purplish-green stalks, branchy, and ascending upon support by their clasps thirty or forty feet high; with one large palmated leaf at each joint, and at the axillae large spreading flowers, with whitish-green petals, and a blue radiated nectarium; succeeded by a large, oval, yellowish fruit. It flowers from July until October; the flowers are very large, conspicuous, and their composition is exceedingly curious and beautiful. The general structure of the singular flowers of this plant is, they come out at the axillae on pedunculi about three inches long, which they terminate, each flower having just close under the calyx a three-lobed involucrum-like appendage; a five-lobed calyx, and a five-petalous corolla, the size, figure, and colour of the calyx, &c., the petals arranging alternately with the calicinal lobes; the whole, including the involucrem, calyx, and corolla, make just 13 lobes and petals, all expanded flat; and within the corolla is the nectarium, composed of a multitude of thread-like fibres, of a blue and purple colour, disposed in circular rays round the column of the fructification; the outer ray is the longest, flat, and spreading on the petals; the inner is short, erect, and narrows towards the centre; in the middle is an erect cylindric club-shaped column, or pillar, crowned with the roundish germin, having at its base five horizontal spreading filaments, crowned with incumbent yellow anthers, that move about every way; and from the side of the germin arise three slender spreading styles, terminated by headed stigmas: the germin afterwards gradually becomes a large oval fleshy fruit, ripening to a yellowish colour.—These wonderful flowers are only of one day's duration, generally opening about 11 or 12 o'clock, and frequently in hot sunny weather burst open with elasticity, and continue fully expanded all that day; and the next they gradually close, assuming a decayed-like appearance, and never open any more; the evening puts a period to their existence, but they are succeeded by new ones daily on the same plant.—This plant and flowers are held in great veneration in some foreign Catholic countries, where the religious make the leaves, tendrils, and different parts of the flower, to represent the instruments of our blessed Saviour's passion; hence the name passiflora. 2. The incarnata, incarnated, or flesh-coloured Italian passion-flower, hath a strong perennial root; slender, herbaceous stalks, rising upon support four or five feet high; leaves composed of three sawed lobes, each leaf attended by a twining tendril; and at the axillae long slender pedunculi, terminated each by one whitish flower, having a greenish calyx, and a reddish or purple radiated nectarium, surrounding the column of the fructification, which succeed to a large, round, fleshy fruit, ripening to a beautiful orange colour.—The flowers of this species are also very beautiful, though of short duration, opening in the morning, and night puts a period to their beauty; but they are succeeded by a daily supply of new ones.—The fruit of this sort is also very ornamental, as ripening to a fine reddish orange colour; but these rarely attain perfection here, unless the plants are placed in the stove; therefore when there is such accommodation, it highly merits that indulgence, where it will exhibit both flowers and green and ripe fruit, all at the same time, in a beautiful manner. 3. The vesperilio, or bat's-wing passion-flower, hath slender, striated, branchy stalks; large, bilobate, or two-lobed leaves, the base roundish and glandular, the lobes acute, widely divaricated like a bat's wings, and dotted underneath; and axillary flowers, having white petals and rays. The leaves of this species have a singular appearance, the two lobes being expanded six or seven inches wide, resembling the wings of a bat upon flight; hence the name vesperilio. As all the species are natives of warm climates, in this country they are mostly of a tender quality, except the first sort, which succeeds very well in the full ground, in a warm situation; only their young branches are sometimes killed in very severe winters; but plenty of new ones generally rise again in spring following; the others, denominated stove kinds, must always be retained in that repository.

PAVING

Pages 1200-1201

the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of ground-floors, streets, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> highways, in such a manner that they may be conveniently walked upon. In <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, the pavement of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> streets, &c. are usually of flint, or rubble-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; courts, stables, kitchens, halls, churches, &c. are paved with tiles, bricks, flags, or fire-stone; sometimes with a kind of free-stone, and rag-stone. In some streets, e.g. of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, the pavement is of brick; churches sometimes are paved with marble, and sometimes with mosaic <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, as the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St Mark at Venice. In France, the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>, streets, courts, &c. are all paved with gres or gritt, a kind of free-stone. In <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> cities of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, they call their brick pavement the burgher-masters pavement, to distinguish it from the stone or flint pavement, which usually takes up the middle of the street, and which serves for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>; the brick which borders it being destined for the passage of people on foot. Pavements of free-stone, flint, and flags, in streets, &c. are laid dry, i.e. in a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a> of sand; those of courts, stables, ground rooms, &c. are laid in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a> of lime and sand; or in lime and cement, especially <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there be vaults or cellars underneath. Some malons, after laying a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> dry, especially of brick, spread a thin mortar over it; sweeping it backwards and forwards to fill up the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a>. The several kinds of pavement are as various as the materials of which they are composed, and whence they derive the name by which they are distinguished; as, 1. Pebble-paving, which is done with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a> collected from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-beach, mostly brought from the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUERNSEY">Guernsey</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERSEY">Jersey</a>; they are very durable, indeed the most so of any stone used for this purpose. They are used of various sizes, but those which are from six to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> inches deep, are deemed the most serviceable. When they are about three inches deep, they are denominated holders, or bowlers; these are used for paving <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>-yards, and other places not accustomed to receive carriages with heavy weights; when laid in geometrical figures, they have a very pleasing appearance. 2. Rag-paving was much used in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, but is very inferior to the pebbles; it is dug in the vicinity of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAIDSTONE">Maidstone</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, from which it has the name of Kentish rag-stone; there are squared stones of this material for paving <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COACH">coach</a>-tracks and foot-ways. 3. Purbeck pitches; <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> stones used in footways; they are brought from the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Purbeck, and also frequently used in court-yards; they are in general from six to ten inches square, and about five inches deep. 4. Squared paving, for distinction by some called Scotch paving, because the first of the kind paved in the manner that has been and continues to be paved, came from Scotland; the first was a clear <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> stone, called blue whynan, which is now disused, because it has been found inferior to others since introduced in the order they are hereafter placed. 5. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRANITE">Granite</a>, a hard material, brought also from Scotland, of a reddish <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, very superior to the blue whynan <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUARRY">quarry</a>. 6. Guernsey, which is the best, and now almost the only stone in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>; it is the same stone with the pebble before spoken of, but broken with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMMERS">hammers</a>, and squared to any dimensions required of a prismoidal <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, set with its smallest base downwards. The whole of the foregoing paving should be bedded and paved in small gravel. 7. Purbeck-paving, for footways, is in general got in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> surfaces about 2½ inches thick; the blue sort is the hardest and the best of this kind of paving. 8. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a> paving, is an exceeding good material for the same purpose, and is got of almost any dimensions of the same thickness as the Purbeck. This stone <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> not admit the wet to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through it, nor is it affected by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FROST">frost</a>. 9. Ryegate, or fire-stone paving, is used for hearths, stoves, ovens, and such places as are liable to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, which does not affect this stone if kept dry. 10. New- 10. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a> flags, are stones about two feet square, and 1½ or two inches thick; they answer very well for paving out-offices; they are somewhat like the Yorkshire. 11. Portland paving, with stone from the island of Portland; this is sometimes ornamented with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> marble dots. 12. Swedland paving, is a black flate dog in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEICESTERSHIRE">Leicestershire</a>, and looks well for paving halls, or in party-coloured paving. 13. Marble paving, is mostly variegated with different marbles, sometimes inlaid in mosaic. 14. Flat brick paving, done with brick laid in sand, mortar, or grout, as when liquid lime is poured into the joints. 15. Brick-on-edge paving, done with brick laid edgewise in the same manner. 16. Bricks are also laid flat or edgewise in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERRING">herring</a>-bone. 17. Bricks are also sometimes set endwise in sand, mortar, or grout. 18. Paving is also performed with paving bricks. 19. With ten inch tiles. 20. With foot tiles. 21. With clinkers for stables and outer offices. 22. With the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of animals, or gardens, &c. And, 23. We have knob-paving, with large gravel-stones, for porticoes, garden-seats, &c. Pavements of churches, &c., frequently consist of stones of several colours; chiefly black and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, and of several forms, but chiefly squares and rectangles, artfully disposed. Indeed, there needs no great variety of colours to make a surprising diversity of tures and arrangements. M. Truchet, in the Memoir of the French Academy, has shown by the rules of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a>, that two square-stones, divided diagonally into two colours, may be joined together chequerwise, 64 different ways: which appears surprising enough; yet two letters, or figures, can only be combined two ways. The reason is, that letters only change their situation with regard to the first and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, the top and bottom remaining the same; but in the arrangement of these stones, each admits of four several situations, in each whereof the other square may be changed 16 times, which gives 64 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a>. Indeed, from a farther <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of these 64 combinations, he found there were only 32 different figures, each figure being repeated twice in the same situation, though in a different combination; so that the two only differed from each other by the transposition of the dark and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> parts.

PAWN

Pages 1200-1200

a pledge <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> gage for surety of payment of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LENT">lent</a>. It is said to be derived a pugno, quia res quae pignori dantur, pugno vel manu traduntur. The party that pawns goods hath a general <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> in them; they cannot be forfeited by the party that hath them in pawn for any offence of his, nor be taken in execution for his debt; neither may they otherwise be put in execution till the debt for which they are pawned is satisfied. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the pawn is laid up, and the pawnee robbed, he is not answerable; though if the pawnee <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the thing, as a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JEWEL">jewel</a>, watch, &c. that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> not be the worse for wearing, which he may do, it is at his peril; and if he is robbed, he is answerable to the owner, as the using occasioned the loss, &c. If the pawn is of such a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> that the keeping is a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> to the pawnee, as a cow, or a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, &c. he may <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILK">milk</a> the one, and ride the other, and this shall go in recompence for his keeping. Things which will grow the worse by using, as apparel, &c. he may not use.

PERIAGUA

Pages 1201-1201

a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> canoe made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of in the Leeward <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, South <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>. It is composed of the trunks of two trees, hollowed and united together; and thus differs from the Canoe which is formed of one tree. PERSIMON (Diospyros Virginiana, Linn.) a tree pretty <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">North</a> America; the fruit of which, when ripe, is sweet and glutinous, with a little astringency. From the persimmon is made a very palatable liquor, in the following manner. As soon as the fruit is ripe, a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> is gathered, which is very easy, as each tree is well stocked with them. These persimmon apples are put into a dough of wheat <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> other flour, formed into cakes, and put into an oven, in which they continue till they are quite baked and sufficiently dry, when they are taken out again; then, in order to brew the liquor, a pot full of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> is put on the fire, and some of the cakes are put in; these become soft by degrees as the water grows warm, and crumble in pieces at last; the pot is then taken from the fire, and the water in it well stirred about, that the cakes may mix with it: this is then poured into another vessel, and they continue to steep and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> as many cakes as are necessary for a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BREWING">brewing</a>: the malt is then infused, and they proceed as usual with the brewing. Beer thus prepared is reckoned much preferable to other beer. They likewise make brandy of this fruit in the following manner: having collected a sufficient quantity of persimons in autumn, they are all together put into a vessel, where they <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> till they are quite soft; then they pour water on them, and in that state they are left to ferment of themselves, without promoting the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a> by any addition. The brandy is then made in the common way, and is said to be very good, especially <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a> (in particular of the sweet sort) which are wild in the woods, be mixed with the persimmon fruit. Some persimons are ripe at the end of September, but most of them later, and some not before November and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>, when the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> first overcomes their acrimony. The wood of this tree is very good for joiners' instruments, such as planes, handles to chisels, &c. but if after being cut <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> it lies exposed to sunshine and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, it is the first wood which rots, and in a year's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> there is nothing left but what is useless. When the persimmon trees get once into a field, they are not easily got out of it again, as they spread so much.

PEZIZA

Pages 1201-1201

cup-mushroom, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, a genus of the class of cryptogamia, and order of fungi. This mushroom is <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BELL">bell</a>-shaped and sessile. Linnaeus enumerates eight <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>.

PHAETON

Pages 1201-1201

in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ornithology</a>, a genus of birds belonging to the order of anthers; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of which are: The <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BILL">bill</a> is sharp, straight, and pointed; the nostrils are <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a>, and the hinder toe is turned forward. There are two <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, viz. 1. The demerius, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> penguin, has a thick, arched bill; the head, hind-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the neck, and the back, of a dusky purplish hue, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> and belly <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> wings, with the tips of the feathers white; tail of a tail, a few <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> bristles; and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> legs. It is found on Penguin <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> of Good Hope. 2. The etherus, or tropic <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>, is about the size of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARTRIDGE">partridge</a>, and has very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> wings. The bill is red, with an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> under the lower mandible. The eyes are encircled with black, which ends in a point towards the tip of the head. Three or four of the larger quills, towards their ends, are black, tipped with white; all the rest of the bird is white, except the back, which is variegated with curved <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of black. The toes are webbed. The tail consists of two long straight narrow feathers, a set of equal breadth from their quills to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>. See Plate CCCXXI. These birds are rarely seen between the tropics, at the remotest distance from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>. Their name seems to imply the limits of their range; and although they are seldom seen but a few degrees <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a> or south of either tropic, yet one of their wintering-places is almost <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> degrees from the northern tropic, viz. at Bermuda. They breed also in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers on some little <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> at the east end of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PORTO_RICO">Porto Rico</a>.

PHARMACY

Pages 1201-1202

(Encycl.) p. 288. Correct thus: "Let the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>-filings be put below a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAWN">lawn</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GAUZE">gauze</a> sieve, and the magnet applied above; it <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> attract them through the pores of the sieve, and thus free them more effectually from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HETEROGENEOUS">heterogeneous</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>."

PHASCUM

Pages 1202-1202

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, a genus of the class of cryptogamia, and order of musci <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> mosses. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> are, that the anthera is covered, and guarded at the margin by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> bristles; and that the calyptra, or veil, is small. There are four <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>.

PHORMIUM

Pages 1202-1202
New s="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand Flax-plant. See Flax-Plant, (Append.) PHOSPHORUS. P. 6168, col. 1. line 35, for quicksilver read quicklime.

PILARETIC

Pages 1202-1202

a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> used to denote those who, without being absolutely mad, are subject to such strong fancies of imagination as in some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> pervert their judgment, and cause them <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> in a way different from the more rational <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of mankind.

PILEUS

Pages 1202-1202

in Roman antiquity, was the ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> hat worn at public shows and sacrifices, and by the freedmen. It was one of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> rewards assigned to such gladiators as were slaves, in token of their obtaining freedom.

PINANG

Pages 1202-1202

the Chinese name of the areca catechu, Lin. See Areca, (Encycl.) PINCHBECK. See SIMILOR and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZINC">ZINC</a>, (Encycl.)

PINGUICULA VULGARIS

Pages 1202-1202

Butterwort, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a> Juncle. The Laplanders receive the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILK">milk</a> of the rein-deer upon the fresh leaves of this plant, which they immediately strain off and let abide till it becomes somewhat acclimatized; and the whole acquires in a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> or two the consistence of cream without separating the serum, and thus becomes an agreeable food. When thus prepared, a small <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the same has the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of rennet in producing the like change on fresh milk. PIUS II. (Pope), before called Aeneas Sylvius <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAR">Bar</a>. Piccolomini, was born at Corsignano of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SIENNA">Sienna</a> in 1405. He was, at the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 26, secretary to Dominico Capranico at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALE">Bale</a>, and had the provostship of St Laurence's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>. Afterwards Frederick III. honoured him with the poetical <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, employed him in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> embassies to Rome, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, &c. He managed several employments with success, especially in the diet with Turks called for the forming of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> against the Turks at Ratibon and Frankfort, where he delivered himself with wonderful eloquence. Calixtus II. made him <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> in 1456; and that pope dying, he was advanced to his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and took the name of Pius II. In 1458 he summoned the Christian kings against the Turks; and would have led some ships himself, but died at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCONA">Ancona</a>, whither he was going in order to embark, in 1464, having sat five years, &c. His works were published at Bale in 1571. He was a person of true courage, singular <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>, the best learned pope that wore the tiara for many ages before.

PLANTS

Pages 1203-1203

Method of preserving them in their original Shape and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">Colour</a>. Wash a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of fine sand, so as perfectly to separate it from all other substances; dry it; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> it through a sieve to clear it from any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> particles which would not rise in the washing: take an earthen vessel of a proper size and form, for every plant and flower which you intend to preserve; gather your plants and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> when they are in a state of perfection, and in dry <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, and always with a convenient portion of the stalk: <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> a little of the dry sand prepared as above, and lay it in the bottom of the vessel, so as equally to cover it; lay the plant <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> flower upon it, so that no <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of it may touch the sides of the vessel: sift or shake in more of the same sand by little upon it, so that the leaves may be extended by degrees, and without injury, till the plant or flower is covered about two inches thick: put the vessel into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STOVE">stove</a>, or hot-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, heated by little and little to the 50th <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>; let it stand there a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> or two, or perhaps more, according to the thickness and succulence of the flower or plant; then gently shake the sand out upon a sheet of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, and take out the plant, which you <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> find in all its <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, the shape as elegant, and the colour as vivid as when it grew. Some flowers require certain little operations to preserve the adherence of their petals, particularly the tulip; with respect to which it is necessary, before it is buried in the sand, to cut the triangular fruit which rises in the middle of the flower; for the petals will then remain more firmly attached to the stalk. A hortus siccus prepared in this manner would be one of the most beautiful and useful curiosities that can be.

PLAY

Pages 1203-1203

in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, &c. See Drama, Tragedy, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMEDY">Comedy</a>, &c. (Encycl.) Play-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">House</a>. The most <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> English play-houses were the Curtain in Shoreditch, and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THEATRE">Theatre</a>. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Shakespeare, who commenced a dramatic writer about the year 1592, there were no less than ten <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRES">theatres</a> open, four private houses, and six that were called public theatres. Most, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not all, of Shakespeare's plays were performed either at the Globe, which was an hexagonal <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, partly open to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> and partly covered with reeds, on the southern side of the river <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, called the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BANK">Bank</a>-side, and a public theatre, where they always acted by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> at the theatre in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-BLACKFRIARS">Blackfriars</a>, which was a private play-house, and where plays were usually represented by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a>-light. Both these belonged to the same <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of comedians, viz. his majesty's servants; which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> they assumed after a licence had been granted to them by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> James in 1603, having before this time been called the servants of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> chamberlain. The exhibitions at the Globe seem to have been calculated chiefly for the lower class of people, and those at Blackfriars for a more select and judicious audience. The former was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, and the latter a winter theatre. Many of our ancient dramatic pieces were performed in the yards of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIER">carrier</a>'s inns; in which, in the beginning of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>'s reign, the comedians, who then first united themselves in companies, erected an occasional stage. The form of these temporary play-houses seems to be preserved in our <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> theatre. Many circumstances concur to render it probable, that our ancient theatres, in general, were only furnished with curtains, which opened in the middle, and a single <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> composed of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a>, sometimes ornamented with pictures. In the year 1605, Inigo Jones exhibited an entertainment at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, in which moveable scenes were used; but they were not then used in the public theatres. When Sir William Davenant first opened, by virtue of his patent, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YORK">York</a>'s theatre in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>'s-Inn fields, in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of the year 1662, with one of his own plays, the siege of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a>, then scenes made their first appearance upon the English stage; and about the same time actresses were also introduced, probably by him, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the foreign theatres; and Mrs Betterton is said to have been the first woman that appeared on the English stage. Before this time <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> were represented by boys or young men. In the time of Shakespeare plays began at one o'clock in the afternoon, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXHIBITION">exhibition</a> was usually finished in two hours; and so late as 1667, they commenced at three o'clock. See Malone's Supplemental Observations to Steevens's edition of Shakespeare. If any persons shall, in plays, &c. jestingly or profanely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the name of God, they shall forfeit 10l. Stat. 1. Jac. I. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 21. And players speaking anything in derogation of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, &c. are liable to forfeitures and imprisonments. 1. Eliz. Also acting plays or interludes on a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a> is subject to penalties, by 1 Car. I. cap. 1. No person shall <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> any new play, or addition to an old one, &c. unless a true copy thereof, signed by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the play-house, be sent to the lord chamberlain 14 days before it be acted, who may prohibit the representing any stage-play; and persons acting contrary to such prohibitions shall forfeit 50l. and their licences, &c. Stat. 10. Geo. II. cap. 28. And by this statute, no licence is to be given to act plays, but in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> and liberties of Westminster, or places of his majesty's residence.

PLEASURE

Pages 1203-1204

(Encycl.) Pleasure and pain are no other than engines in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, whereby we are directed to consult our own preservation, and avoid our ruin. To things that may contribute to the one, as food, venery, &c. she has annexed pleasure; and to those that may conduce to the other, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a>, diseases, &c. pain. She durst not leave it to our <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>, whether we would preserve and propagate the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> not; but, as it were, constrains us to both. Were there no pleasure in eating, nor pain in hunger, what numbers would be starved through negligence, forgetfulness, or sloth? What is it induces people to the office of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>, but pleasure? Without this the world had scarce subsisted to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>. Among the multiplicity of things to be done, and to be avoided, for the preservation of animal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, &c. how should we have distinguished between the one and the the other, but for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a> of pleasure and pain? These are not only spurs to urge us on, but also guides to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> us whether we are to go. Wherever nature has fixed a pleasure, we may take it for granted she there enjoins a duty; and something is to be there done, either for the individual, or for the species. Hence it is, that our pleasures vary at different stages of life; the pleasures, e.g. of a child, a youth, a grown <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>, an old man, &c., all tending to those particular things required by nature in that particular state of life, either for the preservation simply, or jointly for that and propagation, &c. Hence, from the different constitutions of the body, at different ages, it were very easy to account for all the particular tales and pleasures thereof: not by deducing the pleasures mechanically from the disposition of the organs in that state, but by considering what is necessary for the perfection and well-being of the individual in that state, and what is to contribute to that of the species. In a child, e.g. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> preservation in the present state is not enough; it must likewise grow: to bring this to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>, nature has made the returns of hunger, &c. more frequent, as well as more acute, and the pleasures of feeding more exquisite. And that the excess of aliment, in proportion to the bulk of the body, may be dispensed with, she has made one of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> pleasures of this state to consist in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of sportive exercises; by means whereof the parts of the body come to be opened and expanded, and arrive at maturity. This done, the pleasures that conduced thereto disappear; and others, suited to the new state, succeed.

PLUMBAGO

Pages 1204-1204
lead-wort; a genus of the mognynia order, belonging to the pentandria class of plants. There are four species; the most remarkable of which are the Europaea and Zeylonica. The first grows naturally in the southern parts of Europe, and has a perennial root striking deep in the ground. There are many slender channelled stalks, about three feet high, terminated by tufts of small funnel-shaped flowers, of a blue or white colour. The second grows naturally in both the Indies. The upper part of the stalk and empalement are covered with a glutinous juice, which catches the small flies that light upon it. The former species is propagated by parting the roots, and by seeds; but the latter is too tender to thrive in the open air in this country.

POE-BIRD

Pages 1204-1204

in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ornithology</a>, is an inhabitant of some of the South <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">Sea</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, where it is held in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> esteem and veneration by the natives. It goes by the name of Kogo in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-NEW_ZEALAND">New <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>; but is better known by that of Poe-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>. It is somewhat less than our blackbird. The feathers are of a fine mazarine blue, except those of its neck, which are of a most beautiful silver grey, and two <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> three short <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> ones which are on the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PINION">pinion</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> of the wing. Under its throat hang two little tufts of curled snow-white feathers, called its poies, (the Otaheitian word for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EAR">ear</a>-rings); which occasioned the name of poe bird being given to it. It is remarkable for the sweetness of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, as well as the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of its plumage. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> is also delicate food. See Plate CCXLIV.

POINT-BLANK

Pages 1204-1204

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUNNERY">gunnery</a>, denotes the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUN">gun</a> levelled horizontally, without either mounting <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> sinking the muzzle of the piece.—In <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a> point-blank, the shot or bullet is supposed to go directly forward, in a straight line, to the mark; and not to move in a curve, as bombs and highly elevated random-shots do.—When a piece stands upon a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLANE">plane</a>, and is laid level, the distance between the piece and the point where the shot touches the ground first, is called the point-blank range of that piece; but as the same piece ranges more or less, according to a greater or lesser <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>, the point-blank range is taken from that of a piece loaded with such a charge as is used <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a>. It is, therefore, necessary that these ranges of all pieces should be known, since the gunner judges from thence what elevation he is to give to his pieces when he is either farther from or nearer to the object to be fired at; and this he can do pretty nearly by sight, after considerable practice. POLYGALA. At the end of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARAGRAPH">paragraph</a>, delete the remark which follows the word rattle-snake.

POLYGAMY

Pages 1204-1206

(Encyc.) Dr Percival, Phil. Trans. vol. lxvi. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> i. p. 163, has very justly observed, that the practice is brutal, destructive to friendship and moral sentiment, inconsistent with one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> end of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of children, and subversive of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of more than half of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. Besides, it is injurious to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a>, and therefore can never be countenanced <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> allowed in a well-regulated state; for, though the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of females in the world may considerably exceed the number of males, yet there are more men capable of propagating their species than women capable of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> children; and it is a well-known fact, that <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a>, in which a plurality of wives is not allowed, abounds more with inhabitants than any other <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the Turkish empire. Yet Selden has proved, in his Uxor Hebraica, that plurality of wives was allowed of, not only among the Hebrews, but also among all other nations, and in all ages. It is true, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> were more severe in their morals, and never practised it, though it was not forbid among them: and Mark Anthony is mentioned as the first who took the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of having two wives. From that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> it became pretty frequent in the empire, till the reigns of Theodosius, Honorius, and Arcadius, who first prohibited it by express <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> in 393. After this the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VALENTINIAN">Valentinian</a>, by an edict, permitted all the subjects of the empire, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they pleased, to marry several wives: nor does it appear, from the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of those times, that the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> made any opposition to this introduction of polygamy. In effect, there are some even among the Christian calumniators, who do not look on polygamy as in itself criminal. Jureu observes, that the prohibition of polygamy is a positive law; but from which a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> may be exempted by sovereign <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>. Baillet adds, that the example of the patriarchs is a very powerful argument in favour of polygamy. It has been much disputed among the doctors of the civil law, whether polygamy be <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADULTERY">adultery</a>. In the Roman law it is called stuprum, and punished as such, that is, in some <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, capitally. But a smaller <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> is more consistent with the Jewish law, wherein the prohibition of adultery is perpetual, but that of polygamy temporary only. In Germany, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, this offence is Polygamy, differently punished. By a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. it was a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> crime. By the laws of ancient and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, it is punished with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. In Scotland it is punished as <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERJURY">perjury</a>. In England it is enacted by statute 1 Jac. I. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 11, that if any person, being married, do afterwards marry again, the former husband or wife being alive, it is felony, but within the benefit of clergy. The first wife in this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> shall not be admitted as an <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> against her husband, because she is the true wife; but the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> may, for she is indeed no wife at all; and so vice versa, of a second husband. This <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> makes an exception to five cases, in which such second marriage, tho' in the three first it is void, is, however, no felony. 1. Where either party hath been continually abroad for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years, whether the party in England had notice of the other's being living or no. 2. Where either of the parties hath been absent from the other seven years, within this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, and the remaining party hath had no notice of the other's being alive within that time. 3. Where there is a divorce or separation a mensa et thoro by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> in the ecclesiastical <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>. 4. Where the first marriage is declared absolutely void by any such sentence, and the parties loosed a vinculo. Or, 5. Where either of the parties was under the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of consent at the time of the first marriage; for in such case the first marriage was voidable by the disagreement of either party, which this second marriage very clearly amounts to. But if at the age of consent the parties had agreed to the marriage, which completes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>, and is indeed the real marriage, and afterwards one of them should marry again, judge Blackstone apprehends that such second marriage would be within the reason and penalties of the act. Bernardus Ochinus, general of the order of Capuchins, and afterwards a Protestant, published, about the middle of the 16th century, Dialogues in favour of Polygamy, which were answered by Theodore Beza. And about the conclusion of the last century we had at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a> an artful treatise published in behalf of a plurality of wives, under the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Polygamy Triumphatrix: the author whereof assumes the name of Theophilus Aletheus; but his true name was Lyferus: he was a native of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>. It has been answered by several. In the year 1780, the rev. Mr Madan published a treatise, artfully vindicating and strongly recommending polygamy, under the title of Thelyphthora; or, A Treatise on <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">Female</a> Ruin, in its Causes, Effects, Consequences, Prevention, and Remedy, &c. Marriage, according to this writer, simply and wholly consists in the act of personal union, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTUS">actus</a> coitus. Adultery, he says, is never used in the sacred writings but to denote the defilement of a betrothed or married woman, and to this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> he restricts the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a>; so that a married man, in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, is no adulterer, if his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEX">sex</a> be confined to single women, who are under no obligations by espousals or marriage to other men: but, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, the woman who should dare to have even but once an intrigue with any other man besides her husband, (let him have as many wives as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>,) would, ipso facto, be an adulteress, and ought, together with her gallant, to be punished with immediate death. This, he boldly says, is the law of God: and on this foundation he limits the privilege of polygamy to the man; in support of which he refers to the polygamous connections of the patriarchs and saints of the Old <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, and infers the lawfulness of their practice from the blessings which attended it, and the laws which were instituted to regulate and superintend it. He contends for the lawfulness of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> having, like the ancient Jews, more wives than one; and labours much to reconcile the genius of the evangelical dispensation to an arrangement of this sort. With this view he affirms, that there is not one text in the New Testament that even hints at the criminality of a polygamous connection; and he would infer from St Paul's <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> that bishops and deacons should have but one wife, that it was lawful for laymen to have more. Christ, he says, was not the giver of a new law; but the business of marriage, polygamy, &c. had been settled before his appearance in the world, by an authority which could not be revoked. Besides, this writer not only thinks polygamy lawful in a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>, but advantageous in a civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, and highly politic in a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> view. In <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of his notion of marriage, which, according to his account of it, consists in the union of man and woman as one body, the effects of which in the sight of God no outward forms or ceremonies of man's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> can add to or detract from, he grounds his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> argument on the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> words made use of in Gen. ii. 24, to express the primitive <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> of marriage, viz. יָבוֹא רַע, rendered by the LXX. ἀναπληρώσαις πρὸς τὴν γυναῖκα αὐτοῦ, which translation is adopted by the evangelist (Mat. xix. 5.) with the omission only of the superfluous proposition (πρὸς) after the verb. Our translation, "shall cleave to his wife," doth not, he says, convey the idea of the Hebrew, which is literally, as Montanus renders the words, "shall be joined or cemented in his woman, and they shall become (i.e. by this union) one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>." But on this criticism it is well remarked, that both the Hebrew and Greek terms <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> simply and literally <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> or adherence; and are evidently made use of in the sacred writings to express the whole scope of conjugal fidelity and duty, though he would restrain them to the groffer part of it. With respect to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MOSAIC_LAW">Mosaic law</a>, for which Mr Madan is a warm advocate, it was certainly a local and temporary institution, adapted to the ends for which it was appointed, and admirably calculated, in its relation to marriage, to maintain and perpetuate the separation of the Jewish people from the Gentiles. In attempting to depreciate the outward forms of marriage, this writer would make his readers believe, that because none are explicitly described, therefore none existed; and consequently that they are the superfluous ordinances of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> policy. But it is evident, from comparing Ruth iv. 10, 13. with Tobit. vii. 13, 14. and from the case of Dinah, related Gen. xxxvi., that some forms were deemed essential to an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> by the patriarchs and saints under the Old Testament, exclusive of the carnal knowledge of each other's persons. It is also evident in the case of the woman of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SAMARIA">Samaria</a>, whose connection with a man not her husband, is mentioned in John iv. that something besides cohabitation is neces- Polygamy. sary to constitute marriage in the sight of God. Having stated his notion of marriage, he urges, in defence of polygamy, that, notwithstanding the seventh commandment, it was allowed by God himself, who made laws for the regulation of it, wrought <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a> in support of it by making the barren woman fruitful, and declared the issue legitimate to all intents and purposes. God's allowance of polygamy is argued from Exod. xxi. 10; and particularly from Deut. xxii. 15, which, he says, amounts to a demonstration. This passage, however, at the utmost, only presupposes that the practice might have existence among so hard-hearted and fickle a people as the Jews; and therefore wisely provides against some of its more unjust and pernicious consequences, such as tended to affect the rights and privileges of heirship. Laws enacted to regulate it cannot be fairly urged in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of its lawfulness on the author's own <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>; because laws were also made to regulate divorce, which Mr Madan condemns as absolutely unlawful, except in cases of adultery. Besides, it is more probable that the "hated wife" had been dismissed by a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BILL">bill</a> of divorcement, than that she was retained by her husband; and moreover, it is not certain that the two wives, so far from living with the same husband at the same time, might not be dead; for the words may be rendered thus, "if there should have been to a man two wives, &c." The words expressing the original institution of marriage, Gen. ii. 24, compared with Mat. xix. 4, 5, 8, afford insuperable objections against Mr Madan's doctrine of polygamy.
