If we <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> on this subject, from the authority of scripture to the writings of the earliest fathers in the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, there is not to be found the faintest trace of any thing resembling a testimony to the lawfulness of polygamy; on the contrary, many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> occur, in which the practice of it is strongly and explicitly condemned. We shall <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> this article with the words of an excellent anonymous writer, to whose critique on Mr Madan's <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> we are indebted for the above remarks: "It is a word, when we read it, that the primitive institution of marriage limited it to one man and one woman; that this institution was adhered to by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NOAH">Noah</a> and his sons, amidst the degeneracy of the age in which they lived, and in spite of the examples of polygamy which the accursed <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RACE">race</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAIN">Cain</a> had introduced; when we consider how very few (comparatively speaking) the examples of this practice were among the faithful; how much it brought its own punishment with it; and how dubious and equivocal those passages are in which it appears to have the sanction of divine approbation; when to these reflections we add another, respecting the limited views and temporary <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the more ancient dispensations and institutions of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>—how often the imperfections and even vices of the patriarchs and people of God, in old time, are recorded, without any express notification of their criminality—how much is said to be commanded, which our reverence for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOLINESS">holiness</a> of God and his law, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> only suffer us to suppose, were, for wise ends, permitted—how frequently the messengers of God adapted themselves to the genius of the people to whom they were sent, and the circumstances of the times in which they lived;—above all, when we consider the purity, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a>, and benevolence of the Christian law; the explicit declarations of our <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>, and his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> St Paul, respecting the institution of marriage, its <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> and limitation;—when we reflect too, on the testimony of the most ancient fathers, who could not possibly be ignorant of the general and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> practice of the apostolic church; and, finally, when to these considerations we add those which are founded on <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> to the female sex, and all the regulations of domestic economy and national policy, we must wholly condemn the revival of polygamy; and thus bear our honest testimony against the leading design of this dangerous and ill-advised publication."

POLYPE

Pages 1206-1207
or POLYPUS, in zoology, a small freshwater insect, belonging to the genus of hydra, in the class of worms, and order of zoophytes, in the Linnaean system; which, when cut into a number of separate pieces, becomes in a day or two to many distinct and separate animals; each piece having the surprising property of producing a head and tail, and the other organs necessary for life, and all the animal-functions. The first discovery of this animal was owing to M. Leuwenhoek, who, in the year 1703, presented to the Royal Society of London a description of it; and an account of its uncommon way of producing its young: but the discovery of its amazing property of reproducing the several organs from its various pieces was not made till the year 1740, by M. Trembley, at the Hague. The production of its young is indeed different from the common course of nature in other animals: for the young ones issue from the sides of its parent in form of a small pimple or protuberance, which, lengthening and enlarging every hour, becomes in about two days a perfect animal, and drops from off its parent to shift for itself: but before it does this, it has often another growing from its side; and sometimes a third from it, even before the first is separated from its parent. M. Trembley observes, that there is no distinguished place in the body of the polypus by which the young are brought forth. He has seen some of them that have produced young ones from all the exterior parts of their bodies. They breed quicker in hot than in cold weather; and what is very extraordinary is, that there never has yet been discovered among them any distinction of sex or appearance of copulation; every individual of the whole species being prolific, and that as much if kept separate, as if suffered to live among others. If the method of this little animal's producing its young be very amazing, its reproduction of the several parts, when cut off, is much more so. The discovery of this was perfectly accidental; for M. Trembley, who had often met with the creature in the water, and from its fixed residence in one place, and some other observations, not being able to determine whether it was an animal or a vegetable, made the trial by cutting it asunder; when, to his amazement, he found, that in a few days each of those pieces was become a perfect animal, the head part having shot forth a tail, and the tail a head. A thousand other trials, by cutting the animal in different manners, first by M. Trembley, and afterwards, at his request, by Mons. Reaumur and Bernard de de Jussieu at Paris, and Mr Folkes, Mr Baker, and the other naturalists in England, were the result of this; and all succeeded in the same manner by those who repeated them. It is not easy to say what is the size of this creature; for it can contract or extend its body at pleasure from the length of an inch or more, and the thickness of a hog's bristle, to the shortness of a single line, with a proportionate increase of thickness. Its body is round and tubular; at one end of which is the head, surrounded with six, eight, ten, or more arms, with which it catches its prey; and at the other, the anus and tail, by which it fixes itself to any thing it pleases. There have been many different species of it discovered; the most elegant of which, the polype a panache, or plumed polype of M. Trembley, seems much to resemble the wheel-animal (to be called from having the appearance of two wheels in its head) which Mr Leuwenhoek discovered, living in a sheath or case, and affixed to the roots of duckweed. All the species are found in clear and slowly-running waters, adhering by the tail to sticks, stones, and water plants; and live on small insects. They are easily kept alive a long time in glasses, often changing the water, keeping the glasses clean, and feeding them with a small red worm common in the mud of the Thames, or with other small insects. The creature has its name from the Greek πολύς "many," and πούς a "foot," signifying an animal with many feet; but a more apposite one might easily have been invented, since it has in reality no feet at all. What were originally taken for feet, are what have since been called its horns, and of late, more properly, its arms, their office being to catch its prey. This animal is first of a worm-shaped figure, and of the same kind of tender substance with the horns of a common snail: it adheres by one end, like a sucker, to water-plants and other substances; the other end, which is the head, is surrounded by many arms or feeders, placed like rays round a centre: this centre is its mouth; and with these tender arms, which are capable of great extension, it seizes minute worms, and various kinds of water-insects, and brings them to its mouth; and often swallows bodies larger than itself, having a surprising property of extending its mouth wider in proportion than any other animal. After its food is digested in its stomach, it returns the remains of the animals upon which it feeds through its mouth again, having no other observable emunctory. In a few days there appear small knobs or papillae on its sides: as these increase in length, little fibres are seen rising out of the circumference of their heads, as in the parent animal; which fibres soon begin to rise for the purpose of procuring nourishment, &c. When these are arrived at mature size, they send out other young ones on their sides in the same manner; so that the animal branches out into a numerous offspring, united together, and growing out of one common parent. Each of these provides nourishment not only for itself, but for the whole society; an increase of the bulk of one polype, by its feeding, tending to an increase in the rest. Thus a polype of the fresh-water kind becomes like a plant branched out, or composed of many bodies; each of which has this singular characteristic, that if one of them be cut in two in the middle, the separated part becomes a complete animal, and soon adhering to some fixed base, like the parent from which it was separated, produces a circle of arms: a mouth is formed in the centre; it increases in bulk, emits a numerous progeny, and is in every respect as perfect an animal as that from which it was severed. The several strange properties recorded of this animal, though very surprising, are, however, none of them peculiar to it alone. The Surinam toad is well known to produce its young, not in the ordinary way, but in cells upon its back. Mr Sherwood has very lately discovered the small cells in four parts to be without exception full of living young ones. And as to the most amazing of all its properties, the reproduction of its parts, we know the crab and lobster, if a leg be broken off, always produce a new one; and M. Bonet, M. Lyonet, Monf. de Reaumur, and Mr Folkes, have all found, on experiment, that several earth and water worms have the same property, some of them even when cut into thirty pieces. The urtica marina, or sea-nettle, has been also found to have the same; and the sea star-fish, of which the polype is truly a species, though it had long escaped the searches of the naturalists, was always well known by the fishermen to have it also. Polype, marine, is different in form from the freshwater polype already described; but is nourished, increases, and may be propagated after the same manner; Mr Ellis having often found, in his inquiries, that small pieces cut off from the living parent, in order to view the several parts more accurately, soon gave indications that they contained not only the principles of life, but likewise the faculty of increasing and multiplying into a numerous issue. It has been lately discovered and sufficiently proved by Peyssonel, Ellis, Jussieu, Reaumur, Donati, &c. that many of those substances, which had formerly been considered by naturalists as marine vegetables or sea-plants, are in reality animal-productions; and that they are formed by polypes of different shapes and sizes, for their habitation, defence, and propagation. To this class may be referred the corals, corallines, keratophyta, echura, sponges, and alcyonium; nor is it improbable that the more compact bodies, known by the common appellations of star-stones, brain-stones, petrified fungi, and the like, brought from various parts of the East and West Indies, are of the same origin. To this purpose Mr Ellis observes, that the ocean, in all the warmer latitudes near the shore, and wherever it is possible to observe, abounds so much with animal-life, that no inanimate body can long remain unoccupied by some species. In those regions, the ships bottoms are soon covered with the habitations of thousands of animals; rocks, stones, and every thing lifeless, are covered with them instantly; and even the branches of living vegetables that hang into the water, are immediately loaded with the spawn of different animals, shell-fish of various kinds: and shell-fish themselves, when they become impotent and old, are the basis of new colonies of animals, from whose attacks they can no longer defend themselves. For a farther account of this system, see Coral and Corallines.

POLYTRICHUM

Pages 1207-1209

(Encycl.) See Plate CCCXXI. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a>. Popery, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, comprehends the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> doctrines and practices adopted and maintained by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome. The following summary, extracted chiefly from the decrees of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> under Paul III., Julius III., and Pius IV., from the year 1545 to 1563, by successive sessions, and the creed of pope Pius IV., subjoined to it, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DATE">date</a> November 1564, may not be unacceptable to the reader. One of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> tenets, strenuously maintained by popish writers, is the infallibility of the church of Rome; though they are not agreed, whether this privilege belongs to the pope, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> a general council, or to both united; but they pretend that an infallible living judge is absolutely necessary to determine controversies, and to secure peace in the Christian church. However, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> allege, that the claim of infallibility in any church is not justified by the authority of Scripture; much less does it pertain to the church of Rome; and that it is inconsistent with the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and the personal obligations of its professors; and that it has proved ineffectual to the end for which it is supposed to be granted, since popes and councils have disagreed in matters of importance, and they have been incapable, with the advantage of this pretended infallibility, of maintaining union and peace. Another essential article of the popish creed is the supremacy of the pope, or his sovereign power over the universal church. On this subject it is maintained, that every Christian, under pain of damnation, is bound to be subject to the pope; that no appeals may be made from him; and that he alone is the supreme judge of all persons, in all ecclesiastical causes, but that he himself can be judged by no <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>. To this purpose they assert, that the church of Rome is the catholic church; the mother and mistress of all churches; that the pope is the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a> of Christ, successor of St <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>, and the supreme pastor over all the world. And they likewise assert his dominion over temporal princes; pretending that he may overrule what they command; excommunicate and depose them, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they contradict his commands; and absolve their subjects from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a>, and exempt the clergy from their jurisdiction. This exorbitant power hath been challenged by the pope for many successive ages, and in several instances actually exercised. Thus Gregory VII. excommunicated the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Henry IV. and gave away his kingdoms to Rudolphus <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>. Gregory IX. excommunicated the emperor Frederick II. and absolved his subjects from their oath of allegiance. Pope Paul III. excommunicated and deposed Henry VIII., <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of England, and commanded all his subjects, under a curse, to withdraw their obedience from him. Pope Pius V. and Gregory XIII. damned and deposed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, and absolved her subjects from their allegiance. And this practice has been warranted by the decrees of the third Lateran council under pope Alexander III. and by the fourth Lateran council under pope Innocent III. though it is contrary to the express <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of Scripture, to the doctrine and conduct of the apostles and primitive fathers, and to the confessions and practice of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> of Rome, and altogether inconsistent with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> and the welfare of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. Farther, the doctrine of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> sacraments is a peculiar and distinguishing doctrine of the church of Rome: these are <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a>, the eucharist, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENANCE">penance</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> unction, orders, and matrimony. The council of Trent (sess. 7. can. 1.) pronounces an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANATHEMA">anathema</a> on those who say, that the sacraments are more or fewer than seven, or that any one of the above <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> is not truly and properly a sacrament. And yet it does not appear that they amounted to this number before the 12th century, when Hugo de St Victore and Peter Lombard, about the year 1144, taught that there were seven sacraments. The council of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, held in 1438, was the first council that determined this number. These sacraments confer <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> of the council of Trent (sess. 7. can. 8.) ex opere operato, by the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> administration of them: three of them, viz. baptism, confirmation, and orders, are said (can. 9.) to impress an indelible character, so that they cannot be repeated without sacrilege; and the efficacy of every sacrament depends on the intention of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> by whom it is administered (can. 11.) Pope Pius expressly enjoins, that all these sacraments should be administered according to the received and approved <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> of the catholic church. With regard to the eucharist in particular, we may here observe, that the church of Rome holds the doctrine of transubstantiation; the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of paying divine worship to the consecrated <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOST">host</a>; the propitiatory sacrifice of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, according to their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of which Christ is truly and properly put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> as a sacrifice as often as the priest says mass; and solitary masses, in which the priest alone, who consecrates, communicates, and allows <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> only in one kind, viz. the bread, to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAITY">laity</a>. Sess. 14. The doctrine of merits is another distinguishing tenet of popery; with regard to which the council of Trent has expressly decreed (sess. 6. can. 32.) that the good works of justified persons are truly meritorious; deserving not only an increase of grace, but eternal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and an increase of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>; and it has anathematized all who deny this doctrine. Of the same kind is the doctrine of satisfactions; which supposes that penitents may truly satisfy, by the afflictions they endure under the dispensations of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>, or by voluntary penances to which they submit, for the temporal penalties of sin, to which they are subject, even after the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-REMISSION">remission</a> of their eternal <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>. Sess. 6. can. 30. and sess. 14. can. 8. and 9. In this connection we may mention the popish distinction of venial and mortal sins: the greatest evils arising from the former are the temporary pains of purgatory; but no man, it is said, can obtain the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> of the latter without confession to a priest, and performing the penances which he imposes. The council of Trent (sess. 14. can. 1.) has expressly decreed, that every one is assured, who shall affirm that penance is not truly and properly a sacrament instituted by Christ in the universal church, for reconciling those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> to the divine majesty, who have fallen into sin after baptism: and this sacrament, it is declared, consists of two parts, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> and the form; the matter is the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of the penitent, including <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRITION">contrition</a>, confession, and satisfaction; the form of it is the act of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTION">absolution</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the priest. Accordingly it is enjoined, that it is the duty of every man, man, who hath fallen after baptism, to confess his sins once a year, at least, to a priest; that this confession is to be secret; for public confession is neither commanded nor expedient; and that it must be exact and particular, including every kind and act of sin, with all the circumstances attending it. When the penitent has so done, the priest pronounces an absolution; which is not conditional or declarative only, but <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> and judicial. This secret, or auricular confession, was first decreed and established in the fourth council of Lateran, under Innocent III. in 1215, (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 21.) And the decree of this council was afterwards confirmed and enlarged in the council of Florence, and in that of Trent, which ordains, that confession was instituted by Christ, that by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> of God it is necessary to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a>, and that it has been always practiced in the Christian church. As for the penances imposed on the penitent by way of satisfaction, they have been <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> the repetition of certain forms of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>, as pater-nosters, or ave-marias, the payment of stipulated sums, pilgrimages, fasts, or various <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of corporal <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>. But the most formidable penance in the estimation of many, who have belonged to the Romish communion, has been the temporary pains of purgatory. But under all the penalties which are inflicted or threatened in the Romish church, it has provided relief by its indulgences, and by its prayers or masses for the dead, performed professedly for relieving and releasing the souls that are detained in purgatory. Another article that has been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> authoritatively enjoined and observed in the church of Rome, is the celibacy of her clergy. This was first enjoined at Rome by Gregory VII. about the year 1074, and established in England by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANSELM">Anselm</a> archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a> about the year 1175; though his predecessor Lanfranc had imposed it upon the prebendaries and clergy that lived in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>. And though the council of Trent was repeatedly petitioned by several princes and states to abolish this restraint, the obligation of celibacy was rather established than relaxed by this council; for they decreed, that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> contracted after a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VOW">vow</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINENCE">continence</a> is neither lawful nor valid; and thus deprived the church of the possibility of ever restoring marriage to the clergy. For if marriage, after a vow, be in itself unlawful, the greatest authority upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> cannot dispense with it, nor permit marriage to the clergy, who have already vowed continence. To the doctrines and practices above recited may be farther added the worship of images; to justify which, the Papists often leave the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> commandment out of their catechisms: the invocation of saints and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a>, with respect to which the council of Trent decreed, that all bishops and pastors, who have the cure of souls, do diligently instruct their flocks, that it is good and profitable humbly to pray unto the saints, and to have recourse to their prayers, help, and aid; for which practice no scripture command or example, nor any testimony within the first 300 years after Christ, can be pleaded: the worship of sacred relics, by which they understand not only the bodies and parts of the bodies of the saints, but any of those things that appertained to them, and which they touched: and the celebration of divine <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in an unknown tongue; to which purpose the council of Trent hath denounced an anathema on any one who shall say that mass ought to be celebrated only in the vulgar tongue, (see. 25, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>. 22, can. 9.) Though the council of Lateran under Innocent III. in 1215 (can. 9.) had expressly decreed, that, because in many parts within the same <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>, there are many people of different manners and rites mixed together, but of one <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, the bishops of such cities or dioceses should provide fit men for celebrating divine offices, according to the diversity of tongues and rites, and for administering the sacraments. We shall only add, that the church of Rome maintains, that unwritten traditions ought to be added to the holy Scriptures, in order to supply their defect, and regarded as of equal authority; that the books of the Apocrypha are canonical scripture; that the vulgate edition of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a> is to be deemed as authentic; and that the Scriptures are to be received and interpreted according to that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> which the holy mother church, to whom it belongs to judge of the true sense, hath held, and doth hold, and according to the unanimous consent of the fathers. Such are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> and distinguishing doctrines of Popery, most of which have received the sanction of the council of Trent; and that of the creed of pope Pius IV. which is received, professed, and sworn to by every one who enters into holy orders in the church of Rome; and at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of this creed, we are told, that the faith contained in it is so absolutely and indissolubly necessary, that no man can be saved without it. Many of the doctrines of Popery were relaxed, and very favourably interpreted by M. de <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEAUX">Meaux</a>, bishop of Condom, in his Exposition of the Doctrine of the Catholic Church, first printed in the year 1671; but this edition, which was <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with perverting, in endeavouring to palliate, the doctrine of the church, was censured by the doctors of the Sorbonne, and actually suppressed; nor does it appear that they ever testified their approbation in the usual form of subsequent and altered editions.

PORELLA

Pages 1209-1209

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, the name of a genus of mosses, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of which are these: The capsules contain a powder like those of the other mosses; and they have neither operculum, calyptra, nor pedicle; and their manner of shedding their powder is not by separating into two parts, like those of the Selago and Lycopodium, but by opening into several holes on all sides. Of this genus of mosses there is only one known <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; this is called by Dillenius the bluntly pinnated porella, and grows in wet places in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENNSYLVANIA">Pennsylvania</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARYLAND">Maryland</a>, and other parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>.

PORPITES

Pages 1209-1209

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">HAIR</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUTTON">BUTTON</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">STONE</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a name given by authors to a small <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of fossil coral; which is usually of a rounded <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> considerably flattened, and striated from the centre every way to the circumference. These are of different sizes, and of different colours, as greyish, whitish, brownish, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> bluish, and are usually found immersed in stone. See Plate CCCXVII.

POTSDAM

Pages 1209-1210
or Postdam, a town of Germany in the circle of Upper Saxony, with a palace, belonging to the king of Prussia. It is seated in an island ten miles in circumference, formed by the rivers Spree and Havel. The palace is very curious, and finely built distinction by no other motive than his own good pleasure and free will. This opinion was, in a very short time, propagated through all the reformed churches, by the writings of Calvin, and by the ministry of his disciples; and in some places was inserted in the national creeds and confessions, and thus made a public article of faith. The unhappy controversy, which took its rise from this doctrine, was opened at Strasbourg, in the year 1560, by Jerome Zanchius, an Italian ecclesiastic, who was particularly attached to the sentiments of Calvin, and carried on in a manner that contributed very much to exasperate the passions and foment the discord of the contending parties. The Predestinarian opinions have been maintained by considerable numbers, both in Popish and Protestant countries; and in our own country in particular, they have had many zealous advocates. We shall here observe, that they have undergone a kind of relaxation by those who have been denominated Baxterians, from the famous nonconformist minister, Mr Richard Baxter, of the last century. The Baxterians have endeavoured to strike into a middle path between Calvinism and Arminianism, and to unite both these schemes. They profess to believe in the doctrines of election, effectual calling, and other tenets of Calvinism; and, consequently suppose, that a certain number, determined upon in the divine councils, will infallibly be saved. This they think necessary to secure the ends of Christ's interposition. But then, on the other hand, they reject the doctrine of reprobation, and admit, that our blessed Lord, in a certain sense, died for all; and that such a portion of grace is allotted to every man, as renders it his own fault if he doth not attain to eternal happiness. If he improves the common grace given to all mankind, this will be followed by that special grace which will end in his final acceptance and salvation. Whether the Baxterians are of opinion, that any, besides the elect, will actually make such a right use of common grace as to obtain the other and at length come to heaven, we cannot affably say. There may possibly be a difference of sentiment upon the subject, according as they approach nearer to Calvinism or Arminianism.

PREDETERMINATION

Pages 1210-1211

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>. The schoolmen call that concurrence of God, which makes men <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a>, and determines them in all their actions—both good and evil, physical predetermination, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PREDESTINATION">predestination</a>. Divines hold, that God hath no <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> in sin, inasmuch as he only affords his concurrence to the physical part of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> actions, not to the moral part. Physical predetermination, or predestination, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there be any such thing, is that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of God, whereby he excites a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> cause to act; or by which, antecedently to all operations of the creature, or before it could operate in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> either of the order of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> or reason, he really and effectually moves and occasions it to produce all its actions: that is, whatever the creature does or acts, is really done and acted by the agency of God on the creature, who is all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PASSIVE">passive</a>. So that, without such predetermination of God, all creatures must remain in an eternal state of inactivity; and, with such predetermination, it is impossible but that they should do what they are thus put upon doing. It is strongly controverted, whether or no such a physical predetermination be necessary to the action of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> causes; the Scotsits maintain the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a>; urging, that all natural causes are of their own nature determined to a certain action; whence it should seem needless to call in a new predetermination of God, e.g., fire, to make it warm the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. For if an object be, by the course of divine <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVIDENCE">providence</a>, applied to fire; what need a second application of the fire, to make it warm the object applied thereto; since beings are not to be multiplied unnecessarily. And such predetermination some philosophers hold fill less requisite to produce the acts of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a>; at least, say they, the human mind must be allowed the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> power and privilege of a second cause, and therefore be entitled to produce its own acts, as well as other strictly natural agents. The Thomists, on the other hand, stand up strenuously for the physical predetermination: one of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> arguments is drawn from the subordination of second causes to the first. Where there are several subordinate agents, say they, the lower agents do not act, unless first moved and determined thereby by the first; this being the very essence of subordination. Again, the like they argue from the dominion of God over all his creatures: It is of the essence of dominion, say they, to apply and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> things subject thereto, to its own operations; and thus, if the dominion be only moral, morally; but if it be also physical, physically. And that this is the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> in respect of God and his creatures, is confessed.

PRESBYTERY

Pages 1211-1211

an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of the order of prebys ters, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> priests, with lay-elders, for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>. The kirk, or church, of Scotland, is divided into 69 presbyteries, each consisting of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of parishes, not exceeding 24, nor less than 12. The ministers of these parishes, with one ruling elder chosen half-yearly out of every kirk-session, constitute a presbytery; who, meeting in their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town, whence the presbytery is denominated, choose a moderator, or, more properly, a prolocutor, who must be a minister, half-yearly.—They determine all appeals from kirk-sessions, i.e., from the several parochial assemblies; but can try nothing at the first instance cognizable before a kirk-session.—They compose all differences between ministers and people; for which end, they hold presbyterial visitations in each <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>, where they examine the registers of the kirk-sessions, &c.—They inquire into repairs of churches; see that the glebe, &c., suffer no dilapidations; appoint <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> in the parishes; and see that the funds be not misapplied. They alone can exclude from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>; license probationers; suspend, depose, and, in effect, determine all <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> matters within their district. From the presbytery there lies an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a>, in all <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> synods.

PRINGLE

Pages 1211-1212

an eminent physician and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, was a younger son of Sir John Pringle of Stichel, in the shire of Roxburgh, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARONET">baronet</a>; took the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of M.D. at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, 1730; and published there "Dissertatio Inauguralis de Marcore Senilis," 4to. After having been some years professor of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MORAL_PHILOSOPHY">moral <a class="</a>xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, he was in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1745 appointed physician to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>, and physician-general to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> of the forces in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, where the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Stair appears to have been his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>. In February 1746, Dr Pringle, Dr Armstrong, and Dr Barker, were nominated physicians to the hospital for lame, maimed, and sick <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, behind Buckinghamhouse; and in April 1749, Dr Pringle was appointed physician in ordinary to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>. In 1750 he published "Observations on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> and Cure of Hospital and Goal Fevers, in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">Letter</a> to Dr Mac," 8vo (reprinted in 1755); and in 1752 he favoured the public with the result of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> in an admirable treatise under the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of "Observations on the Disorders of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">Army</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMP">Camp</a> and Garrison," 8vo. On the 14th of April 1752, he married Charlotte, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Dr Oliver, an eminent physician at Bath. In 1756 he was appointed jointly with Dr Wintringham (now Sir Clifton Wintringham, bart.) physician to the hospital for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the forces of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. After the accession of his present majesty, Dr Pringle was appointed physician to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>, 1761; physician in ordinary to the queen in 1763, in which year he was admitted of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of physicians in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; and on the 5th of June 1766, he was advanced to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of a baronet of Great Britain. In 1772 he was elected <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, where his speeches for five successive years, on delivering the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a>-medal of Sir Godfrey Copley, gave the greatest satisfaction. Sir John Pringle in 1777 was appointed physician-extraordinary to the king. He was also a fellow of the College of Physicians at Edinburgh, and of the Royal Medical Society at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>; member of the Royal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">Academies</a> at Paris, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STOCKHOLM">Stockholm</a>, Goettingen, and of the Philosophical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOCIETIES">Societies</a> at Edinburgh and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAARLEM">Haarlem</a>; and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> president of the Royal Society till November 1778; after which <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> he gradually withdrew from the world, and in 1781 quitted his elegant <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in Pall Mall (where he had long distinguished himself as the warm friend and patron of literary men of every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a> and profession), and made an excursion to his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. He returned to London in the latter end of that year; died greatly beloved and respected Jan. 18, 1782; and having no children, was succeeded in estate and also (agreeably to the limitation of the patent) in title, by his nephew, now Sir James Pringle, bart. Among this worthy physician's communications to the Royal Society, the following are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a>: 1. "Some Experiments on Substances resisting <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUTREFACTION">Putrefaction</a>," Phil. Trans. No 495, p. 580; and No 496, p. 535; 550; reprinted, with additions, in Martin's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABRIDGMENT">Abridgment</a>, vol. xi. p. 1365. 2. "Account of some Persons seized with the Goal Fever by working in Newgate, and of the manner by which the Infection was communicated to one entire Family," vol. xlviii, p. 42. At the request of Dr Hales, a copy of this useful <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> was inserted in the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">Gentleman</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGAZINE">Magazine</a>, 1753, p. 71, before its appearance in the Transactions. 3. "A remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">Case</a> of Fragility, Flexibility, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISSOLUTION">Dissolution</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BONES">Bones</a>," Ib. p. 297. 4. "Account of the Earthquake felt at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a>," vol. xlii, p. 546. 5. "Account of sinking of a River near Pontypool, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONMOUTHSHIRE">Monmouthshire</a>," ib. p. 547. 6. "Account of an Earthquake felt Feb. 18, 1756, along the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of England, between <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARGATE">Margate</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOVER">Dover</a>," ib. p. 579. 7. "Account of the Earthquake felt at Glasgow and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUMBARTON">Dumbarton</a>; also of a Shower of Dust." Dust falling on a Ship between Shetland and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ICELAND">Iceland</a>," ib. p. 509. 8. "Several Accounts of the Fiery <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-METEOR">Meteor</a> which appeared on <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a>, Nov. 26, 1758, between eight and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> at night," Vol. I., p. 218. 9. "Account of the Virtues of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOAP">Soap</a> in dissolving the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">Stone</a>, in the Cafe of the Rev. Mr Matthew Simons," ib. p. 221. 10. "Account of the Effects of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTRICITY">Electricity</a> in Paralytic <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">Cases</a>," ib. p. 481. And see a letter to him on that subject from Professor Winthrop. "Some Account of the Success of the Vitrum Ceratum Antimonii" was printed in the "Edinburgh Medical Essays," Vol. V.

PROPHECY

Pages 1212-1213

a prediction made by divine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a>. One of the strongest evidences for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of revealed <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> is that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of prophecies which is preserved in the Old and New Testaments; and a greater <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, says an excellent writer, could not be done to Christianity than to lay together the several predictions of scripture with their completions, to show how particularly things have been foretold, and how exactly fulfilled. A <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> of this kind was desired by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a>, and he intitles it the "<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Prophecy;" in which he proposes, that every prophecy of the scripture be sorted with the event fulfilling the same throughout the ages of the world, both for the better <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, and for the better illumination of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> touching those parts of prophecies which are yet unfulfilled; allowing, nevertheless, that latitude which is agreeable and familiar unto divine prophecies, being of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the Author, with whom a thousand years are but as one <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>; and therefore they are not fulfilled punctually at once, but have springing and germinant <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCOMPLISHMENT">accomplishment</a> throughout many ages, though the height <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> fulness of them may refer to some one <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. A work of this kind has been actually executed by the learned bishop Newton, in his Dissertation on the Prophecies. With regard to the credibility of prophecy, it may be observed in general, that it is not at all incredible that God should upon special occasions foretell future events; and, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he affords an extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> to mankind, that he should attest its divine original by this kind of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a>; an evidence which, if the prophecies point to the events, and the events correspond with the prophecies, is in the highest <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> conclusive and convincing. No previous conjecture nor accidental coincidence are sufficient to counteract and invalidate this kind of evidence. As to most of the scripture-prophecies, they comprehend such a variety of particulars; they so minutely describe distant events, to be accomplished in circumstances which no <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> sagacity could foresee or conceive likely to occur; and they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCORD">accord</a> so exactly with the facts to which they refer; that there is no way of evading the conclusion, but by either denying the premises, that such prophecies were ever delivered and recorded, against which fact and history militate; or by pretending, that what we call predictions are only histories written after the events had happened, in a prophetic style and manner. But it is alleged in answer to this absurd <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLEA">plea</a>, that there are all the proofs and authorities which can be had in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of this nature, that the prophets prophesied in one age, and prophecy, that the events happened in another and subsequent age: and we have as much reason to believe these, as we have to believe any <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> matters of fact whatever; and by the same rule which leads us to deny these, we may as well controvert and contradict the credibility of all ancient history. But, besides, Christian writers undertake to prove the truth of prophecy, and consequently the truth of revelation, not by an induction of particulars <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> ago foretold and long ago fulfilled, the predictions of which may be supposed to have been written after the histories, but by instances of things which have confessedly many ages ago been foretold, and have in these later ages been fulfilled, or are fulfilling at this very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>: so that there is no pretence for asserting such prophecies to have been written after the events; but it must be acknowledged, that the events many ages after, correspond exactly with the predictions many ages before. The evidence, therefore, which prophecy furnishes in favour of the truth of religion, is a growing evidence; and the more prophecies are fulfilled, the more testimonies there are and confirmations of the truth and certainty of divine revelation. One of the greatest difficulties in Christianity turns upon the manner of completion of the scripture-prophecies. In the prophets of the Old <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a> are frequent predictions of the Messiah, which the writers of the New frequently urge to the Jews and Heathens as fulfilled in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ; and on this principle evince the truth of his mission. But these texts, thus urged from the Old, in the New Testament, are sometimes not to be now found in the Old; and at other times are not urged in the New in the literal and obvious <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> which they seem to bear in the Old: whence most of the Christian commentators, divines, and critics, ancient and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>, judge them to be applied in a secondary, typical, allegorical, or mystical sense. Thus, e.g. St Matthew, after an account of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a> of the Virgin and the birth of Jesus, says, "All this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet, saying, Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel." But the words, as they stand in Isaiah, whence they are supposed to be taken, do, in their obvious and literal sense, relate to a young woman who was to bring forth a child in the days of Ahaz; as appears from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTEXT">context</a>, and is owned by Grotius, Huetius, Castrilio, Curcellaeus, Epipocus, Hammond, Simon, Le Clerc, Lamy, &c. This prophecy, then, not being fulfilled in Jesus in the primary, literal, or obvious sense of the words, is supposed, like the other prophecies cited by the apostles, to be fulfilled in a secondary, typical, or allegorical sense: i.e. this prophecy, which was first literally fulfilled by the birth of the prophet's son in the time of Ahaz, was again fulfilled by the birth of Jesus, as being an event of the same kind, and intended to be signified either by the prophet, or by God who directed the prophet's speech. Grotius observes this to be the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> in most, if not all, the prophecies and citations quoted from the Old in the New Testament; and Dodwell, with Sir John Marsham, refer even the famous prophecy in Daniel, about the seventy weeks, to the time of Antiochus Epiphanes; showing, that the expressions taken thence by Christ, and urged by him as predicting the destruction of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, have only, in a secondary sense, a respect to that destruction. And even that famous prophecy in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENTATEUCH">Pentateuch</a>, "A prophet will the Lord God raise up unto thee, like unto me; to him shall ye hearken;" which St Luke refers to as spoken of Jesus Christ, is by Simon Grotius, Stillingfleet, &c., understood to signify, in its immediate sense, a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> of a succession of prophets. It is allowed, then, the apostles applied the prophecies which they quote from the Old Testament, in a typical sense; but, unhappily, the rules whereby they quoted them are lost. Dr Stanhope laments the loss of the Jewish traditions or rules for interpreting scripture received among the rabbins, and followed by the apostles. But this loss Surenhusius, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> professor at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, thinks he has retrieved from the Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TALMUD">Talmud</a> and the ancient Jewish commentaries; and has accordingly published to the world the rules whereby the apostles quoted the Old Testament. But the truth is, these rules are too precarious, strained, and unnatural, to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> much <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>. Mr Whitton condemns all allegorical explanation of the prophecies of the Old Testament cited in the New, as weak, enthusiastic, &c., and adds, that if a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> sense of the prophecies be allowed, and there be no other method of showing their completion than by applying them secondarily and typically to our Lord, after having been in the first and primary intention long ago fulfilled in the times of the Old Testament, we lose all the real advantages of the ancient prophecies as to the proofs of Christianity. He therefore sets up a new scheme in opposition thereto: he owns, that taking the present text in the Old Testament for genuine, it is impossible to expound the apostles' citations of the prophecies of the Old Testament on any other than the allegorical foundation; and therefore, to solve the difficulty, he is forced to have recourse to a supposition contrary to the sense of all Christian writers before him, viz., that the text of the Old Testament has been greatly corrupted since the apostolic age by the Jews. His <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a> is, that the apostles made their quotations out of the Old Testament rightly and truly from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEPTUAGINT">Septuagint</a> version, which in their time was in vulgar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, and exactly agreed with the Hebrew original; and that as they made exact quotations, so they argued justly and logically from the obvious and literal sense of the said quotations, as they then stood in the Old Testament; but that, since their times, both the Hebrew and Septuagint copies of the Old Testament have been so greatly corrupted, and so many apparent disorders and dislocations introduced therein, as to occasion many remarkable differences and inconsistencies between the Old and New Testament in respect to the words and sense of those quotations. As to the manner wherein these corruptions were introduced, he says, the Jews, in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> century, greatly corrupted and altered both the Hebrew and Septuagint, especially in the prophecies cited by the apostles, to make their reasoning appear inconclusive: that, in the third century, they put into <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORIGEN">Origen</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> one of these corrupted copies of the Septuagint; which Origen mistaking for genuine, inserted in his Prophecy, Hexapla, and thus brought into the church a corrupt copy of the Septuagint; and that, in the end of the fourth century, the Jews put into the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, who till then had been almost universally ignorant of the Hebrew, a corrupted copy of the Hebrew Old Testament. The disagreement, then, between the Old and New Testament, in respect to the said quotations, he contends, has no <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> between the genuine text of the Old Testament (now nowhere existing), but only between the present corrupted text of the Old and New Testament: and therefore, to justify the reasonings of the apostles, he proposes to restore the text of the Old Testament, as it stood before the days of Origen, and as it stood in the days of the apostles; from which text, thus restored, he doubts not, it will evidently appear, that the apostles cited exactly, and argued justly and logically, from the Old Testament. But this scheme of accomplishing prophecies labours under difficulties at least as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> as the allegorical scheme. Its foundation is incredible, and its superstructure, from first to last, precarious. In effect, it is inconceivable that the Old Testament should be so corrupted; and it may even be made appear, that the Hebrew and Septuagint disagreed in the times of the apostles: add to this, that the means whereby he proposes to restore the true text will never answer that end; nor has he himself, from all the means he is yet possessed of, been able to restore one prophetical citation, so as to make that seem literally which before only seemed allegorically applied. Upon this head it may be observed, that the double sense of prophecies, for which some have zealously contended, and which others have as strenuously opposed, ought not to be understood as if a prophecy equally and indifferently referred to many persons or events; or as if, literally referring to a lower person, it was only figuratively and allegorically to be interpreted of the Messiah, (for a passage only capable of being accommodated to him is not by any means a prediction of him): but it is to be so explained, as that it may appear the Messiah was principally intended, and the prophecy literally referred to him, though it might in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> be applied to some other person; and might have been understood as referring to that inferior person alone, if farther <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> had not been thrown upon it by comparing other prophecies, or by the testimony of those whom on other accounts we have reason to regard as authentic interpreters. Nevertheless it must be acknowledged, that though the tracing of the Messiah in such prophecies as these may serve to illustrate the unity of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, which is a considerable additional <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the truth of a revelation; yet the main stress is to be laid upon such prophecies as evidently and solely relate to the Messiah and his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, rather than on those which are capable of reference to other persons or events.

PROVENCAL POETS

Pages 1213-1214

in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Literature, a name given to certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROFESSIONS">professions</a> of men who sprang up in Provence about the end of the 10th century, comprehending those that were called Troubadours, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Trouveres, Jongleurs, Cantadours, Vilards, and Musarts, in whom the faculties both of music and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> seemed to be united. The first of these were PRU Provencal, so denominated from the art which they professed of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PRUDENCE">Prudence</a>. inventing or finding out as well subjects and sentiments as rhymes, constituting what at that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> was deemed poetry. The jongleurs are supposed to have taken their name from some musical <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> on which they played, probably of a name resembling in its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> that by which their profession was distinguished: whence <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> the jugglers, quasi joculatores, as Menage conjectures, who went about singing their verses in courts and the houses of noblemen, with a viol or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARP">harp</a>, or other instrument, and were dressed in a peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, for the sake of entertaining, in a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURLESQUE">burlesque</a> manner, their protectors and patrons. The canadours, called also chantreteres, were singers of songs and ballads, as were also the musari; and the violars were players on the viol. All these arts were comprehended, in the French <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, under the general denomination of menefraudus, menefraudus, and jongleire. The Provençal poets were not only the inventors and composers of metrical romances, songs, ballads and rhymes, to so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, and of such a kind, as to raise an emulation in most countries of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> to imitate them; but, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we may <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> the Italian writers, the best poets of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, namely Petrarch and Dante, owed much of their excellence to their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the Provençals; and it is also said that the greater <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NOVELS">novels</a> of Boccaccio are taken from Provençal or <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> French romances. The learned Dr Percy, in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on the Ancient English Minstrels, has given a very curious and satisfactory account of these fathers of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> poetry and music; and although he agrees that the several professions above enumerated were included under the general name of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MINSTREL">minstrel</a>, he has in the notes to that essay, p. 42, with great accuracy assigned to each its distinct and peculiar office. Of the ancient writers of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROMANCE">romance</a>, a history is extant in the lives of the Provençal poets, written in French by J. Nostradamus, compiled and published at Lyons in 1575; but a much more satisfactory account of them is contained in the translation of this <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> into Italian, with many additions, by Gio. Mario de Crescimbeni, and published, in 1710, under the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Commentari Intorno all' Istorìa della Volgare Poetìa.

PRUDENCE

Pages 1214-1214

in ethics, may be defined an ability of judging what is best, in the choice both of ends and means. According to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> of the Roman moralist, De Officiis, lib. i. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 43, prudence is the knowledge of what is to be desired <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> avoided. Accordingly he makes prudentia (De Legibus, lib. i.) to be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> of providentia, or foresight. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> (De Legibus, lib. iii.) calls this the leading virtue; and Juvenal, Sat. x. observes, Nullum numen abeit si sit prudentia. The idea of prudence includes ἀνάγκη, or due consultation, that is, concerning such things as demand consultation, in a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> manner, and for a competent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, that the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> taken up may be neither too precipitate nor too slow; and συνειδήσις, or a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of discerning proper means when they occur; and to the perfection of prudence, these three things are farther required, viz. διαίρεσις, or a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> sagacity; ἀγωνία, presence of mind, or a ready turn of thought; and ἐμπειρία, or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>. The extremes of prudence are craft or cunning on the one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, which is the pursuit of an ill end by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> and proper, though not honest means; and folly on the other, which is either a mistake, both as to the end and means, or prosecuting a good end by foreign and improper means.

PTINUS

Pages 1214-1215

a genus of insects belonging to the order of coleoptera. The antennæ are filiform: The last <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> exterior articulations are longer than the others: The thorax is nearly round, without a margin into which the head is drawn back or received: The feet are made for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAPING">leaping</a>. The most remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> are, 1. The pecinicornis. This is produced from a worm that lodges in wood and the trunks of trees, such as the willow, where it makes deep round holes, turns to a winged insect, takes flight, and roosts upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>. It is distinguished by its antennæ peclinated on one side, whence it has the name of feathered. The elytra and thorax are of a deep clay-coloured <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, the antennæ and legs are of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> brown. 2. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERTINAX">pertinax</a>. The form of this insect resembles the preceding one, saving that its antennæ are filiform. It is all over of a deep blackish brown <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> resembling foot. It attacks <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>-furniture, clothes, furs, and especially animals dried and preserved in collections of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, where it makes <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> havoc. When caught, this insect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENDS">bends</a> its legs, draws back its head, and lies as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it was dead till it thinks itself out of danger. It cannot be forced out of this state of inaction either by pricking or tearing; nothing but a strong <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> can oblige it to resume its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> and run away. There are many beautiful varieties of this genus; but they in general escape our <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> by their minuteness, and living among hay, dried leaves, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> other dusty matters, where they undergo their metamorphoses. The larvae of some are found in trunks of decayed trees, in old tables, chairs, &c. See Plate CCCXX.

PULUX

Pages 1214-1214

the FLEA, (Encycl.) This bloodthirsty insect, which fattens at the expense of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, prefers the more delicate skin of women; but preys neither upon epileptic persons, nor upon the dead <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> dying. It loves to nestle in the fur of dogs, cats, and rats. The nests of river-swallows are sometimes plentifully stored with them. Fleas are apterous; walk but little, but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a> to a height equal to 200 times that of their own body. This amazing <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> is performed by means of the elasticity of their feet, the articulations of which are so many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>. Thus it eludes, with surprising agility, the pursuit of the person on whom it riots.—Through the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a> its form appears monstrous; and from observations made on the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> of fleas, we know them to be oviparous. The eggs, which are exceeding smooth and slippery, are deposited at the base of the hairs of animals, and on blankets, &c. In four or five days <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EGG">egg</a>, being hatched, produces a little nimble larva that feeds on greasy <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. When touched, it rolls itself up into a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALL">ball</a>. After it has crept for some time with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> swiftness, it spins a small downy cocoon, which it is careful to keep in concealment. A fortnight after, it issues from its <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>, but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAPING">leaping</a>, and under the form of a flea. Among the memorabilia of fleas, one, they say, has been seen to draw a small silver piece of ordnance to which it was fastened, the firing of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUN">gun</a> nowise daunting its intrepidity. The owner carried it about in a little box lined with velvet, every now and then placing it on her arm to let it feed; but winter put an end to the being of this martial insect. Another flea that became slave to an Englishman, had, for its daily and easy task, to drag its <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> chain and padlock, of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of one grain. A third flea served as a thill-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> to an English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>, who had made an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COACH">coach</a> and six, that carried a coachman with his dog, between his legs, a postilion, two footmen, and four invisible riders.—Mercurial ointment, brimstone, a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FUMIGATION">fumigation</a> with the leaves of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENNY">penny</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a>, or fresh-gathered leaves of that plant sewed up in a bag, and laid in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a>, are remedies pointed out as destructive of fleas.

PYRAMIDS

Pages 1215-1215

(Encycl.) Dr Bryant has lately maintained, with considerable force of argument, this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that the pyramids were designed for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> altars and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, and were constructed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the Deity. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a> was designed for a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a>, what occasion, says he, was there for a well, and for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> which led to other buildings? The apartments near the pyramids he supposes to be designed for the reception of priests, and to be appendages, not to a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>, but to a temple of the Deity. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COFFIN">coffin</a>, he apprehends, was a trough <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> reservoir for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, which by means of the well they drew from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>. The priests of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> delighted in obscurity, and they probably came by the subterraneous passages of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> to the dark chambers within; where they performed their lustrations, and other nocturnal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a>. Many, he adds, of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> temples in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> were caverns in the rock, enlarged by art, and cut out into numberless dreary apartments; for no <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a> upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> was so addicted to gloom and melancholy as the Egyptians. From the top of the pyramids they observed the heavens, and marked the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-CONSTELLATIONS">constellations</a>; and upon the same eminence it is probable that they offered up vows and oblations.

PYROMETER

Pages 1215-1216

(Encycl.) Muschenbroek, who was the original inventor of this machine, has given a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of the expansion of the different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, in the same <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>.
