Having prepared cylindric rods of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, tin, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, he exposed them first to a pyrometer with one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> in the middle; then with two flames; and successively to one with three, four, and five flames. But previous to this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, he took care to cool them equally, by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> them some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> upon the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, when it began to freeze, and Fahrenheit's thermometer was at 32 degrees. The effects of which experiment are digested in the following table, where the degrees of expansion are marked in parts equal to the \( \frac{1}{75} \) <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of an inch. | Expansion of | Iron | Steel | Copper | Brass | Tin | Lead | |--------------|------|-------|--------|-------|-----|------| | By one flame | 80 | 85 | 89 | 110 | 153 | 155 | | By two flames placed <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> together. | 117 | 123 | 115 | 220 | 274 | | It is to be observed of tin, that it <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> easily melt when heated by two flames placed together. Lead <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> melts with three flames placed together, especially <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they burn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>. From these experiments, it appears at first view, that iron is the least rarefied of any of these metals, whether it be heated by one more flames; and therefore is most proper for making <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> instruments which we would have free from any alterations by heat or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, as the rods of pendulums for clocks, &c. So likewise the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> of yards or feet should be made of iron, that their length may be as nearly as possible the same, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> and winter. The expansion of lead and tin, by only one flame, is nearly the same; that is, almost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> of the expansion of iron. It is likewise observable, that the flames placed together, cause a greater rarefaction than when they have a sensible <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> between them; iron, in the former <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>, being expanded 117 degrees, and only 109 in the latter; the reason of which <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> is obvious. By comparing the expansions of the same metal, produced by one, two, three, or more flames, it appears, that two flames do not cause double the expansion of one; nor three flames three times that expansion, but always less; and these expansions differ so much the more from the ratio of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of flames as there are more flames acting at the same time. It is also observable, that metals are not expanded equally at the time of their melting, but some more, some less. Thus tin began to run, when rarefied 219 degrees; whereas brass was expanded 377 degrees, and yet was far from melting. Mr Ellicot found, upon a medium, that the expansion of bars of different metals, as nearly of the same dimensions as possible, by the same degree of heat, were as follow: <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a>, Silver, Brass, Copper, Iron, Steel, Lead, 73 103 95 89 60 56 149 The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> difference between the expansions of iron and brass has been applied with good success to remedy the irregularities in pendulums arising from heat. Mr Graham used to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> the minute alterations, in length, of metal bars, by advancing the point of a micrometer-screw, till it sensibly stopped against the end of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAR">bar</a> to be measured. This screw, being small and very lightly hung, was capable of agreement within the three or four-thousandth part of an inch. On this general principle Mr Smeaton contrived Pyrometer, his pyrometer, in which the measures are determined by the contact of a piece of metal with the point of a micrometer-screw. The following table shows how much a foot in length of each metal grows longer by an increase of heat corresponding to 180° of Fahrenheit's thermometer, or to the difference between freezing and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, expressed in such parts of which the unit is equal to the 1000th part of an inch. | Metal | Length Increase | |------------------------|-----------------| | <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">White</a> glass <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BAROMETER">barometer</a>-tube | 100 | | Martial regulus of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a> | 130 | | Blistered steel | 147 | | Hard steel | 151 | | Iron | 167 | | <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BISMUTH">Bismuth</a> | 204 | | Copper hammered | 218 | | Copper eight parts, mixed with tin one | 225 | | Brass fifteen parts, with tin one | 229 | | Brass wire | 232 | | Speculum metal | 232 | | Spelter folder, viz. brass two parts, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZINC">zinc</a> one | 247 | | Fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEWTER">pewter</a> | 274 | | Grain tin | 298 | | Soft folder, viz. lead two, tin one | 301 | | Zinc eight parts, with tin one, a little hammered | 323 | | Lead | 344 | | Zinc or spelter | 353 | | Zinc hammered half an inch per foot | 373 | We shall close this article with a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of a pyrometer lately invented by M. De Luc, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of a hint suggested to him by Mr. Ramsden. The basis of this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> is a rectangular piece of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> board two feet and a half long, 15 inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and one inch and a half thick, and to this all the other parts are fixed. This is mounted in the manner of a table, with four deal legs, each a foot long and an inch and a half <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, well fitted near its four <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>, and kept together at the other ends by four firm <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>-pieces. This small table is suspended by a hook to a stand; the board being in a vertical situation in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of its grain, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> its legs forward in such a manner as that the cross pieces which join them may form a frame, placed vertically facing the observer. This frame sustains a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a>, which is firmly fixed in another frame that moves in the former by means of grooves, but with a very considerable degree of tightness; the friction of which may be increased by the pressure of four screws. The inner sliding frame, which is likewise of deal, keeps the tube of the microscope in a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> position, and in great part without the frame, insomuch, that the end which carries the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LENS">lens</a> is but little within the space between the frame and the board. This microscope is constructed in such a manner as that the object observed may be an inch distant from the lens; and it has a wire which is situated in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FOCUS">focus</a> of the glasses, in which the objects appear reversed. At the top of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> there is a piece of deal, an inch and a half thick, and two inches broad, laid in a horizontal direction from the board to the top of the frame. To this piece the rods of the different substances, whose expansion by heat is to be measured, are suspended: one end of it slides into a socket, which is cut in the thickness of the board; and the other end, which rests upon the frame, meets there with a screw, which makes the piece move backwards and forwards, to bring the objects to the focus of the microscope. There is a cork very strongly driven through a hole bored vertically through this piece; and in another vertical hole made through the cork, the rods are fixed at the top; so that they hang only, and their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DILATATION">dilatation</a> is not counteracted by any pressure. In order to heat the rods, a cylindrical bottle of thin glass, about 21 inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and four inches in diameter, is placed in the inside of the machine, upon a stand independent of the rest of the apparatus. In this bottle the rods are suspended at a little less than an inch distance from one of the sides, in order to have them near the microscope. Into this bottle is poured water of different degrees of heat, which must be stirred about, by moving upwards and downwards, at one of the sides of the bottle, a little piece of wood, fastened horizontally at the end of a stick; in this water is hung a thermometer, the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALL">ball</a> of which reaches to the middle of the height of the rods. During these operations the water rises to the cork, which thus determines the length of the heated part; the bottle is covered, to prevent the water from cooling to rapidly at the surface; and a thin case of brass prevents the vapour from fixing upon the piece of deal to which the rods are fixed.

PYROPHORUS

Pages 1216-1217

(Encycl.) Mr. Bewly prepares his pyrophorus in the following manner. "I fill, (says he) half <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> three-fourths of the bowl of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>-pipe with a mixture, consisting of two parts of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, previously calcined in a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and of powdered <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a> of tartar each one <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a>; pressing the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> slightly, and filling the remainder of the bowl with fine sand. As soon as the powder becomes hot, the sand lying over it is put into a state of ebullition, which generally continues several minutes. This appearance seems to proceed partly from the vitriolic acid in the alum leaving its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and expelling fixed <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> from the alkali; while another part of it is possibly converted into vitriolic acid air. This phenomenon is succeeded by the appearance of a blue sulphureous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>, proceeding from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of the same acid with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHLOGISTON">phlogiston</a> of the coal, and which continues about ten minutes or a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>. After it ceases, no other remarkable appearance presents itself. The matter is now to be kept in a red-heat 20 minutes or half an hour; or it may continue there two hours longer, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the operator pleases, without any injury to the pyrophorus. The pipe being taken out of the fire, the matter is knocked out of it as soon as it becomes cool, and generally pretty soon afterwards takes fire spontaneously." In another experiment, having added successively various and increasing quantities of fixed alkali to the salt heated as above, till the vitriolic acid contained in the mixture might be considered merely as an evanescent <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, a pyrophorus was still produced on calcining it with charcoal as before. He also mixed equal parts of salt of tartar and vegetable or animal coal, or sometimes three parts of the former with two of the latter, and calcined them in the usual manner; and this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, on being exposed to the air, generally... generally kindled in half a minute or a minute; though, as it contained no sulphur, it did not burn with so much vivacity as the vitriolic pyrophorus. This, which Mr Bewly calls the alkaline pyrophorus, differs in no circumstance from M. De Suvigny's neutral pyrophori, except in its not containing that principle to which he ascribes their ascension. However, lest it might be suspected that the salt of tartar which he employed might accidentally contain vitriolated tartar, or vitriolic acid, he repeated the experiment with tartar calcined by himself, as well as with nitre fixed or alkalised by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFLAGRATION">deflagration</a> with charcoal, and with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> filings; and in all these <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> with the same result. By diversifying in a like manner M. De Suvigny's experiments on the metallic pyrophorus, Mr Bewly found that none of the three vitriols, heated with charcoal alone, in his usual method, could produce a pyrophorus. And thus he found that the addition of an alkaline salt to the composition, which was a part of M. De Suvigny's <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>, was essential to its success. Treating in the usual manner equal parts of calcined green vitriol and charcoal, the powder, which contained no sulphur nor hepar sulphuris, did not acquire any of the properties of a pyrophorus. The vitriolic acid seemed to have been entirely dissipated; having no base to detain it, when dislodged from the metallic earth. The charcoal and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CALX">calx</a> of iron left in this process were calcined again, together with some salt of tartar; and a pyrophorus was produced, which exhibited indications of its containing a scarce perceptible portion of hepar sulphuris. Thirty grains of crocus mariae astragans were calcined with 15 grains of charcoal, and the same quantity of salt of tartar; and the mixture burnt spontaneously, though it contained no hepar sulphuris or vitriolic acid. Having by these experiments evinced that metallic pyrophori may be prepared without vitriolic acid, Mr Bewly proceeded to form an aluminous pyrophorus of the same kind. For this purpose, he procured the earth of alum by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and violent calcination; and examining a part of it, he found, by the usual tests, that it neither contained any sulphur, hepar sulphuris, nor alum uncompounded. This he considered as perfectly pure, though he afterwards found that it contained a small quantity of vitriolated tartar; and yet it repeatedly furnished a pyrophorus, as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> as when alum itself is employed. From these and similar experiments, he infers, that the several kinds of pyrophori are not kindled by moisture, attracted by the vitriolic acid, as M. De Suvigny has maintained; and his conclusion is farther confirmed by some experiments of Dr Priestley, from which it appears, that they are kindled in dry nitrous and deplogisticated air. M. Proust, cited by Mr Bewly, describes a variety of new pyrophori, which neither contain vitriolic acid, nor seem likely to owe their ascension to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTRACTION">attraction</a> of humidity from the air. These principally consist of a coaly matter simply divided by metallic or other earths; such are the sediment left on the filter in preparing Goulard's extract, various <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a> of tartar, or its acid, or the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACETOUS">acetous</a> acid, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, calcareous earths, &c. Mr Bewly, having evinced the insufficiency of M. De Suvigny's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THEORY">theory</a>, and discovered that the pyrophori are not kindled by moisture, attracted (merely) by the vitriolic acid, directed his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the nitrous acid, which Dr Priestley has shown to be a constituent part of atmospherical air, as the probable <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGENT">agent</a> in the production of this phenomenon. The strong <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> which this acid has with phlogiston, and the heat, and even flame, which it is known to produce with certain inflammable matters, manifested that it was equal to the effect; and having excluded the vitriolic acid from having any essential concern in this operation, he suggests, either that the pyrophorus is kindled by moisture attracted by some of the other ingredients which compose it; or that it has the power of decomposing atmospherical air, by suddenly attracting its nitrous acid, and thereby generating a heat sufficient to kindle the phlogistic matter contained in it. This idea appeared plausible, when he farther considered that Dr Priestley produced the purest respirable air with this same acid combined with other principles; and that this as well as <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> air is diminished, and probably in part decomposed, in a variety of phlogistic processes. This ingenious writer concludes, upon the whole, from the experiments he hath made, that the pyrophorus seems to owe its singular <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> to its being a combination of earth or alkali with phlogiston; the vitriolic acid, when present, only occasionally increasing or diminishing the effect, according to circumstances. In the process of calcination, the earth or alkaline principle is not merely mixed, but actually, though loofely, combined with the phlogistic principle of the coal; so that the pyrophorus, considering it in its most simple state, is only a perfectly dry phlogisticated alkali or earth. On these <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DATA">data</a>, the phenomena may be explained in the two following methods; with respect particularly to the influence of moisture and heat upon the pyrophorus. Supposing either the alkaline or earthy principle to have a greater affinity to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> than to the phlogiston with which either of them is united, they may, on being exposed to a moist <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>, attract the humidity, and thereby set the phlogistic principle at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>; which may, in its turn, attract, and be ignited by, the supposed aerial acid, its strong affinity to which is well known:—or, if this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a> be rejected, the inflammable matter may be kindled, merely in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the heat produced by the combination of the alkali, &c., with moisture.

QUARTZ

Pages 1217-1218

is a hard vitrifiable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, something intermediate betwixt rock-crystals and flints, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> opake vitrifiable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. Quartz is a stone well known by metallurgists, mineralogists, and miners, as it is frequently and abundantly found with ores, of which it often forms the matrix. It is also frequently found where no ores are.—The most <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> quartz is more or less of a milky-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and consequently semi-transparent. Some of them have various colours. This stone, which is very hard and very <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a>, is nevertheless cracked throughout its substance; to which also the rock-crystal is very liable, but but much less so than quartz. The fragments of quartz are always angular, and its internal surface has but little gloa. Quartz is a little waved, and has a grey appearance. It is found not only of various colours, but also of various forms. It is frequently found crystallized in caverns and slits of rocks. Its <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CRYSTALLIZATION">crystallization</a> is the same as that of rock-crystal. Quartz may be employed in vitrification, as all other vitrifiable stones are.

QUASIA

Pages 1218-1218

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, a genus of the monogynia order, belonging to the decandria clas of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There is but one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, viz. the amara, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> bitter-

RAGUSA

Pages 1218-1218

a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Ragusa. It is about two miles in circumference, and is pretty well built. It is strong by situation, having an inaccessible mountain on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>-side, and on the side of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a> a strong fort. It has an archbishop's see and a republic; and has a doge like that of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, but he continues only a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> in office. It carries on a considerable trade with the Turks. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 18. 25. N. Lat. 42. 30.

RAPHIDIA

Pages 1218-1218

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a>, a genus of insects, of the neuroptera order; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of which are these: The head is of a horny substance, and depressed <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> flattened: the mouth is armed with two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, and furnished with four palpi: the stemmata are three in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>: the wings are deflected: the antennae are filiform, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as the thorax; the anterior <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of which is lengthened out, and of a cylindrical form: the tail of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> is terminated by an appendix, resembling a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a> crooked bristle.—There are three <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. The most remarkable is the ophiopsis; which for its shape is one of the most singular that can be seen. It has an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> head, shaped like a heart, CCCXXI. with its point joined to the thorax, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> part before. It is smooth, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, flattened, continually shaking, with short antennae, yellowish maxillae, and four palpi. Towards the middle of the upper part of the head, between the eyes, are the three stemmata, placed in a triangle. The thorax, to which this head is fastened, is narrow, long, and cylindrical. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a>, broader, is black like the rest of the body, with the segments margined <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>. The feet are of a yellowish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a>. The wings, which are fatiguated, are <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, diaphanous, veined, and as it were covered with a very fine <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NET">net</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> of black. This insect, for the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of its head, resembles a snake. It is found but seldom, and in woods only. Its larva, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHRYSALIS">chrysalis</a>, and habitation, are absolutely unknown.

RED-BREAST

Pages 1218-1218

in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ornithology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTACILLA">Motacilla</a>, under which article it was omitted. The <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BILL">bill</a> is dusky; the forehead, chin, throat, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, are of a deep <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; the head, hind <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the neck, the back, and tail, are of a deep ash-colour tinged with green; the wings rather darker, the edges inclining to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>; the legs and feet dusky. This <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>, though so very pelucant as to be at constant <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> with its own tribe, yet is remarkably sociable with mankind: in the winter it frequently makes one of the family, and takes refuge from the inclemency of the season even by our firesides. Thomson has prettily described the annual visits of this guest; vide his Winter, l. 246. In the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> this bird retires to breed in the thickest coverts, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the most concealed holes of walls and other buildings. The eggs are of a dull <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, sprinkled with reddish spots. Its song is remarkably fine and soft; and the more to be valued, as we enjoy it the greatest part of the winter and early in the spring, and even through <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>; but its notes are part of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> drowned in the general warble of the season. Many of the autumnal songsters seem to be the young cock <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>-breasts of that year. Red-Start, (Motacilla phoenicurus), in ornithology, was omitted to be described under the article Motacilla, of which it is a species. This bird appears among us only in the spring and summer, and is observed to come over nearly at the same time with the nightingale. It makes its nest in hollow trees, and holes in walls and other buildings; which it forms with moss on the outside, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> and feathers. It lays four or five eggs, very like those of the hedge-sparrow, but rather paler, and more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAPER">taper</a> at the legs end. This bird is so remarkably shy, that it <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> forfeit its nest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the eggs are only touched. It has a very fine soft <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>; but, being a full-bird, is with difficulty kept alive in confinement. It is remarkable in shaking its tail; it moves it horizontally, as a dog does when fawning.—The bill and legs of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> are <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>; the forehead white; the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of the head, hind part of the neck, and the back, are of a deep blue-grey; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a> and throat black; the breast, rump, and sides are red; the two middle feathers of the tail <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, the others red; the wings brown. In the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a>, the top of the head and back are of a deep ash-colour; the rump and tail of a duller red than those of the male; the chin white; the lower side of the neck cinereous; the breast of a paler red.

REPRODUCTION

Pages 1218-1220

(Encycl.) By reproduction is usually understood the restoration of a thing before existing, and since destroyed. It is very well known that trees and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> may be raised from slips and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CUTTINGS">cuttings</a>; and some late observations have shown, that there are some animals which have the same <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>. The polype was the first instance we had of this; but we had scarce <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> to wonder at the discovery Mr Trembley had made, when Mr Bonett discovered the same property in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>-worm. Amongst the plants which may be raised from cuttings, there are some which seem to possess this <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> in so eminent a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, that the smallest portion of them <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> become a complete tree again. It deserves inquiry, whether <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> not the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> Autho- thor of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, when he ordained that certain insects, as these polypes and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>, should resemble those plants in that particular, allowed them this power of being reproduced in the same degree; or, which is the same thing, whether this reproduction will or will not take <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in whatever <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> the worm is cut. In order to try this, Mr Bonett entered on a course of many experiments on the water-worms which have this property. These are, at their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> growth, from two or three inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and of a brownish <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> of reddish. From one of these worms he cut off the head and tail, taking from each extremity only a small piece of a twelfth of an inch in length; but neither of these pieces were able to reproduce what was wanting. They both perished in about 24 hours; the tail first, and afterwards the head. As to the body of the worm from which these pieces were separated, it lived as well as before, and seemed indeed to suffer nothing by the loss, the head-part being immediately used as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the head was thereon, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BORING">boring</a> the creature's way into the mud. There are, besides this, two other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> in which the reproduction will not take place; the one of these is about the fifth or sixth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> from the head, and the other at the same distance from the tail; and in all <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> the condition of the great artery in these parts is the cause of this. What is said of the want of the reproductive power of these parts relates only to the head and tail ends; for as to the body, it feels very little inconvenience from the loss of what is taken off, and very speedily reproduces those parts. Where, then, does the principle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> reside in such worms, which, after having their heads cut off, will have not only the same motions, but even the inclinations, that they had before? and yet this difficulty is very small, compared to several others which at the same time offer themselves to our reason. Is this wonderful reproduction of parts only a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>? or is there lodged in the body of the creature a chain of minute buds or shoots, a sort of little embryos, already formed and placed in such parts where the reproductions are to begin? Are these worms only <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a>? or are they, like more perfect animals, a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> of whose motions are actuated or regulated by a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>? And if they have themselves such a principle, how is it that this principle is multiplied, and is found in every separate piece? Is it to be granted, that there are in these worms, not a single soul (if it is to be so called) in each, but that each contains as many souls as there are pieces capable of reproducing perfect animals? Are we to believe with Malpighi, that these sorts of worms are all heart and brain from one end to the other! This may be; but yet if we knew that it was so, we should know in reality but very little the more for knowing it: and it seems, after all, that in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of this kind we are only to admire the works of the great Creator, and sit <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in silence. The nice <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of feeling in spiders has been much talked of by naturalists; but it appears that these worms have yet somewhat more surprising in them in regard to this particular. If a piece of flick, or any other substance, be brought near them, they do not stay for its touching them, but begin to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a> and frisk about as soon as it comes towards them. There want, however, some farther experiments to ascertain whether this be really owing to feeling or to sight; for though we can discover no distinct organs of sight in these creatures, yet they seem affected by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> or a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a>, and always frisk about it in the same manner at the approach of either; nay, even the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>-light has some effect upon them. A twig of willow, poplar, or many other trees, being planted in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, takes root, and becomes a tree, every piece of which will in the same manner produce other trees. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> is the same with these worms: they are cut to pieces, and these several pieces become perfect animals; and each of these may be again cut into a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of pieces, each of which will in the same manner produce an animal. It had been supposed by some that these worms were oviparous; but Mr Bonett, on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> one of them to pieces, having observed a slender substance, resembling a small filament, to move at the end of one of the pieces, separated it; and on examining it with glasses, found it to be a perfect worm, of the same form with its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARENT">parent</a>, which lived and grew larger in a vessel of water into which he put it. These small bodies are easily divided, and very readily complete themselves again, a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> usually serving for the production of a head to the part that wants one; and, in general, the smaller and slenderer the worms are, the sooner they complete themselves after this operation. When the bodies of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> worms are examined by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a>, it is very easy to see the appearance of the young worms alive, and moving about within them: but it requires great precision and exactness to be certain of this; since the ramifications of the great artery have very much the appearance of young worms, and they are kept in a sort of continual motion by the sypholes and diafloses of the several portions of the artery, which serve as so many hearts. It is very certain, that what we force in regard to these animals by our operations, is done also naturally every day in the brooks and ditches where they live. A curious observer will find in these places many of them without heads or tails, and some without either; as also other fragments of various kinds, all which are then in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of completing themselves; but whether accidents have reduced them to this state, or they thus purposely throw off parts of their own body for the reproduction of more animals, is not easy to determine. They are plainly liable to many accidents, by which they lose the several parts of their body, and must perish very early if they had not a power of reproducing what was lost: they often are broken into two pieces, by the resistance of some hard piece of mud, which they enter; and they are subject to a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, a kind of gangrene, rotting off the several parts of their bodies, and must inevitably perish by it, had they not this surprising property. This worm was a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> instance, after the polype, of the surprising power in an animal of recovering its most essential parts when lost. But nature does not seem to have limited her beneficence in this respect to these two creatures. Mr Bonett tried the same experiments on another species of water-worm, differing from the former in being much thicker. This kind of worm, when divided in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>-season, very often shows the same property: for if it be cut into three or four pieces, the pieces will <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> like dead for a long time, but afterwards will move about again; and will be found in this state of rest to have recovered a head. or a tail, or both. After recovering their parts, they move very little; and, according to this <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>'s experiments, seldom live more than a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a>. It should seem, that the more difficult success of this last kind of worm, after cutting, and the long time it takes to recover the lost parts, if it do recover them at all, is owing to its thickness; since we always find in that species of worms which succeeds best of all, that those which are thinnest always recover their parts much sooner than the others. The water-insects also are not the only creatures which have this power of recovering their lost parts. The earth affords us some already discovered to grow in this manner from their cuttings, and these not less deserving our admiration than those of the water: the common earth-worms are of this kind. Some of these worms have been divided into two, others into three or four pieces; and some of these pieces, after having passed two or three months without any appearance of life or motion, have then begun to reproduce a head or tail, or both. The reproduction of the anus, after such a state of rest, is no longer <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>; a few days do it: but it is otherwise with the head, that does not seem to perform its functions in the divided pieces till about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> months after the separation. It is to be observed, that in all these operations both on earth and water-worms, that the hinder part suffers greatly more than the fore part in the cutting; for it always twirls itself about a long time, as if actuated by strong convulsions; whereas the head usually crawls away without the appearance of any great uneasiness. The reproduction of several parts of lobsters, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CRABS">crabs</a>, &c., makes also one of the great curiosities in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY">natural <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. That, in lieu of an organic part of an animal broken off, another shall rise perfectly like it, may seem inconsistent with the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> system of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>, where the animal is supposed to be wholly formed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EGG">egg</a>. Yet has the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of fact been well attested by the fishermen, and even by several virtuosos who have taken the point into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>, particularly M. de Reaumur and M. Perrault, whose skill and exactness in things of this nature will hardly be questioned. The legs of lobsters, &c., consist each of five articulations: now, when any of the legs happen to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> by any accident, as in walking, &c., which frequently happens, the fracture is always found to be in a part near the fourth articulation; and what they thus lose is precisely reproduced in some time afterwards; that is, a part of a leg shoots out, consisting of four articulations, the first whereof has two claws as before; so that the loss is entirely repaired. If a lobster's leg be broken off by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> at the fourth or fifth articulation, what is thus broken off always comes again; but it is not so if the fracture be made in the first, second, or third articulation. In those cases, the reproduction is very rare if things continue as they are. But what is exceedingly surprising is, that they do not; for, upon visiting the lobster maimed in these barren and unhappy articulations, at the end of two or three days, all the other articulations are found broken off to the fourth; and it is suspected they have performed the operation on themselves, to make the reproduction of a leg certain. The part reproduced is not only perfectly like that retrenched, but also, in a certain space of time, grows equal to it. Hence it is that we frequently see lobsters, which have their two big legs unequal, and that in all proportions. This shows the smaller leg to be a new one. A part thus reproduced being broken, there is a second reproduction. The summer, which is the only season of the year when the lobsters eat, is the most favourable time for the reproduction. It is then performed in four or five weeks; whereas it takes up eight or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> months in any other season. The small legs are sometimes reproduced, but more rarely, as well as more slowly, than the great ones: the horns do the same. The experiment is most easily tried on the common crab.

REST-HARROW

Pages 1220-1220
or CAMMOCK, the Ononis Arvensis. A decoction of this plant has been much recommended to horses labouring under a stoppage of urine. It is the pest of some corn-fields; but in its younger state, before the plant has acquired its thorns, it is a most acceptable food to sheep.

ROSCRUICANS

Pages 1220-1220
ROSCRUCIANS, or Brothers of the Rosy Cross, a name assumed by a sect or cabal of hermetic philosophers, who appeared, or at least were first taken notice of, in Germany, in the beginning of the 16th century. They pretended to be masters of all sciences, and to have many important secrets, particularly that of the f="vol8.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher's stone.—Their society is frequently denoted by the abbreviations F. R. C.

ROUSSEAU

Pages 1220-1221

a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, was the son of a watchmaker at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>, and was born in 1712. In the early <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> he embraced the Roman Catholic <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and travelled into <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. Some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> after, he went into France; and was secretary to M. de Montaign <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> in 1743. Till he was 40 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> he remained entirely unknown in the literary world. His Discourse against the Sciences, which in 1750 was honoured with the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> by the academy of Dijon, first drew him from this obscurity. Though the subject had formerly been treated by the famous Henry Cornelius Agrippa, Rousseau gave his subject all the charms of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a>; displaying the most uncommon resources of genius and knowledge. A variety of writers attacked his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>; dispute on dispute ensued, and he found himself engaged in the most formidable lists of literary controversy. His discourse on the Inequality among Men and of the Origin of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, tho' it supports a false system, is yet done with admirable art; and this performance, especially its dedication to the Republic of Geneva, are among those <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a>-pieces of eloquence, of which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> alone have given us any idea. His <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">Letter</a> to M. d'Alembert on the Project of establishing a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THEATRE">Theatre</a> at Geneva, published in 1757, contains, amidst many paradoxes, some of the most important truths. This letter, in which he decries the stage, was the source of an irreconcilable enmity between him and the celebrated Voltaire. However, it is remarkable, that even Rousseau, this enemy of plays, wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a>, and presented a Pastoral to the theatre; the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> and music of which he composed with the most pleasing <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the simplicity of rural sentiment and manners. The author, who had an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> for music, had cultivated it from his infancy with equal <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>; and his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a> of Music is one of the best works of the kind. His Epistolary <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROMANCE">Romance</a>, to which which the English translator had given the name of Eloisa, is universally known; but of all the works of this celebrated writer, his Emilius, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Treatise on <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">Education</a>, made the greatest noise. The most exceptionable part of this <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> is the third volume; which is almost full of objections to Christianity. This proved fatal to his repose. He had lived from the year 1754 in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> near <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTMORENCY">Montmorency</a>; a retreat which he owed to the generosity of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a>-general of the revenues. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> condemned the last-mentioned work in 1762, and commenced a criminal <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> against the author, which obliged him to fly from that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a>. Being proscribed also in his native <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, he at length found an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a> in the sovereignty of Neufchatel. His first care was to defend his Emilius against the anathemas of the archbishop of Paris. His "Letters from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">Mountains</a>" were published soon after; but this book, less eloquent than his "Letter to the archbishop of Paris," and filled with uninteresting invectives against the magistrates and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a> of Geneva, irritated the Protestant ministers without reconciling him to the Roman clergy. In the year 1753, Rousseau had solemnly abandoned the Roman religion; and, what is remarkable, at the very time that he had determined to reside in a Catholic country. This conversion, however, could not regain the esteem of the Protestant teachers; nor could the protection of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a> secure him against the vengeance of the minister of the village where he resided. He therefore took the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> of visiting England; but here he soon embroiled himself with the celebrated Mr Hume, by whose means he had been placed in an agreeable retreat in <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-DERBYSHIRE">Derbyshire</a>, and who had obtained for him a pension from the king. He again returned to France, where his patrons obtained leave for him to reside in Paris, but on condition that he should not write any thing on the subjects of religion or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. He obeyed this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INJUNCTION">injunction</a> inviolably, and wrote nothing on any subject, but contented himself with the peaceful life of a philosopher. In May 1776 he accepted the invitation of the marquis and marchioness de Girardin, who had prepared a neat little house for him at a small distance from their delightful castle of Ermenonville, about 30 miles from Paris. This retreat was perfectly conformable to the wishes of Rousseau. Every <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> he amused himself in a neighbouring wood in collecting <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> for his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HERBAL">herbal</a>. The marquis, who was himself a philosopher, indulged his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> for rural life, and was enamoured with the writings of the singular Rousseau. They had musical parties frequently, at which he assisted; and he composed several <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIRS">airs</a> in all that simple style of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> for which he had ever been remarked. Among others he set several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> of our Shakespeare to music, and played them himself on the forte piano in the most enchanting manner.—In this sweet retirement he lived two years in the most agreeable manner; and died on the 2d of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1778, in the 66th year of his age. The marquis has since erected a sepulchral monument, to cover the remains of his departed friend. This <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAUSOLEUM">mausoleum</a> is constructed of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> marble, with the bust of the deceased by Houdon; and its decorations are in the best taste. One of its sides exhibits two doves, for Eloisa; another, a mother sucking her child, for Emilius; a third, children sacrificing on the altar of nature; and the fourth, a lyre, with other symbols of poetry and music. The inscription on the monument is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>; and contains a pompous encomium on the genius, sentiments, and moral character of Mr Rousseau. We shall conclude the life of this singular <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> with the character of himself and of his writings, as delivered by the masterly <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PEN">pen</a> of Dr Beattie. "I consider Rousseau," says the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a>, "as a moral writer of true genius. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol17.html#article-SENSIBILITY">Sensibility</a> of heart; a talent for extensive and accurate observation; liveliness and dour of fancy; and a style, copious, nervous, and elegant, beyond that of any other French writer; are his distinguishing characteristics. In argument he is not always equally successful; for he often mistakes <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECLAMATION">declamation</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a> for fact; but his eloquence, when addressed to the heart, overpowers with force irresistible. A greater <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of important facts relating to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> mind are recorded in his works, than in all the books of all the sceptical philosophers <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>. And he appears in general to be a friend to virtue, to mankind, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> religion, and sometimes to Christianity. Yet none even of his best works are free from absurdity. His reasonings, on the effects of the sciences, and on the origin and progress of human society, are diffuse, inaccurate, and often weak; much perverted by theories of his own, as well as by too implicit an admittance of the vague assertions of travellers, and of the systems and doctrines of some favourite French philosophers. And he seems, in these, and frequently too in his own writings, to consider animal <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, and bodily accomplishments, as the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> and perfection of man. His <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of education, though admirable in many parts, is in some injudicious and dangerous, and impracticable as a whole. The character of Julia's lover is drawn with a masterly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> indeed, and well conducted throughout; but the lady has two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, and those incompatible. The wife of Wolmar is quite a different person from the mistress of St Prieux. Wolmar himself is an impossible character; destitute of principle, yet of rigid virtue; destitute of feeling, yet capable of tenderness and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a>; delicate in his notions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, yet not ashamed to marry a woman whom he knew to be to all intents and purposes devoted to another. Some of this author's remarks on the spirit of Christianity, and on the character of its Divine Founder, are not only excellent, but transcendentally so; and I believe no Christian can read them without feeling his heart warmed, and his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> confirmed. But what he says of the absurdities which he fancies to be contained in the Sacred <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, of the impropriety of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>, of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> between those of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ and the tricks of jugglers, of the insignificance and impertinence of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>, of the sufficiency of human reason for discovering a complete and comfortable scheme of natural religion, of the discouraging nature of the terms of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a> offered in the Gospel, of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of evidence that ought to accompany Divine <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-REVELATION">Revelation</a> (which, as he states it, would be incompatible with man's free agency and moral probation); what he says of these, and several other theological <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> importance, betrays a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a>, of which, as a philosopher, as a scholar, and as a man,

SAINTS

Pages 1221-1222

(Encycl.) <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Bellarmine, and other Popish writers, have pleaded, that by praying to the saints, they only intend to express a desire of their intercession, and that their invocation of the saints terminates ultimately in God. Accordingly they have distinguished two sorts of worship; one called *latra*, appropriate to God; and another *dulia*, which, being of an inferior <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, is paid to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a> and saints. However, many of their own writers have exploded this distinction, and others have owned that it is unscriptural. There is another sort of worship, which is of a higher <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> than that paid to saints in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a>, and which is peculiar to the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>: they call *hyperdulia*. After all, those who read their books of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>, their Hours, their Offices, their Rosaries, their Breviaries, and their Missals, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> find many <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> addresses to the saints, which are very different from those prayers whose object is merely to supplicate their intercession. Besides, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>. 25, directs to apply to the saints for their help and assistance, as well as their prayers; and condemns all who think that it is not good and profitable to offer prayers to saints, as chargeable with impious sentiments. And the creed of pope Pius IV. expressly insists upon it as an article of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, that the saints reigning together with Christ are to be invoked. As to the antiquity of this practice, the council of Trent, sect. 25, speaks of it as the usage of the apostolic and catholic <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> from the beginning of Christianity. As to the doctrine of the intercession of saints and angels, there is not the least intimation of it in the writings of the two first centuries; though it must be allowed to have been introduced in the next century, and that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORIGEN">Origen</a> and Cyprian expressly favour this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>. The worship of saints and angels is of a much later <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DATE">date</a>, especially as a standing generally-received doctrine of the church. For though Athanasius was for worshipping the saints, yet Cyril, who lived in the next century, says, We neither call the holy martyrs gods, nor are we used to worship them. St Austin affirms, that neither saints nor angels will be worshipped. Archbishop Usher says, that as to the first 400 years after Christ, for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> parts of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, not one true testimony can be produced out of any father in favour of this doctrine; and cardinal Perron, Richlieu, and other learned writers among the Romanists, own, that the invocation of saints was not practised for the three first centuries. The first symptoms of this worship did not appear till towards the end of the fourth century, and it seems to have sprung out of the regard which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> at that time manifested to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of the martyrs. They frequented their tombs, and erected altars there, praying to God, and engaging themselves to a strict <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the virtues and piety of the departed martyrs: by degrees this veneration degenerated into praises and eulogiums of the saints themselves, in which they used some apotrophies and rhetorical addresses; whence proceeded a superstitious regard to them, and at length a direct invocation and worship of them. Nor does it appear, that any public prayers to saints were established till A.D. 788, by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> council of Nice; and this council was condemned by another held at Frankfort, A.D. 794; and the invocation of saints was likewise condemned by a former council held at Constantinople, A.D. 755, consisting of 388 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>. In the seventh century, Gregory expressly says, that angels refused to be worshipped since the appearance of Christ. In order to convey some idea of the extravagance to which veneration for reputed saints hath arrived in the Romish church, we shall only mention one instance out of many that might be alleged. It is well known that there were three altars in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> church of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, one erected to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Christ, another to the Virgin Mary, and a third to St Thomas à Becket; and the offerings at his shrine amounted to 1000l. when those to the Virgin did not amount to 5l. and those to Christ were nothing; and Rapin informs us, that in one year, viz. A.D. 1420, there were no less than 50,000 foreigners who came in pilgrimages to pay their homage at this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>.

SALT

Pages 1222-1223

(Encycl.) See also <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACIDS">Acids</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol4.html#article-ALKALIES">Alkalies</a> in this Appendix.—Acids and alkalies, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a> of both, when in a concrete form, are salts, and of the purest sort. The bodies, therefore, to which the name of salts more properly belongs, are the concretions of those substances; which are accordingly called acid salts, alkaline salts, and neutral salts. These last are combinations of acid and alkaline salts, in such propor- proportion as to render the compounds neither four nor alkaline to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. This proportionate <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> is called saturation; thus the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a>-salt is a neutral salt, composed of marine acid and mineral alkali combined together to the point of saturation. The appellation of neutral salts is also extended to denote all those combinations of acids, and any other substance with which they can unite, so as to lose, wholly <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, their acid properties. No notwithstanding that the general <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> of salts given above is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> received, yet there are many writers, especially mineralogists, who confine the denomination of salts to those substances only which, besides the general properties of salts, have the power of crystallizing, that is, of arranging their particles so as to form regularly-shaped bodies, called crystals; when the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> superfluous to their concrete existence has been evaporated. Salts of various sorts are found already formed in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, but a great many others are made by art, and even several of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> ones may be imitated. We shall only consider those salts, either natural or <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a>, which are mostly used. The vitriolic acid, when combined with other substances, forms vitriolic salts, which vary both in specific names and properties, according to the various substances with which the acid is combined. Thus the vitriolic acid, combined with mineral alkali, forms the salt called Glauber's salt, or sal mirabile. When it is combined with calcareous earths, it forms vitriolic salts with bases of calcareous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, which are commonly called salenites. When combined with argillaceous earths, it forms <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>. When combined with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, it forms vitriolic salts with metallic bases, to which the general name vitriols is given; and in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> are commonly called copperas. The vitriols principally used are: 1. The martial vitriol; called also English vitriol, green vitriol, or green copperas, which is a combination of vitriolic acid with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>. 2. The vitriol of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, called also blue vitriol, Cyprian vitriol, or blue copperas; which is a combination of vitriolic acid and copper. 3. The vitriol of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZINC">zinc</a>, called also <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> copperas, and Geffar vitriol; which is a combination of the same acid with a semi-metal called zinc. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> peculiar to the vitriolic acid, that all the combinations of it, with those substances with which it can form neutral salts, are susceptible of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CRYSTALLIZATION">crystallization</a>. The nitrous acid, combined with all the substances with which it can mix, forms saline substances, in general called nitrous salts; specifying each particular salt by the name of the substance united to the acid. Thus nitrous acid, with fixed vegetable alkali, forms a saline substance called nitre, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a>. With mineral alkali, forms cubic or quadrangular nitre. When mixed with metallic substances, forms metallic nitrates, which are specified nitre of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>; nitre of silver, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> nitre, lunar crysate, and crysate of silver; nitrous crysate of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>; nitre of copper, &c. The marine acid, combined with various matters, forms marine salts, or simply salts, specified by the names of their particular bases. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-salt, or kitchen-salt, and sal gem, are combinations of marine acid and mineral alkali. When this acid is combined with volatile alkali, it forms sal ammoniac (a). With metals it forms metallic salts, called salt of gold, salt of copper, &c., according to the various metals combined with the acid. The salt of silver is also called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUNA">luna</a> cornua; the salt of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> is often called plumbum cornueum; and the salts of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a>, and of arsenic, are known by the names of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a> of antimony, and butter of arsenic. The acid of tartar (the purest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of which, or that saline substance which first crystallizes, by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a>, in the vessels in which it is purified, is called cream of tartar), and also all other concrete vegetable acids analogous to it, when mixed with various other substances, form compounds, generally called tartarous salts, or soluble tartar, because they are dissolved by water more easily than the acid of tartar itself. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACETOUS">Acetous</a> salts, that is, all salts containing the acid of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, are also combined with various bases, and form saline substances of different names; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which are, the acetous salt of copper, called crysate of Venus, or verdigris, by the chemists, and distilled or crystallized verdigris in commerce; the acetous salt of lead, commonly called salt or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> of lead; and the acetous mercurial salts. Sugar is an essential vegetable salt, of a pleasant sweet taste, containing a vegetable acid combined with earth and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POTASH">Potash</a> is a fixed vegetable alkali, extracted from the ashes of wood. Concrete volatile alkalies are generally called volatile salts; although this name is sometimes also given to the volatile salt of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBER">amber</a>, which is not an alkaline, but an acid salt. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BORAX">Borax</a> is a neutral saline <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, whose origin, whether animal or vegetable, is as yet unknown, its components being not sufficiently examined. It is soluble in water, and very nearly as crystallizable as alum. When borax is exposed to the fire, it first bubbles and foams very much, but afterwards it melts into a clear glaze. When acids are combined with the alkaline part of borax, a substance of a singular nature is separated from it, commonly called sedative salt. Although this substance acts as an acid in borax, by saturating its alkali, yet it has no acid taste, nor doth it turn the tincture of heliotropium to a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>, as other acids do. It is the property of borax to facilitate considerably the fusion of metals, of earths, and other minerals. Some <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a> and earths cannot be vitrified at all, except they are mixed with borax. For this property borax is commonly used as a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLUX">flux</a> (that is, a substance which facilitates the fusion of other bodies) in various <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>; but especially in soldering metals, and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSAYING">assaying</a> ores. Phosphoric salts are combinations of alkaline, earthy, and metallic substances with the acid obtained from the phosphorus of urine. Besides the above-mentioned salts, there are several others to be met with in the writings of the chemical and medical authors; but, as they are of little <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, we shall omit any account of them.

SANDEMANIANS

Pages 1223-1224

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> that originated in Scotland about the year 1728; where it is at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> distinguished by the name of Glasite, after its founder Mr John Glas, who was a minister of the established <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> in that (a) Ammoniacal salts is also a general name given to all neutral salts composed of an acid saturated with a volatile alkali. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>; but being <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of subverting the national covenant, and sapping the foundation of all national establishments by the kirk judiciary, was expelled by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SYNOD">synod</a> from the church of Scotland. His sentiments are fully explained in a tract published at that time, intitled, "The Testimony of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">King</a> of Martyrs," and preserved in the first volume of his works. In <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of Mr Glas's expulsion, his adherents formed themselves into churches conformable in their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> to what they apprehended to be the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of the first churches recorded in the New <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>. Soon after the year 1755, Mr Robert Sandeman, an elder in one of these churches in Scotland, published a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of letters addressed to Mr Hervey, occasioned by his Theron and Aspasio; in which he endeavours to show, that his notion of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> is contradictory to the scripture account of it, and could only serve to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> men, professedly holding the doctrines <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called Calvinistic, to establish their own righteousnesses upon their frames, inward feelings, and various acts of faith. In these letters Mr Sandeman attempts to prove, that faith is neither more nor less than a simple assent to the divine testimony concerning <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, recorded in the New Testament; and he maintains, that the word faith, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a>, is constantly used by the apostles to signify what is denoted by it in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> discourse, viz. a persuasion of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of any proposition, and that there is no <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between believing any common testimony, and believing the apostolic testimony, except that which results from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the testimony itself. This led the way to a controversy, among those who were called Calvinists, concerning the nature of justifying faith; and those who adopted Mr Sandeman's notion of it, and who took the denomination of Sandemanians, formed themselves into church order, in strict fellowship with the churches in Scotland, but holding no kind of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> with other churches.
