The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> opinions and practices in which this sect differs from other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, are, their weekly administration of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUPPER">Supper</a>; their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>-feasts, of which every member is not only allowed but required to partake, and which consist of their dining together at each other's houses in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> between the morning and afternoon <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>; their acts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> used on this occasion, at the admission of a new member, and at other times, when they deem it to be necessary or proper; their weekly collection before the Lord's Supper, for the support of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, and defraying other expenses; mutual exhortation; <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSTINENCE">abstinence</a> from blood and things strangled; washing each other's feet, the precept concerning which, as well as other precepts, they understand literally; <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> of goods, so far as that every one is to consider all that he has in his possession and power as liable to the calls of the poor and church, and the unlawfulness of laying up treasures on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, by setting them apart for any distant, future, and uncertain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. They allow of public and private diversions, so far as they are not connected with circumstances really sinful; but apprehending a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> to be feared, disapprove of playing at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CARDS">cards</a>, dice, &c. They maintain a plurality of elders, pastors, or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, in each church; and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of the presence of two elders in every <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of discipline, and at the administration of the Lord's Supper. In the choice of these elders, want of learning, and engagements in trade, &c., are no sufficient objection; but <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> marriages disqualify for the office; and they are ordained by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> and fasting, imposition of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and giving the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of fellowship. In their discipline they are strict and severe; and think themselves obliged to separate from the communion and worship of all such <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> as appear to them not to profess the simple truth for their only ground of hope, and who do not walk in obedience to it. We shall only add, that in every church transaction, they esteem unanimity to be absolutely necessary. From this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> of the account which they have published of their tenets and practices, it does not seem to be probable that their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> should be very considerable.

SAPOTA

Pages 1224-1224

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>. See ACHRA in this Appendix. SARPLAR of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WOOL">Wool</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of wool, otherwise called a pocket, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> half sack; a sack containing 80 tod; a tod two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; and a stone 14 pounds.—In Scotland it is called sarpliuth, and contains 80 stone.

SASSAFRAS

Pages 1224-1225

a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of laurus; see Laurus, (Encycl.). In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENNSYLVANIA">Pennsylvania</a> and other parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, it grows in a dry loose ground, of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> brick <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, which consists for the most <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of sand mixed with clay. This tree spreads its roots very much, and new shoots come up from them in some places; but these shoots are not good for transplanting, because they have so few fibres besides the root which connects them to the main stem, that they cannot well strike into the ground. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a>, therefore, any one would plant sassafras trees, he must endeavour to get their berries; which, however, is difficult, since the birds eat them before they are half ripe. The cows are very greedy after the tender new shoots, and look for them everywhere. The bark of this tree is used by the women here in dying worsted a fine lasting <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a>-colour, which does not fade in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. They <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> urine instead of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a>; and boil the dye in a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> boiler, because in an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> vessel it does not yield so fine a colour. The wood is made use of for posts belonging to the enclosures, for it is said to last a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> in the ground; but it is likewise said, that there is hardly any kind of wood which is more attacked by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> than this, when it is exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> without cover; and that in a short time it is quite worm-eaten through and through. On <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> some part of the sassafras tree, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> its shoots, and holding it to the nose, it has a strong but pleasant smell. Some people peel the root, and boil the peel with the beer which they are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BREWING">brewing</a>, because they believe it wholesome. For the same reason, the peel is put into brandy, either whilst it is distilling, or after it is made. Professor Kalm informs us, that a decoction of the root of sassafras in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, drank every morning, is used with success in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DROPSY">dropsy</a>. When part of a wood is destined for cultivation, the sassafras trees are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> left upon it, because they have a very thick foliage, and afford a cool <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> to the cattle during the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> heats. Some people get their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a>-posts made of sassafras wood, in order to expel the bugs; for its strong scent, it is said, prevents those <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERMIN">vermin</a> from from settling in them. For two or three years together this has the desired effect; or about as long as the wood keeps its strong aromatic smell; but after that time it has been observed to lose its effect. In Pennsylvania some people put chips of sassafras into their chests, where they keep all sorts of woollen stuffs, in order to expel the moths (or larvae or caterpillars of moths or times) which commonly <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> in them in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. The root keeps its smell for a long while: our author <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> one which had lain five or six years in the drawer of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, and still preserved the strength of its scent. The people here also gather its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, and use it as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TEA">tea</a>. The sassafras-tree generally stands single in the woods, and along the fences round the fields. It flowers in May before the leaves come out; and being entirely covered with them, it is distinguished at a great distance by their beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> colour.

SCALDS

Pages 1225-1225

in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of literature, a name given by the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> inhabitants of the northern countries to their poets; in whose writings their history is recorded.

SCARBOROUGH

Pages 1225-1225

(Encycl.) The waters of Scarborough are chalybeate and purging. Of these there are two <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WELLS">wells</a>, both impregnated with the same principles, in different proportions; though the purging well is the most celebrated, and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> of this is usually called the Scarborough water. When these waters are poured out of one glass into another, they throw up a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>-bubbles; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they are shook for some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> in a phial <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> stoppered, and the phial be suddenly opened before the commotion ceases, they displace an <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> vapour, with an audible noise, which shows that they abound in fixed air. At the fountain they have a brisk, pungent, chalybeate <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>; but the purging water tastes bitterish, which is not usually the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> with the chalybeate one. They lose their chalybeate virtues by exposure and by keeping; but the purging water the soonest. They both putrefy by keeping; but in time recover their sweetness. Four <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> five half pints of the purging water drank within an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, give two or three easy motions, and raise the spirits. The like <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the chalybeate purges less, but exhilarates more, and passes off chiefly by urine. These waters have been found beneficial in hectic fevers, weaknesses of the stomach, and indigestion; in relaxations of the system; in nervous, hysterical, and hypochondriacal disorders; in the green sickness, fever, rheumatism, and asthmatic complaints; in gleet, the fluor albus, and other supernatural evacuations; and in habitual coliciveness.

SCHOONER

Pages 1225-1225

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, a small vessel with two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, whose main-sail and fore-sail are suspended from gaffs, reaching from the mast towards the stern, and stretched out below by booms, whose foremost ends are hooked to an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, which clasps the mast, so as to turn therein as upon an axis, when the after-ends are swung from one side of the vessel to the other.

SENSE

Pages 1225-1226
COMMON, is a term that has been variously used both by ancient and modern writers. With some it has been synonymous with public sense; with others it has denoted prudence; in certain instances, it has been confounded with some of the powers of taste; and, accordingly, those who commit egregious blunders with regard to decorum, saying and doing what is offensive to their company, and inconsistent with their own character, have been charged with a defect in common sense. Some men are distinguished by an uncommon acuteness in discovering the characters of others; and this talent has been sometimes called common sense: similar to which is that use of the term, which makes it to signify that experience and knowledge of life which is acquired by living in society. To this meaning Quintilian refers, speaking of the advantages of a public education: Senium ipsum qui communis dicitur, ubi dicit, cum se a congruis, qui non hominibus solum, sed multis quoque animalibus naturalis est, segregari? Lib. i. cap. 2. But the term common sense hath in modern times been used to signify that power of the mind which perceives truth, or commands belief, not by progressive argumentation, but by an instantaneous, instinctive, and irresistible impulse; derived neither from education nor from habit, but from nature; acting independently of our will, whenever its object is presented, according to an established law, and therefore called sense; and acting in a similar manner upon all, or at least upon a great majority of mankind, and therefore called common sense. The first among the moderns, who took notice of this principle as one of the springs of our knowledge, was Buffier, a French philosopher of the present century, in a book entitled Traité des premières vérités; and this doctrine hath lately, in our SEN [9158] SER sense. our own country, been illustrated and maintained by Drs Reid, Beattie, Oswald, and Campbell. In order to evince, that there is a real and essential difference between this faculty and that of reason, it is observed, that we are conscious, from internal feeling, that the energy of understanding, which perceives intuitive truth, is different from that other energy which unites a conclusion with a first principle, by a gradual chain of intermediate relations: that we cannot discern any necessary connection between reason and common sense: that the one is more in our power than the other; the faculty of reasoning being improveable by culture; whereas common sense, like other instincts, arrives at maturity with almost no care of ours, and it is impossible to teach common sense to one who wants it; though this, like other instincts, may languish for want of exercise: and that a distinction, similar to that which is here maintained, is acknowledged by the vulgar, who speak of mother-wit, as something different from the deductions of reason, and the refinements of science. All sound reasoning, it is said, must ultimately rest on the principles of common sense; that is, on principles intuitively certain, or intuitively probable; and, consequently, common sense is the ultimate judge of truth, to which reason must continually act in subordination. Thus the advocates for this faculty, as an original and distinct power of the human mind, assign to it a very extensive empire, and an authority that is supreme and absolute. And they have proceeded so far, as to substitute in the room of Mr Locke's abstraction, this faculty, as the characteristic of rationality. To this they refer the evidence of mathematical truth, of external and internal sense, of memory, of reasoning from the effect to the cause, of probable or experimental reasoning, of analogical reasoning, of faith in testimony, and, indeed, of all primary truths. To common sense, therefore, all truth must be conformable; this, they say, is its fixed and invariable standard. And whatever contradicts common sense, or is inconsistent with that standard, though supported by arguments that are deemed unanswerable, and by names that are celebrated by all the critics, academies, and potentates on earth, is not truth, but falsehood. In a word, the dictates of common sense are, in respect to human knowledge, in general, what the axioms of geometry are in respect to mathematics: on the supposition that these axioms are false or dubious, all mathematical reasoning falls to the ground; and on the supposition that the dictates of common sense are erroneous or deceitful, all truth, virtue, and science, are vain. And hence it appears, that according to this system, common sense is not only the test of truth, but the standard of moral obligation. See Reid's Enquiry into the Human Mind, on the Principles of Common Sense, 8vo, ed. 2. 1765. Beattie's Essay on the Nature and Immutability of Truth, 8vo, ed. 2. 1771. Oswald's Appeal to Common Sense in behalf of Religion, 8vo, ed. 2. 1768. Campbell's Philosophy of Rhetoric, 8vo, 1776, vol. i. p. 109, &c. This system has been attacked by Dr Priestley; who has again been replied to (by Dr Blacklock, if we are not misinformed) in a late periodical publication at Edinburgh. See Priestley's Examination of Reid, Beattie, and Oswald; also Edinburgh Magazine and Review for the year 1775.

SERPENTS

Pages 1226-1230

(Encycl.) Serpents strike mankind, and other animals, with such terror upon account of their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POISON">poison</a> and some singular properties which elude all the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> of our judgment, that their unexpected approach alarms even the most determined courage. Among the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMPHIBIA">amphibia</a> serpentes we find some genera endowed with a very singular <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, whereby they differ from all others: the greater <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of them live indifferently by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, many of them for one half the year <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> in their winter-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> to all appearance dead: their respiration differs very much from that of birds and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a>; they draw in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> without any <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RECIPROCAL">reciprocal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a>, at least a sensible one: their bodies are of a very rigid <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, abounding with blood, which possesses a very small <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>: the organs of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a>; a singularity occurring in no other animal, unless perhaps a few insects: their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> sounds are hoarse, their aspects ugly, their smell fetid. Some of them are oviparous, others viviparous; and by their having cartilaginous <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BONES">bones</a>, every <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> they shake off their old <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> in the manner of the crab; so that there is no definitive bound to their increase and magnitude. Their singular <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of taking their prey also deserves to be mentioned: being destitute of feet, and consequently not able to pursue it, they <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> hidden under the cover of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a> and the roots of trees, and darting forward with a sudden spring upon any animal which passes by, seizes and devours it. Travellers into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a> inform us, that the Boa constrictor, the greatest of all serpents, lies in ambush among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>, and seizing hares, stags, and other animals, suffocates them by rolling himself round them, and then covering them with his saliva, swallows them. These animals, as they very seldom happen of capture, and beside are not furnished with real and proper <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, have not their jaw-bones jointed with the same articulation as other animals, but only connected at the base with a ligament; so that by expanding them they are able to devour the body of an animal of twice their thickness, or even more: Thus Cleijer relates, that the boa of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JAVA">Java</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> devour a whole buffalo, and other travellers affirm that he is able to swallow a stag. Our own vipers are frequently seen with their bellies greatly swollen out; and being dissected, they will be found to contain a frog or a mouse. A writer in the Amenitates Academicæ, informs us, that he once discovered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> young birds in the stomach of a viper. The American rattlesnake is the most indolent of all the serpents: As he lies under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> of a tree, opening his jaws a little, he fixes his eyes, which glitter very brightly upon any <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> or squirrel which is in it: they are endowed with a wonderful power of fascination; the squirrel utters a mournful and feeble cry, and, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> foreseeing his fate, leaps from bough to bough on every side, seemingly to attempt a sudden escape; but struck with an unknown <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of fascination, he comes <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from the tree, and flings himself with a spring into the very jaws of his enemy. A mouse, having been shut up with one of these fascinating rattle-snakes in an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> box, the mouse sat in one corner, and the rattle-snake was opposite to it; and fixing his his eyes continually upon it, by his look alone it was at last forced to fling itself into the mouth of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a>. The same experiment was repeated in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> with a pregnant <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> viper with the same success; and do we not see in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> instance at home in the toad, a most indolent animal, into whose mouth, as it lies in the shade or under a shrub, butterflies and other insects fly? Weapons. No subject has excited more philosophical controversy than the poison of serpents, with regard to its nature and mode of operating. Antiquity has not been sparing in conjecture and fiction upon this subject, and its errors have been retained with the most reverential obstinacy by the vulgar; among these we are to reckon the fictitious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> fixed in the tail of the serpent, as the painters sometimes have groundlessly enough represented it; some have invented a similar fiction of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> forked tongue, which the serpent vibrates on both sides, and have ascribed its power of producing such noxious effect to this; while others, afflicting an air of superior discernment, have, upon equally good reasons, ascribed it to the teeth in general; these are all errors of a magnitude that the most dilatory <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the subject would have been sufficient to have removed. There is a very small bone closely fixed to the upper jaw, in the inside of the lip of a poisonous serpent, which has a power of moving backward or forward; to this two or three fangs are annexed larger than the teeth, which the serpent, by its assistance, when enraged, darts forward, or withdraws and conceals at his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, in a similar manner to the claws of a cat: these fangs, which the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people name the large teeth of the serpent, are excellently described by Tyson, in the anatomy of the rattlesnake, which he has given in the Philosophical Transactions. "In these (the fangs) we observed a considerable cavity near the base; and near the point a very discernible fissure of some length like the slit of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PEN">pen</a>: the part of the tooth from the fissure to the root was manifestly channelled, which we first discovered by lightly pressing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUMS">gums</a>; we then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the poison ascend through the cavity of the fang and flow out of the fissure; and as these fangs are very acute, so firm and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> toward the point (the fissure being on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> and convex, not the internal side), nothing could be conceived more convenient either for infecting a wound, or to insure the infusion of the poison." Each of the fangs is surrounded with a vesicle furnished with glands secreting a certain fluid; which, upon the vesicle being pressed, seems to flow out of the point of the fang. The serpent when incensed, raising his head, extends the small bone armed with the fangs mentioned above; and attacking his enemy with a force combined of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of his body and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the muscles, he wounds him with the expanded fangs, and the vesicle being compressed the poison immediately flows into the wound: this is clear from the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> of those who, having broken off their fangs with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of forceps, handled the serpent thus disarmed without any hurt. And as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">North</a> Americans, after carefully extracting their venomous fangs, suffer the rattlesnake to bite and gnaw them with his teeth till the blood flows freely, with total impunity; it is certain those people are deceived who <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> the fatal effects of his bite to those harmless weapons. Poison. Antiquity amused itself with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> destitute of all appearance of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, that <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGER">anger</a> was excited by black bile: they applied this fiction without hesitation to the present subject, and founded an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a> upon it to account for the effects of the bite of an incensed serpent; pretending to have discovered an ideal canal which conducted the bile from its vehicle to the mouth of the serpent, whence it flowed into the part bitten, and produced the most fatal symptoms. But toward the end of the last century, this subject was greatly illustrated under the auspices of Ferdinand the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">Second</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>: This <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, desirous of inquiring into that mysterious question, the nature of serpents, invited Steno, Rhedi, and some other philosophers of the first eminence, to his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>; and a multitude of the most poisonous serpents being collected, Rhedi made several experiments upon them, which discovered to him a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of particulars before unknown; of which the following seem to have the best claim to our attention. When he either caused a living viper to bite a dog, or wounded him with the teeth of one newly dead (the poisonous vesicle remaining unbroken), the event was the same. If the bite was repeated, its effect became weaker, and at last was lost, the poison contained in the vesicle being totally exhausted. That the teeth of serpents, when extended to bite, were moistened over with a certain liquor; and when the vesicle at the base was pressed, a drop of poison flowed to the point of the fang. When the poison thus flowing from the vesicle was received in soft <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> or a sponge, an animal bitten by the serpent received no more harm from the wound than from being pricked by a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a>, till after a few days, when the venom was restored afresh: but when an animal was wounded with the point of a needle dipped in the poison, it was tormented with the same pains as if it had been bitten by the viper itself. Preserving some of this poison in a glass, and totally evaporating the moisture in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, when the residuum was diluted again with water, and the point of a needle dipped in the solution, Rhedi found to his great surprize that it had the same effect as when recent. But the boldness of Tozzi, one who charmed vipers, flung all these men who were deeply versed in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY">natural <a class="</a>xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> into the utmost astonishment; they happening to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into discourse (while the prince was present) upon the certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> which would attend any person's swallowing this poison of the viper by mistake, instead of spirit of wine or water; Tozzi, confiding in his art, drank a considerable portion of it without hesitation: they were all astonished at his apparent rashness, and predicted instant death to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>; however, he escaped as safely as if he had drunk only so much water. This event, which struck the prince and his illustrious associates in these philosophical inquiries by its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a>, was well known to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. Lucan, in the 9th book of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHARSALIA">Pharsalia</a>, speaking of the serpent, says, Novia serpentum est admitti sanguine positis <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MORS">Mors</a> virus habet, et fatum dente minatur, Pocula morte careant. Phar. l. 9, v. 614. Mixed with the blood that venom flows alone, His bite is poison, death is in his fang; Yet is the draught innocuous. Nor must we omit observing, that barbarous nations are perfectly acquainted with the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of the poi- son of serpents by which it retains its deadly power after it has been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> kept: they have been possessed of this fatal secret for ages past; it being their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> to tinge the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of their arrows with the juice of spurge, putrid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, but more particularly with the poison of vipers. Some <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Indians continue the practice to this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>; and we have the testimony of Pliny, in his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY">Natural <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, that the Scythians had long ago the same custom: "The Scythians (says that author) dip their arrows in the poison of vipers and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> blood; a horrid practice, as the slightest wound inflicted by one of them defies all the art of medicine." While Rhedi and his associates were thus busied in Tuscany in tracing the footsteps of nature closely and successfully under the guidance of experiment, the philosophers of other countries amused themselves with forming new conjectures and fictions. In France, Moses Charas, first surgeon to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>, a man of considerable reputation, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> upon the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of serpents, endeavoured with all his weight to prove their poison "to consist in heated animal-spirits, and therefore that it is impossible for a viper to give a deadly wound unless it had been before incensed." We shall not go about to deny, that the mental affections can <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENERATE">generate</a> something similar to a poison. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a> of a man in anger, changed to a sallow <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, indicates something like it: men struck with a sudden terror frequently turn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a>, and the humours lodged in the intestinal canal are evacuated by a diarrhoea. But this is evidently discovered in nurses, whose <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILK">milk</a> becomes poisonous when they are greatly irritated; and if it be then taken by a child, provokes a diarrhoea, which frequently terminates fatally. But however this may be, the hypothesis of Charas can receive but little support from it; as that vague doctrine of animal spirits and their irritation, however it might afford a commodious and decent retreat to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> formerly, is now suffered to subside in a very undisturbed oblivion. Bite. The symptoms that attend the bite of the viper are a smarting in the part wounded, as if it were continually pricked with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEEDLES">needles</a>; swelling, paleness, flapping of the eyes, tears, horror with coldness; a weak <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>, afterwards becoming unequal; thirst, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a> sweat, pain in the reins, diarrhoea with griping and vomiting, difficulty of breathing, drowsiness, and convulsions which terminate in death. We are ignorant of what species the hemorrhoid was, which is described by Lucan as causing by its bite a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLUX">flux</a> of blood from every part of the body. But the bite of an American serpent named de la crux kills in the same manner. The dipsas is at present likewise unknown. Lucan informs us, that the person wounded by it was attacked by an unquenchable thirst. This is finely painted by him; where A. Tuscus, standard-bearer of Cato, is described as bitten by that serpent: Non decus imperii, non magis <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JURA">jura</a> Catonis Ardentem tenere virum, quin furgere signa Audaret, totifuge furens exquireret agris Quas polcebat aquas sitiens in corde venenum. Pharsal. I. 9. His wild impatience, not his honoured state, Nor sorrowing Cato's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> command, restrain; Furious, dishonoured in the dust, he flings His sacred eagle, and o'er all the fields Rapid he bursts to seek the cooling stream, To quench the thirsty poison in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>. And a few verses after: Scrutatur venas penitus squalantis arenae Nunc redit <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> Syrtes, et flactus accipit ore, Aquoreaque placet, sed non sibi sufficit humor, Nec semel simulque genus, mortemque venit, Sed pulsat effe stimi; ferroque aperire tumentes Sublinit venarum, atque implere cruore. Now tearing up the sands, some latent vein Frustate he seeks; now to the Syrtes shore Return'd, he swallows down the briny <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a> Mixed with its rolling sands; nor knows his fate And the foul poison's death, but calls it thirst; Then with his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> opens his spouting veins, And drinks the bursting blood. In the monuments of antiquity we find three species of asps. 1. The phytas, with a callous caruncle on its forehead; its colour is cinereous, with a shining green. 2. The chersea, is very long, cinereous, inclining to green; its eyes <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>. 3. The chelidonia is black, with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> belly; its bite is said to produce two or three hiccoughs, change of colour, stupor, cold, and sleep with palpitation. Upon a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of what these authors have written upon these asps, it seems probable that the phytas, which kills by bringing on a lethargic sleepiness, is the same serpent which obtained the specific name of the aspis among the ancients, and that it is the nintipolonga Zeylanica of Bionius and Ray, and the Amodytes of Linnaeus. The phytas seems to have been the serpent made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of by Cleopatra to destroy herself. This woman, to terminate a distipated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> with an easy death, ordered her physicians to prepare a poison for her which might best effect this purpose. They having tried a number of different experiments upon condemned criminals, at last discovered this species of asp, which brings on death without any previous appearance of distemper or hiccup: the face seems in a slight perspiration, an easy insensibility and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETHARGY">lethargy</a> creeps upon the whole frame, and the person bitten seems almost totally ignorant of his approaching <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a>. Having acquainted the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> with their discovery, she applied the asp either to her bosom or her arms; or, according to some authors, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIPPING">dipping</a> the point of a needle in the poison, and prick ing herself with it, she expired in an easy sleep. Most of the colubri are poisonous, and perhaps all the crotali: among these are reckoned Viper, Mysterizans, Berus, Leberis, Lebetinus, Prester, or black viper, Naja, Stolatus, Dipsas, Niveus, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATROPOS">Atropos</a>, Amodytes, Chersea, Aspis, Severus, Laeetus, Atrox, Corallinus. The bite of the naja is so fatal, that a man dies by it in the space of an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, his flesh entirely falling off his bones in a semi-dissolved putrid state: this makes it probable that it is the same serpent which the ancients named the sepe. It is not necessary to enumerate rate anymore, though a number of different species might be mentioned; whole poisons all produced different effects: yet with this diversity, according to Rhedi, they all agree in one particular circumstance, that their venom is not fatal unless introduced into the blood externally. The experiments of Rhedi have not, however, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of some celebrated philosophers, so far cleared the theory of the operation of the poison of the viper, as to leave nothing further to be desired upon that subject. Fontana and Carminati have endeavoured to investigate its operations more clearly. Carminati, from eleven experiments, deduces the following conclusions. 1. That if poison be infilled into a nerve, the animal wounded dies almost instantly; and the whole nervous system, to which it is rapidly conveyed, is deprived of its quality called <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol17.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a>. 2. If a muscle be wounded, it is deprived of its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IRRITABILITY">irritability</a>. This is confirmed by the experiments of Fontana. 3. The poison injected into a wounded muscle or tendon is considerably longer in killing an animal than that introduced into a nerve. 4. The symptoms which precede the death of the animal bitten are, a stupor, lethargy, tremors, convulsions, paralysis of the legs (part wounded), entire dissolution of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a>. The blood is not always coagulated, nor its crisis dissolved. Marks of inflammation are sometimes discovered in certain parts of the animal after death, sometimes not: these are the effects of spasms and convulsions, not of the poison. 5. Not the least sign of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JAUNDICE">jaundice</a> was discoverable in the eyes of any of the animals upon which Carminati made his experiments. 6. The stomach in every one of them was very much inflated; a symptom remarked only by Fallopius and Albertini. 7. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGATURE">ligature</a> applied instantly above the part bitten, if it be so placed as to admit one, was found by some experiments a good preventative against the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFUSION">diffusion</a> of the poison: its compression should be considerable, but not excessive. Cure. It would be endless to attempt to relate all those antidotes which men, compelled by so fatal a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>, have employed against the bite of serpents. We shall confine ourselves only to such as are recommended by the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> of use. The first in point of antiquity, and which recommends itself also to us by its certainty, is to draw the venom out of the wounded part as quickly as possible. This has been attempted by different methods. The most <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> is sucking it out by the mouth; yet the utmost precaution is necessary in the person who performs this operation, that his mouth be perfectly free from the scurvy, and that the skin of the fauces be entirely unbroken; lest he should incur an equal hazard, or perhaps a greater, as the poison must attack a nobler part. Therefore, as the operation is nauseous and full of danger, it will be better to scarify the part with the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>, that the infected blood may have a freer <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EXIT">exit</a> from the opened mouths of the vessels, and to apply a large cupping-glass, by means of which the remaining venom may be extracted; then to foment the part with warm emollient applications, joined with some spirit, as the spirit of sal ammoniac or theriacum; if these be not at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, apply <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOAP">soap</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a> to the wound: the patient may take sudorific and exciting medicines internally, by which is meant emetics or ippecacuanha; and the stronger sudorifics are exhibited with great success. But the present age has added antidotes of three different species to counteract the most vehement effects of this poison, of which <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, has each furnished us with one. 1. Among the Europeans, there has been a strong predilection in favour of the oil of olives, or any other expressed oil: this is directed to be drunk plentifully by the patient, to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of half a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POUND">pound</a> or more, while the wounded part is copiously bathed by Amaranthites. Very full accounts of the happy effects of this treatment are inserted in the Philosophical Transactions of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of the Academy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. We are so far from detracting from the merits of this medicine, that we think it specific against the bite of the common and black viper; yet we must add, that the nature of this antidote is not yet thoroughly investigated and understood, and that we dare not pronounce <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> upon its efficacy and use in every single and particular <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>. Linnaeus, being in Scania, was applied to by a woman who was bitten by the cobra; and notwithstanding he caused her to drink this oil according to the prescribed forms, she nevertheless expired in the greatest agonies. May not this oil fail when applied against the bite of some of the European species of serpents? or is there not some necessary observations omitted in the formula delivered, either respecting the medicine or the patient? This we leave and strongly recommend to the experience of others to determine. 2. Let us now proceed to the American antidotes; of which the powder of the fenega root deservedly claims the first <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. The use of this root has been known to the natives of the woods of North America for many ages past. Its effects against the bite of the rattlesnake almost exceed all <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a>; but the invidious prejudices of those barbarians preferred this secret with so obstinate a silence, that no bribe could purchase it from them, until Tennent happily discovered and published it for the benefit of mankind. He tells us, that the root of the polygala fenega never fails of success unless where some large vessel is wounded, when the medicine has not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> to counteract the rapid progress of the violence of the poison. Upon this subject the reader may consult the Dissertation upon this plant in the second volume of the Amenitates Academicae. A maid-errant at Upsal was bitten by a serpent upon a very dangerous place. The most dreadful symptoms followed the bite, and such as demanded the application of the most decisive remedies. Two dolcs of the powder of this root was attended with so good an effect, that in two days she was almost completely recovered. Beside this root, the Americans have many other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> which they apply upon the same occasion; as the eryngium fetidum, or American fetid eryngo aquaticum, or Virginian aquatic <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DITTO">ditto</a>; veratrum luteum, or Virginian <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>-flowered veratrum; aletris sarinofa, or floridan aletris; uvularia perfoliata, or Virginian perfoliate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-UVULA">uvula</a>; fanicula canadensis, or Canadian fanicle; and the aritlochia serpentaria, or Virginian snake-root: but we shall dismiss these, with a long catalogue of others whose virtues are not yet well known to us. 3. We come now to another antidote of equal celebrity, that made use of by the Asiatics, which is of the greatest antiquity among the Indians, the ophiorrhiza mungos, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> ophiorrhiza. Kæmpfer has given us the history of this plant and its unequalled virtues against the bite of the coluber naja, or cobra di capello. We shall only hint, that as the efficacy of this medicine is so great, it would be much safer to introduce that, or the true lignum colubrinum, instead of the strychnos colubrina, or Indian strychnos, into general practice, whose use, if it have any, is extremely ambiguous. The snake-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, called the pedra de cobras di capello (as if it were a stone extracted from the head of the coluber naja) is very famous throughout all India, and is extolled by Garzia, Kircher, and others, as a specific against the bite of serpents. It is pretended, that if it be applied to a poisoned wound, and suffered to remain upon it until it fall off of itself, that it will extract all the venom. But its use has been suspected by many; nor did it succeed with Rhedi, who tried a variety of experiments with it. Many have been of opinion that the stone is <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a>, and nothing more than the calcined <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HART">hart</a>. See PSYLLI, (Encycl.)

SHELLS

Pages 1230-1231

POLISHING OF. This is an art of no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> standing in the world in its present perfection; and as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-shells is become so <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> among us, it may not be disagreeable to the reader to find some instructions in executing so pleasing a method of adding to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, the rules for which are at present so little known, though the effect of them be so much esteemed. Among the immense variety of shells which we are acquainted with, some are taken up out of the sea, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> found on its shores in all their perfection and beauty; their colours being all spread by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> upon the surface, and their natural polish superior to anything that art could give. Where nature is in herself thus perfect, it were madness to attempt to add any thing to her charms: but in others, where the beauties are latent and covered with a coarser outer skin, art is to be called in; and the outer veil being taken off, all the internal beauties appear. Among the shells which are found naturally polished are, the porcelains, or cowries; the casanders; the dolia, or conchæ globosæ; or tuns; some buccina, the volute, and the cylinders, or olives, or, as they are generally though improperly called, the rhombi; excepting only two or three, as the tiara, the plumb, and the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>-tub rhombus, where there is an unpolishing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FILM">film</a> on the surface, hiding a very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> share of beauty within. Though the generality of the shells of these genera are taken out of the sea in all their beauty, and in their utmost natural polish, there are several other genera, in which all or most of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> are taken up naturally rough and foul, and covered with an epidermis, or coarse outer skin, which is in many rough and downy or hairy. The tellinæ, the mussels, the cochleæ, and many others, are of this kind. The more nice collectors, as naturalists, insist upon having all their shells in their native and genuine appearance, as they are found when living at sea; but the ladies, who make collections, hate the disagreeable outsides, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> have all such polished. It would be very advisable, however, for both kinds of collectors to have the same shells in different specimens, both rough and polished: the naturalist would by this means, besides knowing the outside of the shell, be better acquainted with its internal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> than he otherwise could be, and the lady would have a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> in comparing the beauties of the shell, in its wrought state, to its coarse appearance as nature gives it. How many elegancies in this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> must be wholly lost to us, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it were not for the affluence of an art of this kind! Many shells in their native state are like rough diamonds, and we can form no <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> idea of their beauties till they have been polished and wrought into form. Though the art of polishing shells is a very valuable one, yet it is very dangerous to the shells; for without the utmost care, the means used to polish and beautify a shell often wholly destroy it. When a shell is to be polished, the first thing to be examined is whether it have naturally a smooth surface, or be covered with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TUBERCLES">tubercles</a> or prominences. A shell which has a smooth surface, and a natural dull polish, need only be rubbed with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, or with a piece of chamoy <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, with some <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRIPOLI">tripoli</a>, or fine rotten <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and will become of a perfectly bright and fine polish. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMERY">Emery</a> is not to be used on this occasion, because it wears away too much of the shell. This operation requires the hand of an experienced person, that knows how superficial the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> must be, and where he is to stop; for in many of these shells the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> are only on the surface, and the wearing away ever so little of the shell defaces them. A shell that is rough, foul, and crusty, or covered with a tartarous coat, must be left a whole <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> steeping in hot <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>: when it has imbibed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of this, it is to be rubbed with rough emery on a stick, or with the blade of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>, in order to get off the coat. After this, it may be dipped in diluted aquafortis, spirit of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, or any other acid; and after remaining a few moments in it, be again plunged into common water. This will add greatly to the speed of the work. After this it is to be well rubbed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> cloths, impregnated with common <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>; and when by these several means it is made perfectly clean, the polishing is to be finished with fine emery and a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a>. If after this the shell when dry appears not to have so good a polish as was desired, it must be rubbed over with a solution of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUM">gum</a> arabic; and this will add greatly to its glofs, without doing it any sort of injury. The gum-water must not be too thick, and then it gives no sensible coat, only heightening the colours. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EGG">egg</a> answers this purpose also very well; but it is subject to turn <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>. If the shell has an epidermis, which will by no means admit the polishing of it, it is to be dipped several times in diluted aquafortis, that this may be eaten off; and then the shell is to be polished in the usual way with putty, fine emery, or tripoli, on the hair of a fine brush. When it is only a pellicle that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a> the colours, the shells must be steeped in hot water, and after that the skin worked off by degrees with an old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FILE">file</a>. This is the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> with several of the cylinders, which have not the natural polish of the rest. When a shell is covered with a thick and fatty epidermis, as is the case with several of the mussels and tellinæ; in this case aquafortis will do no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, as it will not touch the skin; then a rough brush and coarse emery are to be used; and if this does not succeed, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>-skin, or, as the workmen call it, fibreskin and pumice-stone, are to be employed. When a shell has a thick crust, which will not give way to any of these means, the only way left is to plunge it several times into strong aquafortis, till the stubborn crust is wholly eroded. The limpets, auris marina, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HELMET">helmet</a>-shells, and several other species of this kind, must have this sort of management; but as the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> is to show the hidden beauties under the crust, and not to destroy the natural beauty and polish of the inside of the shell, the method of using the aquafortis must be this: A long piece of wax must be provided, and one end of it made perfectly to cover the whole mouth of the shell; the other end will then serve as a handle, and the mouth being stopped by the wax, the liquor cannot get in to the inside to spoil it; then there must be placed on a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TABLE">table</a> a vessel full of aquafortis, and another full of common water. The shell is to be plunged into the aquafortis; and after remaining a few minutes in it, is to be taken out, and plunged into the common water. The progress the aquafortis makes in eroding the surface is thus to be carefully observed every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> it is taken out; the point of the shell, and any other tender parts, are to be covered with wax, to prevent the aquafortis from eating them away; and if there be any worm-holes, they also must be flopped up with wax, otherwise the aquafortis would soon eat through in those places. When the repeated dippings into the aquafortis show that the coat is sufficiently eaten away, then the shell is to be wrought carefully with fine emery and a brush; and when it is polished as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> as can be by this means, it must be wiped clean, and rubbed over with gum-water or the white of an egg. In this sort of work the operator must always have the caution to wear gloves; otherwise the least touch of the aquafortis will burn the fingers, and turn them yellow; and often, if it be not regarded, will eat off the skin and the nails. These are the methods to be used with shells which require but a moderate quantity of the surface to be taken off; but there are others which require to have a larger quantity taken off, and to be uncovered deeper: this is called entirely sealing a shell. This is done by means of an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> wheel of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> or tin, impregnated with rough emery; and the shell is wrought <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in the same manner in which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a> are wrought by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAPIDARY">lapidary</a>. Nothing is more difficult, however, than the performing this work with nicety: very often shells are cut down too far by it, and wholly spoiled; and to avoid this, a coarse vein must be often left standing in some <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and taken down afterwards with the file, when the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> it down at the wheel would have spoiled the adjacent parts. After the shell is thus cut down to a proper <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, it is to be polished with fine emery, tripoli, or rotten stone, with a wooden wheel turned by the same machine as the leaden one, or by the common method of working with the hand with the same ingredients. When a shell is full of tubercles, or protuberances, which must be preserved, it is then impossible to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the wheel; and if the common way of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIPPING">dipping</a> into aquafortis be attempted, the tubercles being harder than the rest of the shell, will be eaten through before the rest is sufficiently scaled, and the shell will be spoiled: in this case industry and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol14.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a> are the only means of effecting a polish. A camel's-hair <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> must be dipped in aquafortis; and with this the intermediate parts of the shell must be wetted, leaving the protuberances dry: this is to be often repeated; and after a few moments the shell is always to be plunged into water to stop the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EROSION">erosion</a> of the acid, which would otherwise eat too deep, and destroy the beauty of the shell. When this has sufficiently taken off the foulness of the shell, it is to be polished with emery of the finest kind, or with tripoli, by means of a small stick, or the common polishing stone used by the goldsmiths may be used. This is a very tedious and troublesome thing, especially when the echinated oysters and murices, and some other such shells, are to be wrought: and what is worst of all is, that when all this labour has been employed, the business is not well done; for there still remains several places which could not be reached by any <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, so that the shell must necessarily be rubbed over with gum-water or the white of an egg afterwards in order to bring out the colours and give a gloss; in some <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> it is even necessary to give a coat of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a>.

SHERIDAN

Pages 1232-1232

wife to Thomas Sheridan, M.A., was born in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> about the year 1724, but descended from a good English family which had removed thither. Her maiden name was Chamberlaine, and she was <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Sir Oliver Chamberlaine. The first literary performance by which she distinguished herself was a little pamphlet at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of a violent party-dispute relative to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, in which Mr Sheridan had newly embarked his fortune. So well-timed a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> exciting the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of Mr Sheridan, he by an accident discovered his fair patroness, to whom he was soon afterwards married. She was a person of the most amiable character in every relation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, with the most engaging manners. After lingering some years in a very weak state of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, she died at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BLOIS">Blois</a>, in the south of France, in the year 1767. Her "<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-SYDNEY">Sydney</a> Biddulph" may be ranked with the first productions of that class in ours <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> in any other <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. She also wrote a little <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROMANCE">romance</a> in one volume, called Noujahad, in which there is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of imagination productive of an admirable moral. And she was the author of two comedies, "The Discovery" and "The Dupe."

SIDUS

Pages 1232-1233

GEORGIIUM, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, a new primary planet, discovered by William Herschel, Esq.; of Bath, in the year 1781, for which he obtained from the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> the honorary recompence of Sir Godfrey Copley's medal; and so called in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of his majesty <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> George III. who has taken Mr Herschel under his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a>, and granted to him an annual salary. "From many calculations of our best..." astronomers and mathematicians, says Mr Herschel, I have collected the following particulars, as most to be depended upon. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">Place</a> of the node - $2^\circ 11' 49'' 30''$ Inclination of the orbit - $43' 35''$ Place of the perihelion - $172^\circ 13' 17''$ <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">Time</a> of the perihelion passage Sep. 7, 1799 Eccentricity of the orbit - $0.82034$ Half the greater axis - $19,079,04$ Revolution - $8,333,64$ sidereal years. From my own observations on this planet's apparent diameter, which I have found cannot well be less than $4''$, nor indeed much greater, we infer that its real diameter is to that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> as $4,454$ to $1$; and hence it appears to be of very considerable bulk, and, except <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, by far the largest of the remaining <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> is of a bluish-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and in brilliancy between that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">Moon</a> and of Venus. With a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TELESCOPE">telescope</a> which magnifies about 300 times, it appears to have a very well-defined visible disk; but with instruments of a small power, it can hardly be distinguished from a fixed <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STAR">star</a> of between the sixth and seventh magnitude. In a very fine clear night, when the moon is absent, it may also be seen by the naked eye.*

SIGHING

Pages 1233-1233

an effort of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, by which the lungs are put into greater <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, and more dilated, so that the blood passes more freely, and in greater <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, to the left auricle, and thence to the ventricle. Hence we learn, says Dr Hales, how sighing increases the force of the blood, and consequently proportionably cheers and relieves nature, when oppresed by its too slow motion, which is the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> of those who are dejected and sad.

SILK

Pages 1233-1236

sericum, a very soft, fine, bright, delicate thread; the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> of an insect, called bombyx <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> the silk-worm. See Silk, (Encycl.) The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> were but little acquainted with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> and manufacture of silk; they took it for the work of a sort of spider, or beetle, who spun it out of its entrails, and wound it with its feet about the little branches of trees. This insect they called fer, from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERES">Seres</a>, a people in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SCYTHIA">Scythia</a>, whom we now call the Chinese, who, as they thought, bred it; whence the silk itself they called sericum. But this fer of theirs has very little <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> with our silk-worm, bombyx; the former living five years; but the latter dying annually, enveloped in a yellowish bag, or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALL">ball</a>, which, wound out into little threads, makes what we call silk. It was in the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Cos that the art of manufacturing silk was first invented; and Pamphila, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Platus, is honoured as the inventress. The discovery was not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> unknown to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. Silk was brought them from Serica, where the worm was a native. But so far were they from profiting by the discovery, that they could not be induced to believe so fine a thread should be the work of a worm, and thereupon formed a thousand chimerical conjectures of their own. Silk was a very scarce commodity among them for many ages; it was even sold <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> for weight with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, insomuch that Vopiscus tells us, the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Aurelian, who died A.D. 275, refused the empress, his wife a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> of silk, which she solicited of him with much earnestness, merely on account of its dearth. Others, however, with greater <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, assert that it was known at Rome so early as the reign of Tiberius, about A.D. 17. Galen, who lived about the year of our <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> 173, speaks of the rarity of silk; being nowhere but at Rome, and only among the rich. Heliogabalus, the emperor, who died A.D. 220, is said by some to be the first person who wore a holosericum, i.e. a garment of all silk. The Greeks of Alexander the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> are said to have been the first who brought wrought silk from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> into <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, about 323 years before Christ; but the manufacture of it was confined to Berytus and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TYRE">Tyre</a>, in Phoenicia, whence it was dispersed over the West. At length, two monks, coming from the Indies to Constantinople, in 555, under the encouragement of the emperor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a>, brought with them great quantities of silk-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>, with instructions for the hatching of their eggs, rearing and feeding the worms, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> out the silk, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a> and working it. Upon this, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> were set up at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, Thebes, and Corinth. The Venetians, soon after this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, commencing a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> with the Greek empire, supplied all the western parts of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> with silks for many centuries; though sundry kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> silk manufactures were unknown in those times, such as damasks, velvets, fustians, &c. About 1130, Roger II. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a> established a silk-manufactory at Palermo, and another in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a>; managed by workmen, who were a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the plunder brought from Athens, Corinth, &c. whereof that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> made a conquest in his expedition to the Holy <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">Land</a>. By degrees, Mezeray adds, the rest of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> learned, from the Sicilians and Calabrians, the management of the silk-worms, and the working of silk; and at length the French got it by <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of neighbourhood, a little before the reign of Francis I. and began to imitate them. Thuanus, indeed, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> to most other writers, makes this manufacture of silk to be introduced into Sicily 200 years later, by Robert the Wise, king of Sicily, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of Provence. It appears, by 33 Henry VI. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 5, that there was a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of silk-women in England so early as the year 1455. But these were probably employed in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a>-works of silk and thread; and we find that various sorts of small haberdashery of silk were manufactured here in 1482: but Italy supplied England, and all other parts, with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> manufacture, till the year 1489. In Spain, indeed, the culture and manufacture of silk seem to have been introduced in an early <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> by the Moors, particularly in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MURCIA">Murcia</a>, Cordova, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRANADA">Granada</a>. The silk manufactures of this last town were very flourishing, when it was taken by Ferdinand, &c. at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the 15th century. In 1521, the French, being supplied with workmen from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, commenced a silk manufacture; but it was long after this time before they could obtain raw silk from the worms: and, even in the year 1547, silk was scarce and dear in France; and Henry II. is said to have been the first who wore a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of silk knit stockings, though the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> originally came from Spain, whence silk stockings were brought over to Henry VIII. and Edward VI. After the civil wars, in France, the plantations of mulberry-trees were greatly encouraged by Henry IV. and his successors; and the produce of silk is at this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> very considerable. The great advantage which the new manufacture afforded, made our king James I. very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> for its being introduced into England: accordingly, it was recommended several times from the throne, and in the most earnest terms, particularly in the year 1608, to plant mulberry-trees, &c. for the propagation of silk-worms, but unhappily without effect; though, from the various experiments we meet with in the Philosophical Transactions, and other places, it appears that the silk-worm thrives and works as well, in all respects, in England as in any other part of Europe. However, towards the latter end of this king's reign, i.e. about the year 1620, the broad-silk manufacture was introduced into this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and prosecuted with great vigour and advantage. In 1629, the silk manufacture was become so considerable in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, that the silk-throwsters of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CITY">city</a> and parts adjacent were incorporated under the name of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, wardens, &c. of the silk-throwsters; and in 1661, this company of silk-throwsters employed about 40,000 persons. The revocation of the edict of Nantes, in 1685, contributed in a great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> to promote the silk manufacture in this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>; as did also the invention of the silk-throwing machine at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DERBY">Derby</a>, in 1719.—So <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> in reputation was the English silk manufacture, that even in Italy, as Keyser informs us, in 1730, the English silks bore a higher price than the Italian. Silk, Raw, is that taken from the ball, without fire, and wound without any coction: such as is molt, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not all, that is brought into England from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>; i.e. from Persia by the way of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>, from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, and from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-CHINA">China</a>. The raw silk is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> worked up into two sorts, called organzine and tram. The former is made by giving a throw or twist to each thread of raw silk singly, and then doubling two of these twisted threads together, and twisting them smartly together: this forms the length or warp of a piece when manufactured.
