The tram, or shoot, which makes the breadth of the piece, is formed by twisting two or more threads of raw silk flack. The wafted silk, or refuse in reeling, &c. is collected, carded, and spun, and called <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLAX">flax</a> silk; this is doubled and thrown, and often made into a cheap sort of silk stockings, which are very strong and durable. In the French silk-works, the greatest part of this raw silk passes for little better than a kind of fine floretta; yet, when spun, it makes a bright thread, and serves for the manufacture of stuffs of moderate value and lustre. But the raw silks of the Levant, whence most of ours come, are exceeding fine and beautiful. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> arises hence, that, in France, the best balls are spun and wound in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and only the refuse made into raw silk; whereas, in the Levant, there is no such thing as spinning or winding on the fire, but the silks are all sent in bales, or packs, as they are drawn from off the balls; so that they are only distinguished by their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of fine, middling, and coarse. Silk, Boiled, is that which has been boiled in water, to facilitate the spinning and winding. This is the finest of all the sorts of silk manufactured in France, and is seldom used but in the richest stuffs, as velvets, taffetas, damasks, brocades, &c. There is also another kind of boiled silk, which is prepared by boiling, to be milled, and which cannot receive that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> without being first passed through hot water. By the laws of France, it is prohibited to mix raw with boiled silk; both as such a practice spoils the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a>, and as the raw silk corrupts and cuts the boiled. Silks, Threwed or Twisted, are such as, before their spinning and winding, have received their milling or throwing. This they receive in a different degree, as they are passed oftener or feldomer over the mill; properly, however, throwed silks are those wherein the threads are pretty thick throwed, and twisted several times. The thrown silk comes to us chiefly from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEGHORN">Leghorn</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and Messina. Silks, Slack, are such as are not twisted, but are prepared, and dyed, for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a>, and other works with the needle. Silk, Eastern or East <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a>. That popularly thus called is not the work of the silk-worms, but comes from a plant that produces it, in pods, much like those of the cotton-tree. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> this pod contains is extremely <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, fine, and moderately glossy: it spins easily, and is made into a kind of silk that enters the manufacture of several Indian and Chinese stuffs. Silks, French. It is only in the most southern provinces of France that silk is cultivated, mulberry-trees planted, and worms bred. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> places are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>, Dauphine, Provence, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AVIGNON">Avignon</a>, Savoy, and Lyons. This last <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, indeed, furnishes very few silks of its own growth; but it is the great staple whence the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and the other cities, are to fetch them. At least, they are obliged to have them <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through Lyons, if they bring them from other places, either by land or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. There have been computed to enter Lyons, communibus annis, 6000 bales, the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALE">bale</a> valued at 160 pounds weight; of which 6000 bales there are 1400 from the Levant, 1600 from Sicily, 1500 from Italy, 300 from Spain, and 1200 from Languedoc, Provence, and Dauphine. At the time when the manufactures of Lyons were in their prosperity, there were reckoned to be 18000 looms employed in the silk manufacture; but in 1698 there were not reckoned 4000. However, this manufacture has revived of late, and a great part of Europe has been supplied from thence with <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BROCADE">brocade</a> and rich silks. The decay has not been less notable at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TOURS">Tours</a>: they had formerly there 800 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a> for winding and preparing the silks, 8000 looms to weave them, and 40,000 persons employed in the preparation and manufacturing thereof; but these have been reduced to 70 mills, 1200 looms, and about 4000 persons. Silks, Sicilian. The commerce of the silks of Sicily is very considerable: and the Florentines, Genoese, and Lucceese, are the people who chiefly make it. Great quantities are yearly brought thence, especially from Messina: part whereof they use in their own manufactures, and sell the rest to their neighbours, the French, &c. with profit. The Italians have this advantage, especially the Genoese, over other people, that, that, having larger establishments in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, they are reputed as natives, and pay no duty for the export. Part of the Sicilian silks are raw; the rest are spun and milled; of which last kind, those of St Lucia and Messina are the most valued. The raw unwrought silks are always sold for ready <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a>; the others, sometimes, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> for other goods. Silks, Italian. The silks brought from Italy are partly wrought, and partly raw and unwrought. Milan, Parma, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LUCCA">Lucca</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODENA">Modena</a>, furnish none but the latter kind; Genoa most of the former; <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a> affords both kinds. The finest Italian wrought silk comes from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NOVI">Novi</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BERGAMO">Bergamo</a>, and Bologna; and is imported into England from the ports of Nice, Genoa, and Leghorn. The silk we have from Italy is generally thrown, and serves for warp for our manufactures; and the greater part we import from Piedmont, at an annual expense of no less than 200,000l. and in general at the price of 20s. for every <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POUND">pound</a>. And the king of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>, it is said, hath prohibited the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> of raw silk out of his dominions; though the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> are open in other parts of Italy. Silks, Spanish, are all raw; and are spun, milled, &c. in England, according to the several works they are to be used in. Silks, Turkish, are all raw. One advantage we have in the commerce of the Levant, in silks, wanting in those of Sicily, is, that the latter are confined to a particular season of the year; whereas the former are bought at all times. They are brought from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEPPO">Aleppo</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRIPOLI">Tripoli</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SMYRNA">Smyrna</a>, and from the isle of Cyprus, Candia, &c. But the principal place of commerce, especially for the silks of Persia, is Smyrna. The silks are brought hither in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARAVANS">caravans</a>, from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> to September. The caravans in January are loaded with the finest silks; those of February and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">March</a> bring indifferent ones; the rest, the coarsest. They all come from the several provinces of Persia, chiefly those of Ghilan and Shirvan, and the city of Schamachia, situate near the edge of the Caspian sea; from which three places, a Dutch author affirms us, there have not come less than 30,000 bales of silk in a year. Ghilan produces the best and greatest quantities of silk; next to this comes Shirvan and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ERIVAN">Erivan</a>, then Mazanderan, and lastly <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASTRABAD">Astrabad</a>; but the latter is much inferior, serving only for a manufacture mixed with cotton; that of Mazanderan and Astrabad is seldom or never exported. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARDEBIL">Ardebil</a>, or Ardabil, another city of Persia, not far distant from these silk countries, is the place where silks are laid up, and whence the caravans set out for Smyrna, Aleppo, Scanderoon, and Constantinople; and it is this city, with Schamachia, that have always been esteemed the centre of the silk trade; which has been several times attempted to be removed from Smyrna and the Mediterranean, in favour of Archangel, and the White-sea, by carrying them across Murov, by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-VOLGA">Volga</a> and Dwina, two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRAVERSE">traverse</a> the principal provinces of that vast empire. This new course of the Persian silks into Europe was first proposed by Paolo Centurio, a Genoese, to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CZAR">czar</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALEXIS">Alexis</a> Michael attempted the thing himself; but he was disappointed by the rebellion of the Cossacks, and the surprize of Astrakan. In 1688, the commerce of Persian silks had like to have been removed from Smyrna, by an earthquake, which almost overturned the whole city; and doubtless, the removal had been effected, but for the vigorous means used by the Turks to prevent it. Smyrna, however, still remains in her <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> possession; and the several nations of Europe continue every year to send their fleets to fetch away the silks; and matters are like to remain so, unless the conquests made by the late czar, along the Caspian sea, enable his successors, as it is certain he himself had such a thing in view, to put this trade into another channel. Silks, China, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a>, and Indian. Several provinces of China are so fertile in mulberry-trees, and their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> is so agreeable to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of silk-worms, that the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of silk there produced is incredible; the single <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Tchebiang might supply all China, and even a great part of Europe, with this commodity. The silks of this province are the most esteemed, though those of Nankin and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANTON">Canton</a> be excellent. The silk trade is the principal in China, and that which employs the most <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>; but the European merchants, who <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> in it, especially in wrought silks, are to be careful of the spinning, &c. the waste being usually very great, as the French East India company have found to their cost. In the year 1750, an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> was passed for repealing the duties payable on China raw silk, imported into this kingdom by the East India Company, and intitling such silk, upon exportation, to the same drawbacks and allowances with the raw silk of the produce of Italy. And another act was passed in 1752, for the farther encouragement of the British silk manufacture. Japan would not afford fewer silks than China; but that the Japanese, a barbarous and distrustful people, have interdicted all commerce with strangers, especially with Europeans, excepting with the Dutch; who are said to be admitted on certain impious terms, related by Tavernier, but which we must own we cannot <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>. The Dutch have endeavoured to vindicate themselves from these by the pens of several famous writers. The silks of the states of the Great Mogul are brought in great quantities from Cashem-bazaar, a midland place, whence they are conveyed by a canal of 15 leagues into the Ganges, by which they are forwarded 15 leagues farther, to the mouth of the famous river of Indofian. The silk of Cashem-bazaar is yellowish; as are also those of Peitia and Sicily; there being none, that we know of, naturally white, but that of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>. The Indians, however, whiten this with a ley, made of the ashes of a tree called <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a>'s fig-tree; but as this tree is pretty scarce, and they have not yet found any other that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> serve in its place, the Europeans are forced to take the greatest part of their silks in their native <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>. Cashem-bazaar alone is computed to furnish every year 22,000 bales of silk, each bale weighing 100 pounds; of which the Dutch are said to export 7000 bales annually. Great quantities of both raw and wrought silk are furnished by other parts of Bengal, and by several provinces of Indostan, which partly supply the natives, and afford a very considerable exportation to Europe. Several thousand bales of raw silk are annually imported from Bengal and China; some of which is, in this state, used for making princess-stuffs, but the greater part is prepared for the manufacturers by the silkthrowers. The duty on thrown silk imported is 5s. 1d \( \frac{1}{2} \); and the duty on raw silk, whether of the growth of Italy, Turkey, or India, is 1s. 4d \( \frac{1}{2} \) per pound. The quantity of Bengal and China raw silk imported in 1783, was 3636 Bengal bales, each bale weighing about 150 great pounds, and 1390 China bales, at about 145 small pounds per bale.

SKATING

Pages 1236-1236

an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> on <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ICE">ice</a>, both graceful and healthy. Although the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> were remarkable for their dexterity in most of the athletic sports, yet skating seems to have been unknown to them. It may be looked on, therefore, as a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>; and probably it derived its origin in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, where it naturally became habitual and necessary, not only as a graceful and elegant amusement, but as an expeditious <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of travelling when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> were frozen up during winter. In Holland <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> journeys are made upon skates with ease and expedition; but in general less <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> is there paid to graceful and elegant movements, than to the expedition and celerity of what is called journey skating. It is in those countries alone where it is considered as an amusement, that graceful attitudes and movements can be found; and there is no exercise whatever better calculated to set off the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> to advantage. The acquirement of most exercises may be attained at an advanced <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; but to become an expert skater, it is necessary to begin the practice of the art at a very early <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. It is difficult to reduce the art of skating to a system. It is principally by the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of a good skater, that a young practitioner can form his own practice. The English, though often remarkable for feats of agility upon skates, are very deficient in the article of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>; which is partly owing to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of the skates, which are too much curved in the surface which embraces the ice, consequently they involuntarily bring the users of them round on the outside upon a quick and small circle; whereas the skater, by using skates of a different construction, less curved, has the command of his stroke, and can enlarge <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> diminish the circle according to his own wish and desire. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of Scotland has produced more instances of elegant skaters, than perhaps any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> whatever; and the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> of a Skating Club about 40 years ago, has contributed not a little to the improvement of this elegant amusement. We are indebted for this article to a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of that Club, who has made the practice and improvement of skating his particular <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>; and as the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of our <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> not permit the insertion of a full treatise on skating, we shall give a few instructions which may be of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> towards the attainment of the art.—Those who wish to be proficient should begin at an early period of life; and should first endeavour to throw off the fear which always attends the commencement of an apparently hazardous amusement. They will soon acquire a facility of moving on the inside; and when they do so, they must endeavour to acquire the movement on the outside of the skates; which is nothing more than throwing themselves upon the outer edge of the skate, and making the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> of their body tend towards that side, which will necessarily enable them to form a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEMICIRCLE">semicircle</a>. In this, much assistance may be derived from placing a bag of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> in the pocket next to the foot employed in making the outside stroke, which will produce an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> poise of the body, which afterwards will become <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> by practice. At the commencement of the outside stroke, the knee of the employed limb should be a little bended, and gradually brought to a rectilineal position when the stroke is completed. When the practitioner becomes expert in forming the semicircle with both feet, he is then to join them together and proceed progressively and alternately with both feet, which will carry him forward with a graceful movement. Care should be taken to use very little muscular exertion, but that the impelling <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> should proceed from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> impulse of the body thrown into such a position as to regulate the stroke. At taking the outside stroke, the body ought to be easily thrown forward, the unemployed limb kept in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> line with the body, and the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FACE">face</a> and eyes directly looking forward: the unemployed foot ought to be stretched towards the ice, with the toes in a direct line with the leg. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> of making the curve, the body must be gradually, and almost imperceptibly, raised, and the unemployed limb brought in the same manner forward; so that, at finishing the curve, the body will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> a small <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> backward, and the unemployed foot will be about two inches before the other, ready to embrace the ice and form a correspondent curve. The muscular movement of the whole body must correspond with the movement of the skate, and should be regulated so as to be almost imperceptible to the spectators. Particular attention should be paid in carrying round the head and eyes with a regular and imperceptible motion; for nothing so much diminishes the grace and elegance of skating as sudden jerks and exertions, which are too frequently used by the generality of skaters. The management of the arms likewise deserves attention. There is no mode of disposing of them more gracefully in skating outside, than folding the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> into each other, or using a muff. There are various feats of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> and manoeuvres used upon skates; but they are so various as to render their insertion too tedious. Moving on the outside is the primary object for a skater to attain; and when he becomes an adept in that, he will easily acquire a facility in executing other branches of the art. There are few exercises but will afford him hints of elegant and graceful attitudes. For example, nothing can be more beautiful than the attitude of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> the bow and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARROW">arrow</a> whilst the skater is making a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> circle on the outside: the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MANUAL">manual</a> exercise and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> salutes have likewise a pretty effect when used by an expert skater.

SOLANDER

Pages 1236-1237

was a native of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, and educated at the university of Upsal, where he obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a> of Medicine. That of Doctor of Laws was afterwards conferred upon him by the university of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. Dr Solander's strong propensity for the pursuit of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> knowledge was probably probably not a little increased by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> and encouragement of his preceptor the celebrated Sir <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Linnæus; while the zeal which he showed for these branches of literature, particularly for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, conciliated the esteem and affection of that eminent professor. When Dr Solander went from Upsal to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in the prosecution of his studies, Linnæus furnished him with introductory letters to those learned men who were his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> correspondents in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. In these letters, among other strong expressions of regard, he is said to have employed the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>: *Omnium discipulorum, quos unquam habui, dilectissimus.* The footing thus obtained, Dr Solander soon improved by agreeable manners and extensive knowledge. In no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> he contracted intimacies with the most eminent philosophers in London, particularly with Sir <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Banks, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> and one of the first literary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. He was the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> of Sir Joseph in those different voyages which he made for the sole purpose of extending natural knowledge, and which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> do immortal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of both. When he was not thus engaged, his time was principally spent in the British <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MUSEUM">Museum</a>, where he had obtained an appointment in every respect suited to his philosophical disposition; and in discharging that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the duties of his office which led him to show that most valuable collection to different visitors, it was hardly possible to conceive a more agreeable union of the manners of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> with the knowledge of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>. While he was engaged in conversation with his usual cheerfulness at the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of his friend Sir Joseph Banks, he was suddenly attacked with a fit of apoplexy, which in a few days, notwithstanding the best medical assistance, terminated in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; an event sincerely regretted by all who had the honour of his acquaintance, and by which the literature and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> of London sustained a real loss.

SPHINX

Pages 1237-1237

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a>, a genus of insects belonging to the order of lepidoptera. There are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, all of them <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called moths of different kinds. The name of sphinx is given them on account of the singular attitude of their caterpillars, who apply the hinder <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of their body to a branch of a tree, holding the rest of it erect, like the fabulous sphinx. Most of them spin their cocoon under ground, making them up with small parcels of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> and grains of corn interwoven with threads. The sphinges fly either early in the morning <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> after sunset in the evening. They fly heavily and sluggishly, often emitting a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>. One species, the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATROPOS">atropos</a>, or jasmine hawk-moth, has the thorax marked somewhat like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>'s head. It has a shrill <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, more dismal than the squeaking of a mouse. All the species suck the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NECTAR">nectar</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, though they seldom <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> upon them.

SPHIX

Pages 1237-1237

the ichneumon wasp <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a>; a genus of insects belonging to the order of hymenoptera. The mouth is armed with jaws, but without any tongue. The wings of both sexes are extended without folds, and laid horizontally on the back. The sting is sharp, and concealed within the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a>. The genus is divided into two families. 1. Those in which the abdomen is petiolated, or joined to the thorax by a stalk. 2. Those in which the abdomen is subfusiform, or nearly of an equal size through its whole length. The manner of living is different in the various <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, and so is the general form of the body and their haunts; but though the method of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> be utterly different, yet the same manners appear innate and inherent in all. They agree in being the fiercest of all flies; they <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> attack insects much larger than themselves, and this whether they be defenceless or armed, as they are provided with a sting. The strength in all this savage kind is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a>; their jaws are hard and sharp, and in their sting lies a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POISON">poison</a> suddenly fatal to the creatures with whom they engage. The savage seizes hardly on the animal he attacks, and gives a stroke of amazing force; after which he falls <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> himself were killed, but it is to rest from his fatigue and enjoy his victory. He keeps a steady eye on the creature he has struck till it dies, which happens in a few minutes, and then drags it to the nest to feed the young. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of other insects they destroy is scarce to be conceived; the mouth of their cave is like that of a giant in the days of yore, strewed with the remains of prey. The eyes, the filament that serves as a brain, and a small <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the contents of the body, are all the savage eats, and will kill fifty for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>.

SPLACHNUM

Pages 1237-1237

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, a genus of the cryptogamia musci. There are two <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. 1. The ampullaceum, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> crevet splachnum, is found in bogs and marshes, and often upon cow-dung. It grows in thick tufts, and is about two inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. The leaves are oval-lanceolate, terminated with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> point or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEARD">beard</a>. The top of the filament or peduncle swells into the form of an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a> cone, which Linnæus terms an *apophysis* or *umbraculum*; upon the top of which is placed a cylindrical anthera, like the neck of a crevet. The calyptra is conical, and resembles a small extinguisher. 2. The vesculofum, or acorn-shaped splachnum, is found upon bogs and cow-dung, and upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of rocks on the tops of the Highland <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, as on Ben-Lomond, and in the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of Sky, and elsewhere. This differs little from the preceding, and perhaps is no more than a variety. The filaments are about an inch high. The leaves oval-acute, not so lanceolate and bearded as the other. The apophysis, and the anthers at the top of it, form together nearly an oval <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, not unlike an acorn in its cup, the apophysis being transversely semi-oval and of a blood-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, the anthera short and conical. The calyptra is the same as that of the other. The operculum is short and obtuse, and the rim of the anthera has eight <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> cilia. The anthera of the other is also ciliated, but not so distinctly. It is an elegant moss, and very distinguishable on account of its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a>-coloured filaments and dark-red capsules.

SQUATT

Pages 1237-1237

among miners, a small <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a> of ore, less valuable than a vein <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> load, as reaching only a little way.

STANHOPE

Pages 1237-1238

an eminent divine, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HERTFORDSHIRE">Hertfordshire</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-DERBYSHIRE">Derbyshire</a>, in the year 1660. His father was rector of that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a> of St Margaret's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEICESTER">Leicester</a>, and chaplain to the earls of Chesterfield and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLARE">Clare</a>. His grandfather Dr George Stanhope was chaplain to James I., and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Charles I.; had the chancellorship of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YORK">York</a>, where he was also a canon-residentiary, held a prebend, and was rector of Weldrake in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>. He was for his loyalty driven to doors with eleven children; and died in 1644. Our author was sent to school, first at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UPPINGHAM">Uppingham</a> in Rutland, then at Leicester; afterwards removed to Eaton; and thence chosen to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">King</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, in the place of W. Cleaver. He took the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of B.A. in 1681; M.A. 1685; was elected one of the syndics for the university of Cambridge, in the buffoels of Alban Francis, 1687; minister of Quoi near Cambridge, and vice-proctor 1688; was that year preferred to the rectory of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRING">Tring</a> in Hertfordshire, which after some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> he quitted. He was in 1689 presented to the vicarage of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEWISHAM">Lewisham</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KENT">Kent</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DARTMOUTH">Dartmouth</a>, to whom he had been chaplain, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> to his son. He was also appointed chaplain to king William and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to enjoy that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> under queen <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>. He commenced D.D. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 5, 1697, performing all the offices required to that degree publicly and with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> applause. He was made vicar of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPTFORD">Deptford</a> in 1703; succeeded Dr Hooper as <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a> the same year; and was thrice chosen prolocutor of the lower <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONVOCATION">convocation</a>. His uncommon diligence and industry, assisted by his excellent parts, enriched him with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> stock of polite, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a>, and most useful learning. His discourses from the pulpit were equally pleasing and profitable; a beautiful intermixture of the clearest reasoning with the purest diction, attended with all the graces of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> elocution. The good Christian, the solid divine, and the fine <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, in him were happily united. His conversation was polite and delicate, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> without precipitence, facetious without levity. His piety was real and rational, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> great and universal, fruitful in acts of mercy, and in all good works. He died <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 18, 1728, aged 68 years; and was buried in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHANCEL">chancel</a> of the church at Lewisham. The dean was twice married: 1. to Olivia Cotton, by whom he had one son and four daughters. His <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> lady, who was sister to Sir Charles Wager, survived him, dying October 1, 1730, aged about 54. One of the dean's daughters was married to a son of bishop Burnet. Bishop Moore of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELY">Ely</a> died the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> before queen Anne; who, it has been said, designed our dean for that see when it should have become vacant. Dr Felton says, "The late dean of Canterbury is excellent in the whole. His thoughts and reasoning are bright and solid. His style is just, both for the purity of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, and for the strength and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>; but the periods are formed in peculiar order of the words, that it was an observation, nobody could pronounce them with the same <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> and advantage as himself." His writings, which are an inestimable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> of piety and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> are, "A <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARAPHRASE">Paraphrase</a> and Comment upon the Epistles and Gospels," 4 vols, 1705, 8vo. "Sermons at Boyle's Lectures," 1706, 4to. "Fifteen Sermons," 1700, 8vo. "Twelve Sermons on several occasions," 1727, 8vo. "Thomas à Kempis," 1666, 8vo. "Epictetus's Morals, with Simplicius's Comment, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> of Epictetus," 1700, 8vo. "Parson's Christian Directory," 1716, 8vo. "Rochefoucault's Maxims," 1706, 8vo. "A Funeral Sermon on Mr Richard Sare Bookseller," 1724; two editions 4to. "Twenty Sermons," pub- lished singly between the years 1692 and 1724. "Private Prayers for every Day in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">Week</a>, and for the several Parts of each Day: translated from the Greek Devotions of Bishop Andrews, with Additions," 1730. In his translations, it is well known, Dr Stanhope did not confine himself to a strict and literal version; he took the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of paraphrasing, explaining, and improving upon his author; as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> evidently appear (not to mention any other <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>) by the slightest perusal of St Augustine's Meditations, and the Devotions of Bishop Andrews. STEPHENS'S Medicines for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">Stone</a>, were only a more imperfect method of using <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>-ley in that distemper. See CHITTRICK.

STERNWAY

Pages 1238-1238

is when a ship, instead of advancing, retreats in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, either through the violence of a current <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> any other means.

STONE-CHATTERER

Pages 1238-1238

(<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTACILLA">Motacilla</a> Rubicola), in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ornithology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> omitted to be described under Motacilla. It is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> among us during <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> in garfy grounds. In the winter they disperse into marshes and other places, but do not quit the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. It is a restless and noisy <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>, and perches frequently on some bush, chattering incessantly. The head, neck, and throat, are <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>; but on both sides of the latter is a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, so that it appears on first sight to be encircled with white; the feathers on the back are black, edged with tawny; the lower <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the back <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> above the rump is white; the end and exterior side of the two outmost feathers of the tail are of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> rust-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, the rest are black: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> is of a deep reddish <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>; the belly of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> hue: the quill-feathers are dusky edged with dull <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>; those next the body are marked with a white spot near their bottoms; the coverts of the wings are adorned with another. The head of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FERRUGINOUS">ferruginous</a> spotted with black; and the colours in general are less vivid. In both sexes the legs are black.

SULZER

Pages 1238-1239

a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, was born at Winterthur, in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANTON">canton</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ZURICH">Zurich</a>, October 16, 1720. He was the youngest of 25 children. His early <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> did not <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> much, though it was by no means neglected. He had little inclination for what is called in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>, and made but a small progress in the learned languages, which were to prepare him for the study of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, for which profession his parents designed him. At the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 16, when he went to the academical school of Zurich, he had not the smallest notion of the sciences, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> of elegant literature, and consequently no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for study. The first incident that developed a hidden germ of philosophical genius, was his meeting with Wolfe's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-METAPHYSICS">metaphysics</a>; this was the birth of his taste for science; but he wanted a guide. The clergyman with whom he lodged was an ignorant <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a>; and the academical prelections were, as yet, above the reach of his comprehension. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, a sedentary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> was not the thing he liked, nor to which he had been accustomed; and, moreover, a sociable turn of mind led him often into <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, where he lost much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> in frivolous amusements, yet without corrupting his morals. Who, that observed him at this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, says Mr Formey in his Eulogium, would have thought that Sulzer would one <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> be numbered among the most knowing and wisest men of his time? The learned Gesner was the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> that rendered Sulzer's inclination to study triumphant over his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> for amusement and company. Animated by the counsels and example of this worthy and learned man, he applied himself to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> ardour, and resumed the pursuit of Grecian literature and the Oriental languages. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> became his noble and favourite passion. An <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> settlement in a rural <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>, that exhibited happy objects and occasions for this delightful study, began to render his days happy and useful; and he published, in 1741, Moral Contemplations of the Works of Nature; and, the year following, an Account of a voyage he had made through the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>; which showed, at the same time, his knowledge of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, and the taste and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol17.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a> with which he surveyed the beauties of nature, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> and goodness of its author. He afterwards became private <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> to a young <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAGDEBURG">Magdeburg</a>. This procured him the acquaintance of M. Maupertuis, Euler, and Sack, which opened to his merit the path of preferment, and advanced him successively to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of mathematical professor in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">King</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a> in 1747, and to that of member of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Academy in 1750. In this last <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> he distinguished himself in a very eminent manner, enriched the class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECULATIVE">speculative</a> philosophy with a great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of excellent <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a>, and was justly considered as one of the first-rate metaphysicians in Germany. But his genius was not confined to this branch of science. His Universal <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-THEORY">Theory</a> of the Fine Arts, is a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> production. A profound knowledge of the arts and sciences, and a perfect acquaintance with true taste, are eminently displayed in this <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> secure to its author a permanent and distinguished <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in the republic of letters. The first volume of this excellent work was published in 1771, and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> in 1774. We shall not here give a catalogue of the writings of M. Sulzer; but we cannot help mentioning his Remarks on the Philosophical Essays of the late Mr. Hume, as a work of real merit, which does <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> to the acuteness, while it often detects the sophistry, of the British Bayle. The moral character of M. Sulzer was amiable and virtuous: sociability and beneficence were its characteristic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>; and his virtues were animated by that sacred philosophy that forms the Christian, ennobles man, and is the only source of that heart-felt serenity and sedate fortitude which support humanity, when every other object of confidence fails. His dying moments were calm, humble, and sublime; and when he expired, the placid and composed <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> of his countenance made his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOURNING">mourning</a> friends doubt, for some time, whether it was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> that had suspended his conversation. He had no enemy; and his friends were numerous, affectionate, and worthy of the tender returns he made them. The king of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a> distinguished him by repeated marks of munificence and favour. We learn, however, that his royal protector had never seen him before the end of the year 1777, tho' he had been member of the academy from the year 1750. The audience, indeed, though late vouchsafed, was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> to M. Sulzer, with whom the monarch conversed for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> time with the greatest affability and condescension.

SYNCOPEATION

Pages 1239-1239

in music, denotes a striking <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, whereby the distinction of the several times or parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> is interrupted. However, it is more properly used for the connecting the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> of any measure, or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, with the first of the following measure; so as only to make one note of both. A syncop is sometimes also made in the middle of a measure. Syncopation is also used when a note of one <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> ends or terminates on the middle of a note of the other part. This is otherwise denominated binding. It is likewise used for a driving note; that is, when some shorter note at the beginning of a measure, or half measure, is followed by two, three, or more longer notes before another short note occurs, equal to that which occasioned the driving, to make the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> even, e.g., when an odd <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CROTCHET">crotchet</a> comes before two or three minims, or an odd quaver before two, three, or more crotchets. In syncopated or driving notes, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> or foot is taken up, or put <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, while the note is sounding.

TAGETES

Pages 1239-1240

French Marigold; a genus of the polygamy superflua order, belonging to the syn-genetia class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are three <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; the most remarkable are, 1. The erecta, grows naturally in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>, but has been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> cultivated in the British gardens, where it is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> titled African marigold. Of this there are the following varieties: 1. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">Pale</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> primrose <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, with single, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a>, and fistulous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>. 2. Deep yellow, with single, double, and fistulous flowers. 3. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>-coloured, with single, double, and fistulous flowers. 4. Middling African, with orange-coloured flowers. 5. Sweet-scented African. These are all very subject to vary; so that unless the seeds are very carefully saved from the finest flowers, they are apt to degenerate: nor should their seeds be too long sown in the same garden without changing it, for the same reason; therefore, those who are desirous to have these flowers in perfection, should <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> their seeds with some person of integrity at a distance where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is of a different <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, at least every other year. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> this is done, the varieties may be <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in perfection. This plant is so well known as to need no <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>. It flowers from the beginning of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> till the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FROST">frost</a> puts a stop to it. 2. The patula, grows naturally in Mexico, but has been long in the British gardens, where it is distinguished from the first by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of French marigold. Of this there are several varieties, some of which have much larger flowers than others, and their colour varies greatly: there are some which are beautifully variegated, and others quite plain; but as these are accidents arising from culture, so so they do not merit farther distinction; for we have always found that seeds saved from the most beautiful flowers <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> degenerate, especially if they are sown in the same garden for two or three years together, without changing the seed. These plants are annual, so must be propagated from seeds every <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, which may be sown upon a moderate hot-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a> the beginning of April; and when the plants are come up, they should have plenty of fresh <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>; for if they are drawn too much, they will not afterward become handsome, notwithstanding they have all possible care taken of them. When they are about three inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, they should be transplanted on a very moderate hot-bed, which may be arched over with hoops and covered with mats, for these plants are hardy enough to be brought up without glasses; in this bed they should be planted about six inches asunder each way, observing to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> them until they have taken root; but as the plants acquire strength, they should be moved to the open air by degrees; and about the end of May they should be taken up with a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALL">ball</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> to the root of each plant, and planted into the borders of the parterre-garden, or into pots, for furnishing the courts, &c., shading them carefully from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> till they have taken new root, and also supplying them duly with water. When their flowers appear, if any should prove single, the plants should be destroyed, and then those in pots may be removed to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COURT">court</a>, where the several varieties, being intermixed with other annual plants, afford an agreeable variety. These plants have a strong disagreeable scent, especially when handled; for which reason they are not so greatly esteemed for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> near habitations; but the flowers of the sweet-scented sort being more agreeable, are generally preferred, especially for planting in small gardens.

TAVIRA

Pages 1240-1240
or TAVILA, a considerable town of Portugal, and capital of the province of Algarve, with a handsome castle, and one of the best harbours in the kingdom, defended by a fort. It is seated in a pleasant fertile country, at the mouth of the river Gilao, between Cape Vincent and the Strait of Gibraltar, 100 miles west by north of Cadiz. W. Long. 7° 46'. N. Lat. 37° 18'.

TEA

Pages 1240-1243

(Encycl.) Tea, in the Chinese <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, is called tia, in Fokien it is called te; and as the Europeans landed first in that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, that dialect has been preserved. The Europeans learned to drink this infusion in the 15th century; and since that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> have vied with each other in giving the Chinese the most <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a> for this and other goods which are become fashionable: it grows both in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-CHINA">China</a> and in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a>. It likewise grows in Tonkin; but the best tea, according to Du Halde, comes from Fokien. It was universally believed that all teas come from the same shrub, and are only distinguished by the different ages, gathering, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a>, till <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a> Hill lately supposed that he had discovered that the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> tea comes from the tea-shrub with five petals <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> flower-leaves which Kempfer has described and represented, but that the green tea is taken from the tea-shrub with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a>-leaved <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>. Linnaeus distinguishes it, besides the flowers, by the longer and narrower leaves. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of petals may, however, be considered as dubious, at least as not invariable. See Plate CCCXXII, where a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of each is given; that of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BOHEA">bohea</a> being taken from the Amoen. Acad. vol. 7.; that of the viridis from a print by Miller after a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> of a plant, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a>'s garden at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SION">Sion</a>, which was the first that flowered in England, and the flower consisted of only five petals, like the bohea. [This last figure is rather upon too small a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> comparatively with the other.] After all, there are many sorts and varieties of tea differing one from another in the shape and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the leaves; and differently denominated, from these circumstances, from the places where they grow, or from the various ways of preparing. The general distinction of these, however, is into brown and green, according as they tinge the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>. 1. Brown Teas. Brown tea is honam teé, or kuli-teé, which grows in some places about <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANTON">Canton</a>, and is drunk by the Chinese, but not by the Europeans: its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> being the least agreeable of any. The dried leaves are either <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> or brownish. The tea-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>, which are sold in flower-pots here, scarce grow to the height of an ell. The flower consists of six <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> petals, of which the three lowest are the smallest. An-kay is a coarse sort of tea, from a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of this name. Te-bohú, which we usually call bohea-tea, is called moji by the Chinese. This sort is brought to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> in greater quantities than any of the others. The best sort smells agreeably, and in a short time gives a brown <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> to the water, and consists of leaves of one colour; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> ones are among them, it is a bad sort. Tao-kyonn is the name of the best sort of bohea tea. Kongo, or as the Chinese call it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KONG">kong</a> fo, has an agreeable scent: its leaves are finer than those of te-bohé; though it is scarce distinguishable from the best boheas, except in price; for kongo is somewhat dearer. Sutchong, or footchuen, which the Chinese call faa-tyang, or fu-tiann, is the dearest of all brown teas. It gives a fine yellow green colour to the water, and has an agreeable taste, unless you put too much into the pot, which spoils both taste and colour. Padre sutchong is the best tea that can be drunk. The leaves of this tea are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, yellowish, not rolled up, but expanded; and packed up in papers of half a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POUND">pound</a> each, like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>. If it is not taken <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> care of at tea, it is much altered for the worse. Lin-kifem is a sort of tea which hath narrow rough leaves and footstalks. It is seldom used by itself, but mixed with other sorts. Back bo, or pack bo, is that which we call pecko, which has leaves with dots. It is a mild tea, has a good taste, and is said to be the least heating of any. 2. Of Green Teas, there are Hyson, called by tiann, or hi-kiong by the Chinese. Singlo, or fanglo, is so called from the place whence it comes. The Chinese likewise call it jung-tia. Bing, or imperial tea. Tio ti is rolled up like pease. This sort is rolled up up between the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> in a rounder shape than the others. A smaller kind is called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>-tea. Hyson utchin, is distinguishable from the hyson skin by its narrow and short leaves. Go-bé hath <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> narrow leaves. The Chinese likewise make tea-cakes, which they sell very dear. It is almost incredible what quantities of tea are annually exported into Europe and other parts; and what innumerable hands are employed in so unnecessary an article. The countryman must with great care plant and nurse the tea-shrubs; pluck every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> in due time; separate the new leaves from the old, and dry them with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> accuracy. When the merchant has got the baskets of tea, at a low rate, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> people, he must often take care of it for years together; and is always uncertain when, or at what price, he shall sell it. When the Europeans have fixed upon a place where they <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> make their bargains, they empty the baskets (but let it be noted we are now speaking of bohea tea, for the finer sorts are sold in chests); and if any bad tea is found in these baskets, it is separated from the rest. The good tea is then packed up in new chests, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of which is deducted; and these chests are marked, and lined with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> in the inside. A Chinese gets into these chests, and treads <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the tea as it is emptied out of the baskets; this is very hard labour, and throws the treaders, who is almost naked, into a profuse perspiration. Though great care is taken to prevent anything from coming into the tea, yet it is hardly to be avoided; and sometimes their feet are wounded and bleed. But the tea has already passed through so many dirty hands, that those who <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> that drug have no reason to be disgusted with this last mark of indelicacy in the package. As soon as some of the chests are packed by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of kuleers, or Chinese servants, they are pasted over with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, and carried out of the warehouse to the factories, where they are weighed by the Chinese <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CUSTOM_HOUSE"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol3.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> officers, in the presence of the interpreter, and marked <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> with a stiff <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a>, or with a wooden stamp. Some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> people are satisfied with the leaves of rhambus thea, which they put into their clayey water, instead of tea, to make it more palatable. In the account of the Dutch embassy to China, it is related that the Chinese make use of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of mols instead of tea. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> price of tea, at its first introduction, induced many physicians to think of a substitute; and it is well known that Simon Pauli thought the myrica <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GALE">gale</a> to be the shrub itself. Other succedanea are mentioned by authors; such as the leaves of the Prunus spinosa, floe-tree. Origanum vulgare, wild marjoram. Rubus arcticus, arctic bramble. Veronica officinalis, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> speedwell. Veronica chamaedrys, wild germander. Chenopodium ambrosoides, Mexican sweet blite. Capraria biflora, tweet-weed or goat-weed. The sophistication of tea practised by the smugglers in some of the southern parts of this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> is well known. In particular, they have reduced to a regular <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> the management of the leaves of the ash and elder; which, when prepared, is called snouch, and mixed, as is said, in the proportion of one-third, with the ordinary teas. To what an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> the trade in this sophisticated tea had been carried, to the detriment of the trees, may be imagined, when the reader is informed, that an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> has lately been obtained to prohibit it, under very severe penalties.

THELIGONUM

Pages 1243-1243

dog's cabbage; a genus of the polyandria order, belonging to the monocoea class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There is only one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; viz. the cyno-crambe <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> dog's-cabbage of Dioscorides. This plant grows plentifully in the south of France, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>. It is annual. The stalks trail on the ground like those of chickweed; they grow about a foot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>; their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> are pretty <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>, garnished with oval acute-pointed leaves, standing on pretty long footstalks, which are bordered. At each <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> is placed one of these leaves; and from the same point come out several smaller, of the same shape, on shorter footstalks. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> are produced from the wings of the stalks in clusters, fitting very close; they are small, of an herbaceous <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, so make no <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> appearance. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> flowers grow from the same joint. The female flowers are succeeded by a single roundish seed, which ripens in autumn. It is preserved in botanic gardens for the sake of variety. The seeds of this must be sown in autumn, in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the plants are to remain; for when they are sown in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, the plants rarely come up the same year. They require no other culture but to keep them clean from weeds, and thin them where they are too close.

THEOBROMA

Pages 1243-1243

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, a genus of the polydelphus order, belonging to the pentandria class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are two <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, both natives of the Indies. 1. The first, which is the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CACAO">cacao</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> chocolate-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a> tree, is but of very moderate growth. See CACAO, (Encycl.) and Plate LXVI. 2. The guazuma, or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BASTARD">bastard</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEDAR">cedar</a> of Jamaica, rises with an upright <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a>, branching numerously, and spreading 30 or 40 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a>, heart-shaped, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERRATED">serrated</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> leaves, four inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>; and numerous small yellowish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> at the sides of the branches; succeeded by roundish, tuberculated rough fruit, containing the seed.

THESE ARE THE

Pages 1231-1232

e are the means used by artists to brighten the colours, and add to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of shells; and the changes produced by polishing in this manner are so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, that the shell is often not to be known afterwards for the same it was; and hence we hear of new shells in the cabinets of collectors, which have no real existence as separate <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, but are the polished appearance of others well known. To caution the reader against errors of this kind, it may be proper to add the most remarkable species thus usually altered. The onyx-shell <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> volute, called by us the purple or violet-tip, which in its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> state is of a simple <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, when it is wrought slightly, or polished with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> the surfaces taken off, is of a fine bright <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>; and when it is eaten away deeper, it appears of a fine <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MILK">milk</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, with the lower <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> bluish: it is in this state that it is called the onyx-shell; and it is preserved in many cabinets in its rough state, and in its yellow appearance, as different species of shells. The violet shells, so <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> among the curious, is a species of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a>, or common cowry, which does not appear in that elegance till it has been polished; and the common auris marina shows itself in two or three different forms, as it is more or less deeply wrought. In its rough state it is dusky and coarse, of a pale brown on the outside, and pearly within; when it is eaten <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> a little way below the surface, it shows variegations of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> and green; and when still farther eroded, it appears of a fine pearly hue within and without. The nautilus, when it is polished down, appears all over of a fine pearly <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; but when it is eaten away but to a small depth, it appears of a fine yellowish colour with dusky hairs. The burgau, when entirely cleared of its coat, is of the most beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PEARL">pearl</a>-colour: but when once slightly eroded, it appears of a variegated mixture of green and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>; whence it has been called the parroquet shell. The common <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HELMET">helmet</a>-shell, when wrought, is of the colour of the finest a- gate; and the muscles, in general, though very plain shells in their common appearance, become very beautiful when polished, and show <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> veins of the most elegant colours. The Persian shell, in its natural state, is all over white, and covered with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TUBERCLES">tubercles</a>; but when it has been ground down on a wheel, and polished, it appears of a grey colour, with spots and veins of a very bright and highly polished white. The limpets in general become very different when polished, most of them showing very elegant colours; among these the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TORTOISE_SHELL">tortoise-shell</a> <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-LIMPET">limpet</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a>; it does not appear at all of that colour or transparency till it has been wrought. That elegant species of shell called the junquil-chama, which has deceived so many judges of these things into an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of its being a new species, is only a white chama with a reticulated surface; but when this is polished, it loses at once its reticular <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> and its colour, and becomes perfectly smooth, and of a fine bright yellow; and the violet-coloured chama of New England, when worked down and polished, is of a fine milk-white, with a great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of blue veins, disposed like the variegations in agates. The asses-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EAR">ear</a> shell, when polished after working it down with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FILE">file</a>, becomes extremely glossy, and obtains a fine rose-colour all about the mouth. These are some of the most frequent among an endless variety of changes wrought on shells by polishing; and we find there are many of the very greatest beauties of this part of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>, which must have been lost but for this method of searching deep in the substance of the shell for them. The Dutch are very fond of shells, and are very nice in their manner of working them; they are under no restraint, however, in their works; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the most violent methods, so as often to destroy all the beauty of the shell. They file them down on all sides, and often take them to the wheel, when it must destroy the very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of the species.
