Nor do they stop at this; but, determined to have beauty at any rate, they are for improving upon <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and frequently add some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> and colours with a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a>, afterwards covering them with a fine coat of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a>; so that they seem the natural lineations of the shell: the Dutch cabinets are by this means made very beautiful, but they are by no means to be regarded as instructors in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY">natural <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. There are some artificers of this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATION">nation</a> who have a way of covering shells all over with a different tinge from that which nature gives them; and the curious are often deceived by these tricks into purchasing them as new species. There is another kind of work bestowed on certain species of shells, particularly the nautilus; namely, the engraving on it lines and circles, and figures of flares, and other things: this is too obvious a work of art to suffer any one to suppose it natural. Buonani has figured several of these wrought shells at the end of his work; but it is miserably throwing away labour to do them; the shells are spoiled as objects of natural history by it, and the engraving is seldom worth anything. They are principally done in the East Indies. Shells are subject to several imperfections; some of which are natural, and others accidental. The natural ones are the effect of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, or sicknesses in the fish. The greatest mischief happens to shells by the fish dying in them. The curious in these things pretend to be always able to distinguish a shell taken up with the fish alive, from one found on the shores: they call the first a living, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> a dead shell; and say that the colours are always much the faintest in the dead shells. When the shells have lain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> dead on the shores, they are subject to many injuries, of which the being eaten by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> is not the least: age renders the finest shells livid or dead in their colours. The finest shells are those which are fished up at sea, not found on the shores. The other natural defects of shells are their having morbid cavities, or protuberances, in parts where there should be none. When the shell is valuable, these faults may be hid, and much added to the beauty of the specimen without at all injuring it as an object of natural history, which should always be the great end of collecting these things. The cavities may be filled up with mastic, dissolved in spirit of wine, or with sealing-wax: these substances must be either coloured to the tinge of the shell, or else a pencil dipped in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>-colours must finish them up to the resemblance of the rest; and then the whole shell being rubbed over with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUM">gum</a>-water, or with the white of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EGG">egg</a>, scarce any eye can perceive the artifice: the same substances may also be used to repair the battered edge of a shell, provided the pieces chipped off be not too large. And when the excrescences of a shell are faulty, they are to be taken down with a fine file. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the lip of a shell be so battered that it <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> not admit of repairing by any cement, the whole must be filed down to an evenness, or ground on the wheel.

TIBERIUS

Pages 1243-1243

the third <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of Rome, under whose reign our Saviour suffered. See ROME, no 268.—281.

TIMBER

Pages 1243-1244

(Encycl.) Of all the different kinds known in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, oak is the best for <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>; and even when it lies exposed to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, there is none equal to it. Fir-timber is the next in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of goodness for building, especially in England, where they build upon leaves. It differs from oak in this, that it requires not much seasoning, and therefore no <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> stock is required before-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. Fir is used for flooring, wainscoting, and the ornamental parts of building within doors. Elm is the next in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, especially in England and France; it is very tough and pliable, and therefore easily worked; it does not readily split; and it bears driving of bolts and nails better than any other wood; for which reason it is chiefly used by wheelwrights, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COACH">coach</a>-makers, for shafts, naves, &c. Beech is also used for many purposes; it is very tough and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> when young, and of great strength; but liable to warp very much when exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, and to be worm-eaten when used without in doors; its greatest use is for planks, bedsteads, chairs, and other <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> goods. Ash is likewise a very useful wood, but very scarce in most parts of Europe; it serves in buildings, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> for any other use, when screened from the weather; handspikes and oars are chiefly made of it. Wild-chesnut timber is by many esteemed to be as good as oak, and seems to have been much used in old buildings; but whether these trees are more scarce at present than formerly, or have been found not to answer so well as was imagined, it is certain this timber is now but little used. Walnut-tree is excellent for the joiner's use, it being of a more curious <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> than beech, and not so subject to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>. The poplar, alder, and aspen trees, which are very little different from each other, are much used instead of fir, they look well, and are tougher and harder. The goodness of timber not only depends on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> and situation in which it stands, but likewise on the season wherein it is felled. In this people disagree very much; some are for having it felled as soon as its fruit is ripe, others in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, and many in the autumn. But as the sap and moisture of timber is certainly the cause that it perishes much sooner than it otherwise would do, it seems evident that timber should be felled when there is the least sap in it, viz., from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> that the leaves begin to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> till the trees begin to bud. This <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> usually commences about the end of April in England, because the bark then riles most freely; for where a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of timber is to be felled, the statute requires it to be done then, for the advantage of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TANNING">tanning</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> chiefly regarded the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a> in felling their timber; their rule was to fell it in the wain, or four days after the new moon, or sometimes in the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>. Pliny advises it to be in the very article of the change, which happening to be in the last <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the winter solstice, the timber, says he, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> be incorruptible. Timber should likewise be cut when of a proper age; for when it is either too young or too old, it will not be so durable as when cut at a proper age. It is said that oak should not be cut under 60 years old, nor above 200. Timber, however, should be cut in their prime, when almost fully grown, and before they begin to decay; and this will be sooner or later, according to the dryness and moistness of the soil where the timber grows, as also according to the bigness of the trees; for there are no fixed rules in felling of timber, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> and judgment must <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> here as in most other <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>. After timber has been felled and sawed, it must be seasoned; for which purpose some advise it to be laid up in a very dry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRY">airy</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, yet out of the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, or at least free from the extremities of either; and that it may not decay, but dry evenly, they recommend it to be daubed over with cow-dung. It must not stand upright, but <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> all along, one piece over another, only kept apart by short blocks interposed, to prevent a certain mouldiness which they are otherwise apt to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> in sweating on one another; from which arises frequently a kind of fungus, especially <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there be any fappy parts remaining. Others advise the planks of timber to be laid for a few days in some pool or running stream, in order to extract the sap, and afterwards to dry them in the sun or air. By this means, it is said, they will be prevented from either chopping, casting, or cleaving, but against shrinking there is no remedy. Some again are for burying them in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, others in a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>; and some for scorching and seasoning them in fire, especially piles, posts, &c., which are to stand in water or earth. The Venetians first found out the method of seasoning by fire; which is done after this manner: They put the piece to be seasoned into a strong and violent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>; in this they continually turn it round by means of an engine, and take it out when it is everywhere covered with a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> coaly crust; the internal <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the wood is thereby so hardened, that neither <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EAR">ear</a>' nor water can damage it for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> time afterwards. After the planks of timber have been well seasoned and fixed in their places, care is to be taken to defend or preserve them; to which the smearing them with linseed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, tar, or the like oleaginous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, contributes much. The ancients, particularly <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HESIOD">Hesiod</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, advise the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>-drying of all instruments made of wood, by hanging them up in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIMNEYS">chimneys</a> where wood-fires are used. The Dutch preserve their gates, portculices, drawbridges, sluices, &c., by coating them over with a mixture of pitch and tar, whereon they strew small pieces of cockle and other shells, beaten almost to powder, and mixed with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-sand, which incrusts and arms them wonderfully against all assaults of wind and weather. When timber is felled before the sap is perfectly at rest, it is very subject to the worms; but to prevent and cure this, Mr Evelyn recommends the following remedy as the most approved: Put <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> sulphur into a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CUCURBIT">cucurbit</a>, with as much aquafortis as will cover it three fingers deep; distil it to driness, which is performed by two or three rectifications. Lay the sulphur that remains at bottom, being of a blackish or sand-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a> colour, on a marble, or put it in a glaze, and it will dissolve into an oil; with this oil anoint the timber which is infected with worms. This, he says, will not only prevent worms, but preserve all kinds of woods, and many other things, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a>, nets, and mats, from <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a>, either in water, air, or snow.

TRIBULUS

Pages 1244-1245

CALTROPS; a genus of the mono-gynia order, belonging to the decandra class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are three <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; the most remarkable is the terrestris, with six <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of lobes to each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>. It is a very <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> weed in the south of France, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, where it grows among corn, and on most of the arable <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a>, and is very troublesome to the feet of cattle; for the fruit being armed with strong prickles, run into the feet of the cattle which walk over the land. This is certainly the plant which is mentioned in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>'s Georgics under the name of tribulus, tho' most of his commentators have applied it to other plants. It is called in English caltrop, from the form of the fruit, which resembles those instruments of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> that were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> in the enemies way to annoy their horses.—This hath a slender <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">fibrous</a> root, from which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> out four <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> five slender hairy stalks, which spread flat on the ground, garnished at each <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> with winged leaves, composed of six pair of narrow hairy lobes, almost of equal size; those on the lower <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the stalk stand alternately, but toward the top they are placed opposite. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> come out from the wings of the stalk, standing upon short footstalks; they are composed composed of five <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, obtuse, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> petals, which spread open. In the centre is situated an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> germen, crowned by a headed stigma, attended by ten short lamina, terminated by single summit, and are succeeded by roundish, five-cornered, prickly fruit, which, when ripe, divides into five parts, each having a transverse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CELL">cell</a> containing one or two seeds.—This plant is preserved in botanic gardens for variety. It is propagated by seeds, which should be sown in autumn; for those which are kept out of the ground till spring <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> remain in the ground a whole year before the plants come up. These seeds should be sown on an open <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BED">bed</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, where they are designed to remain; for as it is an annual plant, it doth not bear transplanting very well, unless it be done when the plants are very young. In the spring, when the plants come up, they should be carefully cleared from weeds; and where they come up too <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>, some of the plants should be pulled out to give room for the remaining plants to grow; after this they <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> require no other culture but to keep them clear from weeds. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the seeds are permitted to scatter, the plants will come up the following spring, and maintain their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> if they are not overborne with weeds.

TRILL

Pages 1245-1245
or Plain Shake and Gruppo, in music. The first is defined to be a shake upon one note only, in the making whereof the scholar is directed to sing the first of the examples (Plate CCCXIII. fig. 2.) beginning with the first crochet, and beating every note with the throat upon the vowel o, to the last breath. The gruppo (as described by Playford) appears to be no other than the shake now practised, and which consists in the alternate prolongation of two tones in juxtaposition to each other, with a close on the note immediately beneath the lower of them. The trill (says Playford) being the most usual grace, is made in closes or cadences; and when on a long note, exclamation or passion is expressed there, the trill is made in the latter part of such note; but most usually upon binding notes, and such as precede the closing note. Notwithstanding this, Mr Hawkins is of opinion that the trill is rather a defect than an ornament in singing; as being nothing more than the intermitted prolongation of a single tone. TROPÆOLUM, Indian Cress; a genus of the monogynia order, belonging to the octandra clas of plants. There are two species: 1. The minus, or small Indian cress, grows naturally in Peru. This was first brought to Europe in 1684, and was raised in the gardens of count Bevening in Holland. It has a trailing herbaceous stalk, garnished with leaves almost circular. The foot-stalk is inserted in the centre of the leaf, like a buckler, as in the navelwort; they are smooth, of a greyish colour; the flowers come out from the wings of the stalks, standing upon very long slender foot-stalks, of an admirable structure, composed of five acute-pointed petals; the two upper are large and rounded, the three under are narrow; their tails join together, and are lengthened into a tail two inches long. After the flower is past, the germen turns to a roundish fruit, which is furrowed, and divided into three lobes, each including one streaked seed. It flowers from Midsummer till the frost stops it in autumn. There are two varieties of this, one with a deep orange-coloured flower, inclining to red, and the other with a pale yellow flower. 2. The majus, or greater Indian cress, grows naturally about Lima; this has larger stalks than the former. The leaves are also larger, and their borders are indented almost into lobes; the flowers are larger, and their petals are rounded at their points. There are two colours of this sort as in the former; and one with double flowers, which is propagated by cuttings, for it does not produce seeds.—The first sort is less common at present in the English gardens than the second, though it was formerly more so; the flowers of the latter being larger, make a finer appearance, for which it is preferred; they are both esteemed annual plants, though they may be continued through the winter if they are kept in pots, and sheltered in a good green-ass="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">house, in like manner as that with double flowers is preserved; so may be propagated by cuttings as that is. But, as these ripen their seeds constantly every year, the plants are generally raised from them; these may be sown in April in the places where they are to remain, which should be where their stalks may have support; for they will climb six or eight feet high, when they are trained up, and then their flowers make a good appearance; but when they trail upon the ground, they will spread over the neighbouring plants and become unsightly.—The flowers of these plants are frequently eaten in salads; they have a warm taste like the garden cress, and are esteemed very wholesome; they are likewise used for garnishing dishes. The seeds are pickled, and by some are preferred to most kinds of pickles for sauce.

TRYING

Pages 1245-1245

in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. A ship is said to try <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> a-try, when no sails are abroad but the main-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> or mizen-fall.

TUBIPORA

Pages 1245-1245
or Tubularia, a genus of submarine plants, belonging to the cryptogamia clas, of the hardness of coral, and consisting of cylindric tubes rising from a thin crust of the same sort of matter with themselves. See Plate CCCXVII.

TYLES

Pages 1245-1246

(Encycl.) There are various kinds of tyles for the various occasions of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>; as plain, thack, ridge, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a>, crease, gutter, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAN">pan</a>, crooked, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Flemish, corner, hip, dormar, scallop, altragal, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRAVERSE">traverse</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PAVING">paving</a>, and Dutch tyles. Plain or thack tyles, are those in ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> for covering of houses. They are squeezed flat, while yet soft, in a mould. They are of an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>; and by 17 Edw. IV. c. 4. are to be 10½ inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and 6¼ <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and half an inch and half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> thick. But these dimensions are not over strictly kept to.—Ridge, roof, or crease tyles, are those used to cover the ridges of houses, being made circular breadth-wise, like an half-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a>; they are, by the aforesaid statute, to be 13 inches long, and of the same thickness with the plain tyles.—Hip or corner tyles, are those which <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> on the hips or corners of roofs. As to form, they are first made flat like plain tyles, but of a quadrangular figure, whose two sides are <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, and two ends edges of circles, one end being a little concave and the other convex. The convex end is to be about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> times as broad as the concave end, so that they would be triangular but that one corner is taken off; then, before they are burnt, they are bent on a mould breadthwise, like ridge tyles. They have an hole at their narrow end to nail them on by, and are laid. laid with their narrow end upwards; by statute, they are to be 10½ inches long, and of a convenient breadth and thickness.—Gutter tiles, are those which lie in gutters or valleys in crofs buildings. They are made like corner-tiles, only the corners of the broad end are turned back again with two wings. They have no holes in them, but are laid with the broad end upwards, without any nailing. They are made in the same mould as the corner-tiles, and have the same dimensions on the convex side. Their wings are each four inches broad and eight long. Pan, crooked, or Flemish tiles, are used in covering of sheds, lean-to's, and all kinds of flat-roof buildings. They are in form of an oblong parallelogram, as plain tiles; but are bent breadthwise forwards and backwards in form of an S, only one of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> is at least three times as big as the other; which biggest <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> is always laid uppermost, and the least arch of another tile lies over the edge of the greatest arch of the former. They have no holes for pins, but hang on the laths by a knot of their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. They are usually 14½ inches long, and 10½ broad. By 12 Geo. I. c. 25, they are to be, when burnt, not less than 13½ inches long, and 9½ inches wide, and half an inch thick.—Dormar or dorman tiles consist of a plain tile and a triangular piece of a plain one standing up at right <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> to one side of the plain tile, and swept with an arch of a circle from the other end, which end terminates in a point. Of these tiles there are two kinds, the triangular piece in some standing on the right, in others on the left side of the plain tile. And of these again there are two kinds, some having a plain whole tile, others but half a plain tile. But in them all the plain tile has two holes for the pins at that end where the broad end of the triangular piece stands. Their use is to be laid in the gutters betwixt the roof and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a> or sides of the dormars, the plain <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> lying on the roof, and the triangular part standing perpendicularly by the cheek of the dormar; they are excellent to keep out the wet in those places, and yet they are hardly known anywhere but in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUSSEX">Sussex</a>. The dimensions of the plain tile part are the same as those of a plain tile; and the triangular part is of the same length, and its breadth at one end seven inches, and at the other nothing. Scallop or astragal tiles are in all respects like plain tiles, only their lower ends are in form of an astragal, viz. a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEMICIRCLE">semicircle</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> on each side. They are used in some places for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>-tying—Transverse tiles are a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> plain tiles, having the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PIN">pin</a>-holes broken out, or one of the lower corners broken off. These are laid with the broken end upwards, upon rafters where pinned tiles cannot hang. Flemish or Dutch tiles are of two kinds, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>: the ancient were used for chimney foot-pieces; they were painted with antique figures, and frequently with pictures of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, some with compartments, and sometimes with more fugue devices; but they come much short of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> and colours of the modern ones. The modern Flemish tiles are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> used plastered up in the jambs of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIMNEYS">chimneys</a> instead of chimney-corner <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. These are better glazed, and such as are painted (for some are only <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>) are done with more curious figures and more lively colours than the ancient ones. But both kinds seem to be made of the same whitish clay as our white glazed earthen <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WARE">ware</a>; the modern ones are commonly painted with birds, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, &c. The ancient ones are only five inches and a quarter square, and about three <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of an inch thick; the modern ones six inches and a half square, and three quarters of an inch thick. U, V.

USNEA

Pages 1253-1253

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, a genus of mosses, wholly destitute of leaves, and composed only of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> slender filaments <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> stalks, which are usually <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a>, rigid, and of a cylindric <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. The extremities, or other parts of these, are at times furnished with a sort of orbicular bodies, dry and destitute of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, but seeming to supply the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>. These are hollow, in form of cups, but have no rim. The whole <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> are fixed in the manner of mistletoe to the barks of trees. Micheli has given accounts of flowers and seeds in these plants; but Dillenius suspects the accuracy of this observation, and adds, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there are such, they are too minute to be of any <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in the general distinctions of the plants. See Plate CCCXX.

VAYER

Pages 1246-1246

a Parisian counsellor of state, and preceptor to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Anjou, only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> XIV. was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1688. He was admitted into the French academy in 1639; but his style was less polite than that of his fellow-academics. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> of regular conduct, like that of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> sages; however, his austerity and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> did not prevent his being accused of having no <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. This was probably founded on certain Dialogues written by him, and published under the name of Oratius Tubero, and upon his showing throughout his works in general too <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> an inclination to skepticism. He was greatly affected at the loss of his only son; and his grief disordered him so much, that he married again, though he was above 75, and had no reason to lament his first wife. He died in 1672, aged 84.

VESPA

Pages 1246-1247

the wasp, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a>, a genus of insects of the hymenoptera order; of which the following are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>: The mouth is armed with jaws, but has no rostrum; the upper wings are folded in both sexes; the sting is sharp-pointed, and concealed within the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a>; the eyes are lunular; the body is smooth, without <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>; to which may be added, that the antennae are broken, the first articulation being longer than the rest; the under wings shorter than the upper; the abdomen joined to the thorax by a very short stalk; and the sternum three in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. 1. The crabro, has the antennae and head of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUN">dun</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, somewhat <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>. The upper lip is <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, and the eyes are blackish. The middle of the thorax is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>; brown on the fore-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a>, the sides, and behind. The legs are of the same brown colour, inclining to chestnut. The first segment of the abdomen is black mixed with brown, and slightly edged with lemon colour; the others are black on the upper side, a portion of which is again covered by the upper segment, and yellow underneath. Upon the yellow are seen two black spots on each of the rings; one on each side, connected with the black colour of the upper part. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of wasps makes its nest in the trunks of hollow trees, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> of lofts. Its <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> combs are composed of a substance resembling coarse <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> or ruffly <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a>. It is very voracious, devouring other insects, and even bees. Of those insects, some live in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, others are solitary. A distinguishing character of this genus of flies is their bodies being smooth and apparently without hairs. Their upper wings, when at rest, are folded in two the whole length of them. At the rise of each of those wings is situate a fleshy part, which performs the office of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> to hinder the upper wing from rising. rising too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> in the flapping of their wings; a caution very important to those carnivorous insects who pursue their prey on full stretch of wing. 2. The vulgaris, or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> wasp. These raise subterraneous buildings, live in associations, feed on plunder, and commit <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> outrages on our wall-fruit. This numerous commonwealth is founded by a single <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> impregnated during the autumn, and that has weathered out the severity of the winter. It digs a hole in a dry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, contrives itself a sinuous inlet, or else it takes up with the dwelling-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOLE">mole</a>, where it hastily builds a few cells and deposits its eggs. Within the space of 20 days, they have gone through the different states of larva, chrysalids, and are turned to wasps. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a>, all-wise, provides for every thing. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MULE">mule</a>-wasps, or that are of no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, are the only ones that labour at laying the foundation of the republic. The first eggs that are hatched prove to be <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEUTER">neuter</a> wasps. No sooner are they come into existence, but they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> to work, enlarge the hole, and go about upon wood, lattice-work, and window-sashes, in search of materials for <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. With their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> they cut, hack, and tear off small fibres of wood, which they moisten with a liquor they disgorge, and then convey them to the work-shop. Other labourers are in waiting for them, who with these materials set about the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of the wasp-nest; an edifice outwardly composed of sheets of paper, which not being in contact with each other, dampness cannot penetrate to the inside. This latter part consists of 12 or 15 stories, and between each runs a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLONNADE">colonnade</a> formed by the fastenings which connect the cakes one to the other. Every story is as it were a market-place, where the citizens may take their walks. The cells are hexagonal. It is the cradle in which the mother continues to lay eggs of neuter-wasps to the number of 15000 or 16000; after which it deposits 300 eggs of females, and as many of males. The elder brothers, or first-batched insects, take amazing care of those born after them, by proportioning their food to the delicacy of their stomach. First, it consists of the juice of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> and meats, afterwards it is the carcases of insects. The caterers provide for the labourers. Each one takes his own portion; there is no dispute, no fighting. The republic grows daily more numerous, living in profound peace. Every individual, as soon as he has acquired sufficient strength, flies away to the fields. They then become a gang of banditti; they pillage our wall-trees, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> into our fruit before its maturity, dart with the fierceness of hawks upon our bees, cut their throats to possess themselves of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, plunder and lay waste their commonwealth, riot on the fruits of their labour, and oblige them to remove. During the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of plenty, the wasps bring all the booty to the nest, and share it amongst them. There is nothing then goes forwards but feasting, rioting, and good-fellowship; but concord cannot be lasting among robbers. Towards the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of October <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> begin to run short; when this lively, this <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMICABLE">amicable</a> young brood is fired with a kind of rage, and the nest is now nothing but a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of horror. The neuters and males tear from their cradles the eggs, the larva, the chrysalids, and the new-born insects, without showing mercy to any. They next fight one against another, though their duels seldom proceed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> as those of the bees. The males alone are destitute of stings. The hopes of the state, the solicitude for posterity, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of their native place, no longer exist; the whole commonwealth is overturned to the very foundation. Frosts and rains throw the citizens into a state of languor. They almost all perish, luckily for us and our bees. Some few females escape the disasters of intestine <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WAR">war</a> and the severity of winter, which in the ensuing spring become founders of new republics. One robber is sometimes useful in bringing another to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>. Some butchers hang up before their shop a calf's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a> or any other tender meat. The wasps come in quest of this delicate food; and, fond of enjoying it to themselves, they pursue the blue-bottle flies, from whose eggs are produced the maggots that spoil meat: and this is the only advantage we can reap from wasps. 3. The aerial wasps are a very small species; nor is their society numerous. Their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, as well as their manners, are the same as those of the common wasp; but their buildings are on a different construction. Their nest is fastened to the branch of a tree with a kind of a band, and is in bigness from the size of an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to that of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EGG">egg</a>. Wood reduced to paper is the material part of it, which, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it were of a ruddy colour, might be taken for a large opening rose. It is covered over with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a> impenetrable by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>. One of those nests was neither mollified nor impaired by that element.—There are 25 other species.

VIRGULA DIVINA

Pages 1247-1247
or Boculus divinatorius, &c., a forked branch, in the form of a Y, cut off an hazel-stick, by means whereof people have pretended to discover mines, springs, &c. under ground. The method of using it is thus: The person who bears it, walking very slowly over the places where he suspects mines or springs may be, the effluvia exhaling from the metals, or vapour from the water, impregnating the wood, makes it dip or incline, which is the sign of a discovery. Some dispute the matter of fact, and deny it to be possible. Others, convinced by the great number of experiments alleged in its behalf, look out for the natural causes thereof: The corpulency, say those authors, rising from the springs or minerals, entering the rod, determine it to bow down, in order to render it parallel to the vertical lines which the effluvia describe in their rise. The famous Father Kircher, in his Mundus Subterraneus, in which many interesting particulars are found concerning mines, derides these practices, and denies, from his own experience, the truth of the affections concerning them. He seems, however, to have some faith in sympathies, and proposes even new divining wands of his own invention; the effects of which, though more dependent on physical causes, are not, however, more certain. He believes, for instance, that a wand, one end of which should be made of sal gem, and the other of wood, being suspended and balanced above a mine of salt, would be inclined towards the ground; and he supports his opinion by an experiment. This experiment consists in evaporating over the fire a solution of sal gem below the wand, which is by this means really made to incline. We need not be deeply learned in chemistry to discover, that the wand would have inclined in the same manner if Father Kircher had evaporated pure water instead of a solution of sal gem; because the water would have equally well attached itself to the saline end of the wand; consequently this experiment proves nothing. The same author proposes also to discover mines of

VITEX

Pages 1247-1248

the Agnus Castus, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> Chaste Tree; a genus of the angiospermia order, belonging to the dynastia class of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. There are three <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; of which the most remarkable is the agnus castus, or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> chaste tree. This grows naturally in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a> near <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, by the sides of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, and in the Archipelago in moist places; it has a shrubby stalk 10 or 12 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, sending out branches opposite the whole length, which are angular, pliable, and have a greyish bark, garnished with leaves for the most <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> placed opposite, composed of five, six, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> lobes, which unite at the footstalk, and spread out like the fingers of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, ending in blunt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, of a dark green on their upper side, but hoary on their under. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> are produced in spikes at the extremity of the branches, from seven to fifteen inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, diploped in whorls round the stalks, with intervals between each whorl; they are of the lip-kind; the two lips are each cut into three segments, the middle being larger than the two sides; in some plants <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, and in others blue; these are generally late before they appear; so that in bad seasons they do not open fair. The flowers have an agreeable odour, and make a good appearance in autumn, when the flowers of most other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a> are gone; for, in warm mild seasons, these shrubs are in full flower in the middle of October. This sort is pretty common in many English gardens, where it has been long an inhabitant, but was not much propagated till of late years. It is very hardy; and may be propagated by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CUTTINGS">cuttings</a> early in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, before they shoot.

VITRIFICATION

Pages 1248-1253

the production of glass, one of the most curious and most important operations in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>. See Glass, (Encycl.) The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, and perfect transparency, of glass render it very extensively useful in ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, in chemistry, and in many arts. Almost any form may be given to glass, and all kinds of vessels and utensils may be formed of it, which are capable of resisting the most powerful corrosives and solvents. Glass is capable of receiving and preserving the finest polish. Its properties of transmitting and refracting the rays of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, and of reflecting these rays when one of its surfaces is covered with a metallic coat, render it very useful for constructing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRRORS">mirrors</a>, telescopes, microscopes, and all kinds of optical glasses; for collecting, separating, and decomposing the rays of light; and for exhibiting many wonderful catoptrical and dioptrical appearances and experiments. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> to these admirable properties we add that of imitating the many brilliant precious <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, opaque <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> transparent, we shall easily be convinced that perfect glass is one of the most beautiful and excellent productions of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> industry. Perfect glass, or the most beautiful fictitious crystal, is perfectly similar in appearance to the whitest and most transparent natural vitrifiable stones. The only sensible <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between these natural and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> productions is, that the latter are much less hard and more fusible than natural crystal or any other vitrifiable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. In fact, pure glass or artificial crystal is essentially of the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> as vitrifiable stones; or we may rather say, that it is vitrifiable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> itself rendered more fusible only by certain additions, as we shall soon show. The most simple and elementary of all earths, called by chemists vitrifiable earth, forms the hardest and most transparent of all natural bodies when its integrant parts are united together in a due state of aggregation; but the parts of vitrifiable earth cannot form this aggregation, unless they have been previously so much separated from each other that they possess a mobility, which enables them to unite together according to their natural tendency; the integrant parts of elementary earth may acquire this mobility by two methods; namely, by the interposition of the parts of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a> or of those of fire. Almost all the vitrifiable stones that we know, as diamonds, rock-crystal, and other hard transparent stones, appear to have been once dispersed in infinitely small molecules through much water, from which they have afterwards been deposited, and then have united together and formed the very hard transparent masses which we now see. Possibly some of these stones may have been formed by fire, and by a true fusion. Of these two ways, that of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> and elaboration by water cannot be practised by human art, on account of the many ages required for the operation. By the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> method, namely, fusion, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> required for which is better adapted to the shortness of our lives, we certainly might, with a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, melt vitrifiable earth, and all other kinds of earths; since these, when sufficiently purified, are reduced to the nature of vitrifiable earth; and we might convert these earths into masses of crystal, or of hard transparent stones, as perfect as the natural precious stones. In a word, nothing but a heat sufficiently intense is required to melt any earthly <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, and to convert it into a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a> as brilliant and as hard as the most perfect natural diamonds; but here a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, and hitherto unformidable, difficulty occurs, namely, to produce a heat sufficiently intense to melt the most pure and simple vitrifiable earth; for the most violent heat that art has ever produced is insufficient to melt even many of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> impure earths and stones; and is therefore much less capable of melting that earth, which, because it is the simplest and purest, is also the most unfusable of all natural bodies. Hence we conclude, that although we know by what means the parts of the purest earthly principle may be so united as to form bodies similar to the natural precious stones, yet we cannot possibly put these means <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> means in execution; but if we cannot artificially produce <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> masses of pure earth exactly similar in all their properties to the natural precious stones, we can however very well imitate these beautiful natural productions, not in their hardness and fusibility, but in their transparency and lustre; that is, in their most obvious and striking qualities, by means of compositions of glass or fictitious crystal. The solution of this problem is founded on the following principles. First, pure and elementary earth, which makes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> basis of all vitrifications, and therefore called vitrifiable earth, is indeed fusible with regard to us; but we know, that certain very fusible substances are capable of uniting intimately with this earth, and of communicating to it some of their fusibility; so that by their means we may reduce it to a perfect fusion. Secondly, the substances capable of acting upon the earthy principle are the inflammable principle or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHLOGISTON">phlogiston</a>, and several saline matters; but we may remark, that as these substances do only <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> as fluxes by uniting intimately with the vitrifiable earth, and while they themselves make <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the glass; and also, as the integrant parts of these fluxes are not capable of forming either with each other, or with the parts of vitrifiable earth, so strong an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADHESION">adhesion</a> as that which can be formed between the parts of the pure vitrifiable earth; it follows, that all fictitious crystal must be much less hard than natural crystals or other hard stones, since these contain only pure vitrifiable earth. Thirdly, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the principle, that all <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> bodies partake of the properties of their component parts, fictitious crystals ought to partake so much more of the properties of inflammable and saline matters, and ought to be removed so much more from those of pure vitrifiable stones, as they contain a larger <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of those matters. Accordingly we find, that the smaller quantity of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FLUX">flux</a> that is contained in glass, the greater hardness, lustre, and resemblance to natural stones it has, provided the fusion has been complete. Thus glass is so much more perfect, as it possesses more of the properties of vitrifiable earth. These principles, which are incontestable, being once understood, are easily applicable to the art of making glass; since, if we could produce a fire sufficiently intense, and bad furnaces and vessels capable of sustaining it, we should make glass equal to the precious stones: it is therefore evident, that the most important object in vitrification, is to have furnaces capable of producing the greatest heat, and pots or crucibles capable of resisting, during a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> time, this heat, and also the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the vitreous matter that they contain. These pots, as has been elsewhere observed, ought to be made entirely of the most refractory and purest clay, well washed and cleansed from all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FERRUGINOUS">ferruginous</a>, and pyritous matters, and mixed with a certain proportion of the same clay baked, and pounded not very finely. The quantity of baked clay that ought to be mixed with the crude clay, to prevent the pots from cracking, when dried or when exposed to violent heat, is not absolutely determined, but varies in different glass-houses, according as the crude clay employed be more or less fat, as it is called. The ovens and furnaces are different, according to the quantity of materials to be vitrified. See the article Glass, (Encycl.) In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> works, wood or fossil coal are used; and the furnaces are so constructed that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a> circulates and burns within very intensely. As these furnaces vary much in different countries and glass-houses, and as a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> would not be very intelligible without figures, we shall refer the reader to other works in which these several furnaces are described and represented; particularly to the French edition of Neri's Art of making Glass, with Notes by Merret and by Kunckel; and to an excellent Memoir by Dr D'Antic of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. We shall here say only in general, that these furnaces are placed under large and lofty buildings called halls; that they are covered with a vaulted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a>; and that they have no chimney, but only lateral openings, through which the melted glass is drawn from the pots. Under these openings is built a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLATFORM">platform</a> or banquette, on which the pots containing the glass stand, one of which is opposite to each opening. In the middle of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a>, below the banquette, is a space, across which <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> bars are laid. In this space, which communicates with a large cavity below called the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a>-hole, the fuel is placed. In these furnaces, which have not any chimney, as we have said, the fire is nevertheless very intense. This intense heat is occasioned by the great capacity of the furnace, by means of which a strong draught of air passes continually from the air-hole; besides, the flame being vividly agitated by air, and not being drawn out of the furnace by any chimney, circulates in every <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> within the furnace, and produces a very violent heat. Most glass-houses have also hollow towers that communicate with the cavity of the furnace, and which therefore increase the capacity of the whole. In these the heat is not nearly so intense as in the furnace. They are employed to contain the frit, or the pieces of manufactured glass that are to be annealed. Such is the general disposition of the furnaces of glass-houses. Next to the good condition of the pots and furnaces, the most important and essential matter is the consideration of the kinds and proportion of the fluxes. Of these we may observe two kinds, namely, the inflammable and the saline. As we cannot obtain the pure inflammable principle, we must, when we intend that it should enter into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of glass, choose for this purpose some of the earthy substances with which it is found naturally combined; and these are particularly metallic earths, which are best adapted for conveying phlogiston into vitreous compositions; but all these earths are not equally fit for this purpose. All <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> are composed of an earthy matter intimately combined with a sufficient quantity of the inflammable principle to be very fusible, and at the same time very opaque. Some of these metals, namely, those called perfect, are unalterable by fire, and cannot be entirely, or even partly, deprived of phlogiston; but as every metallic substance is incapable of uniting with earthly matters while it retains its metallic state, therefore no perfect metal can be vitrified. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> is different with those metallic substances, the phlogiston of which may be burnt, or otherwise destroyed. The earths or calxes of most, perhaps of all combustible metals, when not perfectly deprived of all their phlogiston, are capable of being reduced to a vitreous state, by means of their remaining inflammable principle. As they are not then in a metallic state, they can facilitate the fusion of vitrifiable earths, may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> with these an intimate union, and reduce them to a state of perfect vitrification: but these phlogisticated calxes of imperfect metals promote vitrification more or less, ac- Vitrification according to their particular natures. Some of these, as, for instance, tin, cannot be without great difficulty brought to that precise degree of calcination that is necessary to vitrification; because the heat required for this purpose deprives them of all their phlogiston, and renders them in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> degree refractory. Others, in whatever manner they be calcined, either retain too little phlogiston to be sufficiently fusible, although they still retain enough to give them <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; or if they be not calcined so much as to lose their fusibility, they cannot be melted but into opaque masses, so nearly in a metallic state that they cannot be united intimately with vitrifiable earths. Such, especially, are the earths of iron and of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>. Of all metallic earths, that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> is fittest for vitrification. This metal, which contains a large portion of phlogiston, is quickly deprived of so much of it, that it loses its metallic state, and is easily melted into a transparent vitreous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a>; but it has, at the same time, this remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, that when once it has lost as much phlogiston as is necessary to dispose it to vitrification, its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CALX">calx</a> strongly retains as much of it as is necessary to give to it its greatest degree of vitreosity; and that it may be sooner dissipated into vapours by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> action of a very intense fire, than it can be changed into an earth totally <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPHLOGISTICATED">dephlogisticated</a>, and consequently refractory, like the calxes of tin and of regulus of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a>. Besides, the fusible earth of lead is one of those that retain the least colour. All these qualities render it preferable to any other metallic earth for the purposes of vitrification. The earth of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BISMUTH">bismuth</a>, which in the above-mentioned properties resembles the earth of lead, may probably be employed with equal success; but as the calxes of lead are much more common than those of bismuth, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of this semi-metal is not known to manufacturers of glass. In whatever manner the calx of lead has been prepared, provided it be really in a calcined and not in a metallic state, it may be used in vitrification. Accordingly, the grey calx, or ashes of lead, massicot, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>-lead, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LITHARGE">litharge</a>, ceros, and all the precipitates of lead, separated from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a> by unmetallic intermediate substances, being mixed with sand or any other vitrifiable stone, and exposed to a sufficient degree of fire, do always promote the fusion of these matters, and form with them glasses more or less hard and transparent, according to the strength of the fire and the proportion of the ingredients. The earth of lead constantly retains, as we have said, enough of the inflammable principle to preserve its fusibility. When it is exposed singly to the fire, it vitrifies with a very moderate heat. It has more phlogiston than is requisite for its vitrification. The fusibility, fluidity, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> of this glass of lead, when pure, are so great, that it cannot be contained in any crucible, all which it easily pervades; therefore pure glass of lead is never made. But as the calx of lead has more phlogiston than is required for its own vitrification, it may divide this excess of inflammable principle with any unmetallic earths with which it is mixed, and thus may produce their fusion and perfect vitrification. The glasses formed by a mixture of calx of lead with unmetallic earths, have more confidence, hardness, and less fusibility, than pure glass of lead. The proportions of calx of lead and of sand employed in these kinds of glass are from one part to two of calx of lead, to one of sand or of ground flints. We may observe upon the subject of glasses that contain no other flux than phlogiston or metallic earths, of lead, or of any other metal, that none of them are perfectly <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, but are all more or less coloured; because phlogiston is, as chemists know, the principle of colours. Secondly, these glasses have a greater density or specific gravity than any natural crystalline stone, all metallic earths being heavier than any that are not metallic. Thirdly, metallic glasses are generally somewhat less brittle, are less liable to be broken by the alterations of heat and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, and have more of a certain smoothness, or, as it were, uncouthness, not easily to be described, than glasses made altogether of unmetallic earths. These properties can only be attributed to the inflammable principle, a pretty considerable quantity of which is united with them. As these latter qualities of glass are valuable, a certain quantity of calx of lead generally enters into the composition of most fine glasses, which are distinguished from ordinary glass by the name crystal-glass. From what we have said concerning the properties of metallic earths in vitrification, we may perceive, that the more calx of lead, or other metallic earth, enters into the composition of any glass, the more fusible, soft, coloured, and dense this glass is; and reciprocally. The colours given to glass by calxes of lead are shades of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>. Saline substances are the second kind of fluxes used in vitrification; but all these substances are not equally fit for this purpose; nor that they are not all very fusible, but for several reasons hereafter to be mentioned. First, neither the pure and disengaged acids, nor volatile alkalis, nor ammoniacal salts, can be employed as fluxes in vitrification; because none of these saline matters is sufficiently fixed. Their volatility is so great, that they may be totally dissipated by fire before they could act in any degree upon vitrifiable earth. Secondly, none of the neutral salts with basis of fixed alkali, containing either vitriolic acid, or marine acid, can be employed as fluxes in vitrification. This proceeds, not from their want of fusibility, or of the necessary degree of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FIXITY">fixity</a>, but from the union of the acid and the alkali; which is so strong that they cannot act with sufficient force upon other substances, and particularly upon vitrifiable earth. The saline matters fit for vitrification are, fixed alkalis, vegetable and mineral; nitres with basis of fixed alkali; sedative <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BORAX">borax</a>; fusible salt of urine, or rather phosphoric acid. Of all saline matters, fixed alkalis, vegetable and mineral, are most frequently used in vitrification. These alkalis are fusible with a moderate heat; they are so fixed that they can resist during a sufficient time the heat of ordinary vitrifications; and they act powerfully upon flints, sands, and other vitrifiable stones. The proportion of alkali to sand, in order to make good glass, is, from one to two parts of the former ingredient, and two parts of the latter. Nitre produces in vitrification nearly the same effects as fixed alkalis, although it be a neutral salt; the alkali and acid of which are united together nearly as they are in common salt, which however does not produce in vitrification similar effects. The remarkable difference in this respect between these two salts, and In many mixtures, it quitted the vitrifiable earth with which it was mixed, and acted upon the crucible, which it penetrated and dissolved. These experiments seem to show, that arsenic has a greater <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> with clays than with vitrifiable earths. From Mr Pott's experiments, chemists know, that vitrifiable, calcareous, and argillaceous earths, each of which are singly insoluble, do reciprocally promote the fusion of each other, when mixed together nearly in equal proportions, and exposed to a very violent heat; and that from these mixtures matters perfectly vitrified are formed. But as we do not know the cause of this singular fusibility, we cannot determine whether it is produced by a phlogistic or by a saline substance, or perhaps by both. Glasses that contain no other fluxing ingredient than phlogistic matters or metallic earths, partake of the properties of these metallic earths; and also glasses that contain only saline fluxes, partake of the properties of salts. The latter, or saline glasses, when pure and well proportioned, are less heavy, less dense, harder, whiter, more brilliant, more brittle, than the glasses containing calx of lead; and glasses containing both saline and metallic fluxes do also partake of the properties of both these substances. In general, glasses too saline are soft, and easily susceptible of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> by the action of air and water; especially those in which alkalis prevail; which latter glasses are also liable to be attacked by acids, as we evidently see from the properties of the vitrified matter that is made with an excess of alkali, for the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of liquor of flints. Glasses containing too much borax and arsenic, although at first very beautiful, do quickly tarnish and become opaque when exposed to air. From what we have said concerning the properties of fluxes, phlogistic or saline, we may know how to adjust the proportions of these to the sand or powdered flints for the various kinds of glasses. Thus, if we require a glass that is dense, fusible, and not saline, one part and a half of red-lead or litharge may be mixed with one part of sand, and fused together. If equal parts of sand and of calx of lead be employed, a glass somewhat less dense and harder <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> be produced. If a glass be required of very little density, only saline fluxes must be employed. A glass of this kind may be composed of six parts of salt of tartar, or of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POTASH">potash</a>, or of purified soda, mixed with eight parts of sand or of flints; or of four parts of any of the above-mentioned alkalis, mixed with two parts of nitre or of borax, and eight parts of vitrifiable earth. These glasses must be left long in the fire, for the reasons hereafter to be mentioned. When a crystal-glass is required which shall be of an intermediate <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> between the metallic and saline glasses, it may be made from a mixture of one part of the above-mentioned salts, one part of calx of lead, and two parts of sand or other vitrifiable earth. By varying the proportions of these ingredients, many different kinds of glasses may be produced, each of which may be good, if the quantity of each of the fluxes employed be proportionate to its vitrifying power. Several good receipts for glass and fictitious crystal may be found in Neri's Art of Making Glasses, with Notes by Merret and Kunckel; to which <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> we refer for many interesting particulars. See also the article Glass, (Encycl.) We shall however observe, that the proportions of the fluxes necessary to produce any required kind kind of glass cannot be precisely ascertained, for the following reasons. First, the sands, flints, and other stones <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> employed for making of glass, are not all equally fusible. Thus the quartzose sand obtained by washing an earth found near <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NEVERS">Nevers</a>, known to manufacturers of glass and of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-POTTERY">pottery</a> by the name of sand of Nevers, may be almost entirely melted when exposed to a good vitrifying heat; and by a moderate heat its grains may be considerably rounded. There are some other hard stones, which in a violent fire are still more fusible, and convertible into an almost transparent glass without addition. The fusibility of these vitreifiable stones is caused by some unknown <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HETEROGENEOUS">heterogeneous</a> matter united with them. These fusible sands and stones require a much less quantity of flux to promote their vitrification than other sands or vitrifiable stones which are much purer, and therefore more refractory. Secondly, although the phlogistic and saline matters employed as fluxes in vitrification are sufficiently fixed to support the degree of fire necessary for the fusion of glass, they are nevertheless far from being so fixed as vitrifiable earth. The fire necessary for the perfect fusion of glass is even sufficient to evaporate them entirely. Accordingly, in glass-houses where the pots are uncovered, a vapour or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> continually rises from their surface, which is nothing else than the saline and phlogistic fluxes in a state of continual exhalation. Hence the longer glass remains melted in the fire, the harder and more difficultly fusible it becomes, and the more it partakes of the properties of pure vitrifiable earth. Accordingly, even when a very hard glass is required, such a quantity of flux ought to be added as shall at first promote a perfect fusion; and this fusion ought to be continued a long time till a considerable quantity of the flux is gradually distillated, and till the glass has acquired the requisite degree of hardness, provided that the fire be sufficiently strong to maintain the fusion notwithstanding the loss of flux. From these observations it appears, that we cannot precisely ascertain the proportion of flux to vitrifiable earth, unless we knew the fusibility of the sand to be employed, and the degree of heat which can be excited in the furnace. The saline fluxes, and especially the fixed alkalis employed in vitrification, are generally rendered impure by a mixture of several heterogeneous matters, and especially by neutral salts not vitrifiable, and by a certain quantity of inflammable principle. In manufactories of bottles and other common glass, the alkalis employed are not previously purified, but are even mixed with the earth of the ashes of the burnt <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, which earth is also much disposed to vitrification. Accordingly, to make glass of this kind, sand is mixed with common wood-ashes, sometimes even with those which have been lixiviated, together with some unpurified potash, soda, or kelp; and from this mixture a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, dusky, not very transparent glass is produced, which is preferred in common <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-SALE">sale</a> for wine bottles to clearer and more transparent glass. But when a fine, white, and very transparent glass is required, the alkali must be perfectly purified from all heterogeneous matter, by lixiviation and calcination. As too large a quantity of the inflammable principle is the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> cause of the colours and of the opacity of glass, when a perfectly colourless and transparent glass is required, not only the alkalis must be deprived of all their superabundant phlogiston, but also the sands or flints employed must be purified from any of this principle which they may contain. The method used for this purpose is by mixing together the due proportions of sands and salts, by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> this mixture during a considerable time to a red heat, not intense enough to melt it. By this calcination, the phlogiston of these matters is burnt and distillated, all colour is destroyed, and the glass produced is also more clear and brilliant. This first mixture of materials of glass, when calcined, is called the frit; and this frit is used in large manufactories not only for the finer glass, but also for the common brown glass; not with an intention to render this latter kind of glass colourless, but because, during this calcination, the salts and earth begin to act upon each other, and to incorporate in a certain degree; by which a great part of the effervescence and foaming occasioned by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REACTION">reaction</a> of these matters, which happen when they are at once exposed to a melting heat, are avoided. Accordingly, when matters not previously fritted are employed in small experiments, the heat must be applied gradually; otherwise they so swell, that frequently the greatest part of the mixture runs over the crucible. The due degree of heat is an essential point in making of glass; it ought not only to be very strong, but also maintained during a long time. In great manufactories, the glass is kept fused during ten or twelve hours before it is taken out of the pots. Accordingly their glass is always more perfect than that which is hastily made in small quantity in two or three hours. Good glass, although kept in fusion in a very great heat, is not perfectly liquid. It is always somewhat thick, and when taken from the crucible, it may be drawn out into fine wire or threads; which shows that it has a certain consistence and a very sensible tenacity when it is red-hot. It is not transparent while it remains red-hot, not even when it has become perfectly hard. Another remarkable circumstance is, that glass which is so brittle when it is cold and transparent, is very ductile when it is so heated as to be opaque. We might be induced to believe, that the disengaged fire with which the glass is filled when it is red-hot, produces upon it the same effect that phlogiston or combined fire produces upon metals. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DUCTILITY">ductility</a> of red-hot glass is very useful; for by its means all imaginable shapes may be given to glass, and numberless vessels and utensils may be easily formed of it. As soon as glass-vessels have received their intended form, they must be cooled very gradually, otherwise they would have no solidity, and would be of little use, as they would be liable to be broken by the smallest stroke, or by a slight change of heat and cold.
