This inconvenience is prevented in glass-houses by carrying the glass vessels as soon as they are formed, and while yet red-hot, into an oven too little heated to destroy their form, but in which they may be very gradually cooled. This is called <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANNEALING">annealing</a> the glass. Notwithstanding all the care taken in the manufactories of the finer kinds of glass, as crystal-glass and plate-glass, to make them perfectly good, they are nevertheless seldom found quite free from faults. The principal faults in glass are, colours, bubbles, and veins. The colours which generally hurt glass, especially that kind which contains saline fluxes, are shades of green, olive, and blue. These colours are destroyed by manganese; which being added in small quantities, clears the glass, and is therefore sometimes called by artists This effect of manganese cannot easily be explained, for it has the property of tinging glass with a purple colour. Mr Montamy, in his "Traité des Couleurs pour la Peinture en Email," has a very fine and ingenious thought upon this subject; which is, that the manganese destroys the above-mentioned colours, by adding to these a purple tinge, and by the mixture producing a blackish brown colour; and that as blackness is caused merely by an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSORPTION">absorption</a> of the rays of light, therefore the blackish tinge given to the glass by the above mixture of colours, prevents the reflection of so many rays, and thus renders the glass less coloured than before. The causes of the bubbles and of the veins in all glasses, even when most carefully prepared, and the methods of preventing these faults, are not sufficiently known. We shall observe, in concluding this article, that several causes lessen or entirely prevent the transparency of glass, which is one of its most necessary qualities. As we cannot melt vitrifiable earth into transparent masses but by means of fluxes, and a sufficiently strong and long-continued heat; therefore when the vitreous mixture contains too little flux, or is exposed to too little heat, some parts of the vitrifiable earth cannot be entirely fused, and therefore injure more or less, according to their quantity, the transparency of the glass. The same fault may be perceived in glass, when it contains some earthly matter not susceptible of the action of fluxes, as vitrifiable earth is; such as, for instance, most metallic earths that are too much dephlogisticated, particularly the earth of tin. Accordingly, these earths are employed to make opaque or semi-transparent glasses, as enamels, artificial opals, and other such stones. Another remark may be made concerning the transparency of some kinds of glass, that it is destructible by too long exposure to violent heat. As all fluxes, phlogistic or saline, are much less fixed than vitrifiable earth, and as some fluxes are less fixed than others, or less capable of becoming fixed by being mixed with vitrifiable earth; the cause therefore of the loss of transparency which some glasses suffer by a too violent fire is, that a part of their flux is dissipated, so that these glasses are decomposed, and that they contain so much earth that the flux is incapable of keeping them completely fused. It has been observed that glasses formed by a mixture of argillaceous and gypseous or calcareous earths, are more liable than any others to this loss of transparency. UNIVERSE. (Encycl.) As space is in its own nature every way infinite, it gives us an idea of the infinity of the universe, which can therefore be only in part comprehended by us; and that part of the universe which we can have any notion of, is that which is the subject of our senses; and of this the eye presents us with an idea of a vast extended prospect, and the appearance of various sorts of bodies disseminated through the same. The infinite <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABYSS">abyss</a> of space, which the Greeks call το ουρανός, the Latins inane, and we the universe, does undoubtedly comprehend an infinity of systems of moving bodies round one very large central one, which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> called sol, and we the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. This collection of bodies is therefore properly called the solar system, and sometimes the mundane system, from the Latin word mundus the "world." That the universe contains as many solar systems or worlds as there are what we call fixed stars, seems reasonable to infer from hence, that our sun, removed to the distance of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STAR">star</a>, would appear <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JUST">just</a> as a star does, and all the bodies moving about it would disappear entirely. Now the reason why they disappear is, because they are opaque bodies, and too small to be seen at so great a distance, without an intense degree of light; whereas theirs is the weakest that can be, as being first borrowed, and then reflected to the eye. But the sun, by reason of his immense bulk and innate light, which is the strongest possible, will be visible at an immense distance; but the greater the distance, the less bright it will appear, and of a lesser magnitude: and therefore every star of every magnitude may probably be a sun like our own, informing a system of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a> or moving bodies; each of which may be inhabited, like our earth, with various kinds of animals, and flored with vegetable and other substances. We can perceive, says Mr MacLaurin, no bounds of the vast expanse in which natural causes operate; nor can we fix any border or termination of the universe; and we are equally at a loss to trace things to their elements, and to discover the limits which enclose the subdivisions of matter. The objects which we commonly call great, vanish when we contemplate the vast body of the earth. The terraqueous globe itself is soon lost in the solar system; being in some parts seen as a planet or distant star, and in great part of the system unknown, or visible only at rare times to vigilant observers, assisted perhaps with instruments like our telescopes. The sun itself dwindles into a star: its turn's vast orbit, and the orbits of all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMETS">comets</a>, crowd into a point when viewed from numberless places between the earth and the nearest fixed stars. Other suns illuminate other systems where our sun's rays are unperceived; but all these are also swallowed up in the vast expanse of the universe. Even all the systems of the stars that sparkle in the clearest sky, must possess a small corner only of that space over which such systems are dispersed. And after we have risen so high, and left all definite <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> so far behind us, we find ourselves no nearer to a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TERM">term</a> or limit; for all this is nothing to what may be displayed in the infinite expanse, beyond the remotest stars that ever have been discovered. In this view of the universe, an august idea arises in the mind, worthy of the infinite and wise Author of nature, who can never be supposed to have created so many glorious orbs, to answer so trifling a purpose as the twinkling to mortals by night now and then; besides that the far greatest part of the stars are never seen by us at all.

WARBURTON

Pages 1254-1256

bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a>, a learned prelate, was born at Newark upon <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTTINGHAM">Nottingham</a>, Dec. 24, 1698. His father was George Warburton, an attorney, and town-clerk of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, in which this his eldest son received his birth and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>. While at school, the bishop showed no indication of superior genius. His original designation was to the same profession as that of his father and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a>-father; and he was accordingly placed clerk to an attorney, with whom he remained until he was qualified to engage in business upon his own account. He was then admitted to one of the courts at Westminster; and for some years <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> the employment of an attorney and solicitor at the place of his birth. The success he met with as a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MAN">man</a> of business was probably not <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a>. It was certainly insufficient to induce him to devote the rest of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> to it; and it is probable, that his want of encouragement might tempt him to turn his thoughts towards a profession in which his literary acquisitions would be more valuable, and in which he might more easily pursue the bent of his inclination. He appears to have brought from school more learning than was requisite for a practising lawyer. This might rather impede than forward his progress, as it has been generally observed, that an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to literary concerns, and the bustle of an attorney's office, with only a moderate share of business, are wholly incompatible. It is therefore no wonder that he preferred retirement to noise, and relinquished what advantages he might expect from continuing to follow the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a>. It has been suggested by an ingenious writer, that he was for some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> usher to a school. In the year 1724, his first <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, consisting of translations from Caesar, Pliny Claudian, and others, appeared under the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of "Miscellaneous Translations in Prose and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-VERSE">Verse</a>, from Roman Poets, Orators, and Historians," 12mo. It is dedicated to his early <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>, Sir Robert Sutton, and seems to have laid the foundation of his first <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> preferment. At this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> it is probable he had not abandoned his profession, though it is certain he did not attend to it much longer. About Christmas 1726 he came to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; and while there, was introduced to Theobald, Concanen, and others of Mr Pope's enemies, with whose conversation he was extremely pleased. In 1727, he published a work, entitled, "A Critical and Philological Enquiry into the Causes of Prodigies and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">Miracles</a>, as related by Historians," &c., 12mo, and was also dedicated to Sir Robert Sutton. He was at this time in orders, and on the 25th of April 1728, had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to be in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> of Masters of Arts, created at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, on his majesty's visit to that university. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, the same year, he was presented by Sir Robert Sutton to the rectory of Burnt Broughton, in the county of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>; a living which he retained till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, at which he spent a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of his middle life in a studious retirement, devoted entirely to letters, and there planned, and in part executed, some of his most important works. Several years elapsed, after obtaining this preferment, before Mr Warburton appeared again in the world as a writer. It was in this year 1736, that he may be said to have emerged from the obscurity of a private life into the notice of the world. The first publication which rendered him afterwards famous now appeared under the title of "The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">Alliance</a> between <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a> and State; <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-NECESSITY">Necessity</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EQUITY">Equity</a> of an Established <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGION">Religion</a> and a Test-law, demonstrated from the Essence and End of Civil <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, upon the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> Principles of the Law of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> and Nations." At the end was announced the scheme of "The Divine Legation of Moses demonstrated on the Principles of a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> Deity, from the omission of the doctrine of a future state of rewards and punishments in the Jewish dispensation;" and met with a reception which neither the subject, nor the manner in which it was treated, seemed to authorize. It was, as the author afterwards observed, fallen upon in so outrageous and brutal a manner, as had been scarce pardonable, had it been "The Divine Legation of Mahomet."—It produced several answers, and so much abuse from the authors of "The Weekly Miscellany," that in less than two months he was constrained to defend himself, in "A Vindication of the Author of the Divine Legation of Moses, from the Asperities of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">Country</a> Clergyman's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LETTER">Letter</a> in the Weekly Miscellany of February 24, 1737-8," 8vo. Mr Warburton's extraordinary merit had now attracted the notice of the heir-apparent to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>; in whose immediate <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> we find him in June 1738, when he published "<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FAITH">Faith</a> working by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">Charity</a> to Christian Edification; a sermon preached at the last episcopal visitation for <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of Lincoln; with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a>, showing the reasons of its publication, and a postscript, occasioned by some letters lately published in the Weekly Miscellany. By William Warburton, M.A. Chaplain to his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Highness the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>." A <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SECOND">second</a> edition of "The Divine Legation" also appeared in November 1738. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1739, the world was in danger of being deprived of this extraordinary genius by an intermitting fever, which with some difficulty was relieved by a plentiful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the bark. The "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on Man" had now been published some years; and it is universally supposed that the author had, in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of it, adopted the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Bolingbroke, whom on this occasion he had followed as his guide, without understanding the tendency of his principles. In 1738, M. de Croufaz wrote some remarks on it, accusing the author of Spinozism and Naturalism; which falling into Mr Warburton's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, he published a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the first epistle, and soon after of the remaining three, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> letters, of which six were printed in 1739; and the seventh in June 1740, under the title of, "A Vindication of Mr Pope's Essay on Man, by the Author of the Divine Legation." The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> which Mr Pope conceived of these defences, as well as of their author, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> be best seen in his letters. In <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, a firm friendship was established between them, which continued with undiminished fervour until the death of Mr Pope; who, during the remainder of his life, paid a deference and respect to his friend's judgment and abilities, which will be considered by many as almost bordering on servility. In 1741, the second volume of "The Divine Legation" was published; as was also a second edition of the "Alliance between Church and State." Mr Pope's affection for Mr Warburton was of service to him in more respects than merely increasing his fame. He introduced and warmly recommended him to most of his friends, and amongst the rest to Ralph Allen, Esq. of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">Prior</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARK">Park</a>, whose niece he some years afterwards married, and whose great fortune at length came to his only son. In 1742, Mr Warburton published "A Critical and Philosophical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMENTARY">Commentary</a> on Mr Pope's Essay on Man." In which is contained a Vindication of the said essay from the misrepresentations of M. de Refnel, the French translator, and of M. de Croufaz, professor of philosophy and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> in the Academy of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAUSANNE">Lausanne</a>, the commentator. It was at this period when Mr Warburton had the entire confidence of Mr Pope, that he advised him to complete the Dunciad, by changing the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERO">hero</a>, and adding to it a fourth book. This was accordingly executed in 1742, and published early in 1743, 4to, with notes by our author; who, in consequence of it, received his share of the satire which Mr Cibber liberally bestowed on both Mr Pope and his annotator. In the latter end of the same year, he published complete editions of "The Essay on Man," and "The Essay on Criticism;" and, from the specimen which he there exhibited of his abilities, it may be presumed Mr Pope determined to commit the publication of those works which he should leave, to Mr Warburton's care. The publication of "The Dunciad" was the last service which our author rendered Mr Pope in his life-time. "The Divine Legation of Moses" having now been published some time, and various answers and objections to it having started up from different <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, Mr Warburton, in 1744, turned his attention to these attacks on his favourite work; and defended himself in a manner which, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it did not prove him to be possessed of much humility or diffidence, at least demonstrated, that he knew how to wield the weapons of controversy with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASTER">master</a>. His answers are couched in those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> terms of confident superiority, which marked almost every performance that fell from his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PEN">pen</a> during the remainder of his life. At this important crisis, 1745, Mr Warburton printed three very excellent and seasonable sermons, 1. "A faithful <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PORTRAIT">Portrait</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a>, by which it is seen to be the reverse of Christianity, as it is the Destruction of Morality, Piety, and Civil <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBERTY">Liberty</a>. A Sermon preached at St James's Church, Westminster, Oct. 1745, 8vo." 2. "A Sermon occasioned by the present unnatural Rebellion, &c. preached in Mr Allen's Chapel at Prior-Park, near Bath, Nov. 1745, and published at his request," 8vo. 3. "The nature of National Offences truly stated. A Sermon preached on the General Fast-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>, Dec. 18, 1745," 8vo, 1746. Notwithstanding his great connections, his acknowledged abilities, and his established reputation, yet we do not find that he received any addition to the preferment given him in 1728 by Sir Robert Sutton (except the chaplainship to the Prince of Wales), until April 1746, when he was unanimously called by the Society of Lincoln's-Inn to be their preacher. In 1747 appeared his edition of Shakespeare, and his Preface to Clarissa; and in the same year he published, 1. "A Letter from an Author to a Member of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARLIAMENT">Parliament</a>, concerning Literary <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">Property</a>," 8vo. 2. "Preface to Mrs Cockburn's Remarks upon the Principles and Reasonings of Dr Rutherforth's Essay on the Nature Warburton and Obligations of Virtue," &c. 8vo. 3. "Preface to a Critical Inquiry into the Opinions and Practice of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Philosophers, concerning the Nature of a Future State, and their Method of teaching by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> Doctrine," (by Mr Towne,) 8vo, 1747, 2nd edition. In 1748, a third edition of "The Alliance between Church and State; corrected and enlarged." In 1749, a very extraordinary attack was made on the moral character of Mr Pope, from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> where it could be the least expected. His "Guide, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">Philosopher</a>, and Friend," Lord Bolingbroke, published a book which he had formerly <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LENT">lent</a> Mr Pope in MS. The preface to this work, written by Mr <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALLET">Mallet</a>, contained an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> of Mr Pope's having clandestinely printed an edition of his Lordship's performance without his leave or knowledge. A defence of the poet soon after made its appearance; which was universally ascribed to Mr Warburton, and was afterwards owned by him. It was called, "A Letter to the Editor of the Letters on the Spirit of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol14.html#article-PATRIOTISM">Patriotism</a>, the Idea of a Patriot King, and the State of Parties, &c. occasioned by the Editor's Advertisement," &c. which soon afterwards produced an abusive pamphlet, under the title of "A Familiar Epistle to the most impudent Man living," 8vo; a performance, as hath been truly observed, couched in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> bad enough to disgrace even gaols and garrets. About this time the publication of Dr Middleton's Enquiry concerning the Miraculous Powers gave rise to a controversy, which was managed with great warmth and acrimony on both sides, and not much to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of either party. On this occasion Mr Warburton published an excellent performance, written with a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of candour and temper, which, it is to be lamented, he did not always <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>. The title of it was, "Julian; or a Discourse concerning the Earthquake and Fiery Eruption which defeated that <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EMPEROR">Emperor</a>'s attempt to rebuild the Temple at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>," 8vo, 1750. In 1751, he gave the public his edition of Mr Pope's works, with notes, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> volumes 8vo; and in the same year printed "An Answer to a Letter to Dr Middleton, inserted in a pamphlet intituled, The Argument of the Divine Legation fairly stated," &c. 8vo, and "An Account of the prophecies of Arise Evans, the Welch prophet, in the last century;" the latter of which pieces afterwards subjected him to much <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a>. In 1753, Mr Warburton published the fifth volume of a Course of Sermons preached at Lincoln's Inn, intituled, "The Principles of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> and Revealed Religion occasionally opened and explained;" and this, in the subsequent year, was followed by a second. After the public had been some time promised the appearance of Lord Bolingbroke's works, they were about this time printed. Many answers were soon published, but none with more acuteness, solidity, and sprightliness, than "A View of Lord Bolingbroke's Philosophy, in two Letters to a Friend, 1754:" the Third and Fourth Letters were published in 1753, with another edition of the two former; and in the same year a smaller edition of the whole; which, tho' it came into the world without a name, was universally ascribed to Mr Warburton, and afterwards publicly owned by him. To some copies of this is prefixed an excellent complimentary epistle from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">President</a> Montefouqui, dated May 26, 1754. At this advanced period of his life, that preferment which his abilities bilities might have claimed, and which had hitherto been with-held, seemed to be approaching towards him. In September 1754, he was appointed one of his Majesty's chaplains in ordinary, and in the next year was presented to a prebend in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DURHAM">Durham</a>, on the death of Dr Mangney. About the same time the degree of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">Divinity</a> was conferred on him by Dr <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HERRING">Herring</a>, then archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>. In 1757, a pamphlet was published, called "Remarks on Mr <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAVID">David</a> Hume's Essay on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY">Natural <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Religion;" which is said to have been composed of marginal observations made by Dr Warburton, on <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-READING">reading</a> Mr Hume's book; and which gave so much offence to the author animadverted upon, that he thought it of importance enough to deserve particular mention in the short account of his life. On the 11th of October, in this year, our author was advanced to the deanery of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>; and at the latter end of 1758, received the honour so justly due to his merit, of being dignified with the mitre, and promoted to the vacant see of Gloucester. In 1762, he published "The Doctrine of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRACE">Grace</a>; or, the Office and Operations of the Holy Spirit vindicated from the Insults of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INFIDELITY">Infidelity</a> and the Abuses of Fanaticism," 2 vols., 12mo; and in the succeeding year drew upon himself much illiberal abuse from some writers of the popular party, on occasion of his complaint in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOUSE">House</a> of Lords, on the 15th of November 1763, against Mr Wilkes, for putting his name to certain notes on the infamous "Essay on Woman." In making his complaint, the bishop, after solemnly disavowing both the Poem and the Notes, averred, that the former was worthy of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEVIL">Devil</a>; then, after a short pause, added, "No, I beg the Devil's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a>, for he is incapable of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> it." The year 1777 produced a third volume of his Sermons, dedicated to Lady <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MANSFIELD">Mansfield</a>: and with this, and a single "Sermon preached at St Lawrence Jewry, on Thursday April 30, 1767, before his Royal Highness Edward <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YORK">York</a>, President, and the Governors of the London <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HOSPITAL">Hospital</a>, &c." 4to, he closed his literary labours. His faculties continued unimpaired for some time after this period; and in 1769 he gave considerable assistance to Mr Ruffhead in his life of Mr Pope. He also transferred £500l. to Lord Mansfield, Judge Wilmot, and Mr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Yorke, upon trust, to found a Lecture in the form of a course of Sermons; to prove the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of Revealed Religion in general, and of the Christian in particular, from the completion of the prophecies in the Old and New <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, which relate to the Christian Church, especially to the apostacy of Papal Rome. To this foundation we owe the admirable Introductory Lectures of bishop Hurd, and the well-adapted continuation of bishop <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HALIFAX">Halifax</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> Bagot. It is a melancholy reflection, that a life spent in the constant pursuit of knowledge frequently terminates in the loss of those powers, the cultivation and improvement of which are attended to with too strict and unabated a degree of ardour. This was in some degree the misfortune of Dr Warburton. Like Swift, and the great duke of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARLBOROUGH">Marlborough</a>, he gradually sunk into a situation in which it was a fatigue to him to enter into general conversation. There were, however, a few old and valuable friends in whose <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, even to the last, his mental faculties were exerted in their wonted force; and at such times he would appear cheerful for several hours, and on the departure of his friends retreat as it were within himself. This melancholy <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> was aggravated by the loss of his only son, a very promising young <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, who died of a consumption but a short time before the bishop himself resigned to fate, in the 81st year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>.

WATER HEMLOCK

Pages 1256-1256
Common. This plant is very common in England. It is a well known fact in Sweden, that horses will eat it, and that it frequently proves fatal to them by inducing a palsy; this effect, nevertheless, is judged to be owing to an insect which inhabits in great plenty the stalks of this herb, and from this singular effect is called by Linnæus curculio paraplecticus, when in its perfect state, as the larva only exists in this vegetable. The same caterpillar is found in the water-parnip also in England. WATER Hemlock, Long leaved. Happily this plant is not very common in England: the roots are the most virulent vegetable poison that is indigenous here. Linnæus, in the Flora Lapponica, p. 103, gives a dreadful account of the havoc it made among the horned cattle in Lapland, where it is common in the meadows near the sea, and where these cattle will frequently eat it, upon being first turned to grass in the spring, though they afterwards refuse it: yet they will eat the roots at all times, which are the most virulent parts of the plant. Bishop Gunner and Gmelin both confirm these bad effects. It is yet doubtful whether horses are hurt by it; and certain that goats are delighted with it, and eat it without any subsequent ill effect: and the roots are collected by the Norwegian peasants as fodder for those animals.

WATSON

Pages 1256-1257

an elegant historian, was born at St Andrews, in Scotland, about the year 1730. He was the son of an apothecary of that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, who was also a brewer. Having gone through the usual course of languages and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> at the school and university of his native place, and also entered on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, a desire of being acquainted with a larger circle of literati, and of improving himself in every branch of knowledge, carried him, first to the university of Glasgow, and afterwards to that of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of theological studies at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> of Scotland is no less than six years: but during that period, young men of ingenious minds find sufficient leisure to carry on and advance the pursuits of general knowledge. Mr Watson pursued his studies with ardour. Few men ever studied more constantly. It was a rule with him to study eight hours every <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>; and this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAW">law</a> he observed during the whole course of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. An acquaintance with the polite writers of England, after the union of the two kingdoms, became general in Scotland; and in Watson's younger years, an emulation began to prevail of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> pure and elegant English. Mr Watson applied himself with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> industry to the principles of philosophical <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> universal <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>; and by a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of these, with the authority of the best English writers, formed a course of lectures on style or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. He proceeded to the study of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a> or eloquence; the principles of which he endeavoured to trace to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> mind. He delivered a course of lectures in Edinburgh on these subjects; and met with the countenance, approbation, and friendship of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LORD">lord</a> Kaims, Mr Hume, with other men of genius and learning. At this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> he had become a preacher; and a vacancy having happened in one of the churches of St Andrews, he offered himself a candidate for that living, but was disappointed. Mr Henry Rymer, who then taught logic in St Salvador's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a>, was in a very indurated state of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, and entertained thoughts of retiring from the cares and emoluments of his office, to live upon his small salary or stipend. Mr Watson understanding this, purchased, for not a great sum of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, what, in familiar phraseology, may be called the good-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> of Mr Rymer's place; and, with the consent of the other masters of St Salvador's, was appointed professor of logic. He obtained also a patent from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, constituting him professor of rhetoric and belles lettres. The study of logic, in St Andrews, as in most other places, was at this time confined to syllogisms, modes, and figures. Mr Watson, whose mind had been opened by conversation, and by <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-READING">reading</a> the writings of the wits that had begun to flourish in the Scotch <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, prepared and read to his students a course of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-METAPHYSICS">metaphysics</a> and logics on the most enlarged and enlightened <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>; in which he analyzed the powers of the mind, and entered deeply into the nature of the different <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> or knowledge. By his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> II. Dr Watson attained in his lifetime a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of celebrity; and his history of Philip III., published after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, has added to his fame. Of this last performance, however, he has only completed the four first books; the two last were written by the editor of his manuscript, at the desire of the guardians of his children. On the death of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> Tulideph, Dr Watson, through the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Kinnoull, was appointed his successor; in which station he lived only a few years. He married a lady of singular <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and virtue, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> to Mr Shaw, professor of divinity in St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>'s college, St Andrews. By this lady he had five daughters, who have lately obtained a small pension from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, through the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> of Mr Dundas then Lord Advocate for Scotland.

WEATHER

Pages 1257-1260

(Encycl.) Many have laboured with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> diligence to explore the secret causes of the various changes of weather, and to foretell these alterations with certainty, but hitherto with no <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> success. Indeed, in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> at least, the alterations of the weather are so many, and frequently so sudden, that we can scarce suppose them to depend on any constant and regular cause. In the warm climates the weather is much more constant and uniform than with us; and even on the Continent in equal latitudes, it is less variable than here. Between the tropics, and probably for a considerable space northward and southward, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> appears to be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGENT">agent</a> in determining the weather. At one season of the year immense quantities of vapour are raised into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>, which, when the solar influence becomes less, are condensed into violent rains, and thus distinguish the year into the dry and rainy seasons. In those climates also the general course of the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> is evidently influenced by the sun, as Dr Halley has observed, (See Wind, Encycl.) Indeed at some times violent storms of wind, called hurricanes, whirlwinds, and storms of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> occur: but of these the sun can only be accounted the remote cause; the immediate one being most probably the highly electrified state of the atmosphere. The inhabitants of those climates, especially the savages, who are continually exposed to the atmosphere, are able to foretell these tempests some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a> before. The signs which they observe, however, are in fact only the tempest beginning its operations in the atmosphere; and no person whatever is able to foretell an hurricane <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> a storm of thunder a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, or even a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>, before it comes. The reason of this is, that the sources of atmospheric <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTRICITY">electricity</a> are not only invisible to us, but so variable in themselves, that though we knew them at one time, we have not the least security they that would continue the same even for a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DAY">day</a>. In various parts of this <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> it has been shown, that the sun communicates the electric fluid to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and that this fluid must escape somewhere from the earth into the atmosphere in the very same <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> in which it is communicated. As the electric fluid, however, cannot easily diffuse itself in the atmosphere, an accumulation of it over any particular spot must soon take <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; in which <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a> that spot will cease to emit any more electric fluid. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> then a new vein is opened, a current of electric <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> may perhaps be directed from that place which emitted it before; and then the atmosphere, instead of receiving electricity from the earth, will communicate its superfluous quantity to it. In such a situation of the atmosphere, storms of thunder may readily take place; but where there is nearly an equal <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of electricity in the earth and atmosphere, an earthquake is most likely to ensue. (See Earthquake, No. 39. art. 10. Encycl.) Besides the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> accumulation of electricity in the atmosphere, there are other causes, such as severe frosts, which may detain the fluid in various parts of the earth at particular times; and thus be indirectly the cause of thunder, earthquakes, &c. in other places. This will easily show the difficulty, nay the impossibility, of predicting these storms; as the causes of them may be very remote from the place where they happen. An hurricane in Jamaica, for instance, may be occasioned by something in <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-NEW_BRITAIN">New <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, or an earthquake in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a> by something in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>. In our own <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, nothing can be more variable and uncertain than the weather. Some have attempted to deduce its changes from the influence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>; but, though it cannot be doubted that the moon as well as the sun has some influence on our atmosphere, the changes in it are by far too many to be occasioned by any regular and permanent cause.—The wind has likewise been thought considerably to influence the weather; but excepting with regard to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, we cannot find that this is to be depended upon; not to mention that the wind itself makes <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the weather, and ought to have its cause explained as much as the rest. That alterations of the weather, however, do not depend immediately either on the sun, moon, or wind, appears from a circumstance mentioned by Mr <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DERHAM">Derham</a>, viz. that "moles dig before a thaw." This he ascribes to warm vapours which they feel in the earth; but whatever it is, we from thence learn, that the cause of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> lies not in the atmosphere, but in the earth itself, from whence it would seem to be communicated to the atmosphere. But though it is probable that the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the electric fluid in the earth is the cause of those sudden changes which are met with in almost all countries; yet the general determination of the weather, or what is called the climate, evidently depends on some settled and permanent cause. The cold of winter and heat of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> are plainly occasioned by the greater or less obliquity of the sun's rays at those seasons. To the sun also are we to ascribe those regular winds which, though most remarkable within the tropics, are yet in some degree to be met with even in our own country. Along the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Britain, at least to a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, the wind blows from the south-east almost during the whole <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> and summer. This we may naturally suppose to arise from the continual rarefaction of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> by the sun. The cold air rushes in to supply the partial vacuity, but it does not follow the course of the sun directly. The reason of this is, that the air is also rarefied over the continent opposite to Britain; and as the distance is but small, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> of air incumbent on that part of the German ocean which lies to the south-east of this country prevails over that which lies directly to the east, and will not allow it to come in. This continues with occasional variations, owing to unknown motions in the electric fluid till after the summer solstice. The same cause continues still to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a>; but though the heat be now greater on <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LAND">land</a> than it was before, the sun begins soon to lose his influence on the great <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a> which lies to the westward. Thus the eastern parts being more rare than the western, a west wind begins to take place. The earlier wind, however, also continues; the two meet and oppose each other; the contest is decided by thunder and lightning, (see the article Thunder, Encycl.) and seldom fails to end in the total defeat of the east wind. The month of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, therefore, is remarkable in this part of the country for thunder, as the contest generally lasts some weeks. In the month of August the west wind prevails, and continues till the superior density of the cold air in the northern regions counteracts it, and the wind blows from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, north-east, or north-west. As these winds do not directly oppose each other, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of their interference is not thunder, but <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, which usually falls in great quantities in the month of October; after which the cold northerly winds bring <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FROST">frost</a> and snow. Thus notwithstanding the excessive variability of our climate, we may determine the general outline of the weather from evident causes. Thus in the months of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> and February we may reasonably expect frost and snow, from the condensed and cold air in the northern regions prevailing southward to those parts rarefied by the sun. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MARCH">March</a> we very often meet with the same, by reason of the weak influence of the sun at that time; but more frequently there are at that time storms of wind from various <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, but frequently from the west or north. The reason of this is, that the air over the land begins to be rarefied; in consequence of which the denser air rushes in from that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> where the passage is most free.—In April, the rarefaction of the air being greater, and considerable quantities of electric matter thus passing from the earth into it, the winds cease, or become more gentle, and rains commence. In the beginning of May the wind often blows very cold from the north, though the weather is more settled. Why this wind did not take place in April, seems not to easily accounted for; but most probably the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of density between the northern and southern air was not then sufficient to allow of a strong current from any quarter. During the latter part of May and the whole of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, the weather is usually settled and clear; the sun gradually exerting his greatest influence. In July we have thunder and rain, for the reasons already given. The latter part of August and the whole of September are usually dry, with westerly winds, in consequence of the latter having prevailed in the conflict with the east wind. The whole month of October, and great part of November, Weather is usually rainy, on account of the interference of the west and north winds; and in the end of November, and throughout the month of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>, frost and snow come on, though not with such certainty as in January. This, in general, is the weather we may expect throughout the year; but by many accidental causes, not easily discoverable, it may be very much altered. Some of these causes we have endeavoured to point out; but, besides the reasons already given, it is not impossible that an alteration may take place in our atmosphere from causes entirely beyond it, and which exist only in the immense <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of ethereal fluid with which the universe is filled. Such causes, however, as they must be totally without the reach of our investigations, can never be assigned as the reason of any kind of weather; yet in some seasons there is such a general cold over a great part of the earth, that we must certainly imagine the cause to have been very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> in the atmosphere. Of this the year 1782 furnishes us with a notable example. During the whole of that summer the sun appeared almost totally to have lost his influence. No vegetable, not even grass, came to perfection; and the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a> was scarce finished in the month of December. This was the case in Scotland, and it seems to have been similar all over <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. The cause of this extraordinary cold, we cannot discover; but its effects were very obvious and dreadful. The electric fluid being confined over to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a> a space, broke out in the southern parts with fury; and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a> were almost entirely ruined by earthquakes. The earth now poured out such immense quantities of electric matter, that the atmosphere seemed scarce able to contain it. It therefore diffused itself along the lower regions all over Europe. Heat and almost perpetual thunder were the consequence: vegetation was excessively luxuriant; but the immoderate quantity of electricity having occasioned continual fogs which obscured the sun, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> had not their proper flavour; nor was the crop altogether what might have been expected. The electric fluid, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, having fully saturated the lower part of the atmosphere, gradually ascended higher; but as the earthquakes ceased to supply new quantities of it, the southern parts of the atmosphere became negatively electrified with respect to the northern parts. To restore the equilibrium, a vast quantity rushed from the north to the south, visible from the north of Scotland to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> and farther, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-METEOR">meteor</a> which appeared on the 18th of August 1783. The immediate consequence of this was, that the atmospherical vapours being left without a proper quantity of electric matter to support them, violent rains took place and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> for some time; a very severe winter succeeded an hot summer, and no remarkable alteration in the weather took place till May. In most parts of the world, the general state of the weather is determined by their situation with regard to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, &c. In general, mountainous countries are subjected to violent rains, storms of wind, very often thunder and lightning. In some places, particularly the southern part of the continent of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, the weather is almost a continual tempest. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> of Good Hope is also remarkable for storms, but chiefly of wind; while Terra del <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FUEGO">Fuego</a> and the opposite point of the continent is deluged with perpetual rains. The Isthmus of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DARIEN">Darien</a> is also remarkable for rainy weather, while in the whole empire of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERU">Peru</a> it scarce ever rains. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, and some other countries, are likewise destitute of rain, without having the inconvenience of earthquakes to which Peru is subject. The reason of these variations cannot be assigned without a more particular knowledge of the situation of those countries than we can boast of. In general, however, it is known, that high mountains have the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of collecting <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> in their neighbourhood, and consequently of producing rains, thunder, and storms of wind. Where a country is nearly surrounded by a vast extent of sea, it is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> subject to great rains. Hence the climate of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> is more rainy than of continents; and hence probably the reason of the rains in South America and the Isthmus of Darien, which approach to an insular situation. The great drenches of the air in Peru may be occasioned by the violent determination of the vapours to these parts, which deprive that country of its due proportion; but this can only be hinted as a conjecture, and we have not sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DATA">data</a> to establish anything certain. To conclude this article, we ought now to give an account of those alterations in the air which predict a change of weather, or rather inform us that the weather actually is changing. These, however, are but few, and not always certain. The brute <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> are much more sensible of them than we; and give information by various means, according to their peculiar instincts. Those who are much in the open air also will be much better able to perceive these alterations, than such as are not. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BAROMETER">barometer</a> is the most certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDEX">index</a> we have, and will frequently inform us of a change before the least sign of it can be otherwise perceived. But though we are thus informed that some change is about to take place, we are at a loss to know what it is, and can only guess from the season of the year what kind of weather we may reasonably expect. Thus, in the summer-months, if the wind is easterly, the barometer falls, and the clouds in the west seem <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STATIONARY">stationary</a>, or move a little to the eastward, we may certainly expect thunder at no great distance. If the wind is brisk, and the clouds move before it heavily and sluggishly, we are also to expect thunder, but at a distance. Indeed, we may judge of the approach of thunder-clouds by the time of the day in which they appear. When the sun has reached the meridian, his power of rarefying the air above any particular spot is then greatest. Hence, as this luminary is continually moving to the westward, the increase of the rarefaction towards that quarter must prevent any current of air from blowing from the west, and at the same time solicit a current from the east: but if by some other cause a westerly wind shall prevail, and drive the clouds directly against the easterly one, it is then plain that nothing further can stop their progress; they will be violently electrified, and discharge their contents directly over our heads. Hence the vulgar observation in this country, that if thunder begins at eleven in the forenoon, we will probably have but little; but a great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEAL">deal</a>, and very near, if it begins at twelve, or between twelve and one. Another pretty certain indication of an approaching change of weather is a great clearness and transparency in the atmosphere. This is commonly taken notice of when the moon is newly changed. If at that time we see distinctly the part of the moon which is not enlightened by the sun's rays, we are pretty certain that rough stormy weather is soon to ensue. In warm climates this transparency is not confined to the atmosphere, but extends even to the waters of the ocean; and when the bottom is visible at a great depth, it is a certain prognostic of an hurricane. This transparency denotes some internal agitation of the electric fluid; for by a certain <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of it even the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> bodies may be made transparent as glass, (see Electricity, Encycl. n° 4;) and the agitation becoming more and more violent, at last produces the most terrible commotions in the atmosphere. Something similar may be observed with regard to the transmission of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>; for in such states of the atmosphere sounds are heard much more distinctly and at a greater distance than others; but a sufficient <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of observations have not yet been made to determine this matter with any accuracy. It would be tedious to enter into a detail of all the prognostics which are drawn from the various appearances of the clouds, of halos, parhelia, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AURORA_BOREALIS"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol10.html#article-AURORA">aurora</a> borealis, &c. Every person expects rain when the sky begins to grow hazy and dull; and halos and parhelia only appear in such <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>. As for the aurora borealis, it is often seen for many nights together without any remarkable change in the state of the atmosphere. It is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> effect of a constant and regular cause, and is probably too high in the atmosphere to produce any remarkable effect; though it has been thought in some cases to be productive of a current of wind from the south-west, for which a probable reason is assigned under the article Aurora Borealis, n° ult. WHEAT-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EAR">ear</a>, (<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MOTACILLA">Motacilla</a> Oenanthe), in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ornithology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> omitted to be described under Motacilla. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> of passage, and begins to visit us about the middle of March, and continues coming till the beginning of May: it has been observed that the females arrive about a fortnight before the males. They frequent warrens, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWNS">downs</a>, and the edges of hills, especially those that are fenced with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>-walls. They breed in the latter, in old rabbit-burrows, cliffs, and frequently under old <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>; their nest is large, made of dried grass, rabbit's <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, a few feathers, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>; and they lay from six to eight eggs, of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>-blue <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. They grow very fat in autumn, and are esteemed a delicacy. About Eastbourn in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-SUSSEX">Sussex</a> they are taken by the shepherds in great numbers, in snares made of horse hair, placed under a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> turf; being very timid birds, the motion of a cloud, or the appearance of a hawk, will drive them for shelter into those traps, and so they are taken. The numbers annually entrained in that district alone, amount to about 1850 dozen, which sell usually at six-pence per dozen; and what appears very extraordinary, the numbers that return the following year do not appear to be lessened. The reason that such a quantity are taken in the neighbourhood of Eastbourn is, that it abounds with a certain fly which frequents the adjacent hills, for the sake of the wild thyme they are covered with; which is not only a favourite food of that insect, but the plant on which it deposits its eggs. Wheat-ears are much fatter in a rainy season than in a dry one; for they not only feed on insects but on earthworms, which come out of the ground in greater numbers in wet weather than in dry. The head and back of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MALE">male</a> are of a light grey, tinged tinged with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>; over each eye is a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WHITE">white</a> line; beneath that is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> stroke, passing across each eye to the hind part of the head; the rump and lower half of the tail are white; the upper half black; the under side of the body is white, tinged with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>; on the neck it inclines to red: the quill-feathers are black, edged with reddish <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>. The colours of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> are more dull: it wants that black stroke across the eyes, and the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAR">bar</a> of white on the tail is narrower. These birds disappear in September, at least from the northern parts of this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>; but in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HAMPSHIRE">Hampshire</a> many of them continue the whole winter.

WHEN THE DOCTOR WANTED TO EXTRACT INFLAMMABLE AIR FROM METALS BY

Pages 1074-1090

n the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a> wanted to extract inflammable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AIR">air</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> by means of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> only, he directed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FOCUS">focus</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-LENS">lens</a> upon them, whilst they were under the exhausted receiver of the air-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PUMP">pump</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-OR">or</a> were confined by quicksilver. From pure filings of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> carefully sorted with a magnet, and confined by quicksilver in an <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a> glass jar, Dr Priestley, by means of the focus of a lens, obtained some permanently <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> fluid, which, as he observes, was weakly inflammable. In sorting the steel-filings for this experiment, the Doctor observes, that care must be taken not to let any other substance be mixed with them, since the least bit of wood, or any vegetable or animal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, hardly discernible by the eye, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WILL">will</a> yield more inflammable air than a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of iron-filings. "I found (says he) at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIME">time</a>, that eleven grains of steel-filings, from watch-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, yielded a more inflammable air, than the same <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of iron-filings; which agrees with the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a> that steel contains more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHLOGISTON">phlogiston</a> than iron." By directing the focus of the lens upon filings of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZINC">zinc</a> or upon <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>-dust in vacuo, the Doctor obtained an elastic fluid that was strongly inflammable. But from tin he obtained an elastic fluid that was weakly inflammable. With other metallic substances, or with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CALX">calx</a> of any metal whatever, the Doctor had no success. From a mixture of iron-filings and chalk, the Doctor obtained, by means of the lens, a plentiful mixture of fixed and inflammable air, as might be naturally expected. The elastic fluid expelled from <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a> by heat only, is fixed air; but the residuum of it Dr Priestley found to be inflammable. Mr Fontana had a very elegant way to extract inflammable air from <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-RED">red</a>-hot charcoal. With a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of tongs he took a piece of charcoal, when thoroughly ignited, and plunging it in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-WATER">water</a>, brought it instantly under a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGE">large</a>-mouthed receiver, which was filled with and inverted in the water, in order to collect the bubbles of inflammable air that proceeded from the charcoal in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of cooling. After the same manner he treated several pieces of charcoal, or the same piece several successive times, until he got a quantity of inflammable air sufficient for his purpose. By means of heat in a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GUN">gun</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a>, Dr Priestley obtained from pipe-clay, first inflammable, and then fixed air. But a quantity of inflammable air is obtained, together with fixed air, in various <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, as we have already remarked. Pit-coal, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a>, yields inflammable air, which, when fired in a wide-mouthed phial, burns with a bright lambent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>, without <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-EXPLOSION">explosion</a>. By <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> to heat, in a gun-barrel, a mixture of calx of zinc and charcoal, or Prussian blue, Mr de Laffon obtained an inflammable air, which burned without explosion. Dr Priestley found, that when iron-filings and brimstone, moistened with water, were confined by quicksilver, and suffered to ferment in a warm <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, some inflammable air was <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a>. Filings of zinc and brimstone produced the same effect. By taking electric sparks in any kind of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, spirit of wine, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETHER">ether</a>, or spirit of sal ammoniac, Dr Priestley obtained inflammable air. The oil, or other liquor, was confined in a glass tube by quicksilver, and a wire was cemented in the upper <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PART">part</a> of the tube, through which the sparks being sent, went to the quicksilver through the oil; but after that a few sparks had been taken, a quantity of inflammable air was generated, &c. Left the production of inflammable air air should be attributed to the cement which fastened the wire, the Doctor repeated the experiment with ether in a glass syphon; but the inflammable air was generated as before. This elastic fluid does not lose its inflammability by being passed several times from one vessel into another through water. Alkaline air, by taking electric explosions in it, is changed into inflammable air. By means of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>, inflammable air is obtained in greater abundance, and more readily. Iron, zinc, or tin, yield plenty of inflammable air when acted on by <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-DILUTE">dilute</a> vitriolic or marine acids. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> iron is put into strong vitriolic acid, the quantity of elastic fluid that is produced is very little, except heat be applied to the phial, for then the production of elastic fluid is more copious; but this elastic fluid is vitriolic acid air, mixed with a small portion of inflammable air, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a> quantity of it being less when the acid is more concentrated. Zinc, treated after the same manner, produces the like effects, except that it gives more elastic fluid, without the application of heat, than iron does; and the greatest part of the produced elastic fluid is inflammable. In order to obtain the greatest quantity of inflammable air from iron or zinc, the vitriolic acid must be diluted with much water, as about one part of strong oil of vitriol to five or six parts of water. Dr Priestley found, that eleven grains of iron yielded 8½ ounces <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> of inflammable air. According to Mr Cavendish, one ounce of zinc, dissolved either in the vitriolic or marine acid, yields a quantity of inflammable air equal to the bulk of 356 ounces of water; one ounce of iron, dissolved by means of vitriolic acid, yields a quantity of inflammable air equal to the bulk of 412 ounces of water; and one ounce of tin yields half as much inflammable air as iron does. The solutions of iron, tin, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and zinc, in the marine acid, produce marine-acid air, and inflammable air, but in various quantities. The proportion of the former to the latter is as one to eight in iron, as one to six in tin, as three to one in copper and lead, and as one to ten in zinc. Regulus of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a>, dissolved in marine acid, with the application of heat, yields a small quantity of elastic fluid, which is weakly inflammable. Dr Priestley obtained inflammable air, not only by dissolving various substances in marine acid, but also by exposing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> bodies to marine-acid air, which is probably the purest part of the marine acid. Having admitted iron-filings to this acid air, they were dissolved by it pretty fast; half of the elastic fluid disappeared, and the rest was rendered unabsorbable by water, and inflammable. The same effect was produced by almost every substance which contains phlogiston, as by spirit of wine, oil of olives, spirit of turpentine, charcoal, phosphorus, bees-wax, sulphur, dry corkwood, pieces of oak, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>, pieces of roasted beef, and even some pieces of a whitish kind of flint. A greater or smaller portion of the acid air was absorbed, and the rest sometimes was all inflammable, and often was partly acid air, which was soon absorbed on the admission of water, and partly inflammable. In short, it seems as if this acid air, having a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> with phlogiston, separates it from all those substances which contain it even in small quantities, and from that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> becomes inflammable. By means of nitrous acid, inflammable air may be obtained from various substances containing phlogiston; but it is always mixed with nitrous air, and sometimes also with fixed and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COMMON">common</a> or phlogisticated air. If two parts of spirit of wine, mixed with one part of nitrous acid, are put into a phial with a ground-stopper and tube, and the flame of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a> be applied to it, so as to heat it gradually, the inflammable air will be produced very readily; the inflammability of which is, however, not very permanent, for by a little washing in water it may be annihilated. In the solution of most substances in nitrous acid, it generally happens, that the elastic fluid, which is obtained towards the latter end of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>, possesses the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of being inflammable; thus iron, dissolved in nitrous acid, yields nitrous air; but when the nitrous air ceases to be produced, if the heat of a candle be applied to the solution, more elastic fluid will be produced which is inflammable. "The nitrous acid (says Dr Ingenhouz) when mixed with iron-filings in a very diluted state, gives, by the assistance of a moderate <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of heat, a mixture of different <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIRS">airs</a>, partly fixed, partly common air, and partly phlogisticated air. III. Nitrous Air. This is a permanently elastic fluid, which is never found naturally, like fixed or inflammable air, but is entirely <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a>. This elastic fluid consists principally of nitrous acid and phlogiston; so that it cannot be produced but from that acid, or, which is the same thing, from substances containing the nitrous acid and phlogiston; thus, when the nitrous acid is mixed with metals, or with animal or vegetable substances which contain phlogiston, nitrous air is generally produced; but very little or none of this sort of elastic fluid is yielded when the nitrous acid is mixed with metallic calxes, with pure ashes of vegetable substances, or, in short, with any substance which contains little or nothing of phlogiston. In this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CASE">case</a>, if the mixture is exposed to a sufficiently strong degree of heat, the nitrous acid is decomposed, and phlogisticated air is produced; though, in some <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of the process, a little nitrous air is generally produced, which is owing to the small quantity of phlogiston which exists in most, if not in all metallic calxes, &c. The variety of elastic <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a> obtainable when nitrous acid is employed, may be deduced from observing, that the nitrous acid itself, by being decomposed, may <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GENERATE">generate</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPHLOGISTICATED">dephlogisticated</a> air; that, by joining with the phlogiston of the substance with which it is mixed, may generate nitrous air; that, by the mixture of those two elastic fluids, another elastic fluid, namely, phlogisticated air, may be formed; and that, by its acting as an acid, it may expel one or more other elastic fluids from those substances with which it is mixed. All metallic substances, when mixed with the nitrous acid, yield nitrous air. Indeed <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, platinum, and regulus of antimony, as they are not dissoluble in simple nitrous acid, must be dissolved in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AQUA">aqua</a> regia, in order to obtain nitrous air from them. Although all metallic substances, by means of the nitrous acid, may be made to yield nitrous air; yet they do not produce it in equal quantities, with equal facility, and of equal goodness. The following are the more remarkable particulars relating to this matter: Either silver, copper, brass, iron, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BISMUTH">bismuth</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-NICKEL">nickel</a>, when mixed with nitrous acid, yield nitrous air in great quantities.
